Don't trade a kidney for money thinking 'one is enough': the remaining one has to do the work of two, and 86% of kidney sellers later said their health got worse

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortality rateMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Among properly vetted donors screened layer by layer before donation and checked afterward, 31 in 10,000 reached end-stage kidney disease 15 years on, versus 4 in 10,000 among equally healthy people who didn't donate. Kidney sellers get neither screening nor follow-up: 6 years later, 86% said their health had worsened, and three-quarters were still in debt.

Cost
Costs nothing. Just seeing this ledger clearly first.
Benefit
The US compared 96,217 living kidney donors with 20,024 equally matched healthy non-donors, the latter from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III). Estimated risk of reaching end-stage kidney disease 15 years after donation: 30.8 per 10,000 for donors, confidence range 95% CI 24.3–38.5; 3.9 per 10,000 for healthy non-donors, 95% CI 0.8–8.9, P<0.001. End-stage kidney disease's technical name is end-stage renal disease (ESRD); at that stage, staying alive means dialysis or transplant. Estimated lifetime risk of reaching ESRD: 90 per 10,000 for donors, 326 per 10,000 for the unscreened general population, 14 per 10,000 for healthy non-donors. Norway ran its own comparison: on one side 1,901 kidney donors, median follow-up 15.1 years; on the other, 32,621 controls who met donation criteria, median follow-up 24.9 years. Donors' all-cause mortality ran about 30% higher (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.11–1.52). Cardiovascular death about 40% higher (HR 1.40, 1.03–1.91). Reaching ESRD roughly ten times higher (HR 11.38, 4.37–29.6). Total ESRD incidence in that donor group was 302 per million. Another US group of 3,698 kidney donors included 11 ESRD cases, equivalent to 180 per million person-years observed, against 268 in the general population over the same period. Of these donors, 255 returned for checks an average of 12.2±9.2 years after donation. Of them, 85.5% had kidney filtration function (GFR) ≥ 60 ml/min/1.73 m² — 60 is the clinical lower limit of normal. 32.1% had hypertension. 12.7% had proteinuria (protein leaking into the urine). In Chennai, India, 305 kidney sellers were surveyed an average of 6 years after selling: 96% sold to repay debt, receiving an average of US$1,070. Average family income fell by a third after the kidney was removed (P<0.001), the number living below the poverty line increased, and three-quarters were still in debt at the time of the survey. 86% reported worse health than before the surgery, and 79% would not advise others to sell.
Note
Contested: Ibrahim's study used ordinary people as comparators and concluded that donors' survival, and their risk of reaching end-stage kidney disease (ESRD), were similar to the general population's. Muzaale and Mjøen swapped the comparators for "equally healthy people equally qualified to donate", and the excess risk then stood out clearly. The disagreement is over who to compare against, not about the donors. All three studies agree the absolute risk is small (30.8 per 10,000 over 15 years — 30.8 out of 10,000 people). So the point is not that "donating a kidney is dangerous"; the things to weigh are two others. The remaining kidney genuinely pays a price — the hypertension and proteinuria rates are right there. All these figures come from people screened before surgery, checked afterward, and able to return to the hospital if something goes wrong; black-market kidney selling offers none of the three, and the Indian follow-up shows the other ending. The original studies report only self-rated worse health, proteinuria, hypertension, and ESRD incidence — no figures like "how many are bedridden" — and this book won't fill that in for them. For the family-relationship limits of legal donation, fines, and criminal liability, see Section 9, item 22 (don't sell your own organs). For those already on dialysis, cross-province direct settlement and long-term medication, see Section 16, items 1 and 2 (finish medication as prescribed; remote filing for outpatient chronic-disease coverage).
Sources (4 references)

JAMA, 311(6), 579-586. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2013.285141; Mjøen G, Hallan S, Hartmann A, et al. (2014). Long-term risks for kidney donors. Kidney International, 86(1), 162-167. https://doi.org/10.1038/ki.2013.460; Ibrahim HN, Foley R, Tan L, et al. (2009). Long-term consequences of kidney donation. Don't pick up, take apart, or sell metal pieces of unknown origin; keep well away from anything bearing the trefoil radiation symbol

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortality rateMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Radiation has no smell, color, or warmth, and most radioactive sources are just a piece of ordinary metal — so "it looks fine" is no way to judge. For an ordinary person the odds of running into one are extremely low, fewer than 1 incident a year per 10,000 sources. But once you do, it cannot be undone: in Brazil in 1987, people dismantled a radiotherapy machine from an abandoned clinic as scrap metal, and in the end 4 people died.

Cost
Costs nothing. Seeing an unfamiliar metal cylinder, lead pot, or part detached from equipment, walk around it: don't pick it up, don't take it apart, don't put it in your pocket.
Benefit
As of 2025 China had about 178,000 radioactive sources in use and 350,000 radiation-emitting devices (sets). The annual incidence of radiation accidents from sources has held steady below 1 per 10,000 sources. The grading works like this: loss, theft, or loss of control of a Category I or II source constitutes a major radiation accident; Category III is a significant accident; loss or theft of Category IV or V, or exposure of people beyond the annual dose limit, is a general radiation accident. Official case: in June 2020, a blast-furnace pipeline renovation project at a Ningxia steel group's ironmaking plant carried out gamma-ray radiography. A Category II iridium-192 source exposed three workers. One worker (surname Chen) suffered grade III acute radiation skin injury on the left hand. Another (surname Liu) grade IV on the left thumb and index finger, grade III on the middle, ring, and little fingers. The third (surname Fan) grades I-II on the left hand. All three received doses severely exceeding the dose limits set by national standards; the two responsible units had their radiation safety licenses revoked and were fined 70,000 yuan. International case: Goiânia, Brazil, 1987 — a teletherapy machine in an abandoned clinic was dismantled and its 50.8 TBq cesium-137 source extracted, with the sealed capsule holding the source also ruptured. About 112,000 people were monitored; 249 of them were contaminated internally or externally. Of these 249, 129 had moderate to severe contamination and 50 needed close medical monitoring. In the end 4 people died. (Nationwide / international)
Note
If it really happens: get far away, remember the location, don't move it, call 110. The regulations require reporting to the ecology and environment, public security, and health authorities. Distance and time are the only effective protection; a pocket or plastic bag shields nothing. Devices that produce rays only when powered — X-ray machines, CT scanners — leave no radioactivity once switched off. What's truly dangerous is the sealed radioactive source inside equipment. Hospital radiotherapy machines, gamma radiography units on pipelines and boilers, well-logging tools, and material level gauges all contain sources. Opening the housing exposes the source, and outwardly these parts look no different from ordinary metal. So don't count on recognizing a source: parts of unknown origin are never dismantled, never sold, never taken home. China has also had cases of people unknowingly picking up sources. In May 2014, a factory in Nanjing's chemical industry park lost an iridium-192 source during radiography work. A warehouse keeper picked it up during an inspection and put it in his work uniform pocket. He was later diagnosed with mild acute radiation sickness and acute radiation skin injury on the right leg, spent a year in hospital, and years later still had to walk on two crutches. Two other workers said they had seen it; one, on the way to work, thought it was a necklace, picked it up to look, and threw it away. The source belonged to Tianjin Hongdi Engineering Testing Development Co. No official accident report was found for this incident. The picker's injuries come from a follow-up paper published by doctors at the Jiangsu Provincial CDC; the pick-up-and-discard episode rests only on reporting by China Environment News. People in scrap recycling, dismantling, hardware, and construction work face far higher risk than most; on work sites, detour around any cordoned area marked with the trefoil symbol. Nuclear power plant leaks are another class of accident, even less likely for an ordinary person to encounter. The beneficiaries are mainly you and the family members on site with you.

When gambling has you borrowing to gamble and feeling down all the time, call 12356 first, then give a family member your bank cards and payment passwords

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortality rateMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Among people treated at hospitals for gambling problems, suicide deaths ran 15 times the rate of their peers, and total deaths 1.8 times. The signal that predicts who will die by suicide is depression. So when you're borrowing to keep gambling and your mood stays low, call 12356 first.

Cost
Costs nothing. One phone call. Hand your bank cards, payment passwords, and loan apps to a family member. The hard part is first admitting you can't control it.
Benefit
A Swedish national register study identified 2,099 people diagnosed with gambling disorder in specialty care from 2005 to 2016. Gambling disorder means being unable to stop gambling, to the point it disrupts your life. Compared with Swedes of the same age, all-cause mortality for these people at ages 20 to 74 was 1.8 times, and suicide mortality 15 times (both figures are standardized mortality ratios, SMR). During follow-up 67 died, 21 of them by suicide. What predicted suicide death was depression. The authors issued a 2023 correction: suicide was 12.1 times for men and 16.1 times for women. From May 1, 2025, dialing 12356 anywhere in China reaches a psychological assistance hotline open no fewer than 18 hours a day. (Sweden / nationwide)
Note
Grade B because there is only one study, and it counts only people treated in specialty care. These patients are on the sicker side, so 15 times cannot be applied to everyone who plays cards. Handing money to a family member is an experience-based practice, with no direct research; on its own it would be Grade C. For gambling's legal red lines, see Section 9, item 13 (no taking a rake, no online gambling). For whether to repay a family member's gambling debts, see Section 8, item 44 (gambling debts are not marital community property). For what to do once suicidal thoughts surface, see item 32 in this section (tell one person nearby first). The beneficiaries are mainly you — and family who spot the signs can pull you into following this item too.

Men who have sex with men with high-risk exposures: ask a designated HIV hospital about pre-exposure prophylaxis; taking it on schedule cuts infection by more than 70%

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortality rateMoney: a lotTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: large

People not yet infected can take an antiviral drug in advance — pre-exposure prophylaxis. Those who take it on schedule cut infection risk by more than 70%. Those who take it on and off get essentially nothing. It's prescription-only: get checked at a hospital first, then have it prescribed, and keep regular follow-ups after.

Cost
Prescription-only, out of pocket in most places, anywhere from a few hundred to a few thousand yuan. Before prescribing, they test for HIV, kidney function, and hepatitis B. After that, recheck every 3 months. The hard part is taking it on time, every day.
Benefit
The drug is a combination pill of emtricitabine plus tenofovir. The iPrEx trial gave 2,499 men who have sex with men and transgender women daily pills or placebo. Infections fell 44% in the pill group (95% CI 15–63). Those with detectable drug levels in their blood had far stronger protection. The UK's PROUD trial enrolled 544 men who have sex with men. The immediate-treatment group had 86% fewer infections than the group deferred by a year (90% CI 64–96, a 90% confidence range). France's IPERGAY trial used on-demand dosing before and after sex: 86% fewer infections (95% CI 40–98). A meta-analysis used by the World Health Organization pooled the trials. Overall RR 0.49 (0.33–0.73, about 51% lower). In trials where over 70% took the pills, RR 0.30 (0.21–0.45, about 70% lower). Where fewer than 40% did, RR 0.95 — essentially ineffective. China's drug regulator approved the drug for pre-exposure prophylaxis in August 2020. Adults and adolescents weighing at least 35 kg can use it. (Multiple countries / China)
Note
The people in the trials were mostly men who have sex with men, so they are the group who most need to ask. Others with high-risk sex can also ask a doctor whether it suits them. Before prescribing, not being infected must be confirmed — infected people taking it breeds drug resistance — and a self-test kit result cannot serve as the basis. People with hepatitis B can trigger a hepatitis flare by stopping, so it must be tested for first. The World Health Organization recommends on-demand dosing only for men who have sex with men, suited to those averaging fewer than 2 episodes a week. The schedule: 2 pills 2 to 24 hours before sex, then 1 pill each at 24 hours and 48 hours after. Women and people with hepatitis B must take it daily. In the on-demand trials, the pill group had more gastrointestinal and kidney side effects than the placebo group, so follow-up visits cannot be skipped. Domestic pilots began in 2019 among men who have sex with men; the 2024 plan calls for "standardized implementation". No nationwide free policy was found. Get it at the infectious disease department or STD/HIV clinic of a local designated HIV hospital; call the local CDC first to ask which one prescribes. It doesn't prevent syphilis, gonorrhea, or other STDs — condoms are still required; see item 30 in this section (condoms for the whole act of sex). If a high-risk act has already happened, the remedy is Section 13, item 38 (get blocking medication within 72 hours). The beneficiary is mainly you — and it also protects your partner.

Women 65 and older: get a dual-energy X-ray (DXA) bone density scan; postmenopausal women with osteoporosis risk factors needn't wait until 65

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortality rateMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Women 65 and older, and postmenopausal women with osteoporosis risk factors, should get a bone density scan. Screening for risk first, then medicating those at high risk, cuts hip fractures by about 17%. Worked out, that's about 5 fewer hip fractures per 1,000 women screened. No change in overall mortality was seen.

Cost
A hospital dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA for short) scan of the lumbar spine and hip takes a few minutes lying down. Out of pocket it usually runs one to two hundred yuan, prices vary by region. The heel ultrasound you step on in checkup packages is for initial screening only and cannot confirm a diagnosis.
Benefit
The US Preventive Services Task Force's 2025 recommendation: screen women 65 and older for osteoporosis (Grade B recommendation). Postmenopausal women under 65 whose fracture risk is high on risk assessment are also recommended for screening (Grade B). For men the evidence is insufficient and it took no position. The evidence review behind the recommendation pooled 3 randomized trials and 42,009 older European women. The screening approach: assess fracture risk first, scan bone density for those at high risk, and medicate those found high-risk. Hip fractures were about 17% lower in the screened group. Point estimate RR 0.83, confidence range 95% CI 0.73 to 0.93. In absolute numbers, 5 fewer hip fractures per 1,000 screened. Among them, the UK's SCOOP trial enrolled 12,483 women aged 70 to 85: hip fractures about 28% lower in the screened group (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.89), with no detectable difference in mortality. The Chinese Medical Association's 2017 clinical guideline recommends: bone density testing for women over 65 and men over 70. Those younger but with one or more osteoporosis risk factors are also recommended to get tested. In the 2017 to 2018 national survey, osteoporosis prevalence was 20.6% among women over 40 and 5.0% among men. (China)
Note
Contested: SCOOP's prespecified primary outcome was all osteoporotic fractures, which were not significantly reduced in the screened group (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.03) — only hip fractures were. All three trials used "assess risk first, then scan"; none compared bone density scanning alone. The evidence review also estimated that 11.8% to 24.1% of those diagnosed were overdiagnosed — people who would never have fractured because of it in their lifetime. Whether men should be screened: the US says evidence is insufficient, the Chinese guideline sets it at 70 and above; follow your doctor's advice. This item covers whether your bones can take a fall; falling less comes from item 13 (balance and leg strength) — do both together. For what to do after an osteoporosis diagnosis, see item 40 (get on osteoporosis medication once diagnosed). The beneficiaries are mainly you — and your parents too.

Diagnosed with osteoporosis, or fractured from a minor fall? Have a doctor prescribe anti-osteoporosis medication and stick with it — calcium supplements are no substitute

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortality rateMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

For people already diagnosed with osteoporosis, or who have fractured from a minor fall, following the doctor's medication plan cuts hip fractures by about half, and spinal fractures by more than half. Older adults who start a once-a-year infusion right after hip fracture surgery had about 35% fewer refractures over two years. Calcium supplements alone cannot replace these drugs.

Cost
Prescription-only, taken for years on end. Common options: a once-weekly oral pill, or an infusion once a year. Early on, bone density is rechecked yearly; once stable, every 1 to 2 years. The hard part is staying on it with no symptoms.
Benefit
A fragility fracture is one that happens from minor trauma or during everyday activity. The Chinese Medical Association's 2017 guideline names three groups for medication. First, people who have had a fragility fracture of the spine or hip. Second, people with a bone density T-score of -2.5 or below, fractured or not. Third, people with low bone mass who have also had a fragility fracture of the wrist, upper arm, or pelvis, or whose calculated fracture risk is high. The guideline also states that "there is currently insufficient evidence that calcium supplementation alone can replace other anti-osteoporosis drug treatment". Cochrane updated its alendronate review in 2025. Among postmenopausal women who already had osteoporosis or fractures, the medication group had about 51% fewer hip fractures. Point estimate RR 0.49, confidence range 95% CI 0.25 to 0.96. Symptomatic spinal fractures about 55% lower (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.73). The HORIZON trial enrolled 2,127 people operated on for hip fracture, average age 74.5. Starting within 90 days of surgery, an annual zoledronic acid infusion, median follow-up 1.9 years. New fractures fell from 13.9% to 8.6%, about 35% fewer. Deaths fell from 13.3% to 9.6%, about 28% fewer. The guideline notes that within a year of hip fracture, about 20% die of various complications. In the 2017 to 2018 national survey, only 1.4% of women diagnosed with osteoporosis or who had fractured were on medication, and only 0.3% of men. (China)
Note
Contested: a meta-analysis pooling 38 trials found no reduction in overall mortality from these drugs (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.05). Zoledronic acid alone was not significant either (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.13). The authors concluded these drugs should be used only to have fewer fractures. The Cochrane figures' confidence was rated low to moderate as well. In women who hadn't fractured and were at lower risk, alendronate showed no clear effect on hip fractures (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.32). Rare side effects like osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures cannot be fully seen in trials lasting a few years, so keep to the review schedule and don't add or stop drugs on your own. Some people suit injections, some suit pills — the doctor decides which. For how osteoporosis gets found, see item 39 (bone density testing). The beneficiaries are mainly you — and your parents too.

Before stepping onto natural ice, drill a hole and measure the thickness — nothing under 15 cm; avoid river ice and the edges of ice-fishing holes

Grade CValue: FairBasis: mortality rateMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

China's official line: ice must be 15 cm thick before adults may go on it to skate. The US and Canadian floor is 10 cm, and it only counts for new, clear ice. White ice is only half as strong, so the required thickness doubles. On the same sheet of ice, one spot may be a foot thick and a few steps away only an inch or two — so measure as you go.

Cost
Easiest: go to a properly run rink, no extra cost. If you must go on natural ice, bring an ice drill or ice chisel to bore holes and measure the thickness. Add a pair of ice claws — two sharp spikes with handles, worn on your chest. All told, tens to one or two hundred yuan. Measuring every stretch costs some extra time.
Benefit
Science popularization from the China Meteorological Administration says ice must reach 15 cm thick for adults to skate on it. Outdoor rinks also need 15 cm of ice before opening. The Beijing Water Authority says a proper natural ice rink opens only when the ice is 15 cm thick and, for a week after, temperatures hold between -8°C and 1°C with no strong winds. Wild ice often carries holes chopped by anglers; once cut open, they rarely refreeze solid. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources' guide applies only to new, clear ice: don't go on under 4 inches (about 10 cm); at 4 inches, walking and ice fishing are OK. White ice — melted snow that refroze — is only about half as strong as clear ice, so count its thickness at double. On the same body of water, ice may be a foot thick here and only an inch or two a few feet away. Ice over moving water is usually dangerous, especially near streams, bridges, and culverts. Ice near shore can be thinner than farther out. The US National Weather Service's threshold for walking, ice fishing, and skating is also 4 inches. The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety relays the Canadian Red Cross's advice: 15 cm for a few people skating or walking, 20 cm for a larger skating party. These are all safety guidelines; no study has computed how many deaths following them prevents. (Nationwide / US, Canada)
Note
Official guides all say no ice is 100% safe; measuring enough thickness is a threshold, not a guarantee. Early winter just after freeze-up and early spring when thaw begins are the most dangerous. If you do fall in, don't take off your clothes — the air trapped in thick clothing helps you float. Turn back toward the direction you came from; that ice is strongest. Get your arms onto the ice, plant the ice claws into it, kick your legs behind you, and drag yourself up. Once out, don't stand up: lie flat and roll away from the hole, then get warm as fast as possible; if badly frozen, go to a hospital. Seeing someone else fall through, don't run over to grab them — see Section 13, item 25 (seeing someone drowning, don't enter the water yourself): first shout for people and call 110, then extend a pole or throw a rope. The beneficiaries are mainly you and the children you bring out onto the ice.

Fit the guard and wear goggles plus a face shield before using an angle grinder, hold it steady with both hands, and never mount a woodworking saw blade to cut wood

Grade CValue: FairBasis: mortality rateMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

An angle grinder spins extremely fast; a shattered disc flies out and injures people, and with a woodworking saw blade mounted it can kick back violently. In both domestic accidents, a saw blade was mounted and no guard fitted: one man's thigh artery was severed, another's carotid artery cut — neither survived. Guard, goggles plus face shield, both hands on the grips: these cost little.

Cost
Goggles plus a face shield: a few dozen yuan. A glance at the guard and disc before each start-up, and unplug before changing discs — a minute or two extra. The hard part: when it feels like a hassle, still keep the guard on and don't work one-handed.
Benefit
The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety and the Queensland safety authority in Australia list the practices as follows. Check the guard and disc before start-up; don't use discs with cracks, chips, or warping. The disc's rated maximum speed must not be lower than the machine's rated speed. The disc's diameter and center hole must match the machine. Disconnect the power before changing discs. Secure whatever you're grinding or cutting first. Wear protective glasses or goggles, with a face shield over them. Grip both handles with both hands and stand stable. Never use a cutting disc for grinding — the disc shatters more easily that way. Don't set the machine down before the disc has fully stopped. Point sparks and debris where no one stands, and keep nothing flammable nearby. Queensland's alert says a cutting disc's edge design speed is about 70 meters per second. Mounting a 356 mm disc on a 230 mm machine pushes edge speed to at least 120 meters per second, and the disc shatters easily. In February 2016, a local worker using a 230 mm angle grinder was struck in the chest by fragments and died of internal injuries. There are two domestic accident investigation reports. In 2019 in Harbin, a worker swapped the cutting disc for a toothed saw blade and, with no guard, cut wooden planks. The saw blade caught his trousers, severed his thigh artery, and he died of blood loss. In 2024 in Futian, Shenzhen, a worker used an angle grinder fitted with a woodworking saw blade, without a guard or the side handle, to cut a wooden door frame. The machine kicked back, cut his carotid artery, and killed him. The national standard quoted in the report states: "do not fit saw chains, wood-carving blades, or toothed saw blades". In South Korea's emergency department injury surveillance from 2011 to 2018, high-speed rotating cutting tools injured 8,697 people, of whom 4,603 were using grinders of this class. 46.4% were injured on the hands, 23.0% on the head. Compared with other similar tools, grinders carried about twice the odds of severe injury (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.88–2.29). A hospital in Mianyang, Sichuan, admitted 36 inpatients with angle-grinder eye injuries over two years. After surgery, 10 still had best vision below 0.05 even with glasses. Of 742 acute hand and forearm injuries at a Turkish hospital in one year, angle grinders caused 82. All but 8 happened off the job, and 44% were retired people. Of 15 angle-grinder casualties at one Japanese trauma center in 2017 to 2018, 9 were misuse like mounting a saw blade to cut wood. Of them, 2 lost an entire finger and 1 lost part of one. (Canada, Australia / China / South Korea, Turkey, Japan)
Note
Grade C because these practices come from safety-agency guides and accident investigations; no study has computed how many injuries following them prevents. The injury data only show how severe the injuries were, and all of it is one hospital's or one country's caseload. Benefit is set at "medium" by judgment: the consequences can be death, blindness, or lost fingers, but they land only on the person using the angle grinder. The Harbin machine's manual already said not to mount toothed saw blades and that the guard must be fitted. That worker had a hand saw within reach — wood is what hand saws and other woodworking tools are for. Keep loose clothing, dangling jewelry, and long hair secured; they get pulled in. Grinding throws off heavy dust and noise; for the ins and outs of masks and earplugs, see Section 19, item 10 (protective equipment the employer must provide). If a large blood vessel really is cut, press hard on the wound first — see Section 13, item 12 (major bleeding: press hard on the wound with your hand first). The beneficiary is mainly you — and the family member standing alongside helping.
Sources (9 references)

2. Don't die slowly

42 items

This section collects only two kinds of chronic risk: those with a large effect on all-cause mortality, and those with hard evidence. Entries are ordered by value for money, highest to lowest. A few are tagged "randomized trial," meaning people were randomly split into two groups and compared — the most trustworthy kind of result. All the other numbers come from studies that only track records, without assigning groups. The risk ratios such studies produce (HR, RR, and the like) carry two kinds of confounding: the people differ to begin with, and some fell ill first and only then behaved this way. So these numbers indicate direction and rough size only; following the advice does not guarantee a drop of the same size. The entries in this section are grouped by theme below; item numbers are in parentheses. Tobacco, alcohol, and betel nut: quit smoking — the sooner the better (item 1), no smoking at home or in the car (item 2), get medication before you quit (item 3), pick a quit date (item 4), a smoking-cessation clinic, or call 12320 (item 5), e-cigarettes only if you can't quit otherwise (item 6), don't chew betel nut (item 8), drink less or no alcohol (item 19), if your hands shake the moment you stop, don't quit cold turkey on your own (item 20), count what you drink in a week (item 21). What to cut back on: no sugary drinks (item 7), less processed meat (item 18), less ultra-processed food (item 28), no scalding-hot tea or soup (item 30). What to swap in or eat more of: switch to low-sodium salt (item 9), a small handful of nuts a day (item 22), trade red meat for fish and poultry (item 23), swap refined grains for whole grains (item 24), tea three or more times a week (item 25), three to four cups of coffee a day (item 26), your full 5 servings of fruit and vegetables (item 27), chili peppers four or more times a week (item 33), one or two servings of dairy a day (item 34), no need to give up eggs (item 35). Exercise and weight: walk 7,000–8,000 steps a day (item 11), play racket sports (item 14), rack up brief vigorous activity (item 15), weekly strength training (item 16), don't sit too long at a stretch (item 17), keep BMI at 20–25 (item 32). Sleep and night shifts: about 7 hours of sleep a night (item 13), keep naps under half an hour (item 37), catch up on sleep the next night after late nights (item 38), transfer out of night shifts early if you can (item 39). Kitchen oil and fumes: no coal or wood for cooking or heating (item 29), no bulk self-pressed peanut oil (item 40), vegetable oil instead of lard and butter (item 41), run the range hood when stir-frying (item 42). Teeth, medication, and other habits: brush properly and clean between your teeth (item 10), take medication regularly as prescribed (item 12), get out in the sun during the day (item 31), take a bath when you can (item 36).

1

Quit smoking — the sooner the better

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: large

On average, smokers die more than ten years earlier than nonsmokers. Quitting before 40 wipes out about 90% of the death risk that comes from continuing to smoke. The earlier you quit, the more you get back.

Cost
Costs nothing — in fact it saves money. A pack a day runs about 20–30 yuan, and once you quit, that money stays with you. The hard part is getting through withdrawal, usually a few weeks to a few months.
Benefit
A US study that tracked a group of people (observational records only, no groups assigned) found that current smokers live more than 10 years less than never-smokers. Quitting before 40 eliminates about 90% of the excess risk of death from continued smoking. Quitting at 25–34 buys about 10 extra years, at 35–44 about 9 years, at 45–54 about 6 years (reported in the original as life-years). A similar Chinese study: in the 2010s, the risk of death for urban male smokers was 1.65 times that of nonsmokers (RR 1.65); for rural men, 1.22 times. Ten years after quitting for good, the share of risk that comes from smoking is nearly gone.
Note
Breathing other people's smoke kills too: in 2004 about 603,000 people worldwide died of secondhand smoke, about 1% of all deaths that year. Even if you don't smoke yourself, stay away from other people's smoke, and above all don't let children breathe it. For how to quit, see the next four items: item 3 (cessation medication), item 4 (pick a quit date), item 5 (smoking-cessation clinics), item 6 (e-cigarettes).
Sources (3 references)
Jha P et al. (2013). 21st-century hazards of smoking and benefits of cessation in the United States. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128; Chen Z et al. (2015). Contrasting male and female trends in tobacco-attributed mortality in China: evidence from successive nationwide prospective cohort studies. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(15)00340-2; Oberg M et al. (2011). Worldwide burden of disease from exposure to second-hand smoke: a retrospective analysis of data from 192 countries. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61388-8 (the two secondhand-smoke figures)
2

Don't smoke at home or in the car, and don't let guests smoke in your home either

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

About 600,000 people worldwide die each year from breathing other people's smoke, nearly a third of them children. For people chronically exposed to secondhand smoke, the risks of high blood pressure, heart disease, and stroke are each about 30% higher. Smoke inhaled at home hurts you more than smoke inhaled outside.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time. The hard part is speaking up and asking family and guests not to smoke in your home.
Benefit
In 2004, 603,000 people worldwide died from secondhand smoke, about 1.0% of all deaths, 28% of them children. Pooling 57 studies: people exposed to secondhand smoke had about 1.28 times the odds of high blood pressure as the unexposed (odds ratio). Heart disease was 1.39, heart attack 1.50, stroke 1.36. Secondhand smoke inhaled at home carries a higher risk than secondhand smoke inhaled outside the home.
Note
Start with the home, because that's where you spend the most hours, and pooled across studies, secondhand smoke at home is more harmful than secondhand smoke elsewhere. Of the health lost to secondhand smoke, 61% falls on children. For quitting yourself, see item 1 of this section.
Sources (2 references)
Öberg M, Jaakkola MS, Woodward A, Peruga A, Prüss-Ustün A (2011). Worldwide burden of disease from exposure to second-hand smoke: a retrospective analysis of data from 192 countries. Lancet: "603,000 deaths were attributable to second-hand smoke in 2004, which was about 1·0% of worldwide mortality. 47% of deaths from second-hand smoke occurred in women, 28% in children, and 26% in men", "61% of DALYs were in children". https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61388-8; (2026). The Associations Between Secondhand Smoke Exposure and Various Cardiovascular Diseases: A Meta-Analysis. Nicotine & Tobacco Research: 57 studies, "hypertension (OR: 1.28, 95% CI: 1.15 to 1.40), heart disease (OR: 1.39, 95% CI: 1.28 to 1.50), myocardial infarction (OR: 1.50, 95% CI: 1.17 to 1.84), stroke (OR: 1.36, 95% CI: 1.18 to 1.54)", "Home exposure has a higher risk of CVD than non-home exposure". https://doi.org/10.1093/ntr/ntaf111
3

Don't quit smoking on willpower alone; get medication first: it can more than double your success rate

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Willpower alone fails most people. People taking varenicline quit at more than twice the rate of those on a placebo. Those using nicotine patches, gum, and the like do about 50% better than those using no medication. Adding a fast-acting form such as gum to the patch adds another 20%-plus.

Cost
Nicotine patches and gum are over-the-counter; any pharmacy counter carries them. One course runs 8 to 12 weeks and costs a few hundred to over a thousand yuan. Varenicline and bupropion are prescription drugs, from a smoking-cessation clinic or a respiratory department. The cost roughly cancels out against the cigarettes you stop buying over the same period.
Benefit
Pooling 41 randomized trials with 17,395 people: quit rates on varenicline were 2.32 times those on placebo (RR 2.32, 95% CI 2.15–2.51, the credible range; high-certainty evidence). Varenicline also beat bupropion (RR 1.36, about 36% higher) and a single form of nicotine replacement on its own (RR 1.25, about 25% higher). Nicotine replacement versus no medication: 133 trials, 64,640 people, success about 55% higher (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.49–1.61). A patch plus one fast-acting form (gum, lozenge) was about 27% higher than a single form alone (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37; 16 trials, 12,169 people, high-certainty evidence).
Note
Only those three classes of cessation medication are sold in China, and only nicotine replacement is over-the-counter. Common reactions to varenicline are nausea, vivid dreams, and poor sleep; anyone with a psychiatric history should tell the doctor. A course of nicotine replacement usually lasts 8 to 12 weeks — don't stop it abruptly on your own; taper as the doctor says. Medication handles the misery of withdrawal during those few weeks; it does not handle the situations that make you want to smoke. So use it together with item 4 of this section (pick a quit date) and item 5 (smoking-cessation clinics).
Sources (4 references)
Livingstone-Banks J, Fanshawe TR, Thomas KH, et al. (2023). Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 5, CD006103. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD006103.pub8; Hartmann-Boyce J, Chepkin SC, Ye W, Bullen C, Lancaster T (2018). Nicotine replacement therapy versus control for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 5, CD000146. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000146.pub5; Theodoulou A, Chepkin SC, Ye W, et al. (2023). Different doses, durations and modes of delivery of nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 6, CD013308. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD013308.pub2; Shanghai Municipal Health Commission (2021). Choosing the right medication makes quitting a little easier: "The cessation medications visible on the market fall into three main classes: nicotine replacement therapy drugs, bupropion, and varenicline"; "Nicotine replacement therapy drugs are over-the-counter (OTC) and can be bought at pharmacy counters; bupropion and varenicline are prescription drugs, available only at a hospital smoking-cessation clinic or respiratory department, dispensed by a pharmacist against a physician's prescription". https://wsjkw.sh.gov.cn/jtyx/20211119/df50681e01ba49f896d54…
4

Pick a quit date and stop completely that day; don't cut down gradually first

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: medium

Many people plan to smoke a few fewer cigarettes a day and taper down to zero. Yet at six months, 22% of those who picked a date and stopped outright had not smoked again, versus only 15.5% of those who cut down gradually. So pick a date and stop completely that day.

Cost
Costs nothing. Pick a day on the calendar and tell family and coworkers in advance.
Benefit
697 British smokers were randomly split into two groups. One stopped abruptly on the quit date; the other cut its smoking by 75% over the two weeks before that date. Both groups got behavioral support from nurses, and both used nicotine replacement before and after the quit date. At week 4, 49.0% of the abrupt group (95% CI 43.8–54.2, the credible range) had not relapsed, versus 39.2% of the gradual group (34.0–44.4), a relative risk of 0.80 (0.66–0.93). By month 6 it was 22.0% (18.0–26.6) for abrupt versus 15.5% (12.0–19.7) for gradual, relative risk 0.71 (0.46–0.91). Even people who preferred cutting down had a lower week-4 success rate than those who preferred stopping outright (38.3% vs 52.2%).
Note
Contested. Cochrane once had a review devoted to comparing these two methods, and concluded they were about the same (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.79–1.13; 10 trials, 3,760 people), but that review was withdrawn in 2019 and is no longer updated. So the best current evidence is the randomized trial above, and it points toward stopping abruptly. Also, both groups in that trial started nicotine replacement before the quit date — a practice with evidence of its own: starting early beats starting on the quit date itself, with success about 25% higher (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.08–1.44; 9 trials, 4,395 people, moderate-certainty evidence). So the sensible schedule is: pick a date, put the patch on two weeks ahead, and stop completely on the day.
Sources (2 references)
Lindson-Hawley N, Banting M, West R, Michie S, Shinkins B, Aveyard P (2016). Gradual Versus Abrupt Smoking Cessation: A Randomized, Controlled Noninferiority Trial. Annals of Internal Medicine, 164(9), 585–592. https://doi.org/10.7326/M14-2805; Theodoulou A, Chepkin SC, Ye W, et al. (2023). Different doses, durations and modes of delivery of nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 6, CD013308 (the part on starting nicotine replacement early). https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD013308.pub2
5

Go to a smoking-cessation clinic, or call 12320 to ask whether your area has quit services

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: large

Medication and "someone checking in on you regularly" are two different things, and together they work best. People on medication with someone dedicated to following up quit at nearly twice the rate of those who only heard a few sentences of brief advice. The phone counts too: quitlines that call you back proactively raise success rates by another 20–30%.

Cost
A clinic visit costs a few yuan to a few dozen yuan. Behavioral support is usually 4 to 8 sessions of half an hour to an hour each, totaling under 5 hours for most. Calling a hotline is free.
Benefit
Pooling 52 trials with 19,488 people: quit rates on medication plus behavioral support were 1.83 times those under usual care or brief advice (RR 1.83, 95% CI 1.68–1.98, the credible range; high-quality evidence). In the 43 trials that recruited in healthcare settings, it was 1.97 (1.79–2.18). Telephone counseling on its own: among people who had called a quitline themselves, those who received several proactive callbacks did about 38% better than those who only got materials or a single call (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.19–1.61; 14 trials, 32,484 people); among people who hadn't called and were offered telephone counseling by the researchers, about 25% better (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.15–1.35; 65 trials, 41,233 people). Both are moderate-certainty evidence.
Note
How to find one in China: search WeChat for the "China Smoking Cessation Platform" mini-program, which lists quitlines and cessation clinics around the country; you can also call 12320 to ask whether your area has a cessation clinic. Most of the trials above were done abroad, and the intensity of cessation clinics varies widely from place to place, so treat the numbers as directional. For the medication to pair with this, see item 3 of this section (cessation medication).
Sources (3 references)
Stead LF, Koilpillai P, Fanshawe TR, Lancaster T (2016). Combined pharmacotherapy and behavioural interventions for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 3, CD008286. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD008286.pub3; Matkin W, Ordóñez-Mena JM, Hartmann-Boyce J (2019). Telephone counselling for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 5, CD002850. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD002850.pub4; Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (2021). The "China Smoking Cessation Platform" WeChat mini-program officially launches: "Under the guidance of the Healthy China Action Tobacco Control Working Group, the Chinese CDC and the WHO Representative Office in China jointly produced the 'China Smoking Cessation Platform' WeChat mini-program, China's authoritative smoking-cessation resource library. The mini-program mainly includes quitlines, detailed smoking-cessation clinic information, and online cessation service resources"; the same site's footer notes "Health consultation hotline: 12320". https://www.chinacdc.cn/jkyj/yckz/gzdt/202203/t20220310_296…
6

Consider e-cigarettes only after quitting has failed otherwise; if you never smoked, don't touch them

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Switching cigarettes for nicotine e-cigarettes gets about 60% more people to quit than nicotine patches, and that finding is solid. But e-cigarettes are not harmless, and there are no long-term safety data yet. For someone who never smoked, they offer no benefit at all.

Cost
Device plus pods: tens to a few hundred yuan a month. In China you can only buy tobacco-flavored products, and only in shops holding a tobacco monopoly retail license.
Benefit
A continuously updated review covers 80 randomized trials and 29,861 people. Nicotine e-cigarettes beat nicotine replacement therapy by about 61% in quit success (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.23–2.12, the credible range; high-certainty evidence; 11 trials, 4,114 people). In absolute terms, about 4 more quitters per 100 people (1 to 7 more). Rates of serious adverse events were about the same in both groups (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.02, moderate-certainty evidence). Versus behavioral support only or no support, about 75% higher (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.39–2.20, low-certainty evidence).
Note
Contested. The World Health Organization does not recommend e-cigarettes as a quitting tool, citing insufficient long-term safety data and the risk of drawing young people into nicotine. The UK, for its part, has built them into its cessation services. China has not banned e-cigarette sales outright but regulates them tightly; the rules are set out in the E-cigarette Management Measures. Only tobacco flavors may be sold; fruity flavors and refillable devices are banned. They may only be bought in physical stores holding a tobacco monopoly retail license. Selling through any website, online shop, or social app other than the national e-cigarette transaction management platform is illegal, and sales to minors are banned. So the fruity e-cigarettes still floating around come through illegal channels, outside all oversight. E-cigarettes laced with synthetic cannabinoids — the kind that get you "high" — leak out the same way; see Section 22, item 4 (don't take pods offered by others). The trials in the review tested regulated nicotine products only; vape liquid of unknown origin is not among them. Order of operations: try item 3 of this section (cessation medication) first — the evidence there is harder, and cheaper.
Sources (2 references)
Lindson N, Livingstone-Banks J, Butler AR, et al. (2026). Electronic cigarettes for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 8, CD010216. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD010216.pub11; State Tobacco Monopoly Administration (2022). E-cigarette Management Measures (Announcement No. 1 of 2022, effective May 1, 2022), Article 18: engaging in e-cigarette retail requires a tobacco monopoly retail license from the competent tobacco monopoly administrative department. Article 22: "Selling e-cigarette products to minors is prohibited." Article 23, paragraph 2: "No individual, legal person, or other organization may sell e-cigarette products, atomized matter, nicotine for e-cigarette use, or the like through information networks other than the e-cigarette transaction management platform specified in these Measures." Article 26: "Sales of flavored e-cigarettes other than tobacco flavor, and of e-cigarettes to which atomized matter can be added by the user, are prohibited.". http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2022/content_5697988.htm
7

Skip sugary drinks; switching to sugar-free doesn't count as a fix

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

People who drink two or more sugary drinks a day are about 20% more likely to die over a given period than those who hardly drink any; one to two a day, about 14% more. Switching to sugar-free shows no benefit: people who drink two or more artificially sweetened drinks a day are instead about a quarter more likely to die.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time. Switching to water or unsweetened tea saves money. The hard part is breaking the sweet-drink habit, sugar-free versions included.
Benefit
Two large US cohort studies — observational records only, no groups assigned — covered about 118,000 people and some 36,000 deaths. Drinking 2+ servings a day carried about 21% higher risk of death than less than 1 serving a month (HR 1.21); 1–2 a day, about 14% higher (HR 1.14). The European EPIC cohort — observational records only, no groups assigned — covered 450,000 people in 10 countries. Comparing 2+ cups a day with less than 1 cup a month: sugar-sweetened soft drinks, about 8% higher (HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.01–1.16); artificially sweetened drinks (the sugar-free kind), about 26% higher (HR 1.26, 1.16–1.35); all soft drinks combined, about 17% higher (HR 1.17, 1.11–1.22).
Note
The dispute is over sugar-free drinks. The association for artificially sweetened drinks is stronger than for sugary ones, most likely because the causality runs backward: people who are already overweight or have diabetes are the ones who switch to the sugar-free version. So don't conclude from this that sweeteners are more toxic. But it does show that "switching to sugar-free makes it fine" has no evidentiary support. Water or unsweetened tea is the safest switch. Also, these studies only track records — no group-assignment trials — and heavy sugary-drink drinkers tended to live less healthy lives to begin with, so the numbers may run high.
Sources (2 references)
Malik VS et al. (2019). Long-Term Consumption of Sugar-Sweetened and Artificially Sweetened Beverages and Risk of Mortality in US Adults. Circulation. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.118.037401; Mullee A, Romaguera D, Pearson-Stuttard J, et al. (2019). Association Between Soft Drink Consumption and Mortality in 10 European Countries. JAMA Internal Medicine, 179(11), 1479-1490. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.2478
8

Don't chew betel nut

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Betel-nut chewers are about 20% more likely to die over a given period than non-chewers. Their risks of diabetes and metabolic syndrome are nearly 50% higher. The risks of oral cancer and esophageal cancer come on top of that.

Cost
Costs nothing, takes no time, and saves the money spent on betel nut. The hard part is breaking the chewing habit.
Benefit
Pooling 17 Asian studies covering 388,000 people: chewers' risk of death was about 21% higher than non-chewers' (relative risk 1.21, P=0.02); the mortality figure is based on 179,600 of them. Risk of diabetes was about 47% higher (1.47); metabolic syndrome about 51% higher (1.51). Betel nut is itself a known risk factor for oral cancer and esophageal cancer.
Note
The more years of chewing and the more quids a day, the higher the oral-cancer risk. After quitting, the risk declines over time. Betel quid with tobacco added is more dangerous still.
Sources (1 reference)
Yamada T, Hara K, Kadowaki T (2013). Chewing betel quid and the risk of metabolic disease, cardiovascular disease, and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis. PLoS One, 8(8), e70679. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0070679
9

Switch your household salt to low-sodium (potassium) salt

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

For people who have had a stroke, or who are over 60 with high blood pressure, switching the household salt to low-sodium salt lowered the probability of dying within five years by about 12%, and of stroke by about 14%.

Cost
A bag costs a few yuan more than regular salt. Swap it in on your regular shopping trip; no extra time. The taste is nearly unchanged.
Benefit
A trial that randomly split people into two groups, done in rural China: 20,995 people, all stroke survivors or hypertensive patients over 60, followed for 4.74 years. Result: the low-sodium-salt group had about 12% lower risk of death than the regular-salt group (RR 0.88); stroke about 14% lower (RR 0.86); major cardiovascular events about 13% lower (RR 0.87). Events from excessively high blood potassium showed no statistically significant difference between the groups.
Note
Contested. The PURE study only tracked records long-term, no groups assigned. It reported: people excreting under 3 g of sodium a day had about 27% higher risk of death plus cardiovascular events; those excreting over 7 g a day, about 15% higher. By its results, too little and too much are both bad, and the middle is best. But in the rural-China randomized trial cited here, the low-sodium salt only replaces part of the salt, so it won't push sodium anywhere near that low. Also note: the trial subjects were high-risk older adults. Healthy young people would gain far less from switching. Anyone with impaired kidney function, or taking potassium-sparing medications, should ask a doctor before switching.
Sources (2 references)
Neal B et al. (2021). Effect of Salt Substitution on Cardiovascular Events and Death. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2105675; O'Donnell M et al. (2014). Urinary sodium and potassium excretion, mortality, and cardiovascular events. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1311889 (the contesting party: PURE)
10

Brush properly, clean between your teeth once a day, and replace missing teeth promptly

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

People who floss or use interdental brushes daily are about 10% less likely to die over a given period. Older adults who have lost all their teeth are about 90% more likely to die; those left with fewer than 20 teeth, about twice as likely.

Cost
Floss or interdental brushes run a few dozen yuan a year; a dental cleaning is 100–200 yuan a visit. Two or three extra minutes a day. The hard part is turning interdental cleaning into something you do every single day.
Benefit
A Japanese study followed 9,676 people for 6 years. Users of interdental cleaning tools had about 11% lower risk of death (hazard ratio 0.89); users of tongue-coating cleaners, about 23% lower (0.77). Separately, pooling multiple studies of community-dwelling older adults: having not a single tooth meant about 1.87 times the odds of death (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.35–2.59, the credible range); fewer than 20 teeth, about 2.04 times (1.67–2.49).
Note
Contested. These studies only track records. People with bad teeth also tend to have worse overall health and finances. Whether bad teeth drag the body down, or a failing body drags the teeth down, is impossible to say for sure. But the cost here is extremely low, and periodontitis and missing teeth interfere with eating in their own right. For what an implant costs and which dental procedures insurance covers, see Section 24, item 12 (ask for a bundled price before getting a dental implant).
Sources (2 references)
Wang K, Matsuyama Y, Kiuchi S, et al. (2026). Routine oral health practices and all-cause mortality. Journal of Dentistry. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdent.2026.106789; Ko MJ, Seo S, So JS, et al. (2026). Deteriorated oral health and function as risk factors for physical disability and mortality in community-dwelling older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. European Geriatric Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41999-025-01319-4
11

Walk 7,000–8,000 steps a day, or total 150–300 minutes of brisk walking a week

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: a lotWillpower: someBenefit: large

People walking about 7,800 steps a day are about 45% less likely to die over a given period than those walking only 3,500. By time it works the same way: 150–300 minutes of brisk walking a week is about 30% lower than not exercising. Past a certain amount the risk stops falling — for people over 60, 6,000–8,000 steps is enough. Hit either yardstick; one is enough.

Cost
Costs nothing. By steps: 60–90 minutes of walking a day, which you can fold into the commute and grocery runs. By exercise time: 20–45 minutes a day. The hard part is keeping it up over the long run.
Benefit
Pooling 15 cohort studies — observational records only, no groups assigned — totaling 47,471 people and 3,013 deaths. People were sorted into four bands by daily steps; the lowest band's median was 3,553 steps a day, and the other three bands' medians were 5,801, 7,842, and 10,901. Those three bands' risk of death was about 40%, 45%, and 53% lower than the lowest band (HR 0.60, 0.55, 0.47). For people over 60, the benefit flattens out after 6,000–8,000 steps; for those under 60, after 8,000–10,000. Another pooled analysis: benefits start at about 3,867 steps a day, and each additional 1,000 steps a day lowers the risk of death by about 15%. By time: pooling multiple cohort studies (observational records only, no groups assigned), people whose activity reached 1–2 times the guideline minimum had about 31% lower risk of death than those who did no exercise (HR 0.69). That amount is 7.5–15 MET·h a week, roughly 150–300 minutes a week of brisk walking. Those below the minimum were still about 20% lower (HR 0.80). Those at 3–5 times the minimum were about 39% lower (HR 0.61) — the deepest point of the drop. Beyond that the risk does not fall further, but there is no harm either (10x and above was HR 0.69). Another pooled study using accelerometers: the most active quarter on moderate-to-vigorous activity had about 48% lower risk of death than the least active quarter (HR 0.52). An accelerometer is a wearable device that measures how much you actually move.
Note
Steps and exercise minutes describe the same thing with a different yardstick; hitting either one is enough. The stretch from 4,000 to 7,000 steps buys the most; there is no need to force your way to 10,000. Remember these studies only track records: the least-walking, least-moving group includes people who were already too sick to move. They moved little because they were near the end, not the other way around, so the measured gaps tend to run large. The studies that measured activity with devices followed people for shorter periods and had older participants, so the true benefit is not as large as "risk down to 0.52 times." But the trend — the more you move, the better — is clear.
Sources (4 references)
Paluch AE et al. (2022). Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. Lancet Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-2667(21)00302-9; Banach M et al. (2023). The association between daily step count and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: a meta-analysis. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurjpc/zwad229; Arem H et al. (2015). Leisure time physical activity and mortality: a detailed pooled analysis of the dose-response relationship. JAMA Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2015.0533; Ekelund U et al. (2019). Dose-response associations between accelerometry measured physical activity and sedentary time and all cause mortality: systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis. BMJ. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l4570
12

With high blood pressure or high cholesterol, take your meds regularly as prescribed; don't stop on your own

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Every 10 mmHg your blood pressure comes down, the probability of dying falls about 13%, and of stroke about 27%. Each unit a statin lowers LDL cholesterol cuts the probability of dying by about 10%. People who take their medication on time are 30–45% less likely to die than those who frequently miss doses.

Cost
Blood-pressure medicines and statins bought through centralized procurement run a few yuan to a few dozen yuan a month. One dose a day, barely any time. The hard part is staying on them — not stopping just because you feel fine.
Benefit
Pooling multiple randomized trials: every 10 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure cut the risk of death about 13% (RR 0.87). Systolic pressure is the higher of the two blood-pressure numbers. Major cardiovascular events were about 20% lower (RR 0.80); stroke about 27% lower (RR 0.73); heart failure about 28% lower (RR 0.72). Statins bring LDL cholesterol down: each 1.0 mmol/L reduction cut the risk of death about 10% (RR 0.90), and major vascular events about 22% (RR 0.78). Separately, pooling multiple cohort studies (observational records only, no groups assigned): people who took at least 80% of their prescribed doses had a lower risk of death than frequent dose-skippers — about 45% lower for statins (RR 0.55), about 29% lower for blood-pressure medication (RR 0.71).
Note
Follow this only if a doctor has judged you need the medication; healthy people need not take any. The "sticking to medication" numbers come from tracking records — people who stay on their meds are more disciplined to begin with, which inflates the apparent benefit. The two randomized-trial figures above are more reliable. This section has no separate entry on blood sugar: the evidence that pushing blood glucose lower benefits all-cause mortality is not as consistent as it is for blood pressure and cholesterol.
Sources (3 references)
Ettehad D et al. (2016). Blood pressure lowering for prevention of cardiovascular disease and death: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(15)01225-8; Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' (CTT) Collaboration (2010). Efficacy and safety of more intensive lowering of LDL cholesterol: a meta-analysis of data from 170 000 participants in 26 randomised trials. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61350-5; Chowdhury R et al. (2013). Adherence to cardiovascular therapy: a meta-analysis of prevalence and clinical consequences. European Heart Journal. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/eht295
13

Sleep about 7 hours a night, on a fixed schedule

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: a lotWillpower: someBenefit: medium

People who chronically sleep under 7 hours are about 10% more likely to die over a given period. The more erratic the schedule, the higher the risk: the most regular sleepers were 20% to nearly 50% less likely to die than the most erratic. In other words, how regular your schedule is reveals mortality risk better than how long you sleep.

Cost
Costs nothing. It does take time — for most people, time traded away from scrolling on the phone. The hard part is pinning down your bedtime and wake time.
Benefit
Pooling 16 cohort studies, observational records only, no groups assigned: 1.38 million people, 113,000 deaths. Short sleepers' risk of death was about 12% higher (RR 1.12); long sleepers', about 30% higher (RR 1.30). Another pooled analysis binned sleep duration: the 7-hour band had the lowest risk. Below 7 hours, each hour less meant about 6% higher risk (RR 1.06); above 7 hours, each hour more meant about 13% higher (RR 1.13). UK Biobank has wristband records for about 61,000 people, observational records only, no groups assigned. People were sorted into five bands by schedule regularity. The four more-regular bands had 20–48% lower risk of death than the most erratic band. How regular your schedule is predicts mortality better than how long you sleep. Another UK Biobank study measured sleep timing by wristband in 51,562 people, during which 3,853 developed cardiovascular disease. "Social jet lag" is the gap between the midpoints of your weekday and weekend sleep. People with 2 hours or more of it had about 30% higher cardiovascular risk (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.11–1.54). The association held among people of normal sleep duration too.
Note
What needs fixing is sleeping too little and an erratic schedule — there is no need to deliberately cut your sleep time. Long sleepers' higher risk is mostly reverse causation: depression, chronic illness, and sleep apnea make people sleep more. Also, the schedule-regularity claim currently rests on two cohort studies, both observational records only, no groups assigned — B-grade evidence on its own. For catching up after late nights, see item 38 of this section (catch up on sleep the very next night).
Sources (4 references)
Cappuccio FP et al. (2010). Sleep duration and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. Sleep. https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/33.5.585; Yin J et al. (2017). Relationship of Sleep Duration With All-Cause Mortality and Cardiovascular Events: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Prospective Cohort Studies. JAHA. https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.117.005947; Windred DP et al. (2024). Sleep regularity is a stronger Predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: A prospective cohort study. Sleep. https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/zsad253; Kumar N, Krishnamurthy S (2026). Social jet lag is associated with incident cardiovascular disease independent of sleep duration and cardiac genetic risk. Journal of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1111/joim.70133
14

Play a racket sport three times a week, 45 minutes each time

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: large

Regular tennis, badminton, and table-tennis players were about half as likely to die over a given period as non-players, and about 56% less likely to die of cardiovascular disease. Swimmers were about 28% less likely. Running and soccer showed no difference in this dataset.

Cost
Court fees of a few dozen yuan a session. About 2 hours a week. The hard part is rounding up people and a court, and showing up every week.
Benefit
A British cohort study of 80,300 people compared people who did a given sport with people who did not. Racket-sport players' risk of death was about 47% lower (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.40–0.69, the credible range), and cardiovascular death about 56% lower (0.44, 0.24–0.83). Racket sports here means tennis, badminton, and table tennis. For swimmers the two figures were 0.72 and 0.59; for aerobics, 0.73 and 0.64; for cycling, 0.85. Running and soccer showed no statistically significant difference.
Note
Contested. These are tracking studies only. Racket players are healthier to begin with and socialize more. The null result for running also suggests that what is at work may be "which kind of person picks which sport." Don't take this entry to mean running is useless — this section has separate entries counted by total exercise volume.
Sources (1 reference)
Oja P, Kelly P, Pedisic Z, et al. (2017). Associations of specific types of sports and exercise with all-cause and cardiovascular-disease mortality: a cohort study of 80 306 British adults. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 51(10), 812-817. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-096822
15

Rack up 4–5 minutes a day of brief vigorous activity — stair climbing, hurrying on foot

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

For people who otherwise never exercise, just three one-to-two-minute bursts of vigorous activity a day — climbing stairs, hurrying on foot — mean about 40% lower probability of dying over a given period, and nearly half for cardiovascular death, compared with none at all. Vigorous activity means climbing stairs, hurrying on foot, that kind of thing.

Cost
Costs nothing and requires no carved-out exercise time. The hard part is remembering to take the stairs and walk faster, instead of taking the easy way.
Benefit
A UK Biobank study followed 25,200 people who did no dedicated exercise, for an average of 6.9 years, during which 852 died. Some of them had three 1–2-minute bursts of incidental vigorous activity a day. Compared with people who had none, their risk of death and of cancer death fell 38–40%, and cardiovascular death 48–49%. People totaling 4.4 minutes a day of such activity had 26–30% lower risk of death and cancer death, and 32–34% lower cardiovascular death.
Note
Contested. The study measured activity with wearable devices, more reliable than asking people to fill out recall questionnaires. Still, it remains tracking records only, with no group-assignment trial, and only 6.9 years of follow-up. The subjects were complete non-exercisers; this entry does not apply to people who already exercise regularly.
Sources (1 reference)
Stamatakis E, Ahmadi MN, Gill JMR, et al. (2022). Association of wearable device-measured vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity with mortality. Nature Medicine, 28, 2521-2529. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-022-02100-x
16

Do 30–60 minutes of strength training a week

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: medium

People who do 30–60 minutes of strength training a week are 10–20% less likely to die over a given period than those who do none. Training more does not help further. Strength plus aerobic exercise together works best.

Cost
Bodyweight squats and push-ups cost nothing. Train 1–2 times a week, 20–30 minutes each. The hard part is slotting it into the weekly schedule.
Benefit
Pooling multiple cohort studies (observational records only, no groups assigned): people who did strength training had 10–17% lower risk of death than those who didn't. More is not better — the reduction is largest at about 30–60 minutes a week, roughly 10–20%, and more training than that adds no benefit. People who did both strength and aerobic training had a lower risk of death than people who did neither.
Note
These studies only track records, and the activity amounts were self-reported by participants. The evidence that "overtraining turns harmful" is weak; there is no need to limit your training because of it. Strength training also helps older adults prevent falls and keep their muscle — that is covered in Section 1.
Sources (1 reference)
Momma H et al. (2022). Muscle-strengthening activities are associated with lower risk and mortality in major non-communicable diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies. British Journal of Sports Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2021-105061
17

Don't sit too long at a stretch; get up and move every so often

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

The people who sat the most were 2.6 times as likely to die over a given period as those who sat the least. Sitting for very long unbroken stretches adds risk on top. But with 60–75 minutes of moderate activity a day, the extra risk from sitting is mostly wiped out.

Cost
Costs nothing, and getting up a few times takes little time. The hard part is losing track of time once you sit down — set yourself a reminder.
Benefit
A US cohort study, observational records only, no groups assigned, measured sitting with accelerometers. Splitting people into quarters by total daily sitting time: the most-sitting quarter had 2.63 times the death risk of the least-sitting quarter (HR 2.63). Splitting again by how long one unbroken sitting bout lasted: the longest-bout quarter had 1.96 times the risk of the shortest-bout quarter (HR 1.96). So total sitting and the length of a single unbroken bout are each linked on their own. Another pooled analysis combined studies of over a million people, observational records only, no groups assigned. People who sat more than 8 hours a day and barely exercised had 1.59 times the death risk of the other group (HR 1.59) — people who sat under 4 hours a day and were the most active. About 60–75 minutes of moderate activity a day can offset the extra risk from sitting. The most active group showed no statistically significant difference even when sitting more than 8 hours a day — their HR was only 1.04.
Note
The reliable conclusion: how much you move matters more than how long you sit, and with enough exercise the risk from sitting largely disappears. Remember these studies only track records — the heaviest sitters include many who were already sick, and "risk up to 2.63 times" clearly contains "fell ill first, then sat more." Also, in that same pooled analysis, the risk of watching TV more than 3 hours a day showed up at every activity level; the most active group merely pushed that threshold out to 5 hours.
Sources (2 references)
Diaz KM et al. (2017). Patterns of Sedentary Behavior and Mortality in U.S. Middle-Aged and Older Adults: A National Cohort Study. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/M17-0212; Ekelund U et al. (2016). Does physical activity attenuate, or even eliminate, the detrimental association of sitting time with mortality? A harmonised meta-analysis of data from more than 1 million men and women. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(16)30370-1
18

Cut back on processed meat (ham, bacon, sausage, luncheon meat)

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

The heaviest eaters of ham, bacon, and sausage were about 20% more likely to die over a given period than the lightest. Each extra daily serving of processed meat raised the probability by about 20% too.

Cost
Costs nothing — even saves money — and takes no time. The hard part is cutting back on the thing you love eating.
Benefit
Pooling multiple cohort studies (observational records only, no groups assigned): the highest processed-meat group had about 23% higher risk of death than the lowest group (RR 1.23); red meat overall, about 29% (RR 1.29); unprocessed red meat about 10% (RR 1.10), though that last figure showed no statistical significance. Another pooled analysis worked per daily serving: each extra daily serving of processed meat meant about 23% higher risk of death (RR 1.23); each extra serving of red meat, about 10% (RR 1.10).
Note
Contested. The NutriRECS guideline, using the standard GRADE evidence-rating scheme, judged these studies "not very reliable" and issued only a very weak recommendation: keep eating as you are. The two sides argue over how hard the evidence is, not over its direction. No study claims processed meat does you good. Unprocessed red meat's effect is small and shows no statistical significance. What needs reining in is processed meat.
Sources (3 references)
Larsson SC, Orsini N (2014). Red meat and processed meat consumption and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis. American Journal of Epidemiology. https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwt261; Schwingshackl L et al. (2017). Food groups and risk of all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.117.153148; Johnston BC et al. (2019). Unprocessed Red Meat and Processed Meat Consumption: Dietary Guideline Recommendations From the NutriRECS Consortium. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/M19-1621 (the contesting party: the NutriRECS guideline)
19

Drink less alcohol or none at all

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Past 100 g of pure alcohol a week, the more you drink, the earlier you die. 100 g of pure alcohol is about 2.5 L of beer. At age 40, people drinking 100–200 g a week lose about half a year of life; 200–350 g, one to two years; over 350 g, four to five years. Judged on overall health, the best-value amount is none.

Cost
Costs nothing, saves money, takes no time. The hard part is a bit of awkwardness declining drinks in social settings.
Benefit
Pooling 83 prospective studies, observational records only, no groups assigned, of 600,000 current drinkers. The lowest point of the risk of death sat at no more than 100 g of pure alcohol a week. That amount is about 2.5 L of 5% beer, or 300 mL of 40%-ABV baijiu. At age 40, drinking 100–200 g a week meant about 6 months less life expectancy; 200–350 g a week, 1–2 years less; over 350 g, 4–5 years less. The last three figures were reported in the original as life-years. The Global Burden of Disease study (GBD 2016), which adds up all kinds of health loss, put the lowest-risk amount of drinking at 0 drinks a week. One more pooled analysis corrected for study-design biases: people drinking 1.3–24 g a day had about 7% lower risk of death than lifetime abstainers (RR 0.93), but that figure showed no statistical significance. Drinking 45–64 g a day meant about 19% higher (RR 1.19); 65 g a day or more, about 35% higher (RR 1.35).
Note
Contested. The "light drinking helps" side is a pooled analysis of 34 long-term cohort studies. It reported that light drinkers' all-cause mortality was up to 17–18% lower, and set the dose at no more than 4 drinks a day for men and 2 for women — within that range, the more people drank, the lower their mortality. The other side points out that the "non-drinkers" group is contaminated with people who quit for health reasons and people in poor health to begin with. One pooled analysis stripped out exactly these confounders, and once that was done, the protective effect disappeared. The Global Burden of Disease study also puts zero as safest. The safe reading: light drinking does not noticeably shorten life, heavy drinking certainly does. "Starting to drink for your health" has no basis. For drinking less, see item 21 of this section (count your drinks first, then see a doctor). Heavy daily drinkers must not quit cold turkey on their own — see item 20 of this section (don't quit cold turkey on your own).
Sources (4 references)
Wood AM et al. (2018). Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption: combined analysis of individual-participant data for 599 912 current drinkers in 83 prospective studies. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)30134-X; GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators (2018). Alcohol use and burden for 195 countries and territories, 1990–2016: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2016. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31310-2; Zhao J et al. (2023). Association Between Daily Alcohol Intake and Risk of All-Cause Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-analyses. JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.6185; Di Castelnuovo A et al. (2006). Alcohol dosing and total mortality in men and women: an updated meta-analysis of 34 prospective studies. Archives of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1001/archinte.166.22.2437 (the contesting party)
20
