If you drink daily and get shaky and heart-racing when you stop, don't quit cold turkey on your own

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: large

Heavy daily drinkers who stop suddenly can go into withdrawal. The mild form brings shaky hands, sweating, a racing heart, and sleeplessness; the severe form brings seizures or delirium tremens, a medical emergency that can kill. Norway tracked more than 30,000 people: among those who had had delirium tremens, 8% died each year afterward. If you want to quit, start at a hospital, and say exactly how much you drink a day.

Cost
A psychiatric or addiction-medicine appointment costs a few yuan to a few dozen yuan. Severe cases need a few days in the hospital.
Benefit
A 2026 clinical review states plainly: after sudden cessation or a sharp cut in drinking, long-term heavy drinkers develop a withdrawal syndrome, with tremor, autonomic overactivity, anxiety, insomnia, perceptual disturbances, seizures, and delirium tremens — in general internal medicine practice, "common and potentially life-threatening." A Norwegian national registry cohort covered 36,287 people diagnosed between 2009 and 2015 with alcohol dependence, alcohol withdrawal state, or delirium tremens: annual mortality was 8.0% in the delirium tremens group, 5.0% in the withdrawal-state group, 3.6% in the alcohol-dependence group. The delirium tremens group's standardized mortality ratio was 9.8 (95% CI 8.9–10.7, the credible range) — a risk of death about 9.8 times that of the general population of the same age.
Note
How to judge for yourself: drinking nearly every day; shaky hands, sweating, a racing heart, and sleeplessness after a single day without a drink; needing a little in the morning to feel normal — if any one of these applies, don't stop on your own. The hospital's standard approach is benzodiazepines to carry you through those few days, plus thiamine (vitamin B1). This is graded B because the Norwegian cohort says what happened to people who had had delirium tremens, not what happens to people who quit cold turkey on their own — the step between the two is an inference. You should still quit; just switch the venue to a hospital. For what counts as heavy weekly drinking, see item 19 of this section (drink less alcohol or none at all); for drinking less, see item 21 (count your drinks first, then see a doctor).
Sources (2 references)
Caputo F, Lungaro L, Costanzini A, De Giorgio R, Addolorato G (2026). Alcohol withdrawal syndrome in hospitalized patients: a practical review. European Journal of Internal Medicine, 107103. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejim.2026.107103; Bramness JG, Heiberg IH, Høye A, Rossow I (2023). Mortality and alcohol-related morbidity in patients with delirium tremens, alcohol withdrawal state or alcohol dependence in Norway: A register-based prospective cohort study. Addiction, 118(12), 2352–2359. https://doi.org/10.1111/add.16297
21

Want to drink less? First count how much you drink in a week, then talk it over with a doctor for a few minutes

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: small

A doctor who spends a few minutes reviewing your drinking, explaining the risks, and setting a goal with you gets an average cut of 20 g of pure alcohol a week a year later — about half a liter of beer. Longer talks add nothing. For those who can't stop, two drugs used abroad have been shown to work: treating about 12 people gets 1 more person who no longer returns to drinking-to-excess.

Cost
Costs nothing. Counting drinks is one note a day. Mentioning it in passing at a clinic visit costs nothing extra.
Benefit
Pooling 34 randomized trials with 15,197 people: a year later, people who received a brief intervention were drinking 20 g of pure alcohol a week less than those given minimal intervention or none (95% CI 12 to 28 g less, the credible range; moderate-quality evidence). Baseline drinking in these studies averaged 244 g a week. A brief intervention means advice or lifestyle counseling of no more than 5 sessions totaling under 60 minutes; talking longer added no benefit. Medication: pooling 122 randomized trials with 22,803 people, acamprosate got 1 more person per 12 treated (95% CI 8 to 26) to stop returning to any drinking at all; oral naltrexone at 50 mg a day got 1 more per 12 treated (8 to 26) to stop returning to heavy drinking.
Note
The benefit is sized "small" because both bodies of evidence measure how much people drink, not mortality — under this book's rules, surrogate endpoints only get "small." The medication trials were mostly done abroad, most subjects already met the diagnostic criteria for alcohol dependence, and every trial layered the drug on top of psychosocial support, so the numbers are the extra benefit on top of that. For these two drugs' approved uses and availability in China, go by your doctor and the drug label; don't buy them from online shops on your own. Anyone already showing withdrawal should see item 20 of this section (don't quit cold turkey on your own).
Sources (2 references)
Kaner EF, Beyer FR, Muirhead C, et al. (2018). Effectiveness of brief alcohol interventions in primary care populations. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2, CD004148. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD004148.pub4; Jonas DE, Amick HR, Feltner C, et al. (2014). Pharmacotherapy for adults with alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA, 311(18), 1889–1900. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2014.3628
22

Eat a small handful of nuts every day

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People who regularly eat nuts are about 20% less likely to die over a given period than those who don't. Even once a week shows a difference, about 10% lower. The difference is most pronounced at a handful a day.

Cost
28 g a day runs about 200–300 yuan a year. Eat as you go; no time cost.
Benefit
Two US cohort studies, 119,000 people, over 3 million person-years. (A person-year is one person followed for one year.) Compared with people who never ate nuts: less than once a week, risk of death about 7% lower (hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.90–0.96, the credible range); once a week, about 11% lower (0.89, 0.86–0.93); 2–4 times a week, about 13% lower (0.87, 0.83–0.90); 5–6 times a week, about 15% lower (0.85, 0.79–0.91); 7 or more times a week, about 20% lower (0.80, 0.73–0.86).
Note
Buy the plain, unsalted kind. Nuts are not low in calories; don't graze on them like snacks. Remember these studies only follow a group of people over the long term — nut eaters lead healthier lives overall, so take the numbers with a discount.
Sources (1 reference)
Bao Y, Han J, Hu FB, et al. (2013). Association of nut consumption with total and cause-specific mortality. New England Journal of Medicine, 369(21), 2001-2011. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1307352
23

Replace some red meat with fish and poultry

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: small

Two extra weekly servings of processed meat or red meat mean about 3% higher probability of dying over a given period. The same servings of fish or poultry show no such increase. This entry's effect is on the small side for this section — the kind of swap you make in passing, not worth agonizing over.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time. This is swapping one meat for another, not buying more. The hard part is bending a few taste preferences.
Benefit
Pooling 6 US cohort studies with nearly 30,000 people: two extra weekly servings of processed meat meant about 3% higher risk of death (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 1.02–1.05, the credible range). Two extra weekly servings of unprocessed red meat, also about 3% higher (1.03, 1.01–1.05). The same servings as poultry: 0.99 (0.97–1.02); as fish: 0.99 (0.97–1.01). Neither of those two showed a statistically significant difference.
Note
Two servings a week moves the needle very little; don't expect swapping meats to add years to your life. For the same meat budget, you can favor fish and poultry first.
Sources (1 reference)
Zhong VW, Van Horn L, Greenland P, et al. (2020). Associations of Processed Meat, Unprocessed Red Meat, Poultry, or Fish Intake With Incident Cardiovascular Disease and All-Cause Mortality. JAMA Internal Medicine, 180(4), 503-512. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.6969
24

Replace some refined rice and white flour with whole grains

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

People who eat an extra 90 g of whole grains a day are about 17% less likely to die over a given period. 90 g is about three servings. The risk keeps falling all the way to about 200 g a day.

Cost
Brown rice, oats, and whole-wheat noodles cost a bit more than refined rice and white flour; no time cost. The hard part is your palate needing time to adjust.
Benefit
Pooling multiple cohort studies (observational records only, no groups assigned): an extra 90 g of whole grains a day meant about 17% lower risk of death (RR 0.83). 90 g is about 3 servings. The benefit continues up to 210–225 g a day. In another pooled analysis, each extra daily serving meant about 8% lower risk (RR 0.92).
Note
No need to switch everything to whole grains — halfway there already lands you in the stretch where the benefit is most visible. Remember these studies only track records: whole-grain eaters are healthier to begin with, so the numbers run large. Results also vary widely from study to study (I² 83% — the higher this number, the less the studies agree).
Sources (2 references)
Aune D et al. (2016). Whole grain consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all cause and cause specific mortality: systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. BMJ. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.i2716; Schwingshackl L et al. (2017). Food groups and risk of all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.117.153148
25

Drink tea three or more times a week

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Habitual tea drinkers were about 15% less likely to die over a given period. Counting from age 50, that works out to 1.26 extra years of life on average, and 1.41 extra years free of cardiovascular disease.

Cost
A few dozen to a few hundred yuan a year. Brewing a cup takes a few minutes; barely any time.
Benefit
A Chinese study of 100,900 people (China-PAR), half of them followed the full 7.3 years. Habitual tea drinkers' risk of death was about 15% lower (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.79–0.90, the credible range). Counting from age 50 as the starting point: habitual tea drinkers gained 1.41 more years free of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and 1.26 more years of life expectancy.
Note
The dispute: these studies only track records, and among Chinese men, tea drinkers smoke and drink at high rates. The authors adjusted away part of that influence, but not all of it. One more thing: don't drink it scalding — for hot-drink temperature, see this section's entry on hot-drink temperature. Some worry about mycotoxins in tea. Chinese testing of 158 dark-tea samples found aflatoxin in 2 of them; at typical drinking amounts, the intake works out below the internationally accepted value. Another study tested 352 teas for 16 mycotoxins; only ochratoxin A in dark tea exceeded the limit on average. At the amounts Chinese people actually drink, neither study found a dietary risk. Store tea somewhere dry; don't drink any that has gone damp and moldy. Green tea extract capsules are a different matter: swallowing concentrated catechins in a single large dose harms the liver; brewed tea has no such problem. So this entry is about brewed tea only — don't substitute extract supplements for it.
Sources (4 references)
Wang X, Liu F, Li J, et al. (2020). Tea consumption and the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: The China-PAR project. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, 27(18), 1956-1963. https://doi.org/10.1177/2047487319894685; Tea mycotoxins: Cui P et al. (2020). Quantitative analysis and dietary risk assessment of aflatoxins in Chinese post-fermented dark tea. Food and Chemical Toxicology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fct.2020.111830; Zhou H et al. (2022). Mycotoxins in Tea (Camellia sinensis (L.) Kuntze): Contamination and Dietary Exposure Profiling in the Chinese Population. Toxins. https://doi.org/10.3390/toxins14070452; Green tea extract and liver injury: Hu J et al. (2018). The safety of green tea and green tea extract consumption in adults - Results of a systematic review. Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yrtph.2018.03.019
26

Drink three to four cups of coffee a day, no sugar and no foam toppings

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People who drink three to four cups of coffee a day are about 17% less likely to die over a given period than those who don't drink it.

Cost
Brewing it yourself costs 1–2 yuan a day. Making a cup takes a few minutes; barely any time.
Benefit
An umbrella review combined the results of 201 pooled analyses, whose underlying studies were all observational records with no groups assigned. Result: people drinking 3–4 cups of coffee a day had 17% lower risk of death than non-drinkers (relative risk 0.83, 95% CI 0.79–0.88, the credible range).
Note
The dispute: the original authors state outright that the evidence comes almost entirely from tracking records, adding that "reliable randomized controlled trials are needed to judge whether it is causal" — meaning people would have to be randomly split into two groups and compared; tracking records alone cannot settle causation. When you drink it, drink it black: sugar and foam toppings cancel out the benefit. This entry does not apply to pregnant women, or to people with arrhythmia, anxiety, or insomnia.
Sources (1 reference)
Poole R, Kennedy OJ, Roderick P, et al. (2017). Coffee consumption and health: umbrella review of meta-analyses of multiple health outcomes. BMJ, 359, j5024. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.j5024
27

Eat your full 5 servings (about 400 g) of fruit and vegetables a day

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Each extra 200 g of vegetables and fruit a day means about 10% lower probability of dying over a given period. People who eat their full 5 servings a day are about 13% lower than those eating only 2. Eating more than that does not push it lower.

Cost
A few yuan to a dozen-plus yuan a day. Some time every day for washing and cutting. The hard part is buying daily and actually eating the full amount every day.
Benefit
Pooling multiple cohort studies (observational records only, no groups assigned): each extra 200 g of produce a day meant about 10% lower risk of death (RR 0.90), with the benefit continuing up to 800 g a day. Two large US cohort studies plus a pooled analysis of 26 studies: people who ate 5 full servings a day had about 13% lower risk of death than those eating 2 (HR 0.87). The best mix is 2 servings of fruit plus 3 servings of vegetables; beyond that, no further reduction.
Note
Eating 5 full servings is enough; there is no need to stretch to 10 — the two studies agree on that point. Remember these studies only track records, and the confounding is obvious: heavy vegetable eaters differ from everyone else in income, education, and exercise. So "about 10% lower risk" is already the ceiling.
Sources (2 references)
Aune D et al. (2017). Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. International Journal of Epidemiology. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw319; Wang DD et al. (2021). Fruit and Vegetable Intake and Mortality: Results From 2 Prospective Cohort Studies of US Men and Women and a Meta-Analysis of 26 Cohort Studies. Circulation. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.120.048996
28

Cut back on ultra-processed food (chips, instant noodles, pastries, ready meals)

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: a lotWillpower: yesBenefit: large

The heaviest eaters of ultra-processed food were about 20% more likely to die over a given period than the lightest, and 50% more likely to die of cardiovascular disease. But this body of evidence is rated low-confidence — discount the numbers back accordingly.

Cost
Costs nothing — you just buy differently. But you have to cook yourself, or spend time picking minimally processed ingredients, and that takes time every single day. The hard part is long-term resistance to the "as long as it's convenient" pull.
Benefit
An umbrella review combined multiple pooled analyses, whose underlying studies were all observational records with no groups assigned. Result: heavy ultra-processed-food eaters had about 21% higher risk of death than light eaters (RR 1.21), and about 50% higher cardiovascular death (RR 1.50). Those two findings were graded "highly suggestive" and "convincing" respectively. But under the standard GRADE evidence-rating scheme, the certainty is low or very low.
Note
The dispute has three parts. One: the NOVA classification lumps foods with very different nutrition into one category. Two: it overlaps heavily with sugary drinks and processed meat (items 7 and 18), so it is hard to tell which of them is doing the work. Three: under the standard GRADE scheme, the rating is low anyway. So how much extra benefit this entry adds once those two are done is hard to say. The other side's evidence is the same review's low ratings themselves; no primary study has reached the opposite conclusion. So get items 7 and 18 (no sugary drinks, less processed meat) done first, and treat this one as secondary.
Sources (1 reference)
Lane MM et al. (2024). Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses. BMJ. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-077310
29

Don't burn coal or wood for cooking or heating; switch to electricity or gas

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: a lotTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People who burn coal or wood for cooking are about 10% more likely to die over a given period; those burning coal or wood for heating, about 14%. People who have switched to electricity or gas are 13–33% less likely to die than people still burning solid fuels.

Cost
Rural households need to replace the stove, plus fuel costs of a few hundred to over a thousand yuan a year. One switch and it's done; no long-term time cost. City dwellers are mostly on electricity or gas already.
Benefit
A Chinese chronic-disease cohort study, observational records only, no groups assigned, followed 271,000 adults free of cardiovascular disease. People cooking with solid fuels such as coal and wood had about 11% higher risk of death than those using electricity or gas (HR 1.11); those heating with solid fuels, about 14% higher (HR 1.14). People who had already switched from solid fuels to clean fuels were, compared with those still burning them, about 13% lower on the cooking side (HR 0.87) and about 33% lower on the heating side (HR 0.67). Outdoor PM2.5 is a separate ledger. Pooling 104 cohort studies: each 10 µg/m³ more in long-term exposure meant about 8% higher risk of death from natural causes (RR 1.08). Natural causes means death from illness, not accidents.
Note
These studies only track records. Households that switch fuels also tend to be better off, so the "risk down to 0.67 times" figure mixes in the effect of household means. As for outdoor PM2.5, what an individual can do is limited: move house, wear a mask, run a purifier. No air-purifier study has used mortality as an endpoint, so this section gives no numbers for them.
Sources (2 references)
Yu K et al. (2018). Association of Solid Fuel Use With Risk of Cardiovascular and All-Cause Mortality in Rural China. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.2151; Chen J, Hoek G (2020). Long-term exposure to PM and all-cause and cause-specific mortality: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Environment International. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2020.105974
30

Let hot things cool a bit before drinking; skip scalding-hot tea, soup, and coffee

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Drinking very hot tea means about 8 times the probability of esophageal cancer as drinking warm tea; even merely "hot" tea, about 2 times. Drinking less than two minutes after pouring carries 5 times the risk of waiting four minutes or more.

Cost
Costs nothing — just wait two or three extra minutes each time. The hard part is holding back when you're craving it.
Benefit
In a high-incidence esophageal-cancer region of northern Iran, 300 patients were compared with 571 disease-free people. All figures below are against warm-tea drinkers. Drinkers of "hot" tea had about 2.07 times the odds of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.28–3.35, the credible range); of "very hot" tea, about 8.16 times (3.93–16.9). Those who drank less than 2 minutes after pouring had about 5.41 times the odds of those who waited 4 minutes or more (2.63–11.1).
Note
The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies hot drinks above 65 °C as Group 2A, meaning probably carcinogenic. The same assessment found coffee itself not carcinogenic. The high esophageal-cancer rates in China's Chaoshan and Taihang regions are linked to the habit of drinking while piping hot.
Sources (2 references)
Islami F, Pourshams A, Nasrollahzadeh D, et al. (2009). Tea drinking habits and oesophageal cancer in a high risk area in northern Iran: population based case-control study. BMJ, 338, b929. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.b929; Loomis D, Guyton KZ, Grosse Y, et al. (2016). Carcinogenicity of drinking coffee, mate, and very hot beverages. Lancet Oncology, 17(7), 877-878. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1470-2045(16)30239-X
31

Get out in the sun during the day; don't go all day without daylight

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Women who deliberately avoided the sun had life expectancies 0.6 to 2.1 years shorter than those who got the most sun. Nonsmokers who avoided the sun lived about as long as the heaviest sun-exposed smokers.

Cost
Costs nothing. A dozen-odd minutes a day; the commute and the lunch break are enough.
Benefit
A Swedish study followed 29,500 women for 20 years. Compared with the group that got the most sun, deliberate sun-avoiders had life expectancies 0.6 to 2.1 years shorter. The authors write that "non-smokers who avoided sun exposure had a life expectancy comparable to smokers in the highest sun-exposure group."
Note
The dispute: Sweden sits at high latitude with little sun, so the finding cannot be transplanted directly to China. Also, people who avoid the sun may simply have been frail and homebound to begin with. And don't sunbathe to the point of sunburn — you should still cover up under harsh midday light, because sun exposure raises skin-cancer risk.
Sources (1 reference)
Lindqvist PG, Epstein E, Nielsen K, et al. (2016). Avoidance of sun exposure as a risk factor for major causes of death: a competing risk analysis of the Melanoma in Southern Sweden cohort. Journal of Internal Medicine, 280(4), 375-387. https://doi.org/10.1111/joim.12496
32

Keep your BMI at 20–25; if overweight, lose the weight

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: a lotWillpower: yesBenefit: large

The probability of dying is lowest in the BMI 20–25 band. At 27.5–30 it is about 20% higher; at 30–35, about 45% higher; at 35–40, nearly double. East Asians are more sensitive to overweight: every 5 points of BMI means about 40% higher risk.

Cost
Costs nothing. Diet plus exercise takes time every day. This is the most willpower-hungry entry in the whole section: long-term discipline over what you eat and daily movement, and keeping the weight off after losing it is harder than losing it.
Benefit
Individual data from 239 prospective studies were pooled (observational records only, no groups assigned). The analysis kept only three kinds of people: never-smokers, people free of chronic disease at enrollment, and people who survived at least 5 years after joining. Result: the risk of death is lowest at BMI 20–25. At 25–27.5 it is about 7% higher (HR 1.07); 27.5–30, about 20% (HR 1.20); 30–35, about 45% (HR 1.45); 35–40, about 94% (HR 1.94); 40–60, 2.76 times (HR 2.76). For people above BMI 25, each extra 5 kg/m² meant about 39% higher risk in East Asian populations (HR 1.39).
Note
Contested. One side holds that "a bit of extra weight means longer life." Their pooled analysis found overweight people's risk of death about 6% lower, and mildly obese people's about 5% lower. The disagreement is mainly over whether to drop three kinds of data: smokers, the already ill, and the first years after enrollment. These get dropped because serious illness thins people out first. Once the 239-study analysis excluded all three, the risk from overweight reappeared. Also note: no randomized trial has shown that weight loss itself lowers all-cause mortality. The benefit figures above come from comparing people of different weights side by side; they do not guarantee that losing the weight delivers the same reduction. Those trying to lose weight need not work on meal timing — breakfast and 16:8 intermittent fasting offer no extra benefit; see Section 6, item 26 (don't count on breakfast or 16:8 to control your weight).
Sources (2 references)
Global BMI Mortality Collaboration (2016). Body-mass index and all-cause mortality: individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 239 prospective studies in four continents. Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(16)30175-1; Flegal KM et al. (2013). Association of all-cause mortality with overweight and obesity using standard body mass index categories: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.113905 (the contesting party)
33

Eat chili peppers four or more times a week

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People who eat chili peppers four or more times a week are about 23% less likely to die over a given period than those who rarely do, and about a third less likely to die of cardiovascular disease.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time.
Benefit
An Italian study of 22,800 people, half of them followed the full 8.2 years, with 1,236 deaths in total. Those eating chili peppers 4 or more times a week had about 23% lower risk of death than rare eaters (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.66–0.90, the credible range), and about 34% lower cardiovascular death (0.66, 0.50–0.86).
Note
The dispute: this is a tracking study set in the context of the Mediterranean diet — chili eaters may simply eat closer to the region's traditional diet overall. Also note that people with gastroesophageal reflux, hemorrhoids, or irritable bowel will find that chili worsens their symptoms; there is no need to force it.
Sources (1 reference)
Bonaccio M, Di Castelnuovo A, Costanzo S, et al. (2019). Chili Pepper Consumption and Mortality in Italian Adults. Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 74(25), 3139-3149. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2019.09.068
34

Have one or two servings of milk or yogurt a day

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People who drink more than two servings of milk or yogurt a day are about 17% less likely to die over a given period than those who drink none.

Cost
A few yuan a day; no time cost.
Benefit
The PURE cohort covered 21 countries and 136,000 people, followed an average of 9.1 years, with 6,796 deaths in total. People eating more than two servings of dairy a day had about 17% lower risk of death than non-consumers (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.72–0.96, the credible range), trend P=0.0052.
Note
The dispute: PURE includes many low- and middle-income countries, where being able to drink milk every day itself signals comfortable means — a confounder that is very hard to purge. Also, the lactose-intolerant can switch to yogurt or low-lactose milk; there is no need to force down regular milk.
Sources (1 reference)
Dehghan M, Mente A, Rangarajan S, et al. (2018). Association of dairy intake with cardiovascular disease and mortality in 21 countries from five continents (PURE): a prospective cohort study. Lancet, 392(10161), 2288-2297. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31812-9
35

You needn't give up eggs, but not three or four a day

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: small

Each extra half whole egg a day means about 7% higher probability of dying over a given period. Swapping that half for egg whites, fish, poultry, or nuts lowers death risk across the board instead. No need to give up eggs — just not three or four a day.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time.
Benefit
A US cohort study of 521,000 people, with 129,000 deaths in total. Each extra half whole egg a day meant about 7% higher risk of death (hazard ratio 1.07, 95% CI 1.06–1.08, the credible range). Replacing that half egg with an equal amount of egg whites, poultry, fish, dairy, or nuts and legumes lowered the risk of death, and lowered the risks of cardiovascular, cancer, and respiratory deaths as well.
Note
Heavily contested: other long-term studies tracking large groups, and pooled analyses of multiple studies, have found no link between eggs and mortality. The US Dietary Guidelines have already dropped the daily cholesterol ceiling. The only thing to avoid is three or four a day; one a day is nothing to worry about.
Sources (1 reference)
Zhuang P, Wu F, Mao L, et al. (2021). Egg and cholesterol consumption and mortality from cardiovascular and different causes in the United States: A population-based cohort study. PLoS Medicine, 18(2), e1003508. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1003508
36

Take a bath when you can, not just showers

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People who take a tub bath almost every day have about 28% lower risk of cardiovascular events than those who bathe less than twice a week, and about 46% lower risk of cerebral hemorrhage.

Cost
A bit more on water and electricity. Half an hour a session.
Benefit
A Japanese study of 30,000 people followed 19 years, with 2,097 cardiovascular events in total. Almost-daily bathers had about 28% lower risk of cardiovascular events than those bathing no more than twice a week (hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.62–0.84, the credible range); coronary heart disease about 35% lower (0.65, 0.45–0.94); stroke about 26% lower (0.74, 0.62–0.87); cerebral hemorrhage about 46% lower (0.54, 0.40–0.73).
Note
The dispute: the finding comes out of the Japanese population and bathtub culture; most Chinese households are in no position to bathe daily. Also, don't make the water too hot, and don't soak too long. For older adults and people with cardiovascular disease, water that is too hot and soaks that are too long are dangerous in themselves — every year in Japan a large number of elderly people die suddenly in the bathtub.
Sources (1 reference)
Ukai T, Iso H, Yamagishi K, et al. (2020). Habitual tub bathing and risks of incident coronary heart disease and stroke. Heart, 106(10), 732-737. https://doi.org/10.1136/heartjnl-2019-315752
37

Keep naps under half an hour and never more than an hour; if you need one or two hours to get through the day, find out why

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

For people napping an hour or less, the risks of death and chronic disease were not elevated, and their minds were a bit sharper besides. Those napping past an hour had about 30% higher risk of coronary heart disease, and about 20% higher for diabetes and obesity. So set an alarm and wake yourself at half an hour. If you cannot get through the day without an hour or two, that is a signal to get checked out.

Cost
Costs nothing. Set an alarm before lying down; almost no willpower needed.
Benefit
An umbrella review pooled 16 meta-analyses covering 244 health outcomes — an umbrella review is a pooling of already-pooled studies. The conclusion: for people napping less than 60 minutes, all-cause mortality and chronic-disease risks were not elevated, and the mental improvement was the most pronounced (SMD 0.69, 95% CI 0.37–1.00, the credible range). Short naps of 20 to 30 minutes improved physical performance the most (SMD 0.99, 0.67–1.31). People napping more than 60 minutes had about 30% higher risk of coronary heart disease, and about 20% higher risk of diabetes and obesity. Another study had 1,338 adults over 56 wear wristbands to measure their naps directly, rather than relying on self-filled questionnaires. Follow-up ran up to 19 years, during which 926 died. Each extra hour of napping meant about 13% higher risk of death (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.04–1.23); each additional nap a day, about 7% (HR 1.07, 1.02–1.13). People who napped in the morning had about 30% higher risk than those who napped in the early afternoon (HR 1.30, 1.03–1.64).
Note
Contested. Both studies above are observational records only, no groups assigned. Long nappers are more likely to begin with sleep apnea, anemia, hypothyroidism, depression, or some other chronic disease, so how much of "long nappers die more" is caused by the napping itself is unclear. Causal inference using genes (Mendelian randomization, 453,000 plus 541,000 people) supports only one thing: the more frequent the napping, the slightly higher the blood pressure and waistline. It found no causal effect of napping on coronary heart disease or diabetes. So don't treat "napping less" as a mortality-lowering tool. The "find out why" half is the author's advice, grade C: if daytime sleepiness forces long naps, first examine your nighttime sleep — snoring and breath-holding during sleep warrant a sleep-apnea workup — then get a blood count and thyroid tests. For refreshing short naps, see Section 3, item 11 (nap 10 minutes when drowsy in the afternoon). For nighttime sleep duration, see item 13 of this section (about 7 hours a night).
Sources (3 references)
Du P, Li J, Hua Z, et al. (2026). Multiple Health Outcomes of Daytime Napping: A Comprehensive Umbrella Review. Public Health Reviews. https://doi.org/10.3389/phrs.2026.1609013; Gao C, Cai R, Zheng X, et al. (2026). Objectively Measured Daytime Napping Patterns and All-Cause Mortality in Older Adults. JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.7938; Dashti HS et al. (2021). Genetic determinants of daytime napping and effects on cardiometabolic health. Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-20585-3
38

After staying up late, catch up on sleep the very next night; don't bank it for the weekend

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

People who stayed up short and did not make up the sleep the next night had about 15% higher risk of death than people with regular schedules; those severely short and unmade-up, about 42%. Those who made it up showed no visible elevation in risk. So when you have stayed up late, get to bed early the very next night.

Cost
Costs nothing. The hour or two of catching up is sleep you wanted anyway.
Benefit
UK Biobank, 85,618 people with an average age of 61.8, wearing wristbands that logged sleep day by day, median follow-up 8 years. The study first computed each person's own "short-sleep nights," meaning nights slept 2.5 hours or more less than they individually need. The first night after a short-sleep stretch counted as a "recovery night": sleeping more than they need that night counted as repaid. People fell into five patterns this way. Compared with the regular-schedule group, the short-sleep-and-unrepaid group's all-cause mortality risk was about 15% higher (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01–1.31, the credible range). Cumulative shortfalls over 3.5 hours left unrepaid meant about 42% higher (HR 1.42, 1.24–1.63). Neither repaid group showed a significant association — among them, repay-after-short-sleep was HR 1.12 (0.98–1.28). Among people who were already short sleepers, short-and-unrepaid meant about 19% higher (1.19, 1.01–1.40), and severely short-and-unrepaid about 38% higher (1.38, 1.17–1.63). The result replicated in a separate US health survey of 4,586 people.
Note
This is an observational study — records only, no groups assigned. People who cannot repay their sleep may simply be busier or in worse health to begin with, and that layer cannot be fully removed. "No elevated risk in the two repaid groups" only means no difference was detected; their point estimates are still above 1, and repaying does not mean all clear. So repay the debt promptly after a late night, and don't treat this as license to stay up at will. In this study, catching up means sleeping a bit longer the first night after the shortfall — it does not include banking it all for the weekend. Making "scrimp on weekdays, repay on weekends" a fixed weekly rhythm is called social jet lag, and it is itself linked to cardiovascular disease — see item 13 of this section (about 7 hours a night, on a fixed schedule). The entry on fixing your wake time on weekends too is Section 3, item 2 (fix your wake-up time, weekends included), and it does not conflict with this one: this entry tells you to get to bed early that night, not to sleep until noon the next day.
Sources (1 reference)
Li X, Zhang M, Li Z, et al. (2026). Acute sleep rebound following sleep restriction is associated with reduced mortality risk. Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72461-1
39

The longer you work night shifts, the higher your cardiovascular risk; transfer out early if you can

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: a lotTime: moderateWillpower: yesBenefit: large

Night-shift workers have about 13% more cardiovascular disease than non-night workers, and about 27% more cardiovascular death. And it accumulates: every additional 5 years of night work adds about 7% more cardiovascular disease. So tally this one by years — transfer out early if you can. As for night shifts causing cancer, the evidence is much weaker than the rumors.

Cost
Transferring or changing jobs may mean less pay, and the night-shift allowance disappears. Job hunting takes time, and making the decision is hard. If you simply factor this into the choice when picking a job, the cost is zero.
Benefit
Pooling 23 cohort studies, observational records only, no groups assigned. Night-shift workers' risk of cardiovascular events was about 13% higher (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.10–1.16, the credible range); cardiovascular death about 27% higher (RR 1.27, 1.18–1.36). By years: every additional 5 years of night work meant about 7% more cardiovascular disease incidence (RR 1.07, 1.04–1.09) and about 5% more cardiovascular death (RR 1.05, 1.03–1.06). By disease: coronary heart disease incidence about 22% higher (1.22, 1.16–1.28); coronary heart disease death about 22% (1.22, 1.10–1.36); ischemic heart disease death about 39% (1.39, 1.06–1.84); stroke death about 49% (1.49, 1.04–2.12). Stroke incidence was not significant (1.06, 0.95–1.18).
Note
All of these are observational records only, no groups assigned. Night workers differ from everyone else in smoking, weight, and income to begin with, and the adjustment is never clean. On night shifts causing cancer: the evidence is much weaker than the rumors. In a pooled analysis of 12 studies with 12,132 breast-cancer cases, people who had ever worked nights had only about 5% higher risk, with the credible range crossing 1 (RR 1.05, 0.96–1.14). The 20-plus-years band was about 25% higher (1.25, 1.01–1.55), but the finding lost significance after the authors' sensitivity analysis and approached 1 after correcting for possible publication bias — their words were that the link is "far from established." A study following Chinese men for 16.1 years with 8,202 cancer cases found no association between night work and total cancer or most common cancers; only pancreatic cancer in the 11-to-20 cumulative-years band was about 59% higher (HR 1.59, 1.09–2.31). So this entry tallies by the cardiovascular numbers, not by cancer. Not everyone should leave a night-shift post — the per-year ledger is yours to compute. Those already on nights, first fix what can be fixed: quitting smoking, item 1 of this section (quit smoking — the sooner the better); blood pressure and cholesterol, item 12 (take your meds regularly as prescribed); repaying sleep after night shifts, item 38 (catch up on sleep the very next night). Two more countermeasures are worth trying: confine your eating to daytime, and shift your body clock across with bright light plus strict daytime blackout. The latter is the only method proven to actually move the clock. Under ordinary indoor lighting, six consecutive night shifts leave the body clock unmoved; switch to 7,000 to 12,000 lux of bright light plus near-total darkness during the day, and the clock flips over entirely within four days. The light at night must be bright enough, daytime sleep must be strictly blacked out, and you must wear sunglasses on the way home to block the morning light — all three, no exceptions; leave out the last one and the whole thing is wasted. Both countermeasures have only been tested down to metabolic markers and sleep; no trial has measured whether following them lowers cardiovascular risk. On days off, returning to a daytime life pushes the clock right back. Doses, the raw numbers, and the remaining sources, together with how the body tells time, are all in [docs/生物钟和夜班.md](../docs/生物钟和夜班.md).
Sources (4 references)
Xi J, Ma W, Tao Y, et al. (2025). Association between night shift work and cardiovascular disease: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1668848; Esposito G, Bravi F, Santucci C, et al. (2025). Night shift work and breast cancer risk in healthcare workers: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Occupational Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1093/occmed/kqaf040; Shen QM, Li ZY, Tan YT, et al. (2026). Night shift work and risk of total and site-specific cancer: results from a prospective cohort study among Chinese men. Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health. https://doi.org/10.5271/sjweh.4290; Czeisler CA, Johnson MP, Duffy JF, et al. (1990). Exposure to bright light and darkness to treat physiologic maladaptation to night work. New England Journal of Medicine, 322(18), 1253-1259. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199005033221801
40

Buy packaged cooking oil with an SC number; skip bulk self-pressed peanut oil from small workshops

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Damp, moldy peanuts grow aflatoxin, a proven carcinogen that mainly damages the liver. After Guangzhou reined in the small workshops, abnormal liver function fell about 35% among residents who regularly ate self-pressed oil. In Guangxi, pregnant women who ate self-pressed peanut oil had about 90% higher risk of a low-birth-weight baby, and about 80% higher risk of preterm birth.

Cost
Buy from somewhere else, for about the same money. Just glance at the package for a food production license number starting with SC. The hard part is persuading elders used to buying self-pressed oil.
Benefit
Aflatoxin is a Group 1 carcinogen under the International Agency for Research on Cancer (proven to cause cancer in humans), chiefly liver cancer. A Guangzhou study measured aflatoxin B1 in small-workshop self-pressed peanut oil from 2010 to 2022: the median was 1.29 μg/kg, with the middle half of samples between 0.12 and 6.58. After the local small-workshop management regulation came into force, the toxin in the oil immediately dropped by 2.865 μg/kg, then by another 2.593 each year. Abnormal liver function fell in step among residents of the area who regularly ate self-pressed oil (PR 0.650, 95% CI 0.469–0.902, the credible range), about 35% lower. In a Guangxi study following 1,611 pregnant women, 81.7% ate self-pressed peanut oil. Their babies' risk of low birth weight was about 90% higher (aOR 1.9, 1.1–3.2), and of preterm birth about 80% higher (aOR 1.8, 1.1–3.0).
Note
Both studies are tracking records only, with no assigned comparison groups. The Guangzhou endpoint was liver-function blood tests, not liver cancer or death. The median toxin level in self-pressed oil is actually below the national limit of 20 μg/kg for peanut oil; the risk comes from eating it year after year and from the occasional high batch. The national limit applies to all peanut oil, but packaged oil must pass production licensing and factory testing, while small workshops are governed by each province's own rules and get far fewer spot checks. This entry's main beneficiaries are you and the family you eat with.
Sources (3 references)
Lei J, Li Y, Wang Y, et al. (2024). The impact of small food workshops management regulations on aflatoxin B1 in home-made peanut oil and the liver function of high-consumption area residents: an interrupted time series study in Guangzhou, China. Frontiers in Public Health, 12. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1484414; Zhong Y, Lu H, Jiang Y, et al. (2024). Effect of homemade peanut oil consumption during pregnancy on low birth weight and preterm birth outcomes: a cohort study in Southwestern China. Global Health Action, 17. https://doi.org/10.1080/16549716.2024.2336312; IARC (2012). Chemical Agents and Related Occupations. IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, Vol 100F. https://publications.iarc.fr/123; National Health and Family Planning Commission & China Food and Drug Administration (2017). National Food Safety Standard — Limits of Mycotoxins in Foods (GB 2761-2017)
41

Cook with vegetable oil instead of lard and butter; no need to rotate oils for health's sake, and don't count on flaxseed oil to protect your heart

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Cutting saturated fats like lard and butter in favor of vegetable oil means about 17% fewer events like heart attack and stroke, though overall risk of death shows no change. Shuffling back and forth between soybean oil, corn oil, and rapeseed oil — no evidence any difference exists. Eating more flaxseed oil shows no drop in heart-disease risk either.

Cost
Costs little extra. Vegetable oil is already the workhorse in most households. The hard part is giving up the taste habits of stir-frying with lard and mixing it into rice.
Benefit
Cochrane pooled 15 randomized trials with 56,675 people, each lasting at least two years. Cutting saturated fat lowered cardiovascular events overall by about 17% (RR 0.83, 0.70–0.98). All-cause mortality was virtually unchanged (RR 0.96, 0.90–1.03), and cardiovascular death unchanged (RR 0.95, 0.80–1.12). Swapping to polyunsaturated fats (the main components of soybean and corn oil) versus swapping to carbohydrate showed no detectable difference. Data for swapping to monounsaturated fats (the main components of rapeseed and olive oil) were too sparse to say. Another Cochrane review pooled 19 randomized trials with 6,461 people: more omega-6 (linoleic acid) gave RR 1.00 (0.88–1.12) for all-cause mortality and RR 0.97 (0.81–1.15) for cardiovascular events — no visible benefit and no visible harm. A third pooled 86 randomized trials with 162,796 people: more plant-source omega-3 (the main component of flaxseed oil and perilla oil) gave RR 1.01 (0.84–1.20) for all-cause mortality and RR 1.00 (0.82–1.22) for coronary heart disease events — essentially no effect.
Note
The dispute: some argue that too much omega-6 in soybean and corn oil promotes inflammation, so you should eat less of them and rotate your oils. The omega-6 randomized trials above showed no harm, and the authors themselves rated the evidence quality low. The benefit is sized "medium" on about 17% fewer cardiovascular events, with all-cause mortality unchanged. Whichever oil you use, control the amount — the dietary guidelines recommend 25 to 30 g of cooking oil per person a day.
Sources (3 references)
Hooper L, Martin N, Jimoh OF, et al. (2020). Reduction in saturated fat for cardiovascular disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (5), CD011737. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD011737.pub3; Hooper L, Al-Khudairy L, Abdelhamid AS, et al. (2018). Omega-6 fats for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (11), CD011094. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD011094.pub4; Abdelhamid AS, Brown TJ, Brainard JS, et al. (2020). Omega-3 fatty acids for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (3), CD003177. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD003177.pub5; Chinese Nutrition Society (2022). Dietary Guidelines for Chinese Residents (2022). People's Medical Publishing House
42

Run the range hood while stir-frying, pan-frying, or deep-frying — from when you light the stove until you're done

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Among Chinese women who never smoked, those who rarely or never ran the range hood while cooking had roughly twice the lung-cancer risk of those who regularly did. Having lived in homes with poor kitchen ventilation also meant about 50% higher risk, most marked in coal-burning households.

Cost
If you already have a range hood, it costs only a little electricity. If not, one with installation runs a few hundred to over a thousand yuan. The hard part is remembering to turn it on every time you light the stove — and not switching it off because it's noisy.
Benefit
Pooling 10 case-control studies, all of non-smoking Chinese women. Case-control means comparing lung-cancer patients with disease-free people and asking backward about past habits. People exposed to cooking fumes had about 1.74 times the odds of lung cancer (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.57–1.94, the credible range). In 4 of the studies comparing people exposed to fumes who did not use a range hood, it was about 2.11 (1.54–2.89). A Taiwan study compared 1,302 never-smoking women with lung cancer against 1,302 disease-free people, looking only at those who had cooked for more than ten years. Those who ran the hood in two-thirds or more of their cooking years had about half the risk of those at one-third or less (odds ratio 0.49, 0.32–0.76). A Shanghai prospective study followed 71,000 never-smoking women from 1996 to 2009 and found 429 cases of lung cancer. Those who reported having lived in homes with poor kitchen ventilation had about 49% higher risk of lung cancer (HR 1.49, 1.15–1.95). Coal burning plus poor ventilation for more than 20 years meant about 2.03 times (HR 2.03, 1.35–3.05). Coal burning on its own showed no difference (HR 1.03, 0.84–1.26); nor did the type of oil used in cooking.
Note
The dispute: the numbers supporting range-hood use come mainly from case-control studies. Patients recalling the past after diagnosis tend to underreport how often they used the hood, so the numbers may run large. In the Shanghai prospective study, the elevated risk fell mainly on coal-burning homes with poor ventilation; for gas-only homes, that study gives no separate figure for hood use or no use. Hence evidence grade B only, with the benefit sized "large" on a risk difference of about twofold. For not burning coal or wood in cooking, see item 29 of this section (don't burn coal or wood for cooking or heating). This entry's main beneficiary is whoever usually cooks at home.
Sources (3 references)
Xue Y, Jiang Y, Jin S, Li Y (2016). Association between cooking oil fume exposure and lung cancer among Chinese nonsmoking women: a meta-analysis. OncoTargets and Therapy, 9, 2987-2992. https://doi.org/10.2147/OTT.S100949; Chen TY, Fang YH, Chen HL, et al. (2020). Impact of cooking oil fume exposure and fume extractor use on lung cancer risk in non-smoking Han Chinese women. Scientific Reports, 10, 6774. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-63656-7; Kim C, Gao YT, Xiang YB, et al. (2015). Home kitchen ventilation, cooking fuels, and lung cancer risk in a prospective cohort of never smoking women in Shanghai, China. International Journal of Cancer, 136(3), 632-638. https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.29020

3. Don't waste energy

24 items

This section counts energy and time only. It looks at four things: how much attention you can use each day, how fast you react, how often you slip up, and how long it takes to get back after an interruption. All the numbers were measured directly — from experiments, or from records tracking a group of people over time (cohort studies). These numbers are not converted into lifespan, nor into mortality. Most entries in this section carry evidence grade B. That is simply the state of this field; it does not mean the advice doesn't hold. Item 19 is about what to expect when dealing with police, doctors, and tellers; it cites regulations, not experiments, so it is graded C. Item 15 (treating pessimistic thoughts as a symptom) and item 22 (treating "others demand I be perfect" as a symptom) cite mortality and suicide-risk figures on a basis different from the rest of this section, so they are not compared side by side. The entries in this section fall into the following groups by theme; item numbers are in parentheses. Attention at work: turn off non-essential notifications (item 1), batch messages a few fixed times a day (item 5), shut out even a few seconds of interruption (item 6), do one thing at a time (item 7), use earplugs in an open-plan office (item 12), work no more than 49 hours a week (item 13). Sleep and late nights: fix your wake-up time (item 2), sleep a full 7 to 8 hours a night (item 3), no caffeine after 2 p.m. (item 4), no screens in the hour before bed (item 8), sleep when it's time (item 9), no major decisions late at night (item 10), nap 10 minutes when drowsy in the afternoon (item 11). Thoughts in your head: when you catch yourself replaying, switch to something hands-on (item 14), treat pessimistic thoughts as a symptom (item 15), halve the estimate when you feel embarrassed (item 21), treat "others demand I be perfect" as a symptom (item 22). Anger and low mood: leave the scene first when angry (item 17), the first things to do when feeling low (item 18), don't vent anger by smashing things (item 23), write your troubles down for several days running (item 24). People and social media: learn to refuse requests you don't want to take (item 16), treat police and doctors as people working by the rules (item 19), cap the apps that feed you your peers' updates (item 20).

1

Turn off non-essential notifications and keep your phone out of sight while working

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

When your phone pings — even if you never look at it or touch it — your score on an attention task drops. The drop is about as large as if you had actually answered a call or sent a text. Then there's the other case: the phone just sits on the desk and you resist looking at it, and the mental bandwidth you can use shrinks anyway. The more attached you are to your phone, the bigger the drop.

Cost
Costs nothing. A few minutes to change some settings, and almost no willpower.
Benefit
Merely receiving a notification — without looking at it or touching the phone — measurably worsens performance on an attention task. The decline is comparable to actually answering calls or texting. This was done in the laboratory, with college students as subjects. Two further experiments showed that even when people successfully resisted checking, having their own phone nearby still reduced the mental bandwidth available. The most phone-dependent declined the most.
Note
These were single tasks in the laboratory. No one has measured what the effect adds up to when it happens day after day. In jobs that genuinely require being on call, you can keep notifications on for only a handful of contacts.
Sources (2 references)
Stothart, Mitchum & Yehnert (2015). The attentional cost of receiving a cell phone notification. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance. https://doi.org/10.1037/xhp0000100; Ward, Duke, Gneezy & Bos (2017). Brain Drain: The Mere Presence of One's Own Smartphone Reduces Available Cognitive Capacity. Journal of the Association for Consumer Research. https://doi.org/10.1086/691462
2

Fix your wake-up time, weekends included

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

The fifth of people with the most erratic schedules had body clocks about 2.5 hours later than the most regular fifth. That amounts to living in a permanent state of jet lag. The more regular a student's schedule, the better their grades.

Cost
Costs nothing. Sleeping in less on weekends takes a bit of willpower.
Benefit
61 college students kept records for 30 days. The most irregular fifth had body clocks (circadian rhythms) about 2.5 hours later than the most regular fifth. Specifically, the time melatonin secretion began was 00:08 versus 21:32. Their sleepiest, most sleep-hungry window also came about 1.8 hours later. The more regular the schedule, the better the academic performance (correlation r = 0.37).
Note
This is the only study; the sample was small and there was no group assignment. The researchers calculated that the difference in body clocks came mainly from differing daily light exposure. So a fixed wake-up time works only when paired with morning light. For how to recover after the occasional late night, see Section 2, item 38 (catch up on sleep the next evening after staying up late): the fix is to go to bed early the next evening, not to sleep until noon.
Sources (1 reference)
Phillips et al. (2017). Irregular sleep/wake patterns are associated with poorer academic performance and delayed circadian and sleep/wake timing. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-03171-4
3

Sleep a full 7 to 8 hours a night; don't treat 6 hours as enough

Grade AValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: a lotWillpower: someBenefit: large

After two weeks of sleeping only 6 hours a night, your mental performance falls to the level of someone who has gone two days and two nights without sleep. The trouble is you can't feel it. Self-rated sleepiness rises for the first few days and then stops rising; people sleeping 6 hours rate themselves just as sleepy as people sleeping 4. So the statement "I'm fine on 6 hours" is itself a symptom of sleep debt.

Cost
Costs nothing. It means setting aside 1 to 2 more hours a day for sleep. Going to bed earlier takes a bit of willpower.
Benefit
48 healthy adults aged 21 to 38 slept only 6 hours a night for 14 consecutive days. Their mental performance declined cumulatively, reaching the level of someone kept awake for 2 full nights. Yet their self-rated sleepiness rose only in the first few days and then barely increased. There was no difference in self-rated sleepiness between the 6-hour and 4-hour groups. This was a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with people randomly split into two groups. Separately, for short-term sleep loss (acute sleep deprivation of up to 48 hours), the effect size on lapses in simple attention was g = -0.776, and on reasoning accuracy g = -0.125. That part pooled 70 studies.
Note
"I don't feel sleepy" is not evidence of adequate sleep. Long-term 6-hour sleepers have merely gotten used to the feeling; their performance has not caught up. The pooled-studies part refers to wholly sleepless nights. "Chronically short sleep" rests on a single randomized controlled trial. The relationship between sleep duration and mortality risk is calculated separately — see Section 2, item 13 (about 7 hours of sleep a night): measured by mortality, the 7-hour band has the lowest risk.
Sources (2 references)
Van Dongen, Maislin, Mullington & Dinges (2003). The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness. Sleep. https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/26.2.117; Lim & Dinges (2010). A meta-analysis of the impact of short-term sleep deprivation on cognitive variables. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018883
4

No caffeine after 2 p.m.

Grade AValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

A large coffee (400 mg) drunk 6 hours before bed cost people more than an hour of measured sleep that night. Yet their own sleep diaries showed no difference at all. A regular cup of coffee (107 mg) needs to be finished more than 8.8 hours before bedtime to leave sleep unaffected. If you go to bed at eleven, 2 p.m. is your cutoff.

Cost
Costs nothing. For people in the habit of an afternoon coffee, resisting it takes a bit of willpower.
Benefit
400 mg of caffeine taken 6 hours before bed reduced objectively measured total sleep time by 1.1 to 1.2 hours compared with a placebo — the placebo being a caffeine-free comparison drink. Yet the sleep diaries the participants wrote themselves reported no difference; they couldn't perceive it. Pooling multiple studies (meta-analysis): caffeine cut total sleep time by 45 minutes on average, and the share of time in bed actually spent asleep (sleep efficiency) fell by 7%. A cup of coffee (107 mg) needs to be finished more than 8.8 hours before bedtime to leave sleep unaffected.
Note
The Drake study came from a single laboratory, and its 400 mg dose was on the large side — roughly two to three cups of coffee. Slow caffeine metabolizers need an even earlier cutoff. What you win by cutting caffeine is sleep duration, which stacks with item 3 (sleep a full 7 to 8 hours a night).
Sources (2 references)
Drake, Roehrs, Shambroom & Roth (2013). Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5664/jcsm.3170; Gardiner et al. (2023). The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2023.101764
5

Batch email and messages a few fixed times a day

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

The same people were compared across two weeks. In the week when they limited email to checking 3 times a day, their daily stress was clearly lower — and they sent and received just as much email. Unrestricted, people checked email 15.5 times a day on average.

Cost
Costs nothing. It takes a little time to tell colleagues how often you'll reply. Resisting the urge to check email constantly takes a bit of willpower.
Benefit
124 adults, compared with themselves across two weeks (within-subject design). In the week limited to checking email 3 times a day, daily stress was significantly lower than in the unrestricted week (effect size Cohen's d = 0.37). The volume of email received and answered did not differ between the two weeks. At the start, with no limit, people checked email 15.5 times a day on average.
Note
One study only, with a small-to-medium effect; it measured stress, not output. Instant messaging has not been studied directly; this is an extrapolation.
Sources (1 reference)
Kushlev & Dunn (2015). Checking email less frequently reduces stress. Computers in Human Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2014.11.005
6

For work requiring sustained thought, shut out even a few seconds of interruption

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

An interruption averaging 2.8 seconds doubled the error rate on the steps that followed. A 4.4-second interruption tripled it. Field tracking also found that an interrupted task took on average 25 minutes to get back to, with two other things done in between. Interrupted people worked faster, but their stress, frustration, and effort were all higher.

Cost
Costs nothing. Close the door, put on headphones, or hang up a "do not disturb" sign.
Benefit
An interruption averaging 2.8 seconds doubled the per-step error rate on tasks done step by step in sequence (sequential tasks); 4.4 seconds tripled it. This was done in the laboratory. Another study observed 24 office professionals (information workers) in the field. They switched work topics every 11 minutes on average. 57% of work topics were interrupted. Getting back to an interrupted task the same day took an average of 25 minutes 26 seconds, with 2.26 other tasks done in between. A further experiment with 48 people: interrupted participants worked faster, but reported more stress, frustration, time pressure, and effort.
Note
That field study split interruptions into two kinds: someone coming to find you, and something you opened yourself. A closed door blocks only the first kind. For the second, combine with item 1 (turn off non-essential notifications) and item 5 (batch your messages).
Sources (3 references)
Altmann, Trafton & Hambrick (2014). Momentary interruptions can derail the train of thought. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0030986; Mark, Gonzalez & Harris (2005). No task left behind? Examining the nature of fragmented work. CHI 2005. https://doi.org/10.1145/1054972.1055017; Mark, Gudith & Klocke (2008). The cost of interrupted work: More speed and stress. CHI 2008. https://doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357072
7

Do one thing at a time; don't reply to messages during meetings

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Every task switch makes you slower and more error-prone. People who routinely run several screens at once have not trained up a gift for doing several things simultaneously — they actually perform worse on task-switching tests.

Cost
Costs nothing. Not replying to messages during meetings takes a bit of willpower.
Benefit
After a task switch, responses are markedly slower and errors more frequent. This part comes from a review of multiple studies. Another laboratory study used college students. Heavy media multitaskers — people who routinely use several media at once — are more easily pulled off course by irrelevant stimuli and irrelevant memories. On task-switching tests they performed worse, not better.
Note
How much switching back and forth costs varies a great deal with the work, so no single number is given here. The Ophir study was a snapshot comparison; it cannot tell whether "multitasking harms attention" or "people with worse attention multitask more."
Sources (2 references)
Monsell (2003). Task switching. Trends in Cognitive Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1364-6613(03)00028-7; Ophir, Nass & Wagner (2009). Cognitive control in media multitaskers. PNAS. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0903620106
8

No glowing screens in the hour before bed; if you must read, read paper or e-ink

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: medium

Reading on a glowing screen before bed delayed falling asleep by about 10 minutes compared with a paper book. Melatonin was suppressed by 55%. The next day's body clock shifted more than 1.5 hours later; people were groggier in the morning and took longer to feel fully awake.

Cost
Costs nothing. Putting the phone down for the hour before bed means fighting the habit long-term; it takes willpower.
Benefit
In the laboratory, the same people cycled through both conditions (crossover trial). Reading a light-emitting e-book before bed delayed falling asleep by about 10 minutes versus a paper book (25.7 vs 15.8 minutes). Evening melatonin was suppressed by 55%. The next day's body clock (circadian rhythm) was delayed by more than 1.5 hours, with melatonin onset at 22:31 versus 21:01. The next morning participants were sleepier and took longer to feel fully awake.
Note
Small sample, done under tightly controlled laboratory conditions. At everyday phone brightness and usage lengths, the effect may not be this large. How much a phone's night mode helps was not tested in this study.
Sources (1 reference)
Chang, Aeschbach, Duffy & Czeisler (2015). Evening use of light-emitting eReaders negatively affects sleep, circadian timing, and next-morning alertness. PNAS. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1418490112
9

Sleep when it's time; don't stay up late for games, short videos, or porn

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: large

In 2025, people in China slept an average of 6.97 hours a night, falling asleep at 0:10 on average. Those who used a phone or tablet before bed were more than twice as likely to sleep too little and 2.7 times as likely to be sleepy in the daytime. The numbers were nearly the same when the device merely sat in the bedroom unused. So the easiest fix is to keep the phone out of the bedroom.

Cost
Costs nothing. The hard part is fighting the "just one more episode" pull night after night. Keeping the phone out of the bedroom is the lowest-effort version.
Benefit
In 2025, residents of China averaged 6.97 hours of nighttime sleep, falling asleep at 0:10 on average (Chinese Sleep Research Society). People who used a portable device before bed were about 2.17 times as likely to sleep too little (OR 2.17), about 1.46 times as likely to have poor sleep quality (OR 1.46), and about 2.72 times as likely to be sleepy in the daytime (OR 2.72). With the device merely present in the bedroom but not used, the numbers were similar: about 1.79, 1.53, and 2.27 times (OR 1.79/1.53/2.27). This pooled 20 cross-sectional surveys covering 125,198 children and adolescents. Another cross-sectional survey: among 844 adults aged 18 to 94, those who kept using their phone after lights out took longer to fall asleep, spent a lower share of time in bed actually asleep, and were more fatigued in the daytime.
Note
Contested. The cost of staying up late itself is covered in item 3 of this section (sleep a full 7 to 8 hours a night). As for how pornography affects ordinary people's energy and mental performance, there is currently no reliable evidence settling whether it is the cause. One analysis pooling multiple studies argues that so-called "pornography problems" stem mostly from a mismatch between a person's values and their own behavior, not from the content itself. Another study pooled data from 280 men and found no relationship between viewing time and erectile function during partnered sex. This entry targets only the sleep time it crowds out. As for the 6.97-hour and 0:10 figures, the Chinese Sleep Research Society's website has no press release posted (checked September 2026); rely on the Health News report republished by the Fujian Provincial Health Commission.

(2018). Pornography Problems Due to Moral Incongruence: An Integrative Model with a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. No major decisions or important messages late at night

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: small

When well rested, people quickly learn to avoid the high-risk option. After two sleepless nights in a row, they keep picking the high-risk one instead — more so the older they are. No one has measured how much a few lost hours of sleep matter, but push important decisions until after you've slept.

Cost
Costs nothing. You're just putting things off until after you've slept.
Benefit
34 healthy adults took the Iowa Gambling Task — an experiment measuring risky decision-making — after 49.5 hours without sleep. When rested, they quickly learned to avoid the high-risk options. Sleep-deprived, they chose the high-risk options more. Older participants were affected more. This is a single experiment; it is the only study.
Note
The study looked at the extreme case of two consecutive nights without sleep. What happens to ordinary people who stay up until 2 a.m. has not been tested directly. The "no messages" half is the author's experience (grade C) — sending the next day is not too late.
Sources (1 reference)
Killgore, Balkin & Wesensten (2006). Impaired decision making following 49 h of sleep deprivation. Journal of Sleep Research. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2869.2006.00487.x
11

When drowsy in the afternoon, nap 10 minutes, not half an hour

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

A 10-minute nap freshens you up on the spot, and the effect lasts two and a half hours. At 5 minutes it's essentially useless. At 20 minutes you wait half an hour before it kicks in. At 30 minutes you wake into a stretch of grogginess during which you perform worse than if you hadn't napped at all.

Cost
Costs nothing. Takes 10 minutes, plus a place to lie down or put your head down.
Benefit
After a short night, a 10-minute nap immediately improved sleepiness, fatigue, vigor, and mental performance, with part of the benefit lasting past 155 minutes. A 5-minute nap offered almost nothing. The benefit of a 20-minute nap appeared only after 35 minutes. A 30-minute nap first brought a stretch of sleep inertia: right after waking, performance was actually worse, improving only later.
Note
One laboratory study only, with healthy young participants. Don't force it if you can't fall asleep. Whether lying down with eyes closed for 10 minutes helps has no research behind it. Naps longer than an hour have instead been linked to higher mortality and coronary heart disease risk — see Section 2, item 37 (keep naps under half an hour).
Sources (1 reference)
Brooks & Lack (2006). A brief afternoon nap following nocturnal sleep restriction: Which nap duration is most recuperative? Sleep. https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/29.6.831
12

In an open-plan office, use earplugs or find a quiet room for memory-dependent work

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: small

When background noise rose from 39 to 51 decibels, people remembered fewer words, felt more tired, and wanted to work less. During breaks, watching nature footage with sound restored energy better than going on listening to office noise.

Cost
Earplugs cost a few dollars. Booking a quiet meeting room takes some time.
Benefit
Students worked in a simulated open-plan office. When background noise rose from 39 to 51 decibels (dB, LAeq), they recalled fewer words, rated themselves more fatigued, and were less willing to work. During breaks, watching nature films with sound pulled their energy ratings back up better than listening only to a river sound or to office noise.
Note
One laboratory study only. The most disruptive noise is speech whose content you can make out. White-noise headphones help with exactly this, but the study did not test headphones.
Sources (1 reference)
Jahncke, Hygge, Halin, Green & Dimberg (2011). Open-plan office noise: Cognitive performance and restoration. Journal of Environmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvp.2011.07.002
13

Don't work more than 49 hours a week

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Records from British munitions factories during World War I show that up to 49 hours a week, output rises in step with hours worked. Past 49 hours, each extra hour yields less and less. Working 70 hours a week produced almost the same as working 56 — the extra 14 hours counted for nothing.

Cost
You may lose some overtime pay. You may also have to spend effort talking it through with your boss.
Benefit
Output records of workers in British munitions factories during World War I: up to 49 hours a week, output was proportional to hours worked. Past 49 hours, the growth in output began to slow. It peaked at about 63 hours. Output at 70 hours was almost no different from output at 56 hours — the extra 14 hours were wasted.
Note
The data come from factories a hundred years ago, doing physical labor, with a mostly female workforce. Whether the same threshold applies to knowledge work is uncertain; the author himself says other trades may sit higher or lower. What is reliable is the direction: past some point, more hours produce almost nothing more. The specific figure of 49 is not reliable.
Sources (1 reference)
Pencavel (2015). The Productivity of Working Hours. The Economic Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecoj.12166
14

When you catch yourself replaying the same upsetting thing, switch to something hands-on

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Replaying the same upsetting thing never produces an answer. It only deepens depression, drives negative thoughts in harder, makes problems harder to solve, makes actually starting harder, and wears out the people around you willing to listen. When you notice you're going in circles, go do something with your hands.

Cost
Costs nothing. The hard part is noticing you're replaying in the first place (it's called rumination); the noticing itself takes practice.
Benefit
A review of multiple studies finds that replaying the same upsetting thing (rumination) worsens depression. It also entrenches negative thinking and weakens problem-solving. It interferes with actually acting, and it wears out the people around you willing to listen. It is associated with anxiety, binge eating, heavy drinking, and self-harm.
Note
The review gives direction only, no numbers. "Switch to another activity" is the author's own practice. The literature supports just one sentence: redirecting your attention beats continuing to circle. Which activity to switch to has never been compared.
Sources (1 reference)
Nolen-Hoeksema, Wisco & Lyubomirsky (2008). Rethinking Rumination. Perspectives on Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-6924.2008.00088.x
15

Treat thoughts like 'things are certainly going to get worse' as symptoms, not facts

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

In a 20-year twin study, each step up in pessimism meant about 13% higher odds of dying during the period, and about 20% higher odds of dying from cardiovascular disease. The reverse did not hold: high optimism scores brought no matching benefit. So what you treat is pessimism, not "insufficient positivity."

Cost
Costs nothing. The hard part is treating such thoughts as a symptom rather than as facts.
Benefit
2,978 Australian twins over age 50, followed for an average of 20 years, during which 1,068 died. For every 1 standard deviation higher on the pessimism scale, the risk of dying during the period rose about 13% (hazard ratio 1.134). The credible range for that figure was 95% CI 1.065–1.207, P=8.85×10⁻⁵. Cardiovascular deaths rose about 20% (1.196, 1.045–1.368, P=0.0093). There was no link to cancer deaths. Optimism scores showed no clear association with mortality either.
Note
Contested. This is observation only; no groups were assigned. One might say "they were pessimistic because they were already sick"; the author counters that if that were so, cancer deaths should have been linked too. But undetected factors remain possible. Optimism had no protective effect, so there is no need to force yourself to "think positive." What matters is not treating pessimistic expectations as accurate forecasts of the future.
Sources (1 reference)
