Whitfield JB, Zhu G, Landers JG, Martin NG (2020). Pessimism is associated with greater all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, but optimism is not protective. Scientific Reports, 10, 12609. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-69388-y
16

Cut back on relationships that drain you and learn to refuse requests you don't want to take

Grade CValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: medium

The loss from one person who drains you is larger, and more consistent, than the gain from one who supports you. So subtract first, add later.

Cost
Costs nothing. There will be some short-term social friction, and you may lose some relationships. Saying no takes considerable willpower.
Benefit
A survey of 120 widowed women aged 60 to 89: the link between upsetting interactions and psychological well-being was more consistent and stronger than the link for pleasant ones. On this result, the loss caused by one person who drains you exceeds the benefit from one who supports you.
Note
The sample was unusual, and it was a one-time questionnaire, so no ordering can be read. It measured well-being, not energy. Its placement in this section is the author's inference. There is no objective standard for which relationships count as "draining" — you have to judge for yourself.
Sources (1 reference)
Rook (1984). The negative side of social interaction: Impact on psychological well-being. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.46.5.1097
17

When angry, leave the scene first; treat the other person as weather, not an enemy

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Reinterpreting what just happened, or putting yourself in the other person's position, both measurably bring the emotion down — the second works better. Clamping down and not showing your feelings does nothing. Also: people who punished the offender went on ruminating about the episode longer afterward; those who didn't retaliate moved on faster. The pleasure revenge would bring is something people overestimate in advance.

Cost
Costs nothing. In the moment you hold your tongue, walk away, and decide later whether to deal with it. That takes a little practice.
Benefit
Pooling 306 experimental comparisons (meta-analysis): reinterpreting what happened (cognitive reappraisal) had an effect size on emotion of d = 0.36. Perspective-taking d = 0.45. Distraction d = 0.27. Suppressing feelings was ineffective (d = -0.04). Three further experiments showed: people who punished the offender went on ruminating about them longer afterward; those who didn't punish "moved on" faster. People overestimated in advance how satisfying revenge would feel.
Note
The pooled-studies part measured emotional intensity, not energy, with small-to-medium effects. The revenge part rests on a single set of experiments, hence grade B. The "empty boat" is a parable from Zhuangzi's "The Mountain Tree": an empty boat bumping into yours doesn't anger you; a manned one does — yet it's the same bump. It's an analogy, not evidence. If you have actually suffered a loss, take the legal routes in Sections 8 and 9 — far cheaper than blowing up on the spot.
Sources (2 references)
Webb TL, Miles E, Sheeran P (2012). Dealing with feeling: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of strategies derived from the process model of emotion regulation. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0027600; Carlsmith KM, Wilson TD, Gilbert DT (2008). The paradoxical consequences of revenge. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012165
18

When feeling low, start with the best value-for-effort moves: get moving, get sunlight, sleep on time, talk to someone, call 12356

Grade AValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: large

For depression, brisk walking and jogging work best, and the higher the intensity the more effective — details in Section 22, item 6 (when your mood is bad, go walk or run). Light therapy is strongly effective for seasonal depression and works for non-seasonal depression too. Online self-help cognitive behavioral courses work; when symptoms run heavier, having someone guide you works better. If thoughts turn dark, call 12356 first.

Cost
Free, or nearly free. A few brisk walks, jogs, or strength sessions a week. Get outside into the sunlight during the day. Settle into a fixed schedule. When thoughts turn dark, one phone call.
Benefit
Pooled 218 randomized controlled trials with 14,170 people (network meta-analysis). The comparators were people doing other activities. Against them, walking or jogging had an effect size on depression of g = -0.62 (95% confidence interval -0.80 to -0.45). Yoga -0.55, strength training -0.49. The higher the intensity, the better the effect. Pooling the light-therapy studies: effect size 0.84 (0.60 to 1.08) for seasonal depression, 0.53 (0.18 to 0.89) for non-seasonal. Another analysis pooled individual patient data across studies. It looked at internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (online self-help courses). Guided and unguided both beat the control group. For moderate-to-severe cases (PHQ-9 above 9), guided worked better. 12356 is the national psychological assistance hotline, open at least 18 hours a day.
Note
All of these are supports for mild-to-moderate depression. For moderate-to-severe cases and suicidal thoughts, seek care — call 12356 first (see Section 1, item 25). Exercise trials are mostly small, and unlike drug trials they cannot blind people to who is exercising. The light-therapy studies run only to 2003 and were also small. "Sleep on time" and "talk to someone" are the author's experience, with no dedicated citations. Don't treat "get moving" as a demand you place on depressed people; a ten-minute walk counts.
Sources (4 references)
Noetel M et al. (2024). Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-075847; Golden RN et al. (2005). The efficacy of light therapy in the treatment of mood disorders: a review and meta-analysis of the evidence. American Journal of Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.162.4.656; Karyotaki E et al. (2021). Internet-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Depression: A Systematic Review and Individual Patient Data Network Meta-analysis. JAMA Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2020.4364; National Health Commission (2024). Notice on adopting "12356" as the nationwide unified psychological assistance hotline number (Guo Wei Yi Zheng Han [2024] No. 259). https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202412/content_6994470…
19

Treat police, doctors, and tellers as people working by the rules, not as characters: what moves your case is paperwork and deadlines, not emotion

Grade CValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: small

Police, doctors, and tellers are people working by the rules of their posts, governed by paperwork, deadlines, and oversight. How pleasant the other person's attitude is has almost nothing to do with whether your matter gets done, or in how many days. So get your receipts, note the deadlines, appeal through the channels — don't try to argue them into agreement.

Cost
Costs nothing. What changes is your expectations and your sequence of actions. The first time, you have to resist the urge to "argue them into agreement."
Benefit
Swap the moves you make when dealing with institutions: from "pleading, getting angry, retelling your grievance over and over" to "getting the paperwork, noting the deadlines, appealing through the channels." What you save is the time spent communicating repeatedly and ruminating. This is a one-time shift in mindset, not a daily time saving. What you can actually check against is the deadlines themselves — they are all in writing. For public-order cases, counted from the date of acceptance, handling may not exceed 30 days; for major or complex cases, this can be extended by 30 days with approval from the public security organ at the next level up. Where a case with a complainant is decided not to be filed, the notice of non-filing must be served within 3 days. The complainant may apply for reconsideration within 7 days, and the public security organ must reach a decision within 30 days. If unsatisfied, they may apply for review to the next level up within a further 7 days.
Note
Why grade C: the judgment that "many people treat the person behind the counter as a character, not as someone at work" has no literature to cite. Only the rules half is citable: deadlines, paperwork, and remedy channels are all in writing. The figures cited in this entry come entirely from the two Ministry of Public Security regulations in Section 8, item 39 (what happens after you report to the police). Following procedure cannot fix "the other person's bad attitude," nor does it guarantee success; what changes is your expectations and your first move. Bank tellers and government service windows are the same: their operations leave records, get double-checked, and errors bring accountability. So keep your slips, ask for receipts, complain through the channels, and don't guess blindly about "whether they'll screw me over." Legitimate priorities are posted in the open — for instance, emergency rooms triage by condition, not first come first served (Section 24, item 7, emergency triage). To thank a doctor who saved you, use a thank-you letter and the satisfaction rating — see Section 24, item 11. To "give something so they take you more seriously" is bribery when aimed at law-enforcement officers, and explicitly an aggravating factor — see Section 8, item 40. If you meet clear differential treatment, complain; don't treat it as an unwritten rule to imitate.
Sources (2 references)
Ministry of Public Security (2020). Procedures for Handling Criminal Cases by Public Security Organs (as amended by MPS Order No. 159; Articles 171, 178, and 179). http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2020/content_5549884.htm; Ministry of Public Security (2013, amended 2019). Procedures for Handling Administrative Cases by Public Security Organs (MPS Orders No. 125 and No. 149). http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2013/content_2321117.htm
20

Don't make 'how everyone else is doing' daily reading: set limits on or delete apps that feed you your peers' updates

Grade AValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: large

People in the habit of comparing themselves online to those doing better tend to have worse moods and lower self-esteem. People who deactivated Facebook for four weeks saw a small rise in well-being — but also a real drop in how much they knew about current events. People who capped each of three social platforms at 10 minutes a day saw loneliness and depression fall after three weeks.

Cost
Costs nothing. Setting limits on an app, or deactivating the account, takes minutes. The hard part is not reopening it afterward — fighting the pull long-term.
Benefit
Pooling multiple studies (meta-analysis): 54 independent samples, 94 effect sizes, N = 36,583, using a three-level random-effects model. The average correlation between online upward social comparison and psychological maladjustment was r = 0.330 (95% CI 0.289–0.370, the credible range). Broken down by outcome: socially evaluative negative emotions such as fear of being looked down on 0.438, anxiety 0.382. Depression 0.306, lower well-being 0.268, lower self-esteem 0.263. Age, cultural background, and year of data collection did not change the strength of the association. Results from long-term follow-up studies were no stronger than those from cross-sectional surveys. Separately, a randomized controlled trial with 2,743 U.S. Facebook users. Of these, 61% were willing to accept deactivation for less than $102. Participants were randomly split into a four-week deactivation group and a control group. Deactivation freed up 60 minutes a day for the average participant. The subjective well-being index rose by 0.09 standard deviations. By subscale: life satisfaction 0.12, anxiety 0.10, depression 0.09, happiness 0.08. After correcting for chance in multiple comparisons, these still held. The authors offered a benchmark: psychological interventions designed to lift people's mood. Such interventions raise subjective well-being by about +0.34 standard deviations and reduce depression by about -0.23. So this effect is roughly 25% to 40% of a standard psychological intervention. The contemporaneous costs: the current-events knowledge index fell 0.19 standard deviations, and political polarization fell 0.16 standard deviations. After the experiment ended, the deactivation group still used Facebook 12 minutes a day less than the controls (0.31 standard deviations, a 23% reduction). A further randomized controlled trial with 143 undergraduates, randomly split into two groups. One group limited Facebook, Instagram, and Snapchat to 10 minutes per platform per day; the other used them as usual. After three weeks, the limited group's loneliness and depression had fallen significantly. Both groups' anxiety and fear of missing out were lower than at the start.
Note
The "correlation" half shows only that two things occur together; it cannot be read as who causes whom, and the authors themselves say more long-term follow-up research is needed. The randomized half can speak to causation, but its participants were U.S. Facebook users before the 2018 midterm elections, so transplanting it onto Chinese platforms is a stretch. The Hunt study had only 143 undergraduates, and it stands alone. The effect sizes are all modest — don't expect deleting an app to solve your mood problems. What you're blocking is the "watching how everyone else is doing" kind of use; keeping in touch with family and friends, looking up information, and job hunting are not included. If you truly can't hold the line, start by turning off push notifications, "people you may know," and the home feed. For the overall screen-time ledger, see Section 4, items 15 and 16 (hard caps on short videos; skip rolling news). For what to do first when feeling low, see item 18 of this section (get moving, get sunlight, sleep on time). On recovering a sense of identity through buying things, see Section 6, item 23. On spending more money to "move up a notch," see Section 6, item 24.
Sources (4 references)
Lei Y, Hu S, Sun Y, Zheng L (2026). "Looking up" linked to feeling down: a meta-analysis of online upward social comparison and psychological maladjustment. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1825169; Allcott H, Braghieri L, Eichmeyer S, Gentzkow M (2020). The Welfare Effects of Social Media. American Economic Review, 110(3), 629–676. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20190658; Allcott H, Braghieri L, Eichmeyer S, Gentzkow M (2019). The Welfare Effects of Social Media. NBER Working Paper No. 25514 (the specific figures cited in this entry were checked verbatim against this version; the published version's abstract does not contain the numbers). https://www.nber.org/papers/w25514; Hunt MG, Marx R, Lipson C, Young J (2018). No More FOMO: Limiting Social Media Decreases Loneliness and Depression. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 37(10), 751–768. https://doi.org/10.1521/jscp.2018.37.10.751
21

When you think 'everyone saw me embarrass myself,' cut that estimate in half

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: small

Wear an embarrassing T-shirt into a room of people, and you'll figure nearly half of them can tell whose face is printed on it; in reality fewer than a quarter do. Wear a T-shirt you consider flattering, and you'll overestimate the count sixfold. After a chat, people also routinely underestimate how much the other person liked them. So when you think "everyone will remember how I embarrassed myself," halving the estimate is still too high.

Cost
Costs nothing. Just ask yourself one extra question in the nervous moment: did they really see?
Benefit
Experiment one: participants put on a T-shirt printed with Barry Manilow's face and walked into a room with other participants. The wearers estimated on average that 46% of observers would correctly identify whose face was on the shirt. The observers actually got it right 23% of the time — the estimate was exactly double reality. Subtracting actual from estimated for each session, the average overestimate was 23 percentage points (95% CI 9–38, the credible range). Excluding the two sessions with only two and three observers, it was 27 percentage points (11–43). Experiment two: participants wore self-chosen T-shirts they considered flattering. Average estimate 48%; observers actually got it right 8% — six times. Another series of studies covered three settings: paired conversations between strangers, first-year college roommates, and adult workshops. The result: people systematically underestimate how much their conversation partners like them, and how much the partners enjoyed the conversation. The authors call it the "liking gap." It held across conversations of different lengths and persisted for months among new roommates.
Note
Why grade B: these are all small laboratory and campus studies, in the settings of wearing a shirt and chatting with strangers. There is no direct evidence for carrying them over to "being talked about by colleagues" or "saying the wrong thing in a meeting." These numbers show only the direction and rough magnitude of the overestimate; they cannot be applied as conversion factors. Nor is what others think always unimportant. In settings that genuinely evaluate you — interviews, defenses, performance reviews, medical reports — the evaluation is real; prepare as needed. What deserves the discount is only the everyday feeling that "everyone is watching me"; what you're countering there is your own estimation bias.
Sources (2 references)
Gilovich T, Medvec VH, Savitsky K (2000). The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 211–222. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.78.2.211; Boothby EJ, Cooney G, Sandstrom GM, Clark MS (2018). The Liking Gap in Conversations: Do People Like Us More Than We Think? Psychological Science, 29(11), 1742–1756. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797618783714
22

Treat 'others demand I be perfect' as a symptom, not a fact

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: small

People who feel "the people around me demand I be perfect, and I'll be rejected if I fall short" are more prone to suicidal thoughts. "I demand perfection of myself" is far more weakly tied to suicidal thoughts — about a third as strong. Even after subtracting the thoughts people already had, the first kind of feeling still tracked later increases in such thoughts, though not by much.

Cost
Costs nothing. The hard part is treating the thought as something to be handled, rather than as an accurate reading of other people's real demands.
Benefit
Pooling multiple studies (meta-analysis): 45 studies, N = 11,747, across undergraduates, medical students, community adults, and psychiatric patients, using a random-effects model. Below are the weighted average correlations with suicidal thoughts. Perfectionistic concerns r = .28 (95% CI .24–.32, the credible range; 42 studies, 7,936 people). Perfectionistic concerns is an umbrella covering socially prescribed perfectionism, concern over mistakes, doubts about actions, and the gap between reality and one's standards, among others. Socially prescribed perfectionism on its own also came to r = .28 (.25–.32, 30 studies, 3,640 people). Perfectionistic strivings r = .10 (.07–.13, 31 studies, 4,588 people) — an umbrella covering self-oriented perfectionism and personal standards. Parental criticism r = .20 (.11–.29). Now the link to suicide attempts. Perfectionistic concerns r = .12 (.07–.17, 15 studies, 5,275 people). Socially prescribed perfectionism r = .19 (.08–.29, 8 studies, 689 people). The follow-over-time portion: after subtracting suicidal thoughts present at the start, socially prescribed perfectionism still moved in the same direction as suicidal thoughts at later follow-up, though modestly. Self-oriented and other-oriented perfectionism showed no detectable association.
Note
Why grade B: most of the included studies were one-time questionnaires, so no ordering can be read. The correlation strength is moderate (r about .28), explaining roughly a few percent to a tenth of the variance. It measured suicidal thoughts and attempts, not deaths themselves, so the benefit is rated small on the "surrogate endpoint only" rule. The authors themselves say the perfectionistic concerns and suicide-attempt results look affected by publication bias — meaning studies with unflattering results went unpublished. After adding back an estimated set of missing studies, the direction of the conclusions held. High standards are not themselves a problem, and you needn't lower them because of this. The difference lies in where the standards come from, and whether falling short makes you feel "I as a person am finished." Like the pessimistic expectations in item 15 (treat thoughts like 'things are certainly going to get worse' as symptoms, not facts), it is something you can treat as a symptom. For suicidal thoughts, call 12356 first and move lethal means out of reach — see Section 1, item 25. For what you can do when someone near you voices such thoughts, see Section 8, item 15. For depression screening in children, see Section 30, item 8.
Sources (1 reference)
Smith MM, Sherry SB, Chen S, Saklofske DH, Mushquash C, Flett GL, Hewitt PL (2018). The perniciousness of perfectionism: A meta-analytic review of the perfectionism-suicide relationship. Journal of Personality, 86(3), 522–542. https://doi.org/10.1111/jopy.12333
23

Don't vent anger by smashing things, hitting a punching bag, or going for a run; slow your body down first

Grade AValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Punching a bag, throwing things, going for a run — the arousal-raising ways of venting don't, on the whole, dispel anger. Slow breathing, mindfulness, and meditation — the ways that calm the body down — measurably lower both anger and the urge to lash out.

Cost
Costs nothing. In the heat of anger, switch for a few minutes to things that slow your heartbeat: breathe slowly, sit down, be still. The hard part is that venting is exactly what you most want to do in that moment.
Benefit
Pooling 154 studies (meta-analysis), 184 samples and 10,189 people in all. Body-calming methods, such as deep breathing, mindfulness, and meditation, reduce anger and aggression. Effect size g = -0.63, 95% CI -0.82 to -0.43 (the credible range). The result held across people of different genders, ethnicities, ages, and cultures. Arousal-raising activities, such as punching a bag, jogging, and cycling, were ineffective overall. Their effect size was g = -0.02, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.09. The authors' conclusion: venting anger, or going for a run, are not workable ways to cool down.
Note
It measured anger and aggression, not energy. Recording the basis as time is the author's classification: one fight avoided is one mess less to clean up. For in-the-moment techniques, see Section 22, item 8 (cyclic sighing), and item 17 of this section (leave the scene first when angry). Running isn't useless. Over the long run, it works on low mood — see Section 22, item 6 (when your mood is bad, go walk or run). It's just the wrong tool for cooling down on the spot. While angry, don't drive, don't send messages, don't make decisions. If someone is hitting you, leave first and call the police. What needs handling then isn't your emotions — see Section 8, item 43 (when you're a victim of domestic violence).
Sources (1 reference)
Kjærvik SL, Bushman BJ (2024). A meta-analytic review of anger management activities that increase or decrease arousal: What fuels or douses rage? Clinical Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2024.102414
24

If something weighs on your mind, you can write your thoughts and feelings down for a few days running — but don't expect it to cure you

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: small

Writing down what's eating you helps on average, but only a little. The pooled findings disagree; two pooled analyses came out with no effect. It costs almost nothing, so it's worth a try. When emotional problems get serious, don't let it substitute for seeing a doctor.

Cost
Costs nothing. The common protocol in the research is 3 to 4 sessions of 15 to 20 minutes. Write about something that troubles you — your deepest thoughts and feelings about it.
Benefit
One analysis pooled 146 randomized studies (meta-analysis), in which participants wrote or spoke about things of personal importance. The average effect was positive and significant, but small: effect size r = .075. Another pooled analysis included only randomized controlled trials — 30 trials pooled — and found no significant effect on either physical health or mental health. Pooling 16 randomized trials of cancer patients and survivors, none of the three outcomes — psychological, physical, or quality of life — was significant. For the psychological outcome, g = 0.04, 95% CI -0.06 to 0.14 (the credible range).
Note
Contested. On the supporting side, the pool of 146 studies found a positive but very small effect. On the opposing side, two pooled analyses restricted to randomized controlled trials found no significant effect. The frequency and duration in the Cost field come from the earliest experimental design, described in the abstract of the Mogk pooled analysis. It costs almost nothing, takes little time, and can be done alone — useful when you don't want to talk to anyone or have no one around to talk to. It doesn't measure energy; recording the basis as time is the author's classification. If writing makes you feel steadily worse, stop and call 12356 instead — see Section 1, item 25 (12356).
Sources (3 references)
Frattaroli J (2006). Experimental disclosure and its moderators: a meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.6.823; Mogk C, Otte S, Reinhold-Hurley B, Kröner-Herwig B (2006). Health effects of expressive writing on stressful or traumatic experiences - a meta-analysis. Psycho-Social Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2736499/; Zachariae R, O'Toole MS (2015). The effect of expressive writing intervention on psychological and physical health outcomes in cancer patients--a systematic review and meta-analysis. Psycho-Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1002/pon.3802

4. Don't waste time

18 items

This section counts time only. It looks at how many hours you can win back per day, week, or year, or how much the share of things finished on time can improve. Time is not converted into lifespan here, nor into money. Where money comes in, the method is given, not a verdict. Most entries in this section rest on a single study or on aggregate statistics from time-use surveys, so the grades are mostly B and C.

1

Rewrite 'I plan to do it' as 'at what time, in what place, and when X happens I do Y'

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Rewrite "I'm going to do this" as "at 8 on Tuesday morning, when I sit down at the desk, I start with the introduction." Across 94 pooled tests, people who phrase their goals this way achieve them at a clearly higher rate — a medium-to-large effect. All you change is the wording of one sentence; it costs nothing and takes no effort.

Cost
Costs nothing. A minute or two per task to write one "if...then..." sentence. For example: "at 8 on Tuesday morning, when I sit down at the desk, I start with the introduction."
Benefit
Pooling 94 independent tests: people who first write their plan as an "if...then..." sentence achieve their goals at a higher rate. In psychology this phrasing is called an implementation intention. Effect size d = 0.65, which counts as medium to large. It helps at three points: getting started, holding out when disturbed, and pulling out of endeavors doomed to fail.
Note
The trick works only on things you genuinely want to do. If you don't actually want the goal, no number of sentences will help. Also, these studies mostly recruited students and mostly looked at health habits; the same effect in work settings is not guaranteed.
Sources (1 reference)
Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1
2

Write down your exit conditions before you start

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Before you start, write one sentence: if by such-and-such date I haven't hit such-and-such marker, I stop. Pooled across multiple studies, this phrasing genuinely helps people pull out of endeavors that won't pan out. What you save is all the time you would otherwise keep pouring in.

Cost
Costs nothing. Five minutes at the start to write "if by such-and-such date I haven't hit such-and-such marker, I stop." The hard part is owning it when the day comes — stopping in front of others stings a little.
Benefit
Pooling multiple implementation-intention studies, the result is: an "if...then..." plan made in advance also helps people pull out of endeavors doomed to fail. The source's own wording is disengagement from failing courses of action. The time saved is the time you would otherwise have kept investing.
Note
Set exit conditions when you have just started and your judgment is still calm. Set later, they get warped by what you've already sunk in. When deciding, count only future costs and future returns — see item 3. Also, "willingness to disengage" is just one sub-finding within a pooled set of studies; no one has separately computed how much time it saves.
Sources (1 reference)
Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1
3

When deciding whether to continue, weigh only future costs and future returns — never what you've already sunk

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Money and time already sunk make people want to keep going. Across 98 pooled datasets, the tendency is reliably there. So when deciding whether to continue, count only what you still must invest and what you can still get back. Whatever is already spent, leave out of it.

Cost
Costs nothing. The hard part is accepting one thing: the time you put in earlier is gone and cannot be recovered.
Benefit
Money, effort, and time already invested make people want to keep going. In psychology this is called the sunk cost effect. Pooling 98 datasets, the analysis confirmed the tendency is reliably present. Avoiding the tendency means you won't keep pouring in time "so it won't go to waste."
Note
The Arkes and Blumer theater experiment worked like this. The Ohio University theater sold season tickets, randomly charging buyers the full $15, $2 off, or $7 off. In the first half of the season, the full-price group attended an average of 4.11 shows, versus 3.32 and 3.29 for the other two groups. In the second half there was no clear difference among the three. Roth and colleagues found the effect fades over time, and older people are affected less.
Sources (2 references)
Arkes, H. R., & Blumer, C. (1985). The psychology of sunk cost. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 35, 124–140. https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(85)90049-4; Roth, S., Robbert, T., & Straus, L. (2015). On the sunk-cost effect in economic decision-making: A meta-analytic review. Business Research, 8(1), 99–138. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40685-014-0014-8
4

Estimate timelines from how long similar past tasks actually took, not from the plan

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Students estimated they would finish their theses in 33.9 days; it actually took 55.5, and only 29.7% finished within their own estimate. Another group was made to first recall how long a similar task took last time, then estimate — and the on-time completion rate rose from 29.3% to 60.0%.

Cost
Costs nothing. A few minutes before estimating to look up how long the last similar task actually took.
Benefit
Students predicted they would finish their theses in 33.9 days; it actually took 55.5 days. Only 29.7% finished within their own estimate. The researchers asked a second group to first connect their past experiences to the task at hand, then estimate. That group's on-time completion rate rose from 29.3% in the control group to 60.0%. The optimism that shrinks timelines no longer appeared in this group.
Note
The Buehler study recruited only Canadian university students — a single study with small samples: 37 people, and about 40 per group. Estimating from the historical data of similar projects is called reference class forecasting; for how it is done in engineering practice, see Flyvbjerg. After pooling multiple studies, Halkjelsvik noted that underestimating is more common than overestimating, but the size of the gap varies a great deal with the task and the research method.
Sources (3 references)
Buehler, R., Griffin, D., & Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366–381. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.67.3.366; Flyvbjerg, B. (2006). From Nobel Prize to project management: Getting risks right. Project Management Journal, 37(3), 5–15. https://doi.org/10.1177/875697280603700302; Halkjelsvik, T., & Jørgensen, M. (2012). From origami to software development: A review of studies on judgment-based predictions of performance time. Psychological Bulletin, 138(2), 238–271. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0025996
5

Send an agenda before meetings; no agenda, no meeting; stand up when you can

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Meetings with an agenda sent beforehand left attendees more likely to find the meeting useful. In an experiment, seated meetings ran 34% longer than standing ones, and the quality of the decisions made was no different.

Cost
Costs nothing. The organizer spends 5 to 10 minutes before the meeting writing an agenda. Standing meetings require participants to go along.
Benefit
Two surveys, with 958 and 292 respondents respectively. The result: meetings with an agenda sent beforehand left attendees more likely to rate the meeting as effective, a relationship that holds up statistically. In another experiment, 55 groups met seated and 56 standing; the seated meetings ran 34% longer. The quality of the decisions made did not differ between the two formats.
Note
The standing-meeting experiment used five-person groups on laboratory tasks; the conclusion cannot be copied straight to long or large meetings. Leach measured how effective attendees felt the meeting was, not how much work it actually produced.
Sources (2 references)
Leach, D. J., Rogelberg, S. G., Warr, P. B., & Burnfield, J. L. (2009). Perceived meeting effectiveness: The role of design characteristics. Journal of Business and Psychology, 24(1), 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10869-009-9092-6; Bluedorn, A. C., Turban, D. B., & Love, M. S. (1999). The effects of stand-up and sit-down meeting formats on meeting outcomes. Journal of Applied Psychology, 84(2). https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.84.2.277
6

Cut the meeting count; anything solvable asynchronously in writing gets no meeting

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

The more meetings in a day, the more exhausted people are and the heavier their own workload feels. Cut one meeting and the time saved is exactly the length of that meeting, not a minute discounted.

Cost
Costs nothing, but needs colleagues and your boss to go along. The hard part: writing a clear paragraph takes more energy than saying a sentence out loud.
Benefit
Two surveys of employees working more than 35 hours a week, with 676 and 304 respondents. How much time meetings take up does not have a fixed effect on work attitudes and well-being; it depends on two things: how well the meetings are run, and how much the job depends on other people. Another study had people keep a diary for a week: the more meetings in a day, the higher the fatigue and the self-perceived workload. The time saved equals the length of the meetings you cut.
Note
Contested: Rogelberg 2006 found the link between meeting load and well-being is not one-directional. In jobs highly dependent on other people, more meetings were not a bad thing. Also, no study has directly compared "switching to written asynchronous communication" with meetings; this entry is the author's own inference.
Sources (2 references)
Rogelberg, S. G., Leach, D. J., Warr, P. B., & Burnfield, J. L. (2006). "Not another meeting!" Are meeting time demands related to employee well-being? Journal of Applied Psychology, 91(1). https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.91.1.83; Luong, A., & Rogelberg, S. G. (2005). Meetings and more meetings: The relationship between meeting load and the daily well-being of employees. Group Dynamics: Theory, Research, and Practice, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1037/1089-2699.9.1.58
7

Split big tasks into subtasks before estimating and starting

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

When people estimate a timeline, they don't automatically break the task into pieces and add them up. List the subtasks first, then estimate, and you'll undershoot by less. Once split, every small step is something you can start immediately — which makes procrastination less likely.

Cost
Costs nothing. The splitting itself takes 5 to 15 minutes.
Benefit
When estimating, people don't on their own split a many-headed task into pieces. Writing the literature review, writing the discussion, tidying the references — these were several tasks all along. Listing subtasks before estimating reduces the tendency to underestimate timelines, a bias called the planning fallacy. Once split, every small step becomes an action you can start right away, and procrastination falls with it. In the research, the factors most predictive of procrastination include how aversive the task feels and how far off the task sits.
Note
How fine to split: aim for "each subtask can be finished in one sitting"; splitting too fine wastes time in itself. Also, the Kruger and Evans finding was verified from the abstract only as to direction; the exact percentages were not checked against the original text.
Sources (2 references)
Kruger, J., & Evans, M. (2004). If you don't want to be late, enumerate: Unpacking reduces the planning fallacy. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 40(5), 586–598. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2003.11.001; Steel, P. (2007). The nature of procrastination: A meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure. Psychological Bulletin, 133(1). https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.133.1.65
8

Give anything without an external deadline a deadline of your own

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

When someone else set a deadline, 80.6% of students finished by it. Finished within the time they themselves predicted: only 38.7%. When things get done is decided almost entirely by the deadline, hardly at all by your own estimate. So for anything with no deadline, set one yourself — and stand by it.

Cost
Costs nothing. The hard part is standing by it once set: if you shrug when the day arrives, you never set one.
Benefit
Students with an external deadline: 80.6% finished before it. Finished within their own predicted time: only 38.7%. Completion time tracked the deadline almost entirely — correlation r = 0.82, and the closer this number is to 1, the tighter the tracking. The link to their own prediction was very weak.
Note
Tell other people your self-set date, and it moves closer to the externally-set kind. To be clear, what the research validated is that deadlines set by others work. Self-imposed ones — timeboxing, the Pomodoro technique — have never been tested directly; this is an extrapolation.
Sources (1 reference)
Buehler, R., Griffin, D., & Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366–381. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.67.3.366
9

See procrastination as dodging discomfort, not as lack of effort

Grade AValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Procrastination has little to do with laziness or character. What best predicts whether someone procrastinates is how unpleasant the task itself feels, whether they believe they can do it, and how easily they get pulled away by whatever is in front of them. So what helps is making the task less unpleasant and shrinking the first step — not scolding yourself and then grinding on.

Cost
Costs nothing. Only the diagnostic direction changes: first ask what makes the task unpleasant, then find a fix.
Benefit
A meta-analysis pooling 691 correlations found several strong, stable correlates of procrastination: how aversive the task is, how far off the deadline is, self-efficacy (believing you can do it), impulsiveness, and conscientiousness with its facets of self-control, distractibility, organization, and achievement motivation. Neuroticism, rebelliousness, and sensation-seeking were only weakly related to procrastination. The author explains the pattern with temporal motivation theory: the present appeal of a task shrinks rapidly as its rewards recede into the distance.
Note
The benefit is rated "medium" because these studies point to direction only; no one has measured how many hours they save. For concrete moves, see item 1 of this section (rewrite as "at what time, in what place, and when X happens I do Y"), item 7 (split big tasks into subtasks), and item 8 (give deadline-less things a date of your own). These are pooled correlational studies; they cannot show who causes whom.
Sources (1 reference)
Steel P (2007). The nature of procrastination: a meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure. Psychological Bulletin, 133(1), 65–94. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.133.1.65
10

Put what you need within reach and move what you want to avoid out of the way; don't rely on resisting in the moment

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

The farther away things are, the less people take them. Moving the same snacks farther away clearly cut how much people ate — a medium-sized effect. Offering fewer options also clearly cut how many people took them. None of this requires resisting in the moment; a few minutes of setup does it.

Cost
Costs nothing, a few minutes at a time. Put the phone in another room; lay the books and the laptop out on the desk.
Benefit
A Cochrane review including 24 randomized trials. Placing food farther away reduced how much was consumed — standardized mean difference -0.60 (95% CI -0.84 to -0.36, the credible range; 12 studies, 1,098 people, low-certainty evidence) — a medium effect. Reducing the options available cut the choice of the target food even more: standardized mean difference -1.13 (95% CI -1.90 to -0.37, 3 studies, 154 people, low-certainty evidence). Regression analysis showed: the farther away and the fewer the options, the stronger the effect.
Note
Why grade B: all 24 studies included in this review concerned food — not one covered alcohol or tobacco; 14 were done in the laboratory, and all came from high-income countries. So carrying "farther away, less use" over to phones and games is an extrapolation with no direct trial. One thing has been directly tested: keeping the phone out of sight — see Section 3, item 1 (turn off non-essential notifications and keep your phone out of sight while working).
Sources (1 reference)
Hollands GJ, Carter P, Anwer S, et al. (2019). Altering the availability or proximity of food, alcohol, and tobacco products to change their selection and consumption. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 9, CD012573. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD012573.pub3
11

To make yourself follow through, put money on the line — but first ask whether you'd actually stake it

Grade AValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

To force yourself to follow through, you can collect a bonus when you succeed, or post a deposit that is refunded only on success, plus a reward. Among people willing to take part in either, the deposit format got 13 percentage points more to succeed. But only 13.7% were willing to post a deposit, versus 90% for the bonus — so deposits work only for people willing to stake the money.

Cost
Deposit-style plans require putting up your own money first, forfeited on failure. The trial used a $150 deposit.
Benefit
A U.S. randomized trial with 2,538 people assigned employees and their friends and family to four incentive programs or usual care. Acceptance rate: reward-based (about $800 on success) 90.0%; deposit-based ($150 upfront, plus a $650 reward) 13.7%. Six-month prolonged smoking abstinence rates: the four incentive programs ranged from 9.4% to 16.0%, usual care 6.0%. Reward-based 15.7%, deposit-based 10.2%. But among only the 13.7% willing to take part in both, the deposit format beat the reward format by 13.2 percentage points on six-month abstinence (95% CI 3.1 to 22.8, the credible range).
Note
This trial tested smoking cessation; carrying it over to theses or fitness is an extrapolation, hence the benefit is rated "medium." When choosing a scheme, first ask whether you would actually use it. A method most people won't accept does them no good, however strong its effect. So pick the one you'll accept — staking a smaller amount still beats staking nothing. For quitting smoking itself, see Section 2, item 3 (smoking-cessation medication).
Sources (1 reference)
Halpern SD, French B, Small DS, et al. (2015). Randomized trial of four financial-incentive programs for smoking cessation. New England Journal of Medicine, 372(22), 2108–2117. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1414293
12

Measure new habits in months, not '21 days'

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: medium

"21 days to form a habit" has no basis. In a 12-week tracking study, the time for an action to become something you do without thinking ranged from 18 days at the fast end to 254 days at the slow. Still finding it hard after two or three weeks is normal. Missing a day along the way doesn't reset progress to zero.

Cost
Costs nothing. What it takes is repeating the same action in the same setting every day, for months.
Benefit
96 volunteers each chose one eating, drinking, or activity behavior and did it every day in a fixed setting (for example, "after breakfast") for 12 weeks, rating their degree of automaticity daily. Data from 82 people were usable for analysis, and the model fitted successfully for 62 of them. The days needed to reach 95% of each person's automaticity plateau ranged from 18 to 254. The study also found that missing one performance opportunity had no material effect on the habit-formation process.
Note
This is the only study, with 96 people doing simple actions (like eating a piece of fruit after a meal). How long complex pursuits take — running three times a week, writing every day — no one has measured. So still finding it effortful after two weeks is not evidence of failure. To make the repetition actually happen, anchor the action to a fixed setting — see item 1 of this section (rewrite as "at what time, in what place, and when X happens I do Y").
Sources (1 reference)
Lally P, van Jaarsveld CHM, Potts HWW, Wardle J (2010). How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world. European Journal of Social Psychology, 40(6), 998–1009. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.674
13

If procrastination already affects your life, use self-help materials backed by randomized trials; a therapist isn't a must

Grade AValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Procrastination painful enough to disrupt your life is treatable. Ten weeks working through cognitive behavioral self-help materials — guided or entirely self-directed — was clearly better than doing nothing. Guided and unguided showed no difference, so working through it on your own works too.

Cost
A self-help book costs a few dollars, and some are free. The investment is about ten weeks: one chapter to read and one exercise to do each week.
Benefit
150 people were randomized to three groups: therapist-guided self-help, unguided self-help, or waitlist control. After ten weeks, the between-group effect sizes on the Pure Procrastination Scale were d = 0.70 for the guided group (95% CI 0.29–1.10, the credible range) and d = 0.50 for the unguided group (0.10–0.90); on the Irrational Procrastination Scale, 0.81 (0.40–1.22) and 0.69 (0.29–1.09) respectively. Rates of clinically meaningful improvement: guided 31.3% to 40.0%, unguided 24.0% to 36.0%. The two groups showed no significant difference on any outcome.
Note
The participants were Swedish adults using Swedish-language materials; no ready-made equivalent exists in Chinese, hence the benefit is rated "medium." The materials' ingredients are the usual ones: behavioral activation, behavioral experiments, stimulus control, and instruction on motivation and work methods. Stimulus control is item 10 of this section (move what you want to avoid out of the way). If the procrastination comes with marked low mood or anxiety, start with Section 3, item 18 (get moving, get sunlight, sleep on time, talk to someone, call 12356).
Sources (1 reference)
Rozental A, Forsell E, Svensson A, Andersson G, Carlbring P (2015). Internet-based cognitive-behavior therapy for procrastination: A randomized controlled trial. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 83(4), 808–824. https://doi.org/10.1037/ccp0000023
14

Let your hourly wage decide which chores to outsource

Grade BValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: a lotTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People in China spend an average of 1 hour 17 minutes a day on housework. Among those who actually did housework that day, it was 1 hour 59 minutes. People who spend money to buy time report higher life satisfaction. And the same sum spent buying time feels better in the moment than spending it on things.

Cost
It takes outsourcing money — how much depends on the service you buy. And it takes a one-time calculation of your own hourly wage.
Benefit
Residents of China spend an average of 1 hour 17 minutes a day on housework; counting only those who did housework, the average was 1 hour 59 minutes. This is the 2024 survey, covering 38,500 households and 107,000 people. Another study sampled 6,271 people across four countries and found higher life satisfaction among those who spend money to buy time. The researchers also ran an experiment in real life: the same sum spent buying time brought greater in-the-moment happiness than buying physical things.
Note
First compute your hourly wage: one month's after-tax income divided by one month's actual working hours. Then check what outsourcing the chore would cost. If the going rate is below your hourly wage, and the time you save will genuinely go to earning or resting, outsource. Everyone's wage and outsourcing prices differ, so run the numbers yourself. Also, Whillans measured how happy people were after spending money to buy time, not how many hours it saved.
Sources (2 references)
Whillans, A. V., Dunn, E. W., Smeets, P., Bekkers, R., & Norton, M. I. (2017). Buying time promotes happiness. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1706541114; National Bureau of Statistics (2024). Bulletin of the Third National Time Use Survey (No. 2). https://www.stats.gov.cn/sj/zxfb/202410/t20241031_1957216.html
15

Set hard caps on short videos and aimless scrolling

Grade CValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: large

People in China spend an average of 5 hours 37 minutes online a day. Among those who actually went online that day, 6 hours 3 minutes. In 2018, by the same measure, it was only 2 hours 42 minutes. This is the largest number in this section. Cut one hour a day, and you gain 365 hours a year.

Cost
Costs nothing. The moves take minutes: turn off push notifications, delete the app, or set a daily time limit on it. The hard part is keeping your hands off — not tapping in.
Benefit
Residents of China spend an average of 5 hours 37 minutes a day online; counting only those who actually went online that day, 6 hours 3 minutes. 92.9% used the internet that day. These are 2024 figures. In 2018, by the same measure, it was only 2 hours 42 minutes. This is the largest number in this section. Cutting one of those hours a day equals 365 extra hours a year. Separately, per the China Internet Network Information Center, as of June 2025 internet users averaged 30.6 hours online per week, 1.9 hours more than six months earlier. There were 1.068 billion short-video users, 95.1% of internet users.
Note
Time online includes work, study, and socializing — not all of it is waste. It is graded C because no study has computed "how much is saved after capping, and where that time went"; only aggregate statistics are in hand. For the "watching how everyone else is doing" category, randomized trials have measured how much time is saved and how much mood changes — see Section 3, item 20.
Sources (3 references)
National Bureau of Statistics (2024). Bulletin of the Third National Time Use Survey (No. 2). https://www.stats.gov.cn/sj/zxfb/202410/t20241031_1957216.html; National Bureau of Statistics (2019). Bulletin of the 2018 National Time Use Survey. https://www.stats.gov.cn/sj/zxfb/202302/t20230203_1900224.html; China Internet Network Information Center (2025). The 56th Statistical Report on China's Internet Development. https://www.cnnic.net.cn/NMediaFile/2025/0730/MAIN175384666…
16

Skip TV and rolling news; take in the information you need at set times

Grade CValue: HighBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Americans over 15 watch 2.6 hours of TV a day — half of all their leisure time. People in China watch an average of 1 hour 40 minutes, and adults aged 75 to 84 watch 3 hours 16 minutes. Switch the information you need to set, batched viewing, and this whole block is what you save.

Cost
Costs nothing. The hard part is breaking the grab-and-turn-on habit, and you may miss some breaking news.
Benefit
Americans over 15 watch 2.6 hours of TV a day. Their total leisure time is 5.2 hours, so TV takes half. These are 2025 figures. Residents of China watch an average of 1 hour 40 minutes of TV a day; those aged 75 to 84, 3 hours 16 minutes. These are 2018 figures.
Note
Only aggregate statistics are in hand. No study has computed where the saved time goes after people cut back on TV and news. "Batched viewing" is the author's own practice.
Sources (2 references)
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2026). American Time Use Survey — 2025 Results. https://www.bls.gov/news.release/atus.nr0.htm; National Bureau of Statistics (2019). Bulletin of the 2018 National Time Use Survey. https://www.stats.gov.cn/sj/zxfb/202302/t20230203_1900224.html
17

Invest time once to learn the keyboard shortcuts and automation of the software you use most

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Most people who have used Word for years still click the toolbar icons. In a controlled comparison, shortcuts beat both menus and icons for speed. Learning this is a one-time cost that pays back on every operation, every day after. The longer you do the same kind of work, the more it returns.

Cost
Costs nothing. It takes a one-time investment of a few to a few dozen hours of learning. The hard part: at first you're slower than with the mouse.
Benefit
The study looked at 251 experienced Word users: most rarely used the faster keyboard shortcuts, still relying mainly on clicking the icon toolbars. A controlled comparison confirmed that of the three methods — menus, icons, shortcuts — shortcuts were fastest. The time saved accumulates a little at a time with each daily operation. People who do the same kind of work long-term gain the most.
Note
Learn only the operations you'll use more than ten times a day; learning everything is another form of waste. To be clear, that efficiency experiment had only 6 participants, and its abstract gives no seconds saved per operation.
Sources (1 reference)
Lane, D. M., Napier, H. A., Peres, S. C., & Sándor, A. (2005). Hidden costs of graphical user interfaces: Failure to make the transition from menus and icon toolbars to keyboard shortcuts. International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327590ijhc1802_1
18

When choosing where to live, put commute time near the top; shorten your one-way commute

Grade BValue: FairBasis: timeMoney: a lotTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

The longer the commute, the worse people say their lives are going. That loss is not made up in wages or housing. Thirty fewer minutes each way saves 5 hours a week.

Cost
The cost is high. You may pay more rent, or move to a smaller place. Moving itself takes time too.
Benefit
Residents of China spend an average of 50 minutes a day on travel; counting only those who traveled that day, 1 hour 2 minutes. These are 2024 figures. German data following the same people over years show that longer commuters have consistently lower subjective well-being (how good they feel their life is going). And the loss is not compensated in income or housing. A review pulling multiple studies together also confirms: the longer the commute, the less satisfied people are with it, regardless of the mode of transport. Thirty fewer minutes each way saves about 5 hours a week.
Note
Contested: after pooling multiple studies, Chatterjee and colleagues note that no stable relationship is visible between commute length and overall life satisfaction. People, they argue, can generally trade away the losses of a long commute through better jobs or housing. Also note: travel-time statistics cover all trips, not just commuting. And if you can shift your hours to off-peak, the same route runs shorter too.
Sources (3 references)
Stutzer, A., & Frey, B. S. (2008). Stress that doesn't pay: The commuting paradox. Scandinavian Journal of Economics, 110(2), 339–366. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9442.2008.00542.x; Chatterjee, K., et al. (2020). Commuting and wellbeing: A critical overview of the literature with implications for policy and future research. Transport Reviews, 40(1), 5–34. https://doi.org/10.1080/01441647.2019.1649317; National Bureau of Statistics (2024). Bulletin of the Third National Time Use Survey (No. 2). https://www.stats.gov.cn/sj/zxfb/202410/t20241031_1957216.html

5. Don't waste money

45 items

This section only counts money: how much you can save, how much the yearly benefit differs, and how much a sum of money pays back on long-run average. None of these is converted into lifespan or time. The entries that involve investing only explain how to do the math, using only verified historical data; none of it constitutes investment advice. The entries in this section are grouped by theme below; the numbers in parentheses are entry numbers. Everyday spending: turn off auto-renewals (item 1), recheck your phone and broadband plans (item 4), decline extended warranties on electronics (item 11), prefer drugs chosen in centralized procurement (item 12), drink boiled tap water (item 14), pay per session at the gym (item 21), set a cooling-off rule on big purchases (item 23), don't stockpile for crossed-out prices (item 24). Impulse spending and spending on kids: don't buy lottery tickets (item 5), don't tip streamers (item 8), a child's game top-ups and tips can be reclaimed (item 9), anyone who has your child read out a verification code is a scammer (item 10), count beads and designer toys as money spent (item 33), accept only CMA reports for jewelry and jade (item 34), blind boxes, card pulls, and other randomized sales (item 35). Online shopping and consumer rights: sign a written contract for prepayments (item 22), rely on platform rules when shopping online (item 29), when something bought in a livestream goes wrong (item 30), claim ten times the price for unsafe food (item 31), check spot checks and certification before buying big-ticket items (item 32), buy packaged food if you want to read the ingredients (item 36). Tax, housing provident fund, and medical insurance: individual income tax reconciliation (item 2), the provident fund can also be withdrawn for rent and renovations (item 3), medical insurance family account sharing (item 13), personal pension accounts (item 20). Saving, borrowing, and investing: walk away on sight of high returns (item 6), convert borrowing costs to annualized rates first (item 7), don't trade stocks frequently (item 15), don't invest borrowed money (item 16), broad-based index funds as your core holdings (item 17), pick funds with lower fees (item 18), don't stake your money in one place (item 19), save an emergency fund first (item 27), compare before prepaying your mortgage (item 28), sell losing stocks by the rules (item 37), buy US stocks via QDII or Stock Connect (item 38), don't buy virtual currencies (item 45). Insurance: prefer pure-protection insurance (item 25), buy enough third-party liability coverage (item 26), insure only losses you couldn't withstand (item 39), buy term life insurance on the earner first (item 40), cancel within the free-look period (item 41), tell deposits from insurance at the bank counter (item 42), never use surrender agents (item 43), name a specific person as beneficiary (item 44).

1

Turn off every auto-renewal; renew manually when it expires

Grade CValue: HighBasis: MoneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

What you save is the subscriptions you stopped using long ago but that still charge you every month. Going through the auto-debit lists in Alipay, WeChat, Apple, and Android takes under 20 minutes. Under the rules, a merchant must clearly remind you before charging, and must give you an entry point where you can cancel at any time — one that is easy to find and easy to tap.

Cost
Nothing. Go through the "auto-debit" lists in Alipay, WeChat, Apple, and Android, 10 to 20 minutes each time. Afterward, every renewal takes one extra tap of your own.
Benefit
The savings equal the total of the subscriptions you no longer use but are still being charged for. It differs from person to person; there is no single number. Regulators require merchants to clearly remind you before renewal and to give you a "simple, cancel-anytime" option, with no extra charge for canceling (China, in force since 2021)
Note
For services you genuinely use often, annual payment is usually cheaper than monthly, and keeping auto-renewal can actually be the better deal. What you want to turn off is the ones you forgot about long ago that are still charging you.
Sources (1 reference)
State Administration for Market Regulation (2021, amended 2025). Measures for the Supervision and Administration of Online Transactions (SAMR Order No. 37, Article 18). https://www.samr.gov.cn/zw/zfxxgk/fdzdgknr/fgs/art/2025/art…
2

Do your annual individual income tax reconciliation each March–June, claiming every special additional deduction you qualify for

Grade AValue: HighBasis: MoneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

People who usually get money back: those who worked only a few months of the year, changed jobs mid-year, or never claimed deductions like children's education, mortgage interest, rent, or supporting elderly parents. It takes about ten-odd minutes on your phone. If your annual comprehensive income is under 120,000 yuan, or the tax you owe is under 400 yuan, you can skip it.

Cost
Nothing. Do it in the "Individual Income Tax" app; ten-odd minutes and it's done.
Benefit
It combines wages and salaries, remuneration for labor services, author's remuneration, and royalties into one final settlement. Overpayments are refunded; shortfalls must be paid. You can skip it in two cases: your annual comprehensive income does not exceed 120,000 yuan, or the tax you need to make up does not exceed 400 yuan. These two provisions were set by a 2023 announcement of the State Taxation Administration and apply through December 31, 2027. Conversely, these people usually get money back: those with income in only a few months of the year, those who changed jobs mid-year, and those who never claimed deductions such as children's education, mortgage interest, rent, or supporting the elderly
Note
If you owe tax, you must file too — not filing is against the law. There are seven special additional deductions: children's education, continuing education, treatment of serious illness, housing loan interest, housing rent, supporting the elderly, and care of infants under 3. Of these, you may claim the housing loan interest or the rent, but not both.
Sources (2 references)
State Taxation Administration (2025). Measures for the Administration of Annual Reconciliation and Settlement of Individual Income Tax on Comprehensive Income (Article 6), with its official interpretation. https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/202502/content_7006465.htm; Ministry of Finance and State Taxation Administration (2023). Announcement on Extending Certain Policies for Individual Income Tax Comprehensive Income Reconciliation. https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202308/content_6900594…
3

The housing provident fund isn't only for buying a home: you can withdraw it for rent, renovations, and property fees; from September 20, 2026, follow the new regulations

Grade AValue: HighBasis: MoneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

The housing provident fund isn't money you can touch only when buying a home. The new regulations list nine situations in which you can withdraw; renting, renovating the home you live in, and paying property fees all count. Once you file an application, the provident fund center must tell you within 3 days whether the withdrawal is approved.

Cost
Nothing. Just go file the withdrawal procedure once.
Benefit
The amended regulations list nine situations in which withdrawal is allowed. They include paying rent, renovating the home you live in, and paying property fees on the home you live in. The provident fund management center must decide, within 3 days counting from the day it accepts your application, whether to approve or deny the withdrawal
Note
The money in the account is your own salary contributions plus the matching part your employer puts in. Left untouched, it earns interest at a very low rate. The regulations also state that if an employee dies or is declared dead, heirs and legatees may withdraw the account balance. Which documents you need and how the process works are set locally by each city's provident fund management center. Check your local center's service guide before making the trip.
Sources (1 reference)
State Council (2026). Decision of the State Council on Amending the Regulations on the Administration of Housing Provident Funds (State Council Decree No. 844, adopted at the 93rd executive meeting of the State Council on July 31, 2026, "effective from September 20, 2026"): amended Article 24, "An employee may withdraw the balance stored in the employee's housing provident fund account in any of the following circumstances: (1) paying rent; (2) purchasing, building, rebuilding, or carrying out major repairs on the employee's own home; (3) repaying the principal and interest of a home purchase loan; (4) renovating the employee's own home; (5) paying property fees on the employee's own home; (6) leaving the workforce or retiring; (7) complete loss of the capacity to work and termination of the labor relationship with the employer; (8) settling abroad; (9) other housing consumption circumstances approved by the State Council." Article 25: "The housing provident fund management center shall decide whether to approve or deny the withdrawal within 3 days of accepting the application." Article 18 on the contribution ratio: "in no case lower than 5% of the employee's average monthly wage of the preceding year." https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2026/issue_12946/202608/content_…
4

Recheck your phone and broadband plans every year; downgrade what you don't use, and complain if the carrier won't let you switch

Grade AValue: FairBasis: MoneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

The old plan you're on is often tens of yuan a month pricier than what they sell to new customers now. Tens a month becomes several hundred yuan a year thrown away. Under the rules, a carrier without legitimate reason cannot refuse to let you switch, cannot drag its feet, and cannot set up special pricing just for people who switch. If it stonewalls you, complain.

Cost
Nothing. One look at your bill, ten-odd minutes. The hard part is standing up to customer service when they resist downgrading you.
Benefit
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology's rules state that carriers must not "refuse, block, or delay providing number portability services to users without legitimate reason," must not "use technical means such as interception or restriction to affect the service quality of number-portability users," and must not "create special tariff and marketing schemes for number-portability users." Old plans are often tens of yuan a month more expensive than the ones on sale now. Never switching means throwing away several hundred yuan a year
Note
First check in the carrier's app how much data and call time you actually used over the past six months, then pick a plan based on that usage. If customer service says "downgrades must be done at a service hall" or "you can't change during the contract period," demand written grounds. If they can't produce them, call 12300 and complain
Sources (1 reference)
Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (2019). Provisions on the Administration of Number Portability Services (MIIT Xin Guan [2019] No. 242). http://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2019-11/13/content_5451…
5

Don't buy lottery tickets

Grade AValue: HighBasis: MoneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

By rule, lotto and numbers games must pay out at least 50% of sales as prizes; for the Double Color Ball it's 51%. That means for every 1 yuan you put in, you get back 0.51 yuan on average over the long run — a steady 49% loss. In 2024, lottery sales nationwide totaled 623.486 billion yuan, of which 161.031 billion yuan went straight into the public welfare fund, a part that never appears in prizes.

Cost
Nothing. Not buying is saving.
Benefit
The Ministry of Finance sets minimum prize shares of sales: 50% for lotto and numbers games, 65% for instant tickets, 73% for sports betting games. The Double Color Ball reserves 51% of sales for prizes — of every 100 yuan sold, only 51 yuan goes back out as prizes. For you, that's 0.51 yuan back per 1 yuan spent on average over the long run, a 49% loss. In 2024 national lottery sales were 623.486 billion yuan, of which 161.031 billion yuan went into the public welfare fund and never returned to the people who bought the tickets (China, 2024)
Note
Over the long run you are guaranteed to lose; that's built into the system and has nothing to do with luck. Buying anyway is fine, but treat it as a 2-yuan entertainment expense per ticket, never as investing.
Sources (3 references)
Ministry of Finance (2015). Notice on Regulating and Strengthening the Management of Lottery Fund Composition Ratios (Cai Zong [2015] No. 94). http://m.mof.gov.cn/czxw/201511/t20151113_1560814.htm; Ministry of Finance (2025). MOF Announcement 2025 No. 8 (lottery public welfare funds raised and allocated in 2024). http://zhs.mof.gov.cn/zhengcefabu/202508/t20250828_3970977.htm; China Welfare Lottery Double Color Ball Game Rules (Article 14). https://mzj.nc.gov.cn/ncsmzj/flcp/202111/5dccc1a5da89434e94…
6

Walk away on sight of 'high returns,' 'principal guaranteed,' or 'sure to win'

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: MoneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

The regulators' own rule of thumb: returns above 6% warrant a question mark, above 8% is dangerous, and above 10% you should prepare to lose your entire principal. Legitimate wealth management is no longer allowed to promise principal protection or guaranteed returns. Money lost in illegal fundraising is, by rule, yours to bear — when it blows up, nobody bails you out.

Cost
Nothing. Just pause when you hear these words.
Benefit
The then-chairman of the banking and insurance regulator said this at the 2018 Lujiazui Forum. Verbatim: "Returns above 6% should raise a question mark, above 8% is very dangerous, and above 10% you should be prepared to lose all your principal." The new asset-management rules require financial institutions to "not promise principal protection or guaranteed returns," and stipulate that "when redemption difficulties arise, financial institutions must not advance funds to redeem in any form." So legitimate wealth management no longer has any principal guarantee. Losses from illegal fundraising are "borne by the fundraising participants themselves"; when it collapses, nobody repays you (China, 2018 and 2021)
Note
The 6%, 8%, and 10% lines are rules of thumb drawn by a regulator, not legal text. The remark was made in the context of cracking down on illegal fundraising, aimed at wealth-management products and investment companies promising high returns. Not investment advice.
Sources (4 references)
Guo Shuqing (2018). Preventing and Defusing Financial Risks, Striving to Cross the Major Threshold (speech at the 10th Lujiazui Forum, published on the National Financial Regulatory Administration website): "In cracking down on illegal fundraising, we strive through many channels to make the public understand that high returns mean high risk — returns above 6% should raise a question mark, above 8% is very dangerous, and above 10% you should be prepared to lose all your principal." https://www.nfra.gov.cn/cn/view/pages/ItemDetail.html?docId…; Republished by the Tianjin Local Financial Administration. https://jrgz.tj.gov.cn/ztlm/ztzl/jrjfwphjr/202006/t20200625…; People's Bank of China et al. (2018). Guiding Opinions on Regulating the Asset Management Business of Financial Institutions (Yin Fa [2018] No. 106, Articles 2 and 6). https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2018/content_5323101.htm; State Council (2021). Regulations on the Prevention of and Disposal of Illegal Fundraising (State Council Decree No. 737, Article 25). https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2021/content_5588815.htm
7

Don't pay only the credit card minimum, and don't take installments or consumer loans for spending; if borrowing is unavoidable, convert the interest to an annualized rate before comparing

Grade CValue: FairBasis: MoneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Paying only the minimum is a loan with interest accruing daily, about 18% a year, and it voids your interest-free grace period. Installments advertised as "0.6% monthly fee" run about 13.8% a year, not 7.2% — because the principal shrinks every month while the fee keeps being charged on the original amount. To compare loans, look only at the annualized rate, not daily interest or monthly fee rates.

Cost
Nothing. Keep enough cash to pay the statement in full before the due date. The hard part is resisting the urge to spread big purchases into installments. When borrowing is unavoidable, spend a few minutes asking each lender's annualized rate.
Benefit
Before 2020, credit card overdraft rates had a band: a cap of "a daily rate of 0.05% (five ten-thousandths)" and a floor of 0.7 times that cap. 0.05% a day comes to 18.25% a year, simple interest: at 18.25% a year, interest does not compound back into the principal. From 2021, pricing became a matter for card issuers and cardholders to negotiate. Once you pay only the minimum, interest accrues daily on the full unpaid principal, and the interest-free period is voided at the same time. The central bank already requires issuers to display the annualized rate (the rate converted over a whole year) prominently, and they "must not display only the daily rate or daily repayment amount." From 2021, every lender, in advertising and in contracts, must prominently state the annualized rate. Daily and monthly rates may appear alongside, but must not be more prominent than the annualized rate. The annualized rate must include the interest plus all fees directly tied to the loan. For installment repayment, your actual cost is computed on the principal remaining after each payment. The People's Bank of China gave a worked example: borrow 100,000 yuan, repay over 12 months, paying 0.5% of the original principal each month as an installment fee, plus a 1,000-yuan service fee at the time of borrowing. On simple interest, the annualized rate is about 12.80%. On compound interest (the internal rate of return method), about 13.58%. Judging by the fee rate alone, you'd think it costs only 0.5% × 12 + 1% = 7% a year. The real figure is nearly double, because the principal falls every month while the fee keeps being charged on the full 100,000 yuan. By the same method, a credit card installment of 12 periods at 0.6% per period with no other fees is nominally 7.2% a year. On compound interest, the annualized rate is about 13.8%, roughly 1.9 times the nominal number. Across 6 to 36 installments, the multiple stays between 1.8 and 2. If your lender is a private individual or an ordinary company, that is private lending. If the agreed rate exceeds 4 times the one-year LPR at the time of signing, courts do not uphold the excess. The one-year LPR on August 20, 2026 was 3.0%, so 4 times is 12%. Interest deducted from the loan upfront does not count: courts compute the principal as the money actually received. This cap does not bind licensed financial institutions such as banks and consumer finance companies, nor seven types of local financial organizations including microloan companies, pawnshops, and financial leasing firms. So you cannot apply the 12% line to their loans — go by the annualized rate written in the contract (China, 2020 and 2021)
Note
The 18.25% figure comes from multiplying 0.05% × 365 directly, without compounding. Compounded monthly it would run even higher. Some banks offer discounts — go by the annualized rate stated on your own bill. When you truly can't cover your cash flow, first look for legitimate channels with lower rates; don't ride the minimum payment and let interest snowball. When comparing two loans, ask for the annualized rate computed on compound interest. If the lender quotes simple interest, regulations require it to be labeled "simple"; simple interest will run somewhat lower than compound.
