For blind boxes, card pulls, and other randomized sales, count the money as never coming back

Grade AValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: small

Sellers must put the draw rules, draw probabilities, and limited-edition quantities in a conspicuous place; they may not manipulate the results backstage or set up empty boxes. Guarantee mechanisms and caps on spending and draw counts are only "encouraged" in the document. For blind boxes bought online, where the seller disclosed clearly and you confirmed, the 7-day no-reason return no longer applies once unsealed.

Cost
Costs nothing. Just fix the budget before you buy. The hard part is stopping even when you didn't pull the one you wanted.
Benefit
The basis is the Guidelines for Regulating Blind Box Business Practices (Trial). Article 9 lists the key information that must be prominently publicized so consumers know it before buying: product name, category, styles, draw rules, product distribution, limited-edition release quantities, draw probabilities, and product value ranges. The same article sets three prohibitions. One: no covertly inducing purchases by manipulating draw results backstage or arbitrarily adjusting draw probabilities. Two: no refusing or deliberately delaying the delivery of blind boxes through cash conversion, buybacks, or trade-ins. Three: no empty boxes. Article 11 merely "encourages" operators to establish guarantee mechanisms — guiding rational consumption by setting caps on draw time, draw amount, and draw count. Article 17 covers blind box goods sold over the internet: where the operator has fully informed and warned, and the consumer confirmed at the single purchase, the 7-day no-reason return may not apply after unsealing. Operators may not replace the consumer's confirmation step with a default-checked box. Article 21: no gambling, directly or in disguise, in the name of blind boxes. Article 23: no selling blind boxes to minors under 8; selling to minors aged 8 and up requires lawful confirmation that the relevant guardian's consent has been obtained (nationwide)
Note
This document is a guideline governing how operators should behave; it is not itself a basis for penalties. When something actually goes wrong, it's handled under the Product Quality Law, the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, and the Law on the Protection of Consumer Rights and Interests. Three situations give you concrete grounds to complain: probabilities not publicized, publicized probabilities not matching reality, and receiving an empty box. Before complaining, screen-record the rules on the page and the unboxing process. The no-return-after-unsealing rule has preconditions: the seller fully informed you, you confirmed at the single purchase, and no default checkbox stood in for your confirmation. Sales to minors have their own rules: sellers may not sell to children under 8, and for ages 8 and up they must first confirm guardian consent has been obtained. For refunds when a child tops up games or tips on a phone, see item 9 in this section (children topping up and tipping on phones). For the 24-hour cooling-off rule on big non-essential purchases, see item 23 (a 24-hour cooling-off period for big non-essential purchases). For the cycle of "bored as soon as you own it, so you buy again," see section 6, item 23 (don't expect purchases to improve your mood).
Sources (1 reference)
State Administration for Market Regulation (2023). Guidelines for Regulating Blind Box Business Practices (Trial) (Guo Shi Jian Ji Fa [2023] No. 39, Articles 9, 11, 17, 21, and 23). https://www.samr.gov.cn/zw/zfxxgk/fdzdgknr/zfjcs/art/2023/a…

If you care what's in your food, buy packaged: bulk counters aren't legally required to list ingredients

Grade AValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: small

The law requires an ingredients list only on prepackaged food, not on bulk. A bulk counter needs only the name, production date, shelf life, and who produced it. So "no additives listed" doesn't mean "none added" — only that the law doesn't require listing them. If you care, buy the prepackaged version, where the ingredients and additive names are printed on the label.

Cost
Costs nothing. The same product prepackaged usually costs a bit more than bulk. A glance at the ingredients list takes seconds.
Benefit
Food Safety Law Article 67 requires prepackaged food to carry a label stating nine items. Item 2 is the "ingredients or ingredient list"; item 7 is "the generic names in the national standard of the food additives used." Article 68 demands far less of bulk food, in the original text: a food seller offering bulk food must mark on the container or outer packaging "the food's name, production date or production batch number, shelf life, and the name, address, and contact details of the producer or seller." That article mentions no ingredients list and no additives. Frozen aquatic products show the gap most starkly. GB 2760—2024 permits phosphoric acid and phosphates as water-retention agents — commonly called water-retaining agents — in frozen aquatic products, at a maximum of 5.0 g/kg measured as phosphate. Use within that limit is legal. The problems are overdosing and ice glazing to add weight. After the 2025 CCTV March 15 Gala exposed shrimp "illegally overdosing on water-retention agents (compound phosphates) and ice glazing for weight," market regulators required producers to "clearly label on the product the water-retention agent (e.g., phosphate) ingredient, the net content (excluding the glaze weight), and the ingredient list" (nationwide; Food Safety Law third 2025 amendment, effective December 1, 2025)
Note
"Not labeled" doesn't mean "not added" — only that the law doesn't require labeling. To know the ingredients, buy the prepackaged version. For frozen shrimp, frozen fish fillets and the like, the net content on the prepackaged label is the weight after the glaze is deducted — price per that figure to get the true price. Bulk is priced by the posted price and can shrink a lot once thawed. Water-retention agents within the limit are legal and not a safety issue — don't treat them as poison. Overdosing and ice glazing are money problems: you paid seafood prices for water. Conversely, the four things a bulk counter must display may go undisplayed: name, production date, shelf life, and the producer's or seller's name, address, and phone. Missing any one violates Article 68. You can not buy it, or call 12315. For how to label when you open your own shop selling bagged food, see section 12, item 9 (prepackaged food labels). This item's beneficiaries are you and your family — the top two tiers.

Sell losing stocks by the rules you set in advance too; don't count on averaging down to come back

Grade AValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

People's instinct is to sell winners and cling to losers. In seven years of records from ten thousand US accounts, a stock that had risen was over 50% more likely to be sold than one that had fallen. The same people were also more eager to add to losing positions. Yet the losing stocks they kept went on to underperform the sold ones by 3.4 percentage points on average over the following year.

Cost
Costs nothing. The hard part is admitting this position has already lost, then selling it.
Benefit
The study examined all trading records of 10,000 accounts at a US discount broker from 1987 to 1993. The proportion of gains realized (PGR) was 0.148; the proportion of losses realized (PLR) was 0.098 — a gap of 0.050 with a t-statistic above 35. Counted by day, a stock that had risen was over 50% more likely to be sold than one that had fallen. The same accounts were also more active about adding to losers: the proportion of losing stocks bought again was 0.135, versus 0.094 for winners, a t-statistic of 19. The study also tested the idea that "what you keep will come back." The result ran the other way: the winners that were sold beat the losers left unsold by an average of 3.4 percentage points of excess return over the following year. Excess return means the portion above the market index. The authors also worked out an example from the averages: selling 1,000 dollars' worth of a losing stock rather than a winning one yields about 4.4% more return over the following year. That 4.4% includes the tax saved by realizing the loss early. The tax offset is computed under the US tax system (US, 1987 to 1993)
Note
This item governs "sell or not"; item 15 (don't trade stocks frequently) governs "stop meddling so much" — the two don't conflict. Setting rules in advance and following them actually means fewer moves. Averaging down is arithmetically correct: buy a bit more and your average cost is lower. The mistake is treating it as a comeback plan; its real effect is to raise how much of your money is staked on this one stock — see item 19 (don't stake your money on one stock). The tax part is computed under the US system and doesn't transfer to China; the rest still stands. These are US account data from the 1980s to 1990s, with trading costs and taxes different from A-shares. Not investment advice.
Sources (1 reference)
Odean T (1998). Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses? The Journal of Finance 53(5):1775-1798. https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00072

To buy US stocks and other overseas assets, use QDII funds or Stock Connect; don't open accounts with offshore brokers, and don't spend your annual forex quota on it

Grade AValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Offshore brokers such as Tiger, Futu, and Longbridge may no longer open accounts for mainland residents from May 2026. Existing accounts can only sell and move the money out during the two years — no more buying. The annual forex quota can't be spent on overseas stocks either: violators can't use the quota that year or for the 2 years after. To buy overseas assets, go through QDII funds or Stock Connect.

Cost
Costs nothing. You can buy QDII funds in your own bank's or broker's app in minutes. The trade-off is fewer products to choose from than offshore brokers offer.
Benefit
On May 22, 2026, eight departments — the CSRC, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the Ministry of Public Security, the People's Bank of China, the State Administration for Market Regulation, the National Financial Regulatory Administration, the Cyberspace Administration of China, and the State Administration of Foreign Exchange — issued the Implementation Plan for the Comprehensive Rectification of Illegal Cross-Border Securities, Futures, and Fund Business Operations. The overall requirement is "after two years of concentrated rectification, completely eliminate the illegal cross-border operations of overseas securities, futures, and fund institutions." Overseas institutions may not conduct marketing or solicitation within the mainland, nor "provide trading services such as account opening, trade order processing, and fund transfers." For those who already hold accounts, the plan states: "overseas institutions are prohibited from illegally providing buy trades, funds transfers-in, and similar services within the mainland to existing investors; only one-way sell trades and transfers-out of funds are allowed." After the two-year period, "mainland websites, trading software, and accompanying servers are to be shut down completely." The same day, the CSRC announced that it intends to confiscate all illegal gains of the relevant domestic and offshore entities of Tiger, Futu, and Longbridge and punish them severely according to law. The accompanying Q&A makes clear the aim to "guide mainland investors to invest overseas through lawful channels such as Stock Connect, Qualified Domestic Institutional Investors (QDII), and the Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect." On the forex side, the SAFE's Individual Foreign Exchange Purchase Application Form states that individual forex purchases "may not be used for capital-account items not yet opened, such as buying property abroad, securities investment, life insurance, or investment-linked return-and-dividend insurance." Violators go on a "watch list" and "forfeit the individual facilitation quota for the current year and the following two consecutive years," and also face administrative penalties and referral for anti-money-laundering investigation, with the information entered into their personal credit records (nationwide, from May 2026)
Note
These documents target the offshore institutions; they prescribe no penalties on the investor personally. Already holding an offshore brokerage account? Just sell and move the money back within the two years. Each of the three lawful channels has its own opening conditions — ask your own bank or broker first. US stocks having risen a lot in the past doesn't mean they will in the future. Buying QDII follows the same methods as item 17 (broad-based index funds) and item 19 (don't stake your money on one stock, one platform, or one property): pick broad-based indexes, and don't bet on a single market. Overseas cash withdrawals have a separate quota — see section 21, item 6 (overseas withdrawals). Not investment advice.

Insure only the losses you couldn't withstand; cover the ones you could with your emergency fund

Grade CValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Not all of your premium comes back in claims — part goes to the insurer's costs and profit. So what's worth insuring is the loss that rarely happens and would break the household if it did: major illness, injuring someone with your car, the household earner dying. Small losses your savings can absorb go to the emergency fund.

Cost
Costs nothing. What there is to do: list the big losses your household could face and see which ones savings couldn't withstand. Half an hour, once.
Benefit
Only part of the premiums an insurer collects goes out as claims; the rest pays for sales and operating costs, plus company profit. Regulators require companies selling individual short-term health insurance to publish a "comprehensive claims ratio" on their websites every six months — roughly the claims paid as a share of premiums; if you want to know how much a company actually pays out, check its website. So for any given loss, insurance is on average a small money-loser over the long run. What you get in exchange is turning one household-crushing expense into a small annual payment. The smaller the loss and the more easily you could pay it, the worse the trade. By this standard, the ones this book has already covered are worth buying. One-year medical insurance: section 7, item 20 (one-year medical insurance). Car owners: item 26 in this section (third-party liability insurance). Those going abroad: section 21, item 4 (medical care abroad). Anyone with family living on your income: item 40 in this section (term life insurance) (nationwide, from 2021)
Note
Grade C because no official numbers exist for computing which insurance pays off; what's given here is the trade-off method. Screen-break insurance, flight-delay insurance and the like involve losses of a few hundred yuan you could pay yourself — by this standard you can skip them. Critical illness insurance replaces the income lost while illness keeps you out of work; if your savings could carry one or two years out of work, you can consider skipping it. Basic medical insurance is social insurance — it doesn't follow this trade-off, keep paying it; see section 7, item 9 (resident medical insurance). For what backstops small losses, see item 27 in this section (emergency fund). This item's beneficiaries are you and your family.

Notice on Issues Concerning Regulating Short-Term Health Insurance Business (CBIRC Ban Fa [2021] No. 7, comprehensive claims ratio disclosed on company websites every six months). https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2021-01/12/content_557…
40

If anyone lives on your income, buy term life insurance on the earner first — not on the kids

Grade CValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: a lotTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Term life insurance covers a fixed number of years; if the person dies within them, the family receives a payout. It exists for the family members living on your income — say the mortgage isn't paid off or the children are still young. If nobody depends on you, you don't need it. Children don't earn, and for death insurance bought on children, the law caps what can be paid out.

Cost
A few hundred to a few thousand yuan a year, depending on age, coverage amount, and term (author's rough estimate; no official figures). Before applying, disclose health conditions truthfully — half an hour, once.
Benefit
The regulator defines life insurance as personal insurance with a person's life as the subject matter, divided into term life, whole life, endowment, and other types. Term life pays the benefit on the insured's death, over a fixed number of years. Whole life covers for life. Accident insurance pays only for death or disability caused by accidents — not for death from illness — so it can't replace life insurance. A contract with death as the payment condition requires the insured's own consent to and acknowledgment of the sum insured, or the contract is void. Parents insuring their minor children's deaths are exempt from that restriction, but the total death benefit paid on a child may not exceed the cap set by the regulator. Life insurance coverage is typically in the hundreds of thousands of yuan, hence Benefit: large. There is no official basis for how much coverage to buy. The author's method: the outstanding mortgage, plus the children's expenses up to adulthood, plus a few years of household spending (nationwide, 2015 amendment)
Note
Grade C because the official material provides only definitions and caps; "insure the adults first" is inferred from "whose income, if cut off, would break the household." If a child dies, the household doesn't lose an income. If the earner dies, the mortgage and the children's expenses remain. With limited money, buy term life and one-year medical insurance on the earner first, then the children's medical insurance. For honest disclosure and guaranteed renewal, see section 7, item 20 (one-year medical insurance). This item's beneficiaries fall in tier 2: your spouse and children.
Sources (2 references)
China Insurance Regulatory Commission (2011). Administrative Measures for the Insurance Clauses and Premium Rates of Life Insurance Companies (CIRC Order No. 3 of 2011, Articles 8 and 12). http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2012/content_2163594.htm; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2015 amendment). Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China, Articles 33 and 34. https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=2c909fdd678bf17901678bf7c4…
41

Regret a personal insurance policy of over a year? Cancel within the free-look period and you get nearly all the premium back

Grade AValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Personal insurance over one year always has a free-look period. Bought at a bank, it's 15 days from receiving the policy, and surrender during it costs at most a 10 yuan handling fee. Surrender after the free-look period and you get back only the refundable part of the policy — usually less than you paid. When the insurer's follow-up call asks whether everything is clear to you, don't say it is if it isn't.

Cost
Costs nothing. Call the insurer's service line or go to the counter — ten-odd minutes. The hard part is, after signing, calmly reading the contract through within the 15 days.
Benefit
For personal insurance with an insurance period over one year, the regulator requires the policy to state from which day the free-look period runs and how many days it lasts, and also to state what rights the policyholder has during it. Long-term health insurance must have a free-look period of no less than 15 days. Insurance with a period over one year bought at a bank must stipulate a 15-day free-look period in the contract, counted in calendar days from the day you receive the policy and sign for it in writing. The cover of such policies must print this notice: "You have the right to a full surrender refund (minus a handling fee of no more than 10 yuan) within 15 days of receiving the insurance contract. Surrendering after 15 days involves losses." After the free-look period, you can still cancel the contract at any time; the insurer must return the policy's cash value (the refundable part of the policy) as the contract provides, within 30 days. Financial regulators' risk warnings note that for long-term personal insurance surrendered after the free-look period, the cash value is often below the total premiums paid. For new personal insurance policies over one year, the insurer must call you back during the free-look period, confirming that you know the loss from surrendering and your free-look rights (nationwide, from 2010 and 2019)
Note
The free-look period is a rule for personal insurance over one year. One-year medical and accident insurance isn't required by the regulations — whether there is one depends on the terms. Policies not bought at a bank: go by the number of days written in the contract, and flip to the "free-look period" clause as soon as you get the policy. Savings-type and dividend-type policies take the most money, so the free-look period is most worth using there — see item 25 in this section (pure-protection). Benefit is set at "medium" because what you save is the gap between premiums paid and cash value, commonly several hundred to several thousand yuan, with no official statistics. This item's beneficiary is you.
Sources (6 references)
General Office of the China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission (2019). Administrative Measures for Health Insurance (CBIRC Order No. 3 of 2019, Article 15). https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2019-12/04/content_545…; China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission (2022). Basic Service Provisions for Life Insurance Business (CIRC Order No. 4 of 2010, Article 15). http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2010/content_1702219.htm; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2015 amendment). Risk Alert on Guarding Against Illegal Surrender Agencies. https://www.nfra.gov.cn/branch/ningxia/view/pages/common/It…
42

Before signing at a bank counter, check whether what you're holding is a deposit or insurance

Grade BValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Banks can sell insurance as agents, but may not pass it off as deposits. An insurance contract's cover must print "Insurance Contract" and the insurer's name in large type, and may not contain the words "deposit" or "savings." If the cover says an insurance company, the money isn't a deposit — surrendering after the free-look period loses you money. Buyers over 65 at a bank can in principle only buy products with guaranteed returns.

Cost
Costs nothing. Two extra minutes reading the contract cover before signing.
Benefit
The rules state that banks may not sell insurance bundled together with savings deposits, funds, or bank wealth-management products; may not draw simple analogies between insurance returns and deposits; and may not present non-guaranteed returns as guaranteed. Insurance documents and promotional materials may not use the bank's name or logo, nor phrases like "deposit," "savings," or "launched jointly with the bank." The insurance policy cover must print "Insurance Contract" in type no smaller than size 72 and the insurer's name no smaller than size 2. Three groups of people can in principle only be sold products with determinable policy benefits: policyholders over 65; policyholders over 60 buying periodic-premium products; and those whose stated annual income is below the local per-capita disposable income of residents. Policies for these three groups must also be passed to the insurer for manual underwriting — no automatic issuance at the branch. Insurance company personnel may not sell insurance inside bank branches. Insurance of over one year sold by banks carries a 15-day free-look period; surrendering after it means losses (nationwide, from October 2019)
Note
Grade B because the rules are crystal clear, but there are no official figures on "how much misled people lost." Elderly family members are most likely to run into this while depositing money at a bank — check the cover for them when you accompany them. Already signed? Surrender within the 15 days per item 41 in this section (free-look period). For how to complain if you feel misled, see item 43 in this section (surrender agents). This item's beneficiaries are you and the elders in your family.
Sources (1 reference)
General Office of the China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission (2019). Administrative Measures for Commercial Banks Acting as Agents for Insurance Business (CBIRC Ban Fa [2019] No. 179, Articles 30, 31, 32, 36, 42, and 49). https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2019-12/03/content_545…
43

To surrender a policy, deal with the insurer yourself — never 'surrender agents'; if you feel misled, complain via 12378

Grade BValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Those online shouting "full refund of premiums, no win no fee" are mostly illegal surrender agents. They take 30–50% of whatever you get back, plus your ID, bank card, and verification codes. Surrender the policy and your coverage is gone too. Feeling misled? Start with the insurer's customer service; if that stalls, call 12378 — free the whole way.

Cost
Costs nothing. Calling the insurer or going to the counter yourself takes an extra trip or two versus handing it to a middleman.
Benefit
In February 2026, the National Financial Regulatory Administration, the Cyberspace Administration of China, the Ministry of Public Security, the People's Bank of China, and the CSRC jointly issued a risk alert. It says claims like "full surrender refund" are false information inconsistent with the Insurance Law and other laws and regulations. "Rights-protection agents" charge steep service fees, and if you try to quit midway you may even be sued for "breach of contract." They also collect your SIM card, bank cards, policies, home address, your child's school, and similar information; once this is resold, you can run into telecom fraud and card theft. The Ningxia Financial Regulatory Bureau's June 2026 alert goes into more detail: these intermediaries stipulate an agency fee of 30% to 50% of the surrendered amount after success, with heavy breach penalties for quitting midway. They coach people to invent grounds like sales misleading or forged signatures for their complaints; those who follow along may violate the Public Security Administration Punishments Law, and in serious cases may be implicated in complicity in false accusation or extortion. Insurance liability terminates the moment you surrender. Buying similar insurance later may cost more or be refused, because you're older or health problems have shown up. Genuinely misled? Complain and negotiate with the insurer's official customer service first; if that goes nowhere, call 12378, the banking-and-insurance consumer complaint and rights-protection hotline — free throughout. If you merely can't pay premiums for the moment, first ask the insurer about reduced paid-up insurance, policy loans, and similar services. Reduced paid-up means you stop paying premiums from then on, with the sum insured scaled down proportionally (nationwide, 2026)
Note
The Hunan Financial Regulatory Bureau reported a case in 2025. A woman was talked into agent-handled surrender by a "friend," paid a "consultation fee," and still got only the cash value. Three months after surrender she was diagnosed with breast cancer — the critical illness policy was already gone. Whether to surrender is your own calculation: if you still need the coverage and can't pay, ask about reduced paid-up first. Surrendering yourself within the free-look period: see item 41 in this section (free-look period). This item's beneficiary is you.
Sources (3 references)

Risk Alert on Guarding Against the Traps of Illegal "Rights-Protection Agent" Short Videos and Livestreams (reposted on the CAC official website). https://www.cac.gov.cn/2026-02/06/c_1772110875635198.htm; Ningxia Financial Regulatory Bureau (2026-06-16). Risk Alert on Guarding Against Illegal Surrender Agencies. https://www.nfra.gov.cn/branch/ningxia/view/pages/common/It…; Hunan Financial Regulatory Bureau (2025-07-23). Risk Alert on Guarding Against the Illegal "Surrender Agent" Black and Gray Industries. https://www.nfra.gov.cn/branch/hunan/view/pages/common/Item…
44

Name a specific person as the beneficiary, and remember to claim the money after a death: within 5 years for life insurance, 2 years for other policies

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

No beneficiary named, or the beneficiary died first? Then the insurance money counts as an estate and goes first to pay the debts the deceased owed. A beneficiary written as "wife so-and-so" who later divorced counts as unspecified when the death occurs. Your family must know this policy exists: for life insurance, claims must be made within 5 years of learning of the event; for other insurance, 2.

Cost
Costs nothing. Fill it in once when you buy the policy; changing the beneficiary later requires written notice to the insurer.
Benefit
The Insurance Law provides that the beneficiary is designated by the insured or the policyholder; designated by the policyholder, it requires the insured's consent. In three situations the insurance money counts as the insured's estate and is distributed under inheritance rules. One: no beneficiary was designated, or the designation is unclear. Two: the beneficiary died before the insured and there is no other beneficiary. Three: the beneficiary forfeited or waived the benefit right by law and there is no other beneficiary. Where beneficiary and insured die in the same event and the order cannot be established, the beneficiary is presumed to have died first. Money counted as estate first settles the deceased's taxes and debts; only the remainder is divided. The Supreme People's Court's interpretation spells out: a beneficiary written as "name plus identity relationship" counts as no designated beneficiary if the relationship has changed by the time of the event. A beneficiary change not notified to the insurer has no effect against the insurer. The limitation period for claiming the money is 5 years for life insurance and 2 years for other insurance, both counted from the day you knew or should have known of the event. Life insurance coverage is typically in the hundreds of thousands of yuan, hence Benefit: large (nationwide, 2015 amendment and from 2021)
Note
Once the limitation period passes, the insurer can refuse to pay and a lawsuit rarely gets it back. So at minimum, your family should know which insurers you've bought from. After a divorce, a remarriage, or the birth of a child, go back and update the beneficiary. For claiming money place by place after someone dies, see section 25, item 9 (claiming them one by one). For why "dying to settle debts" doesn't work, see section 29, item 13 (repaying debts). This item's beneficiaries fall in tier 2: your spouse and children.
Sources (3 references)
Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2015 amendment). Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China, Articles 26, 39, 41, and 42. https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=2c909fdd678bf17901678bf7c4…; Supreme People's Court (2020 amendment). Interpretation (III) on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 9, Paragraph 2, Item 3, and Article 10. https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=ff808181799df4000179ac03d7…; National People's Congress (2020). Civil Code of the People's Republic of China, Article 1159. https://flk.npc.gov.cn/detail?id=ff808081729d1efe01729d50b5…
45

Don't put money into virtual currencies like Bitcoin or Tether, and don't go along when someone pulls you in: the transactions aren't legally protected — if you lose, you can't get it back even in court

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Mainland China doesn't recognize virtual currency as money; an individual's coin purchase can be ruled void, and the loss is yours to bear. One person bought Tether from an individual, paying about 448,000 yuan; when the platform later blocked withdrawals, the court dismissed his suit for the money. Theft is a different matter — the thief is still convicted of theft.

Cost
Costs nothing. Don't buy coins, and don't join crypto groups promising "signals" or "sure profits." The cost is missing out when coin prices rise.
Benefit
In February 2026, the People's Bank of China and seven other departments issued Notice Yin Fa [2026] No. 42. It states that virtual currencies like Bitcoin, Ether, and Tether "are not legal tender and should not and cannot circulate in the market as currency." Exchanging RMB for coins, coin for coin, and token-issuance fundraising are all illegal financial activities, "strictly prohibited without exception." Overseas institutions may not provide such services to mainland residents either. On the individual-investment side, the notice's own words: "Any unit or individual investing in virtual currencies, real-world asset tokens, and related financial products, where this violates public order and good morals, the relevant civil juristic acts are void, and the losses arising therefrom are borne by themselves." The 2021 Notice Yin Fa [2021] No. 237 is repealed at the same time; this sentence is retained in the new notice. Court case: from February 2018 to July 2019, a person surnamed Tang bought Tether from two people claiming to be platform merchants, paying about 448,000 yuan (precisely 448,000 yuan). The platform later blocked withdrawals and logins. He sued to recover the money. The court held that exchanging RMB for virtual currency made the investment act void, with the losses borne by himself, and dismissed the claim; the second instance upheld it (Yixing, Jiangsu, released March 2025). Theft is another matter: someone's virtual coins worth over 4 million yuan were stolen from their account by a "hacker," and one of the thieves was sentenced to 7 years for theft and fined 20,000 yuan (Zhengzhou, Henan)
Note
"Losses borne by yourself" governs money disputes between you and the coin seller or the signal group — the court won't recover your investment for you, so don't count on suing afterward. Being robbed or scammed out of coins is a criminal case; report it as usual. Holders of coins also need to guard against QR-code theft: in Lianshui, Jiangsu, someone met another party and scanned a code, and about 57,000 Tether were swept out of the wallet — worth about 394,000 yuan (precisely 393,665.461434 yuan); a People's Court Daily article argued the case should be handled as theft. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation warned in 2022 about a similar trick: your wallet pops up a list of permissions; once you click agree, the other party can transfer out your coins without limit. Its defense advice: don't connect your wallet to sites you're unsure about, and periodically use a third-party authorization checker to see which sites your wallet has granted coin-transfer permissions to. Using your own bank card to receive money, buy coins, or move coins for others is a different matter and can lead to criminal conviction — see section 9, item 5 (a "side gig" that has you receive money with your own card). For how to recognize "investments" promising high returns, see item 6 (walk away on sight of 'high returns,' 'principal guaranteed,' or 'sure to win'). For lawful channels to buy overseas assets, see item 38 (buying US stocks through QDII funds or Stock Connect). Not investment advice.
Sources (5 references)

The Criminal-Law Characterization of Illegally Stealing Virtual Currency. http://www.sdcourt.gov.cn/jningzcfy/386500/386502/31441533/… (reposted on the Zoucheng People's Court website); Federal Bureau of Investigation (2022).
