6. The Don't List

29 items

This section collects the things that "look cheap and effective." Open the original studies, and their benefit is close to zero, exactly zero, or in some cases negative. The ranking weighs two things: how much money people spend on them, and how solid the evidence is. The higher up an item sits, the more urgent it is to quit first. The entries in this section are grouped by theme below, with item numbers in parentheses. Supplements: multivitamins (item 1), ordinary fish oil (item 2), vitamin D (item 3), antioxidant supplements to prevent cancer (item 4), chondroitin for knee arthritis (item 5), vitamin C for colds (item 6), big money on health supplements (item 10), long-term probiotics (item 11), detox and colon-cleanse products (item 13). Checkups and incidental findings: whole-body PET-CT and tumor-marker packages (item 7), generic checkup packages (item 18), high uric acid with no flares — skip the drugs (item 19), painless gallstones — skip the surgery (item 20), don't cut calcium to prevent kidney stones (item 21). Wellness claims: fitness bands for weight loss (item 8), organic food (item 9), cold showers to boost immunity (item 12), forcing yourself to drink water (item 14), blue-light glasses (item 16), blood donation as health care (item 17), breakfast or intermittent fasting to control weight (item 26), proper lifting posture to prevent back pain (item 29). Buying luck and mood: paying for fortune-telling and horoscopes (item 15), crystals, beads, and Pixiu charms (item 22), shopping to improve your mood (item 23), spending more to move up a notch (item 24). Willpower and sex: willpower like a muscle (item 25), masturbation ruining health (item 27), sexual orientation conversion (item 28).

1

Don't take multivitamins for longevity or heart-disease prevention

Grade AValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Some 14,000 male doctors took a daily multivitamin for eleven years. Just as many of them had a major cardiovascular event or died as the men who took none. Pool the 9 trials covering more than 50,000 people and there's no visible effect on death either. Skipping the purchase saves 200 to 700 yuan a year. People diagnosed with an actual nutrient deficiency, and pregnant women taking folic acid, are not covered by this item.

Cost
About 0.5 to 2 yuan a day, 200 to 700 yuan a year. Taking it costs no time — it's one pill. Take it long enough and it breeds dependence: skip a day and it feels like something's missing from your routine.
Benefit
The PHS II trial enrolled 14,641 male doctors and followed them for 11.2 years (a median — half were followed longer, half shorter). Major cardiovascular events hit takers and non-takers at the same rate. Major cardiovascular events HR 1.01 (HR is the hazard ratio; 1 means the two sides are identical). 95% CI 0.91–1.10 is the uncertainty range around that number. Death was the same: all-cause mortality HR 0.94 (0.88–1.02). USPSTF, the US agency that grades preventive measures, pooled 9 randomized controlled trials covering 51,550 people in 2022 and found no association between multivitamins and total mortality. It assigned grade I, meaning the evidence is insufficient — it can't be called either way. It looks like a good deal because "one pill covers every nutrient" sounds right, and a day's worth costs mere cents.
Note
Controversy: the same male doctors were also followed for cancer. Takers developed cancer about 8% less often (0.86–0.998, P=0.04 — just barely over the "probably not chance" line). Deaths from cancer were about 12% lower (0.77–1.01). That range crosses 1, so it may be pure chance. The benefit is tiny, and it has only ever been seen in male doctors. People diagnosed with an actual deficiency, pregnant women (folic acid), and people whose everyday diet is genuinely lopsided don't count here — supplement as your doctor says.
Sources (3 references)
Sesso HD et al. (2012). Multivitamins in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.14805; US Preventive Services Task Force (2022). Vitamin, Mineral, and Multivitamin Supplementation to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2022.8970; Gaziano JM et al. (2012). Multivitamins in the Prevention of Cancer in Men. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.14641 (the cancer result in the Note)
2

Don't take ordinary fish oil to prevent cardiovascular disease

Grade AValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Two large trials enrolled 26,000 people and 15,000 people with diabetes respectively. Those who took 1 gram of fish oil a day had just as many major cardiovascular events and just as many deaths as those who took none. "Eating fish is good for you" is not the same as "fish oil capsules are good for you." Skipping the purchase saves 400 to 1,000 yuan a year.

Cost
About 1 to 3 yuan a day, 400 to 1,000 yuan a year. Taking it costs no time.
Benefit
The VITAL trial enrolled 25,871 people, who took 1 gram of fish oil daily and were followed for 5.3 years (median). Neither major cardiovascular events nor deaths showed any difference between the two groups. Major cardiovascular events HR 0.92 (HR is the hazard ratio; 1 means the two sides are identical). 95% CI 0.80–1.06 is the uncertainty range around that number; it crosses 1, meaning no visible difference. All-cause mortality HR 1.02 (0.90–1.15). The ASCEND trial enrolled 15,480 people with diabetes, also 1 gram a day, followed for 7.4 years on average, and likewise found no difference. Serious vascular events RR 0.97 (0.87–1.08). All-cause mortality RR 0.95 (0.86–1.05). It looks like a good deal because many people take "eating fish is good for you" straight over to "fish oil capsules are good for you."
Note
Controversy: one trial did work. The REDUCE-IT trial enrolled 8,179 people who already had cardiovascular disease or diabetes, were all on statins, and still had elevated triglycerides (135–499 mg/dL). They took 4 g of a prescription pure-EPA drug daily; the event rate was 17.2% versus 22.0%. Risk about a quarter lower (HR 0.75, 0.68–0.83). But that is a high-dose prescription drug for high-risk patients, not the fish oil supplements ordinary people buy. This item also doesn't cover eating fish itself.
Sources (3 references)
Manson JE et al. (2019). Marine n-3 Fatty Acids and Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1811403; ASCEND Study Collaborative Group (2018). Effects of n-3 Fatty Acid Supplements in Diabetes Mellitus. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1804989; Bhatt DL et al. (2019). Cardiovascular Risk Reduction with Icosapent Ethyl for Hypertriglyceridemia. New England Journal of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1812792 (the high-purity prescription fish oil trial in the Note)
3

Don't give vitamin D to people who aren't deficient, for longevity's sake

Grade AValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

People who weren't deficient in vitamin D to begin with supplemented for 5 years, and their rates of cancer, cardiovascular disease, and death all matched those who took nothing. People who test as genuinely deficient, have osteoporosis, or get little sun long-term are not covered by this item — they supplement as their doctor says.

Cost
About 0.2 to 0.5 yuan a day, 100 to 200 yuan a year. The money isn't much; the real price is believing you've already done your prevention.
Benefit
The VITAL trial enrolled 25,871 people, who took 2,000 IU daily and were followed for 5.3 years (median). Cancer, cardiovascular trouble, and death all showed no difference. Invasive cancers HR 0.96 (HR is the hazard ratio; 1 means the two sides are identical; 95% CI 0.88–1.06 is the uncertainty range). Major cardiovascular events HR 0.97 (0.85–1.12). All-cause mortality HR 0.99 (0.87–1.12). The D-Health trial enrolled 21,315 Australians over 60, who took 60,000 IU a month for 5 years. Again no difference: all-cause mortality HR 1.04 (0.93–1.18). The death rate was 5.3% versus 5.1%. It looks like a good deal because some studies only track and record without intervening at all, find that people with low vitamin D levels die more often, and that gets misread as "topping it up works."
Note
Controversy: neither trial specifically recruited people who were truly deficient in vitamin D, so the conclusions apply only to "people who weren't deficient to begin with." Those who test as genuinely deficient, have osteoporosis, get little sun long-term, or are infants and young children should still supplement as their doctor says. Only total death, cancer, and cardiovascular outcomes were examined here; nothing else.
Sources (2 references)
Manson JE et al. (2019). Vitamin D Supplements and Prevention of Cancer and Cardiovascular Disease. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1809944; Neale RE et al. (2022). The D-Health Trial: a randomised controlled trial of the effect of vitamin D on mortality. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-8587(21)00345-4
4

Don't take antioxidant supplements (beta-carotene, vitamin E, vitamin A) to prevent cancer

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

This one isn't just useless. Pool 78 trials covering nearly 300,000 people and those taking antioxidant supplements die at a slightly higher rate. In the two big trials run specifically on smokers, beta-carotene raised lung cancer rates by 18% to 28% and deaths by 8% to 17%. Smokers and people exposed to asbestos should especially stay away.

Cost
About 0.5 to 2 yuan a day. For a smoker, the real cost is lung cancer risk creeping up along with it.
Benefit
Cochrane pooled 78 randomized controlled trials and 296,707 people. Total mortality among antioxidant takers RR 1.02 (RR is the risk ratio; 1 means the two sides are identical; 95% CI 0.98–1.05 is the uncertainty range). Looking only at the more rigorous trials that are harder to skew: RR 1.04 (1.01–1.07), slightly higher. Beta-carotene alone RR 1.05 (1.01–1.09); vitamin E alone RR 1.03 (1.00–1.05). The ATBC trial enrolled 29,133 male smokers, who took 20 mg a day: lung cancer up 18% (3%–36%), total mortality up 8% (1%–16%). The CARET trial enrolled 18,314 smokers or people exposed to asbestos. Their lung cancer risk was about 28% higher (RR 1.28, 1.04–1.57) and their death risk about 17% higher (all-cause mortality RR 1.17, 1.03–1.33). It looks like a good deal because the chain of reasoning — "antioxidants fight aging, and fighting aging prevents cancer" — sounds like common sense at every step.
Note
USPSTF, the official US agency that grades preventive measures, gave beta-carotene and vitamin E a D grade in 2022, meaning: recommend against their use. Smokers and asbestos-exposed people have already been harmed by this. Antioxidants that occur naturally in fruits and vegetables don't count — keep eating those.
Sources (3 references)
Bjelakovic G et al. (2012). Antioxidant supplements for prevention of mortality in healthy participants and patients with various diseases. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD007176.pub2; The Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta Carotene Cancer Prevention Study Group (1994). The effect of vitamin E and beta carotene on the incidence of lung cancer and other cancers in male smokers. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199404143301501; Omenn GS et al. (1996). Effects of a combination of beta carotene and vitamin A on lung cancer and cardiovascular disease. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199605023341802
5

Don't expect glucosamine/chondroitin to fix knee arthritis

Grade AValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Of people with knee osteoarthritis who took a placebo for 24 weeks, six in ten said their pain eased. Those taking glucosamine or chondroitin scored only four or five percentage points above that — small enough to be coincidence. Spend 700 to 1,800 yuan a year and what you're buying is mostly that 60% placebo effect.

Cost
About 2 to 5 yuan a day, 700 to 1,800 yuan a year.
Benefit
The GAIT trial enrolled 1,583 patients with knee osteoarthritis for 24 weeks. Even among those taking the placebo, 60.1% said their pain was relieved. Glucosamine scored only 3.9 percentage points above that (P=0.30). Chondroitin, 5.3 points (P=0.17). The two together, 6.5 points (P=0.09). All of these gaps are too small to rule out chance. The real drug used as an active control in the same trial, celecoxib, came in 10.0 percentage points higher (P=0.008). It looks like a good deal because "supplying the raw material for cartilage" sounds exactly on target, and six in ten people say even the placebo works.
Note
Controversy: within the same trial, among those who were in severe pain from the start, the combination worked for 79.2% versus 54.3% of the control group (P=0.002). But the authors say this was dredged out of the data after the fact — a lead, not a conclusion. What actually has evidence for knee arthritis is weight loss and muscle training; see Section 2.
Sources (1 reference)
Clegg DO et al. (2006). Glucosamine, chondroitin sulfate, and the two in combination for painful knee osteoarthritis. NEJM. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa052771
6

Don't rely on vitamin C to prevent colds

Grade AValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: small

Taking vitamin C every day will basically not reduce how many colds you catch, and starting it only after a cold has begun works sporadically at best. Daily use shortens a cold by about 8% — half a day less misery — and whether that's worth 300 to 500 yuan a year, do your own math. Marathon runners and soldiers marching in cold climates are the exception: with supplementation, about half as many of them catch colds.

Cost
An effervescent tablet runs about 1 to 2 yuan — 300 to 700 yuan a year.
Benefit
Cochrane pooled 29 controlled trials and 11,306 people. For ordinary people taking vitamin C daily, the number of colds barely falls. Incidence of colds RR 0.97 (RR is the risk ratio; 1 means the two sides are identical). 95% CI 0.94–1.00 is the uncertainty range. In the trials where people started taking it after catching a cold, the original text reports "no consistent effect": some trials found benefit, others didn't. In the same review, long-term daily use shortened the miserable part of a cold by about 8% (adults, 95% CI 3%–12%), and by 14% in children (7%–21%). Marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers marching in cold climates are the exception: across 5 trials and 598 people, about half as many caught colds. Incidence RR 0.48 (95% CI 0.35–0.64). It looks like a good deal because it's cheap, it's sweet-and-sour and pleasant to drink, and the belief that "vitamin C prevents colds" has been circulating for half a century.
Note
Controversy: in the same review, daily use does shorten the misery of a cold — by about 8% in adults (3%–12%) and 14% in children (7%–21%). That works out to roughly half a day less illness per cold. Marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers marching in cold climates are the exception: across 5 trials and 598 people, about half as many caught colds (RR 0.48, 0.35–0.64). The vast majority of people belong to neither of those groups.
Sources (1 reference)
Hemilä H, Chalker E (2013). Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4
7

Don't get a 'whole-body PET-CT' or 'tumor marker package' with no symptoms

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

When people without symptoms get scanned, the most common finding is a false alarm. More than eight in ten of those getting whole-body CTs have at least one "abnormality" flagged, and nearly four in ten get called back for follow-up — yet most findings are benign. Women screened with ovarian-cancer markers were slightly more likely to die of ovarian cancer, and some went through surgery for nothing because of a false alarm.

Cost
A whole-body PET-CT runs about 7,000 to 10,000 yuan per scan, plus a dose of ionizing radiation. Tumor-marker packages cost a few hundred yuan. The real cost comes later: one flagged "abnormality" that turns out to be a false alarm (that's called a false positive), and then all the follow-up scans, tissue biopsies, and operations behind it — the money and the suffering pile up in that stretch.
Benefit
USPSTF, the US agency that grades preventive measures, gave screening for ovarian cancer with CA-125 and ultrasound in symptom-free women a D grade, meaning: recommended against. The basis is the PLCO trial. Ovarian cancer deaths: 0.34% in the screened group versus 0.29% under usual care. RR 1.18 (95% CI 0.82–1.71). Screening brought no benefit. The share who went under the knife for nothing because of a false positive ranged from 0.2% to 3.25% across trials, and up to 15% of those people suffered serious surgical complications. Another study gave whole-body CT screening to 1,192 symptom-free people: 86% had at least one "abnormality" flagged, and 37% were advised to get further testing. The original text says "most findings were described as benign." It looks like a good deal because "one scan checks the whole body, catch it early, treat it early" is deeply intuitive.
Note
The tumor-marker part is backed by randomized controlled trials. The whole-body CT and PET-CT part rests only on "following what happened to people who got scanned" — no comparison groups — so the evidence is a tier weaker, roughly Grade B. The screenings that do have evidence — colorectal, cervical, and breast cancer, and low-dose chest CT for high-risk people — are a different matter; see Section 1. Someone who already has symptoms, or a patient with a confirmed cancer getting a PET-CT, is being treated, not screened — that's a different story.
Sources (3 references)
US Preventive Services Task Force (2018). Screening for Ovarian Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement. JAMA (the same recommendation also has an official USPSTF page). https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2017.21926, https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recomm…; Furtado CD et al. (2005). Whole-body CT screening: spectrum of findings and recommendations in 1192 patients. Radiology. https://doi.org/10.1148/radiol.2372041741
8

Don't expect activity tracking on your band or watch to make you lose weight

Grade BValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Overweight people on identical diet and exercise plans: those wearing fitness bands lost 3.5 kg over two years, while those without them lost 5.9 kg. For weight loss, buying a device doesn't help — the exercise itself is what works.

Cost
Devices run 200 to 2,000 yuan. Plus the daily distraction of checking all those numbers.
Benefit
The IDEA trial enrolled 471 overweight or obese adults and followed them for 24 months. Everyone got the same diet and exercise plan; the only difference was whether they wore a wearable device. The wearers lost 3.5 kg (95% CI 2.6–4.5, the uncertainty range). The non-wearers lost 5.9 kg (5.0–6.8) — more. The gap between the groups was 2.4 kg (1.0–3.7, P=0.002). It looks like a good deal because "you can't manage what you don't measure" sounds sensible, and the device only needs buying once.
Note
This rests on a single trial, using early-2010s devices worn on the upper arm, so it can't be stretched to "all wearables are useless." Exercise itself does work; see Section 2. The conclusion is one sentence: if you want to lose weight, a device is not money you need to spend.
Sources (1 reference)
Jakicic JM et al. (2016). Effect of Wearable Technology Combined With a Lifestyle Intervention on Long-term Weight Loss: The IDEA Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2016.12858
9

Don't pay a premium for organic food in the name of 'being healthier'

Grade BValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

There is no strong evidence that organic food is more nutritious. Only 3 studies have actually looked at people's health after eating it, and none found a difference. Organic produce is indeed 30 percentage points less likely to test positive for pesticide residues, but a detection is not a violation. Eating more fruits and vegetables works in itself; whether they're organic makes no difference to that.

Cost
Usually 1 to 3 times the price of the conventional equivalent.
Benefit
One systematic review pooled 17 studies in humans and 223 studies measuring food composition, and concluded there is "a lack of strong evidence that organic foods are significantly more nutritious than conventional foods." Only 3 of the studies looked at people's health after eating (they looked at allergies and symptomatic infections), and found no difference between the two sides. Organic produce was 30 percentage points less likely to test positive for pesticide residues, but a detection is not a violation. It looks like a good deal because "no pesticides means safer, and safer means healthier" sounds like common sense at every step.
Note
Studies that directly track people's health after eating organic food are very scarce. So the conclusion is "no evidence it's better," not "proven to have no benefit." Environmental impact, animal welfare, and taste are outside this item. Eating more fruits and vegetables works in itself; organic or not makes no difference to that.
Sources (1 reference)
Smith-Spangler C et al. (2012). Are organic foods safer or healthier than conventional alternatives?: a systematic review. Ann Intern Med. https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-157-5-201209040-00007
10

Don't spend big on health supplements, herbal pastes, and tonics to 'condition your body'

Grade CValue: ExceptionalBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

The common ingredients — multivitamins, fish oil, vitamin D — have been checked one by one in the first six items of this section, and none showed any effect. The line on the packaging, "health food is not medicine and cannot replace drugs in treating disease," is printed there because the regulator requires it. Most of this money is spent on gifts for parents and carried to their door — the sentiment is fine; only the product is wrong.

Cost
Anywhere from a few hundred yuan to over 10,000. Once it's boxed as a gift set, the price often multiplies several times over.
Benefit
What you get back is the money you don't spend. The reasoning is in the first 6 items of this section: the most common ingredients in health supplements — multivitamins, fish oil, vitamin D, antioxidants, glucosamine, vitamin C — showed none of their promised benefits in randomized controlled trials, with the numbers in each item's Benefit row. Regulation only sets what a product may claim; it is not evidence that the product works. SAMR rules require the front of every health food package to devote no less than 20% of its area to one sentence: "Health food is not medicine and cannot replace drugs in treating disease." The same rules confine health food's purpose to "supplementing dietary nutrients, maintaining or improving the body's health, or reducing disease risk factors." It looks like a good deal because "it doesn't cure, it only conditions" is a claim that can't be wrong no matter how you put it, and no one can prove it false. And when the money is spent as a gift, it runs on human sentiment, not evidence.
Note
The conclusion is "no evidence of support," not "proven useless," which is why this gets only Grade C. For products with clearly listed ingredients, check the research on each one against the earlier items. People diagnosed with an actual deficiency or under medical treatment should follow their doctor. What's being rejected is the product, not the sentiment. If an elderly parent already bought it and is already taking it — as long as it hasn't replaced their medication and hasn't caused problems — there's no need to go pick a fight; arranging their vaccines and screenings matters more. The same money spent on the following instead is backed by the book item by item. Take them for their annual flu shot: Section 1, item 20. The shingles vaccine after 50: Section 1, item 21. The pneumococcal vaccine after 65: Section 1, item 22. Buy a blood pressure monitor and see that they take their antihypertensives as prescribed until blood pressure reaches target: Section 1, item 7. Retrofit the bathroom and stairs at home and practice balance and leg strength with them: Section 1, item 13. Age-appropriate cancer screening — go along for one: Section 1, items 17 to 19. If they are already bedridden long-term, pressure-sore protection and long-term care insurance are in Section 17, items 7 and 8. If you must bring something to the door, bring fruit, rice and flour, or food they love — more solid than an herbal paste. What really needs blocking is two kinds: pay-upfront "investment for retirement" schemes, and anything that would push out their medication; see Section 17, item 5.
Sources (1 reference)
State Administration for Market Regulation (2019). SAMR holds a special press conference on the 'Guidelines for Warning Wording on Health Food Labels' and the 'Measures for the Administration of the Health Food Raw Materials Catalogue and the Health Function Catalogue.' https://www.samr.gov.cn/tssps/sjdt/tpxw/art/2023/art_4b658b…
11

Don't take probiotics long-term without a gut problem

Grade BValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: small

Across 45 trials in healthy adults, probiotics do not durably change the gut microbiome — stop taking them and it reverts — and blood lipids don't improve either. Specific situations like diarrhea brought on by antibiotics have their own separate evidence and are not covered by this item.

Cost
About 2 to 5 yuan a day, 700 to 1,800 yuan a year.
Benefit
One review pooled 45 trials in healthy adults and concluded it "failed to support that probiotics can induce lasting changes in the gut microbiota, or improve blood lipids in healthy adults." The gut bacteria do shift, but only temporarily; stop and they go back. It looks like a good deal because "gut health" is a claim broad enough to never be wrong, and the price per bottle is low.
Note
The same review does note some small improvements in healthy people — more formed, better-textured stools, and more Lactobacillus in women's vaginas. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, and one particular strain used on one particular condition, each have their own separate evidence and are different stories. This item targets only healthy people taking probiotics daily as a supplement.
Sources (1 reference)
Khalesi S et al. (2019). A review of probiotic supplementation in healthy adults: helpful or hype? Eur J Clin Nutr. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41430-018-0135-9
12

Don't force yourself into cold showers to 'boost immunity'

Grade BValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: small

In a trial of 3,018 people, those taking cold showers called in sick 29% fewer times, but their total sick days matched everyone else's — so it isn't fewer illnesses. Pooling 11 trials in 2025, markers of inflammation briefly rose after a cold shower, while immune markers were unchanged. Take cold showers if you like them; just don't book it as an investment in your health.

Cost
Costs nothing. It does cost 30 to 90 seconds of discomfort a day, and willpower to keep it up through winter. People with cardiovascular disease should be careful — cold shock is a risk for them.
Benefit
A randomized controlled trial in the Netherlands enrolled 3,018 people who finished their hot shower with 30, 60, or 90 seconds of cold. They called in sick 29% fewer times (IRR 0.71, a ratio of counts). But the paper states plainly that "there was no significant between-group difference in sick days": total days ill were the same on both sides. Quality of life, work productivity, and anxiety showed no meaningful differences either. A 2025 systematic review pooled 11 randomized trials and 3,177 people. Immediately after cold-water immersion and 1 hour later, markers of inflammation were elevated. Immune markers were unchanged. Stress fell only at the 12-hour time point. The authors themselves say the evidence is "limited by few RCTs and small samples" — meaning there are too few randomized trials of this kind, and each has few participants. It looks like a good deal because it's free, and the intuition that "suffering must be doing something" runs deep.
Note
Controversy: the 29% drop in the number of sick calls is real and doesn't look like chance. But total days of illness didn't fall, so it looks more like "going to work sick anyway" than actually being sick less. Athletes using cold water to recover after training is a different question, not covered here. Cold showers themselves do no harm to healthy people — just don't count them as a health investment.
Sources (2 references)
Buijze GA et al. (2016). The Effect of Cold Showering on Health and Work: A Randomized Controlled Trial. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0161749; Cain T et al. (2025). Effects of cold-water immersion on health and wellbeing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0317615
13

Don't buy detox, colon-cleanse, enzyme, or alkaline-water products

Grade CValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

The detox industry is big business, yet the clinical evidence behind it is vanishingly thin, and no one has rigorously tested the detox diets actually sold on the market. When researchers went looking for a link between dietary acid-alkaline balance, alkaline water, and cancer, only 1 qualifying study turned up — and it found no association either.

Cost
A few hundred to a few thousand yuan. The kind that "detoxes" by starving you can also drive your blood sugar low and leave you short on nutrients.
Benefit
That review's conclusion: "despite the burgeoning detox industry, there is very little clinical evidence to support these diets," and "no randomized controlled trials of commercial detox diets exist." Another systematic review looked specifically at whether dietary acid-alkaline balance, alkaline water, and cancer are connected: it screened 8,278 papers and only 1 qualified for inclusion, and it too found no association. The authors wrote that "promotion of alkaline diets and alkaline water to the public for cancer prevention or treatment is not justified." It looks like a good deal because "your body holds toxins that need flushing out" and "an acidic constitution causes cancer" both sound remarkably like physiology.
Note
All that can be said is "no evidence of support," so this gets only Grade C. Clearing out the waste products of metabolism is already the liver's and kidneys' full-time job. As long as those two organs aren't sick, no extra "detoxing" is needed.
Sources (2 references)
Klein AV, Kiat H (2015). Detox diets for toxin elimination and weight management: a critical review of the evidence. J Hum Nutr Diet. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.12286; Fenton TR, Huang T (2016). Systematic review of the association between dietary acid load, alkaline water and cancer. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2015-010438
14

Don't force down water to hit '8 glasses a day'

Grade CValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: small

Someone traced the origin of the "8 glasses a day" rule and found not a single study supporting it. Food and other drinks already carry plenty of water, so you don't need to drink that much. Drink when you're thirsty; check the color of your urine and that's enough. People working in hot weather, exercising hard, or with a history of kidney stones, plus older people who no longer feel thirst keenly, do need to drink deliberately on top of that.

Cost
Costs nothing. It costs a little time and attention to remember to drink, plus more trips to the bathroom at night.
Benefit
One literature review chased down the "8×8" claim — 8 glasses of 8 ounces of water each per day. Its conclusion: "no scientific studies were found in support of 8×8." It also writes that "surveys of food and fluid intake of thousands of adults strongly suggest that such large amounts are not needed," because food and other beverages already supply plenty of water. The claim looks like a good deal because water is free, 8 is a tidy number, and "drink more water" never sounds harmful in any setting.
Note
What's being rejected is the number — "you must finish X glasses a day" — not water drinking itself. Drink when thirsty, check the color of your urine, and that's enough. People working in high heat, exercising hard, or with a history of kidney stones, and older people who feel thirst less keenly, should drink deliberately — they're a different case.
Sources (1 reference)
Valtin H (2002). "Drink at least eight glasses of water a day." Really? Is there scientific evidence for "8 x 8"? Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol. https://doi.org/10.1152/ajpregu.00365.2002
15

Don't pay for fortune-telling, tarot, or horoscopes to make decisions

Grade BValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

There's a classic classroom experiment: every student received the identical "individual personality analysis," yet nearly all found it strikingly accurate. That is exactly why fortune-telling seems accurate. Astrologers picked the right profile about as often as blind guessing. And the cost isn't just a few dozen yuan: the fortune-telling ring in Xixian, Henan, collected "incense money" and "offering packages" of up to 3,888 yuan; the ringleader got eleven years.

Cost
Costs nothing. What's hard is giving up a shortcut for making decisions and thinking for yourself from now on.
Benefit
The classic classroom experiment: after a personality test, the "individual analysis" students received was in fact the same for everyone, yet most judged it highly accurate. The author's conclusion: "acceptance by the person or the interpreter does not prove the interpretation correct." Of 39 students rating the analysis's accuracy on a 0-to-5 scale, 34 gave it a 4 or a 5; averaging over the table's distribution gives about 4.26. That explains why fortune-telling always seems accurate — the phenomenon is called the Barnum effect. Astrology has also been put through a double-blind test, published in Nature. Astrologers had to pick, from three personality-test profiles, the one matching a birth chart. Out of 116 they matched 40; pure guessing would get 38.5, and the astrologers themselves had predicted they'd match 58.5. Official case: prosecutors in Xixian, Henan, reported an online fortune-telling scam ring that lured people in with free palm readings, then collected "incense money" and "offering packages" of up to 3,888 yuan. More than 50 victims; over 2 million yuan recovered; the ringleader sentenced to eleven years in prison and fined 100,000 yuan.
Note
Both of these are single studies. Forer's paper doesn't state the average score directly; 4.26 was computed from the distribution in its Table 1. This item only says "it predicts poorly" — it passes no judgment on any faith. Spending a few dozen yuan on entertainment doesn't count; using it to decide on quitting a job, getting married, or investing is where the money is lost.
Sources (4 references)
Forer BR (1949). The fallacy of personal validation: A classroom demonstration of gullibility. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 44(1):118-123 (Table 1 score distribution: one person at 2, four at 3, eighteen at 4, sixteen at 5; N=39). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0059240; Carlson S (1985). A double-blind test of astrology. Nature 318:419-425 (Table 2: 116 first choices, 40 correct, 38.5 expected by chance, astrologers predicted 58.5; "The data are consistent with chance, inconsistent with astrological hypothesis"). https://doi.org/10.1038/318419a0, full text on the second author's homepage https://muller.lbl.gov/papers/Astrology-Carlson.pdf; Supreme People's Procuratorate (2026). Xixian, Henan: after three years of sustained tracking, a batch of online fortune-telling scam rings is broken up. https://www.spp.gov.cn/zdgz/202607/t20260728_732935.shtml
16

Don't buy blue-light glasses to 'protect your eyesight,' and don't believe months of screen work will ruin your eyes — but aching, red eyes need emergency care

Grade AValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Blue-light filtering lenses don't work; skipping them saves several hundred to a thousand yuan in lens markup. Compared with ordinary lenses, wearers show no difference in eye fatigue or in how clearly they can see, and no evidence of macular protection was found either. Sore, dry eyes from screen work recover; what genuinely wrecks eyes is welding arc light, ultraviolet light, lasers, and acute glaucoma attacks.

Cost
Costs nothing — it actually saves the several-hundred-to-thousand-yuan markup on the lenses.
Benefit
Cochrane's 2023 systematic review covered 17 randomized controlled trials of 5 to 156 participants each, with follow-up from under 1 day to 5 weeks. Because the data were sparse, the trials recruited very different people, and follow-up was inconsistent, the authors did not pool them into one total. The results below are all against lenses without blue-light filtering. At follow-up under one week, self-reported eye strain showed "probably no difference," low certainty of evidence. In one trial of 120 people the two groups differed by 9.76 units. The uncertainty range around that difference was 95% CI −33.95 to 53.47 — a range straddling positive and negative, meaning no visible difference. Critical flicker fusion frequency, an objective measure of eye fatigue, showed "probably little to no difference," low certainty. Best-corrected visual acuity showed "probably no effect." The groups differed by 0.00 logMAR (95% CI −0.02 to 0.02). This one rests on a single study of 156 people, moderate certainty. Whether daytime alertness is affected can't be determined (2 trials, 42 people, very low certainty). The review also found no evidence supporting macular protection.
Note
Screens cause eye strain and dry eye — the signs are aching eyes, dryness, and blurring after long sessions. A break and more blinking relieve it. It does recover, which is not the same as "your eyes have been ruined." That sentence is ophthalmology consensus, not a conclusion of the Cochrane review in the Sources block, so it only counts as Grade C. What actually causes rapid, irreversible eye damage is intense light sources: welding arc light, ultraviolet light, lasers. An eye injury from welding arc is called "welder's flash" (photokeratitis) and is a legally recognized occupational disease. Blocking it takes goggles and face shields, not blue-light lenses — see Section 19, item 10 (protection against dust, noise, and chemical hazards). What all-night screen sessions threaten isn't the screen itself — with one exception: eyes aching and red, a rainbow ring around lights, plus headache, nausea, and vomiting means an acute angle-closure glaucoma attack; it can crush the optic nerve within days and needs an ophthalmology emergency room that same day — see Section 13, item 6 (eye emergencies). Dilated pupils in the dark plus long periods with the head bowed pushing the lens forward are its two triggers; those at high risk are over 50, farsighted, or with shallow anterior chambers. Screen-related dry eye, dragged out long enough, also becomes a chronic condition needing a doctor — it doesn't vanish after one night's sleep. If your eyes stay uncomfortable, or your vision is genuinely declining, see an ophthalmologist to find the cause; don't just swap your lenses and call it done. On preventing myopia in children and teenagers, see Section 30, items 4, 12, and 9 (2 hours outdoors a day, cycloplegic refraction, and not buying "myopia cure" products).
Sources (1 reference)
Singh S, Downie LE, Anderson AJ, Keller PR, White SJ, Ang M, Wolffsohn JS (2023). Blue-light filtering spectacle lenses for visual performance, sleep, and macular health in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 8, CD013244. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD013244.pub2
17

Don't treat blood donation as health care: 'detox, lower blood lipids, prevent heart attacks' has no randomized-trial support, while frequent donation really does cause iron deficiency

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: small

The claims that donating blood detoxes you, lowers blood lipids, or prevents heart attacks don't hold up. People healthy enough to keep donating were healthier to begin with; strip that away and the mortality drop from donating one extra unit a year shrinks from nearly 20% to 7.5%. In trials that actually split people into groups, deaths showed no difference. On the flip side, donating too often genuinely leaves people fatigued and cold-intolerant — the cause is iron deficiency.

Cost
Costs nothing. One donation — forms, the blood draw, plus the observation rest afterward — takes about an hour. For weeks afterward, the body is busy replacing the iron it lost.
Benefit
The Kuopio study in Finland followed 2,862 men aged 42 to 60 for nearly 9 years on average. Of those, 153 had donated blood in the 24 months before the analysis began, and 1 of them (0.7%) had an acute heart attack; 316 of the 2,529 non-donors did (12.5%) (difference between the two proportions P<0.0001). After stripping out age and other coronary risk factors, donors' heart attack risk was about 88% lower. Relative risk 0.12 (95% CI 0.02–0.86, P=0.035). But this comes from follow-up records only, with no randomized groups. The Nordic SCANDAT database holds 1,182,495 donors, followed for a cumulative 9,526,627 person-years, with 15,401 deaths. Adjusting only for characteristics like age and sex, each additional donation per year came with 18.6% lower mortality (95% CI 16.8%–20.4%). Strip out the "healthy donor effect" — you're only allowed to keep donating as long as you stay healthy — and the drop shrinks to 7.5% (5.7%–9.4%). The authors' conclusion: it "cannot be interpreted as firm evidence of a health benefit." The FeAST randomized controlled trial enrolled 1,277 patients with symptomatic lower-limb artery disease, randomly assigned to one group having iron reduced by regular blood draws every 6 months and one serving as control. The main outcome was all-cause death: 125/636 (20%) versus 148/641 (23%). HR 0.85 (HR is the hazard ratio; 1 means the two sides are identical). 95% CI 0.67–1.08, P=0.17. Death plus nonfatal heart attack and stroke combined: 180 (28%) versus 205 (32%), HR 0.88 (0.72–1.07, P=0.20). Neither comparison showed a difference. The INTERVAL randomized trial enrolled 45,263 whole-blood donors into three donation intervals: men at 12, 10, and 8 weeks; women at 16, 14, and 12 weeks. Shorter intervals collected clearly more blood over two years (the men's 8-week group gathered 1.69 units more than the 12-week group, 95% CI 1.59–1.80). Quality of life, physical activity, and cognition showed no differences between groups. But donation-related discomfort was more common, including fatigue, shortness of breath, faintness, dizziness, and restless legs (legs too uncomfortable at night to lie still). Average hemoglobin and ferritin were also lower, and donations deferred for low hemoglobin more frequent (P<0.0001 across the measures). Iron deficiency impairs the body's heat production: 10 women with iron-deficiency anemia, 8 with iron stores already depleted but no anemia yet, and 12 control women sat in 28 °C water for 100 minutes. The anemic group's rectal temperature was 36.0±0.2 °C versus 36.2±0.1 °C in controls (P=0.001). Oxygen consumption 5.28±0.26 versus 5.99±0.29 mL·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹ (P=0.04). The thyroid hormones thyroxine and triiodothyronine were also lower (P<0.002). The claim seems to hold up because blood donors are, by definition, healthy people who have been screened over and over — and the hypothesis "letting iron out protects the heart" failed its randomized test.
Note
What's being rejected is "donating for your own body," not blood donation itself. Blood is for others; in this book's tiers of beneficiaries it falls in tier ④ (strangers). What does flow back to you is the share the system gives. Article 14 of the Blood Donation Law provides that voluntary unpaid donors who need blood in hospital are exempt from the collection, storage, separation, and testing fees, and spouses and immediate family can be exempted or charged less under provincial government rules. A January 2024 notice from the National Health Commission and other agencies states that 28 provinces already waive these charges directly at discharge when unpaid donors or their relatives use blood in hospitals within the province. Holders of the Voluntary Blood Donation Dedication Award can also, under local "three frees" policies, ride public transport free, enter government-invested parks free, and skip the standard outpatient consultation fee at public hospitals. If you donate, keep to the legal intervals. Article 9 of the Blood Donation Law sets 200 mL per donation as the general rule, never more than 400 mL, with at least 6 months between donations; the promoted age range is 18 to 55. Don't compress the interval to chase honors or a group quota. Women, people of low body weight, and those with heavy periods are already short on iron; frequent donors can pay out of pocket for one ferritin test. If you stay fatigued or cold-intolerant after donating, or your legs feel so restless at night that you can't help moving them (that's restless legs), don't guess that your "vitality got injured" — get a complete blood count and ferritin. If iron deficiency shows up, supplement as your doctor says and lengthen your donation interval. The cold-intolerance evidence involves only 10 people — enough to explain why it happens, not how many people it happens to.

Don't rely on generic checkup packages to prevent disease; get the few evidence-based screenings for your age and sex

Grade AValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

People who get regular general health checks die at the same rate as those who don't — and just as many of them die of cardiovascular disease or cancer. The few evidence-based screenings for your age and sex are enough. From 35 you can get a free blood pressure check every year; from 65, one free health exam a year.

Cost
Costs nothing — it actually saves several hundred to several thousand yuan a year in package fees. The obligation it trades for is remembering which items to check and how far apart.
Benefit
Cochrane's 2019 systematic review update covered 17 randomized controlled trials. For total mortality it pooled 11 trials, 233,298 participants, and 21,535 deaths: the general-health-check group came out the same as the control group, RR 1.00. RR is the risk ratio; 1 means the two sides are identical. 95% CI 0.97–1.03 is the uncertainty range. For cardiovascular death it pooled 9 trials, 170,227 people, and 6,237 deaths: RR 1.05 (95% CI 0.94–1.16). For cancer death it pooled 8 trials, 139,290 people, and 3,663 deaths: RR 1.01 (95% CI 0.92–1.12). Neither showed a difference either. The authors' conclusion: "general health checks are unlikely to be beneficial." Under the National Basic Public Health Service Program, permanent residents 35 and older get one free blood pressure measurement a year, and people 65 and older get one free health exam a year. The free exam includes a physical, complete blood count, urinalysis, fasting blood glucose, and an ECG. Liver function covers AST, ALT, and total bilirubin. Kidney function covers serum creatinine and blood urea. Lipids cover total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL cholesterol, and HDL cholesterol. And finally an abdominal B-ultrasound of the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and spleen (nationwide).
Note
What's being rejected is "treating an annual package as disease prevention," not all testing. Also, the free annual blood pressure check from 35 and the free annual exam from 65 already come from the National Basic Public Health Service Program — you don't pay for them. Keep getting tested when there's a reason to. Blood pressure, blood sugar, and hepatitis B: Section 1, items 7, 8, and 14. Breast, cervical, and colorectal: Section 1, items 17, 18, and 19. H. pylori and low-dose CT: Section 1, items 23 and 24. Bone density testing for women over 65: Section 1, item 39 (bone density testing). Get tested after high-risk exposures: Section 1, item 31. Starting ages and testing intervals are all written there. Checkups organized by your employer or paid for by someone else: go. What to block is buying packages and adding items with your own money. People who already have a chronic condition, have symptoms, or are getting tests a doctor ordered for their condition are not covered — that's care, not screening. The most common no-evidence items in packages are tumor markers and whole-body imaging; see item 7 in this section (whole-body PET-CT and tumor-marker packages). What to do about high uric acid that has never flared, or gallstones that have never hurt, see item 19 in this section (asymptomatic high uric acid) and item 20 (asymptomatic gallstones). One more thing: most trials in the Cochrane review were run in high-income countries where seeing a doctor is easy to begin with; regions with strained medical resources shouldn't copy this conclusion wholesale.
Sources (2 references)

National Basic Public Health Service Specifications (3rd edition) (health management services for the elderly, health management services for hypertension patients). https://www.nhc.gov.cn/ewebeditor/uploadfile/2017/04/201704…

Don't start urate-lowering drugs just because a checkup found high uric acid that has never caused gout

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: small

For people whose uric acid is above range but who have never had a gout flare or grown tophi, the American College of Rheumatology recommends against starting urate-lowering drugs for now. It takes 24 people treated for 3 full years to prevent one gout flare. Hoping the drugs protect the kidneys falls flat too: on medication, kidney function declined just as fast as on placebo. Treat once it has actually flared.

Cost
Costs nothing — it actually saves long-term drug costs and the money for regular follow-up tests, and avoids one unnecessary round of medication risks.
Benefit
The American College of Rheumatology's 2020 gout guideline addresses asymptomatic hyperuricemia: blood uric acid >6.8 mg/dL with no previous gout flare and no tophi under the skin. The guideline conditionally recommends that these people not start any urate-lowering drug. The drugs include allopurinol, febuxostat, and probenecid. The certainty of the evidence was rated "high." A footnote under the table states that "by attributable risk, 24 patients must be treated for 3 years to prevent one gout flare." The CKD-FIX randomized controlled trial enrolled 363 people with stage 3 or 4 chronic kidney disease, no gout history but at risk of worsening, randomized to 100–300 mg allopurinol daily or placebo. The trial ran 104 weeks. eGFR is a marker of kidney function, in mL/min/1.73 m². One group changed by −3.33 a year (95% CI −4.11 to −2.55). The other changed by −3.23 a year (−3.98 to −2.47). The groups differed by −0.10 (−1.18 to 0.97), P=0.85 — kidney function fell at the same speed. Serious adverse events 46% versus 44%. The PERL randomized controlled trial enrolled 530 people with type 1 diabetes and early-to-moderate diabetic kidney disease, on allopurinol for 3 years, then 2 months off to wash the drug out. Allopurinol did lower blood urate from 6.1 to 3.9 mg/dL. But after the washout, the groups' kidney-function measure GFR differed by just 0.001 mL/min/1.73 m². The uncertainty range around that difference was 95% CI −1.9 to 1.9, P=0.99. Albumin leaking into the urine was actually 40% higher in the allopurinol group (0 to 80). It looks like a good deal because the intuition "the number is out of range, so medicate it down" runs deep.
Note
What's being rejected is "starting lifelong urate-lowering drugs after never having flared," not "high uric acid doesn't matter." The same guideline also lists exceptions where starting can be considered. First, a first flare happening alongside stage 3 or worse chronic kidney disease. Second, blood uric acid >9 mg/dL (about 535 µmol/L). Third, a history of urinary stones. People who have already flared, grown tophi, or show bone erosion on imaging should be on the drugs; see Section 16, item 9 (once gout is diagnosed, stay on urate-lowering drugs long-term). About 7.4% of Han Chinese carry a genotype called HLA-B*5801, versus only 0.7% of white people. Carriers taking allopurinol are more prone to severe, life-threatening drug rashes, and Asians run 3 times the risk of hypersensitivity syndrome as white people. This is a drug you can simply put off starting — no reason to take on that extra risk. Before truly starting, test for the genotype first; see Section 16, item 9 (once gout is diagnosed, stay on urate-lowering drugs long-term). The two kidney trials were run in chronic kidney disease and type 1 diabetes patients, so they can't be stretched to "high uric acid is completely harmless to the kidneys." What they reject is only the one practice of "taking drugs to lower urate to protect the kidneys."
Sources (3 references)
FitzGerald JD, Dalbeth N, Mikuls T, et al. (2020). 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout. Arthritis Care & Research, 72(6), 744-760 (Table 1 and its footnote). https://doi.org/10.1002/acr.24180; Badve SV, Pascoe EM, Tiku A, et al. (2020). Effects of Allopurinol on the Progression of Chronic Kidney Disease. New England Journal of Medicine, 382(26), 2504-2513. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1915833; Doria A, Galecki AT, Spino C, et al. (2020). Serum Urate Lowering with Allopurinol and Kidney Function in Type 1 Diabetes. New England Journal of Medicine, 382(26), 2493-2503. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1916624

Don't have your gallbladder removed preventively just because a checkup found stones that have never hurt

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Of people with stones in the gallbladder who have never had pain, about eight in ten stayed symptom-free across nearly nine years. Left alone, about 0.1% to 0.3% a year develop emergencies like cholecystitis or pancreatitis. Gallbladder removal isn't zero-risk either: in about 1.5% of operations the bile duct gets injured. So both the European and the UK guidelines say: no symptoms, no surgery.

Cost
Costs nothing — it actually saves one general-anesthetic operation and one hospital stay. The obligation it trades for is remembering which signals mean go to the hospital the moment they appear.
Benefit
The Italian MICOL population survey ultrasound-scanned 11,229 people aged 29 to 69. It found gallstones in 856, of whom 580 had no symptoms, followed for 8.7 years on average. Of those 580, 453 (78.1%) never developed symptoms, 61 (10.5%) developed mild symptoms, and 66 (11.4%) severe symptoms. Over the follow-up, 189 gallbladder removals were performed in total, 41.3% of them on people without symptoms. The authors' conclusion: "expectant management remains an effective approach for most patients" — expectant management means watchful waiting, no surgery. An American HMO — a managed-care health provider — ran tracking statistics on 691 people with diagnosed gallstones, followed for 78±61.6 months on average. The 135 without symptoms were followed for 58±50.2 months (median 46.3 months): only 10% developed gallstone symptoms, and 7% had surgery. Of the 50 deaths in the whole group, only 2 were related to the bile ducts, and both were in the symptomatic group. The authors' conclusion: "patients with silent stones do not need surgery before symptoms develop" — silent meaning stones that keep quiet and never flare. UK NICE guideline CG188, recommendation 1.2.1, puts it this way: "people with asymptomatic gallstones found by chance, whose gallbladder and bile ducts are both normal, should be told they do not need treatment until symptoms develop." The European liver association's 2016 gallstone guideline sets the risks on both sides side by side. Symptom-free people develop symptoms at about 0.7% to 2.5% a year. Acute cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, obstructive jaundice (bile duct blocked, skin turning yellow), or cholangitis strike 0.1% to 0.3% a year. After a first bout of colic, complications rise to 1% to 3% a year — which is why most people get a warning pain before anything serious. On the surgical side, of 51,041 gallbladder removals in the Swedish national registry, 1.5% injured the bile duct. About a fifth of those (0.3%) were partial or complete cuts of the duct. One-year mortality was 3.9% for those with a bile duct injury versus 1.1% without. The guideline also notes that 10% to 40% of patients still have discomfort after removal, or symptoms that come back after a good stretch. The guideline's conclusion: in people without symptoms, surgery — open or laparoscopic — does not extend life, because the operation's own risk of death and complications exceeds the risk of not removing it; and dealing with it after symptoms appear also costs less overall. A 1983 decision analysis put concrete numbers on it: a 30-year-old man having prophylactic removal lived 4 days less on average than watchful waiting; a 50-year-old, 18 days less. Removal versus non-removal has never been compared in a randomized trial to this day. Prophylactic removal looks like a good deal because of the intuition "it will hurt sooner or later — better to remove it once, while young."
Note
Controversy. The 2021 Chinese expert consensus on biliary surgery lists some asymptomatic gallstones as surgical indications, and a commentary in the same journal names this as one of the points in dispute. The consensus full text is behind a subscription, so exactly which situations it includes could not be verified (TODO: to be checked). The other counterargument is small stones: stones under 5 mm are more associated with pancreatitis. A Dutch decision analysis found that for these people, prophylactic removal might extend life or shorten it, depending on how common and how lethal pancreatitis is. The European guideline also lists exceptions that do warrant removal: a calcified gallbladder wall (porcelain gallbladder) and gallbladder polyps of 1 cm or more — those two should come out. When other major abdominal surgery is being done, removing it at the same time can be considered. This item covers one situation only: stones in the gallbladder, which have never hurt. Stones in the common bile duct are a different matter. The same guideline states explicitly in recommendation 1.3.1 that bile duct stones must be cleared and the gallbladder removed, whether or not there are symptoms. Go to the hospital the same day — don't tough this one out with this item's conclusion — if any of the following appears: constant cramping pain in the right upper abdomen or upper abdomen, fever with chills, yellowing of the whites of the eyes or the skin, or darkening urine. When a doctor recommends surgery after reviewing imaging, ask which specific reason it rests on — bile duct involvement, a polyp present at the same time, an abnormal gallbladder wall — and don't rebut them with this item. What this item blocks is only "removing it for no reason other than stones showing up on a scan." Both studies above followed cohorts forward in time without randomized groups. But the question they answer is "what happens if you leave it alone," not "which treatment is better," which fits the use here. Also, both followed people for 4 to 9 years; over longer horizons the symptom rate will climb.

Don't cut out calcium to prevent kidney stones

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

People who have passed calcium oxalate stones are often told to cut back on calcium — the trial evidence is exactly the opposite. Men with recurrent stones who ate a normal amount of calcium while cutting animal protein and salt had half as many recurrences over five years as those on a low-calcium diet. The UK guideline also states plainly: don't restrict calcium.

Cost
Costs nothing. It actually makes life easier — no more guarding every meal for hidden calcium.
Benefit
A 5-year randomized controlled trial enrolled 120 men with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and high urinary calcium (called idiopathic hypercalciuria). They were randomly split into two groups. One ate a normal amount of calcium, 30 mmol a day; that group also cut animal protein (52 g a day) and salt (50 mmol of sodium chloride a day). The other ate the traditional low-calcium diet, 10 mmol a day. Over 5 years, recurrences were 12/60 versus 23/60. Unadjusted relative risk 0.49 (95% CI 0.24–0.98, the uncertainty range), P=0.04 — the normal-calcium group's recurrence risk was half. Over the follow-up, urinary calcium fell by about 170 mg a day in both groups. But the oxalate excreted in urine diverged: the low-calcium group's rose by 5.4 mg a day on average, while the normal-calcium group's fell by 7.2 mg a day on average. UK NICE guideline NG118, recommendation 1.8.1, states: do not restrict dietary calcium. Adults should keep 700 to 1,200 mg a day; children and teenagers 350 to 1,000 mg a day by age. Cutting calcium looks like a good deal because of the intuition "stones are made of calcium, so eat less calcium."
Note
Controversy: this trial was run only in men, and all of them had recurrent calcium oxalate stones with high urinary calcium, so it can't be stretched to every type of stone. Also, the trial group changed three things at once — normal calcium, less animal protein, less salt — so the whole benefit can't be booked to "not cutting calcium"; low salt and less animal protein were working too. What's being rejected is "deliberately cutting out calcium-containing foods," not "you should take more calcium." What was changed here is the calcium in everyday meals; calcium supplements are a different matter — whether to take supplements after stones is a question for your doctor. The drink-more-water item is Section 16, item 8 (after kidney stones, get water up to 2.5–3 liters a day).
Sources (2 references)
Borghi L, Schianchi T, Meschi T, et al. (2002). Comparison of two diets for the prevention of recurrent stones in idiopathic hypercalciuria. New England Journal of Medicine, 346(2), 77-84. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa010369; National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2019). Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management. NICE guideline NG118, recommendation 1.8.1. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng118/chapter/Recommendations

Don't buy crystals, beads, or Pixiu charms to 'turn your luck,' 'attract wealth,' or 'nurture yourself'

Grade BValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

The claims that wearing them changes your luck, attracts wealth, or nurtures you have no verifiable support. It's the same mechanism that makes fortune-telling seem accurate: the words are vague enough that you do the fitting yourself. When a seller's claims reach into curing disease, that's false advertising — a livestream shop was penalized for it in 2026. Buying them as decoration is fine.

Cost
Costs nothing. All that's required is not counting "turning your luck" or "nurture" among your reasons for buying. What's hard is not following along when everyone around you wears one and swears it works.
Benefit
The classic classroom experiment showed that everyone received the same vague "personal analysis," yet nearly all judged it highly accurate — the Barnum effect. That explains where the feeling of "things really have gone smoother since I put it on" comes from. That author's conclusion: "acceptance by the person does not prove the interpretation correct." Official case: on June 4, 2026, SAMR published a batch of typical "fake crackdown, source cleanup" cases from traditional craft markets. Among them, a jewelry store in Sihui, Guangdong, fabricated the materials of its goods on livestream. It also falsely claimed the products had effects such as "preventing and treating rheumatism, boosting immunity, improving sleep quality, and clearing blood vessels." The store used scripted performances to mislead and deceive consumers, violating Article 9(1) of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law (nationwide).
Note
One conclusion only: its claimed powers can't be verified, and no predictive ability can be measured. No faith or custom is being judged here, nor gifts, keepsakes, or heirlooms. Keep two things apart: claims by merchants are covered by written rules you can complain to, while "turning your luck" has neither research behind it nor any way to prove it false — only a personal budget can hold the line. Before buying, treat it as an ordinary ornament and ask yourself: "if it changed nothing at all, would I still pay this price?" How to check materials and certificates, and why it's a bad investment: Section 5, items 33 and 34 (count beads and luxury watches as money spent; for gems, accept only CMA reports). On paying for fortune-telling: item 15 in this section (fortune-telling, tarot, horoscopes).
Sources (2 references)

Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0059240; State Administration for Market Regulation (2026). SAMR publishes a batch of typical 'fake crackdown, source cleanup' cases from traditional craft markets. https://www.samr.gov.cn/xw/zj/art/2026/art_1529399cfe874b87…

Don't expect purchases to lift your mood or your sense of standing

Grade BValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: medium

The more people prize money and possessions, the less happy they report feeling — but the link is weak, and it can't tell you which causes which. Other research finds that spending on an experience brings more happiness than spending on things. So when your mood is low, money spent on a trip out or a meal with people is more likely to help than a stuffed shopping cart.

Cost
Costs nothing. What's hard is holding off on the order when your mood is low.
Benefit
One meta-analysis (pooling many studies) covered 259 independent samples and 753 effect sizes. The result: the more people value material things, the lower their self-reported well-being. On the most commonly used kind of multidimensional scale, the correlation is r = -0.19 (adjusted ρ = -0.24). On scales measuring only the "importance of money" aspect, the link is weaker, r = -0.08 to -0.11. Broken down by which outcome was measured, the strength varies. It's strongest with risky health and consumer behaviors and negative self-evaluations, r = -0.28 to -0.44. It's weakest with life satisfaction and negative emotions, r = -0.13 to -0.15. The authors also ran a mediation analysis (testing what carries the effect through), which suggests the negative link may run through unmet psychological needs. Another study: in two surveys of different populations, respondents said money spent on gaining a life experience made them happier than money spent on things. In a follow-up lab experiment, recalling a good mood after spending on an experience also beat recalling a purchase (the nationwide basis doesn't apply; both studies used foreign samples).
Note
Controversy: most of the included studies asked a group of people at a single point in time whether two things moved together, and can't establish which comes first. The authors themselves say in the conclusion that pinning down direction will take more experiments and long-term follow-up studies. So don't read this as "buying things makes people unhappy" — only as "counting on purchases to make you happy is a bad bet." And the link is weak: r = -0.19 explains only a few percentage points of the variation, and people differ widely. Both studies used foreign samples; no comparable data exist for Chinese populations. This item doesn't oppose spending on things you love — it opposes using shopping as a tool for regulating emotions, because that trains your first response to the next bad mood to be another order. Concrete money-saving moves: Section 5. What actually has evidence when your mood is low: the second half of Section 22 and Section 29. The budget added to be "a notch above others": item 24 in this section (moving up a notch).
Sources (2 references)
Dittmar H, Bond R, Hurst M, Kasser T (2014). The relationship between materialism and personal well-being: A meta-analysis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 107(5), 879-924. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037409; Van Boven L, Gilovich T (2003). To do or to have? That is the question. Don't spend extra on a new house, car, or social circle just to 'move up a notch among the people around you'

Grade BValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Compare people with the same income: the more their neighbors earn, the less well-being they report. It only happens between neighbors with the same education as you whom you see often. So the extra money to move somewhere everyone is better off than you buys a step down, not up. But when incomes rise together, people do feel better off — absolute levels still count.

Cost
Costs nothing. All it takes is one extra question before raising the budget: is this markup buying the thing itself, or my standing in this group. What's hard is not following when everyone around you upgrades.
Benefit
The US National Survey of Families and Households (NSFH) revisited the same people across two waves. The authors matched this data to local average income (PUMA), estimated from the 1990 census 5% sample. After stripping out one's own income and a series of personal characteristics, the result: the higher the neighbors' income, the lower the respondent's reported well-being. The effect is large, robust to a different estimation method, and highly significant. In the authors' words, the drop in well-being from "neighbors' income rising" is of the same order of magnitude as from "one's own income falling by the same amount." Switching to comparing each person with their own former self (adding individual fixed effects), the coefficient kept its direction and a similar size, though significance fell to the 10% level. Restricting the comparison to within the same state and the same survey wave (state and wave fixed effects) left the result basically unchanged. That rules out both "people who like moving to poorer places were already happier" and some unmeasured state-level factor. The effect is stronger among people who interact with their neighbors often, and not significant among those whose friends are all outside the community. Renters and homeowners show no difference — which doesn't support the explanation "expensive places have high housing costs, so there's less money left to spend." Well-being fell only with the income of equally educated neighbors, and barely responded to the income of neighbors with different education. And it travels mainly through "satisfaction with one's own material situation," not through satisfaction with family life or other domains. Finally, when one's own income and the neighbors' rise by the same proportion, well-being still rises.
Note
There are several reasons for Grade B: the data come from questionnaires repeatedly revisiting the same people; there is only this one study; and the sample is foreign. The outcome measured was respondents' self-reported well-being, not money. The authors did use statistical tools to rule out several confounders — each person compared with their own past, and comparisons within the same state and wave — but it is still not a randomized trial. No comparable data exist for Chinese populations. Benefit is rated "medium" following the basis used by item 23 in this section (don't expect purchases to lift your mood). The money saved can indeed reach five figures in yuan. But there are no numbers for how much well-being that saving buys, so it isn't booked as "large" on five-figure grounds. This item doesn't oppose paying for a bigger house, a quieter community, or a shorter commute — those buy the thing itself. What it blocks is the single reason "my coworkers all upgraded; I can't fall behind them." How housing should be ranked: Section 4, item 18 (put commute time near the front when choosing a home). Shopping to regulate mood: item 23 in this section (don't expect purchases to lift your mood). Endless upward comparison online: Section 3, item 20 (don't make "how other people are doing" your daily reading).
Sources (2 references)
Luttmer EFP (2005). Neighbors as Negatives: Relative Earnings and Well-Being. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 120(3), 963–1002. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/120.3.963; Luttmer EFP (2004). Neighbors as Negatives: Relative Earnings and Well-Being. NBER Working Paper No. 10667 (the wording and magnitudes cited in this item were checked verbatim against this version). https://www.nber.org/papers/w10667
