44

A family member ran up gambling debts? Don't rush to pay: the law doesn't protect gambling debts, and money borrowed to gamble isn't joint marital debt

Grade BValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Money owed at the gambling table gets no protection from the courts. If the lender knew the money was for gambling and lent anyway, the courts won't protect that either. Money one spouse borrowed to gamble cannot be counted as debt the couple repays together. Without a trial, the court cannot make the spouse who never borrowed bear responsibility.

Cost
Costs nothing. The hard part is keeping your wallet shut when the creditor comes knocking and the family begs in tears. If the creditor really sues, you'll have to answer in court.
Benefit
The Supreme People's Court's 2017 notice makes four points. Debts incurred in gambling, drug use, and other unlawful or criminal activities receive no legal protection. Where the lender knew or should have known the money was borrowed for gambling or drugs and lent anyway, it receives no legal protection. Where one spouse borrowed in their own name and used it for unlawful or criminal purposes, courts do not support their demand to treat it as joint marital debt. Without trial proceedings, the spouse who never borrowed cannot be made to bear civil liability (nationwide, from 2017)
Note
Graded B because this is an internal court notice with no figures, and whether the creditor knew depends on evidence. The notice was issued under the then-current Marriage Law; how joint marital debt is determined after the Civil Code took effect — see Section 10, item 12 (a spouse's large borrowing). Loans the creditor didn't know went to gambling must still be repaid — by the one who borrowed. To prove the money went to gambling you need transfer records, gambling-platform records, or police handling materials — keep such things on hand routinely. If the creditor really sues, first-instance ordinary procedure runs from 6 months, simplified procedure 3 months. Each side pays its own attorney fees; the losing party doesn't cover yours. If the creditor waylays or detains people at your door, see Section 9, item 15 (collecting debts without detaining anyone), and call the police directly. If they themselves have gambled to the point of wanting to die, see Section 1, item 37 (borrowing to repay gambling: call 12356 first). The beneficiaries are mainly the spouse and immediate family.
Sources (1 reference)
Supreme People's Court (2017). Notice on Properly Adjudicating Cases Involving Marital Debt According to Law (Fa [2017] No. 48, Articles 2, 4). https://www.court.gov.cn/fabu/xiangqing/36982.html
45

An acquaintance asks you to 'lend your face' or 'be a witness' for their loan, or to read out a verification code? Refuse: it's an AB loan — the borrower is you, not a guarantor

Grade BValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

"Lend your face, be a witness" really means borrowing from the bank in your name. The borrower is you, not a guarantor — once the money is forwarded to the acquaintance, the bank still comes after you. The broker deceived you, but as long as the bank was unaware, you cannot rescind the loan contract. The acquaintance's written pledge that "I'll repay it" doesn't bind the bank either.

Cost
Costs nothing. The hard part is refusing relatives and friends to their face. If they say "you'd just be a witness" or "you carry no responsibility," refuse all the same. Don't hand your phone, ID card, or bank card to the broker, and don't scan your face or sign as the broker arranges. Verification codes are for you alone — don't read them out even to a close acquaintance.
Benefit
The NFRA's Fujian bureau described the scheme in its 2022 risk advisory. Customer A's qualifications fall short and the loan won't come through. The broker says to add a guarantor and sends A to find a well-qualified B. In practice, the broker applies for the loan using B's identity information, and the money goes to A. The original text says "the borrower is in substance B," and that B "only learned when the bank came collecting that they were the borrower, not the guarantor." The Shandong bureau's 2024 advisory says brokers promise B "no responsibility whatsoever." The broker also coaches B in advance on how to handle the bank's pre-loan investigation, while B in fact applies for the loan as the borrower. The Shanghai Putuo District court publicized a case in 2024: a salesperson downloaded the bank app on B's phone and applied for the loan directly in B's name. The money reached B's account, B transferred it to A, and A paid more than 80,000 yuan in fees. The eight-member broker gang drew 10 months to 4 years for contract fraud. Even with the brokers sentenced, the loan doesn't become someone else's. Civil Code Article 149 provides that where a third party committed the fraud, the deceived party can seek rescission only if the counterparty "knew or should have known." Here the counterparty is the bank; so long as the bank was unaware, the contract cannot be rescinded. Where rescission is possible, the court must be asked within 1 year of learning of the fraud (Article 152). The borrower must repay within the agreed term (Article 675). A contract binds only its parties (Article 465). Transferring a debt to someone else requires the creditor's consent (Article 551). So A's written pledge doesn't bind the bank; the money can only be recovered by suing A yourself. Scanning your face for someone without reading the contract — the court upholds that too. The Shizhong District court of Neijiang concluded a case in 2025: Jiang wanted to borrow from a microloan company but couldn't borrow alone. Zhang's son, behind her back, gave her identity information to Jiang to make her a co-borrower. The loan process required her to scan her face in person; she scanned, but never read the contract. The court held that she "should have foreseen the importance of facial recognition and its legal consequences," and ordered her to repay the remaining principal of more than 60,000 yuan together with Jiang. The Electronic Signature Law states that "a reliable electronic signature has the same legal force as a handwritten signature or a seal." The Anti-Telecom and Online Fraud Law provides that no one "may provide real-name verification assistance"; violators face fines and, in serious cases, detention. Ordinary first-instance procedure concludes within 6 months, and can be extended. Attorney fees are not among the statutory litigation fees and come out of your own pocket (nationwide)
Note
The beneficiary is mainly you; the A who comes asking is most likely family or a friend. A chief procurator in Shanghai Pudong wrote that B often goes along, knowing full well the loan is in their own name, out of reluctance to lose face, and ends up as the bank's collection target. If you truly want to help, first ask exactly what capacity you'd hold on the contract; if it's a loan contract, don't sign. Willing to guarantee? Then sign a surety contract as guarantor — see item 18 (guaranteeing for others). If a loan has already been taken out in your name, report to the police first, then call the lending bank at the number on its official website and explain, keeping all chat and transfer records. To see how many loans stand in your name, check your credit report — see item 9 (check your credit report). In the bank's pre-loan interview, don't recite the broker's script; lying can land the liability on you — see Section 9, item 6 (polished materials for a loan). Face scans and electronic confirmations count as signatures too — see item 17 (read the whole document before signing). Courts don't always hold the named person liable: in 2021 the Guangzhou Internet Court ruled for a woman whose ID had been stolen — she reported it and registered the loss on the spot, and the bank, unable to prove she herself had done the face scan, lost. So if your ID is lost, report and register the loss immediately, and keep the receipt. When an institution demands a face scan you may ask for another method — that's a separate matter, see Section 14, item 9 (a face scan is not something you must accept). For the same family of tricks that borrow your name, see item 28 (name-only legal representative). Don't lend out your phone or your accounts — see item 8 (don't lend anyone your bank card). Graded B because the regulators gave the scheme and the cases, but no statistics on how many people were defrauded or for how much.

Fit good locks on doors and windows, put a motion-activated light outside, and actually lock up when you leave: these are what deter burglary; an alarm alone shows little effect

Grade BValue: FairBasis: moneyMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

UK data show households with door locks plus window locks had about one-twelfth the chance of being burgled of households with nothing installed. Add a motion-activated light outside and it falls to roughly one in thirty. An alarm alone, with nothing else, shows no measurable burglary prevention. This covers burglary, not robbery with someone home.

Cost
Swap the door lock for one that deadbolts only with a key, add window locks, fit a motion-activated light outside — usually a few dozen to a few hundred yuan. Replacing the whole security door runs over a thousand yuan. The hard part is actually locking doors and windows every time you leave — remember it even with windows open in summer.
Benefit
The crime survey for England and Wales asked 37,416 households which security devices they had from 2008 to 2012, then compared against burgled households. Households with no security at all were only 4.9% of all households but 36.6% of households burgled by entry. The authors computed "protection multiples": how many times smaller the burglary odds were than for households with nothing installed. Door locks plus window locks: 12.54 times — burglary odds fall to about one-twelfth. "Door locks" here means double locks or "deadlocks" (the bolt retracts only with a key). Door locks, window locks, plus an outside motion-activated or timer light: 34.41 times. Add an indoor timer light: 49 times. Single devices alone: an outside light about 3 times, door locks about 2.8 times; window locks alone show no measurable difference. Homes with five devices were no better off than homes with the right three. An alarm alone, with nothing else, left burglary odds higher than installing nothing at all. Homes with dummy alarm boxes also had higher odds of break-in attempts that failed. Locks only count when actually locked: from 1993 to 2006/07, burglaries by picking locks, smashing windows, or removing door panels fell from 31 to 7 per 1,000 households — a 77% drop. The kind where doors and windows were unlocked and the intruder simply walked in stayed at 7 per 1,000 households, unchanged (England and Wales)
Note
The controversy: the alarm half of the finding has counter-evidence. The same authors, using 1992–1996 data, found that adding an alarm did lower burglary odds back then. They also caution that the counter-intuitive result deserves care — one possibility is that burglary victims are the ones who install alarms. All figures are UK figures, and the comparisons merely contrast households with and without devices, with no grouped controls — hence grade B. These figures cover burglary only; there is no data that door locks stop home-invasion robbery. If someone really is inside, back away first and call the police — see item 10 (in a conflict, call the police and keep your hands off). When there is no retreat, see item 11 (against assault you can't escape, fighting back is allowed). Renters: agree with the landlord before changing locks or adding window locks. The Civil Code provides that a tenant who installs or alters fixtures without the landlord's consent can be required to restore the original state or pay compensation. When buying a security door, note that burglar-resistant security doors are covered by the mandatory national standard GB 17565-2022, effective January 1, 2024. The beneficiaries are mainly you and your family.

9. Legal red lines ordinary people can easily cross

26 items

This section runs two calculations: your personal freedom, and your money. The things below are ones ordinary people often assume are "no big deal," yet they can actually get you detained, fined, or in serious cases imprisoned. Each entry gives the specific numbers in the statutes, plus cases published through official channels. The Public Security Administration Punishments Law cited in this section is the 2025 revision, effective January 1, 2026; its article numbers differ from the old law. The Criminal Law cited is the consolidated text "as amended through Criminal Law Amendment (XI)," reposted by the Beijing Public Security Traffic Management Bureau, and the corresponding amendment is noted in the text. The entries are ranked from high to low by "easiest to trip over by accident" plus "heaviest consequences." The entries in this section are grouped by theme below, with entry numbers in parentheses. Posting and forwarding online: don't forward disaster news of unknown veracity (No. 1), don't share content insulting heroes and martyrs (No. 2), read-and-close what's on overseas websites (No. 3), don't send porn videos to group chats (No. 4). Collecting money for others, loan fraud, and insurance fraud: "part-time jobs" that have you collect money with your own card (No. 5), "packaging documents" to defraud lenders (No. 6), don't withdraw money from a bank card you found (No. 7), claim discounts under your real identity (No. 8), never lend out your ID card (No. 16), don't stage accidents for insurance claims (No. 21). Everyday little things: throw nothing from balconies or windows (No. 9), don't buy replica guns online (No. 10), register drones under your real name first (No. 11), play cards without taking a rake or organizing games (No. 13), don't eat wild game (No. 14). Conflicts and the police: don't seize people when collecting debts (No. 15), cooperate when police stop you (No. 17), do the math before hitting someone (No. 19), don't carry batons or stun guns for self-defense (No. 26). Sex, children, and your body: don't secretly film people (No. 12), no sex with anyone under 14 (No. 18), adoption registration through civil affairs if you can't raise a child (No. 20), don't sell your organs (No. 22), don't buy sex — detention is the default (No. 23). Copyright and derivative works: fan translations, re-uploads, and pirated e-books (No. 24), get permission before selling fan fiction (No. 25).

1

In group chats, don't forward disaster, epidemic, or police news of unknown veracity; no photoshopping, no AI-fabricated 'scene' images

Grade AValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Forward a disaster, epidemic, or police message knowing it's fake, and the penalty is as heavy as if you had made it up yourself. Not being the one who invented it changes nothing: 5 to 10 days of detention, plus a fine of 1,000 yuan. Serious disruption of social order means up to 3 years; serious consequences, 3 to 7 years. Photoshopped and AI-fabricated "scene" images both count as making it up yourself.

Cost
Costs nothing. Before forwarding, check whether it's an official notice. If you're not sure, don't forward it — and don't edit images or add "rumor has it." The hard part is resisting the urge to be the first one to break the news.
Benefit
Whoever deliberately spreads rumors or falsely reports hazards, epidemics, disasters, or police situations, disrupting public order: 5 to 10 days of detention, plus a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. The lighter tier is up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Fabricating false hazards, epidemics, disasters, or police situations and spreading them online: up to 3 years. Knowingly and deliberately passing falsehoods along falls in the same tier. The premise is serious disruption of social order — the statute's wording is "seriously disrupting social order." Causing serious consequences: 3 to 7 years (nationwide)
Note
Forwarding something you know is fake and making it up yourself are handled under the same provision. "I only shared it" is no defense. Photoshopped and AI-generated fake scene images count as fabricating them yourself. In 2025 the Ministry of Public Security published several batches of typical cases of online rumors about disasters and hazards. The MPS website was down while this section was written, so no specific cases are cited.
Sources (3 references)
Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (2025 revision, Article 29). https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2015). Criminal Law Amendment (IX) (Article 32, i.e., Paragraph 2 of Article 291-1 of the Criminal Law). https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/201802/t20180205_364562.shtml; National People's Congress (2020). Criminal Law (as amended through Criminal Law Amendment (XI), Article 291-1). https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index… (reposted by the Beijing Public Security Traffic Management Bureau)
2

Don't post or share images, memes, or comments insulting heroes and martyrs; don't joke about the national flag or anthem

Grade AValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Joke about heroes and martyrs, the national flag, or the national anthem, and the lighter penalty is 5 to 10 days of detention or a fine of 1,000 to 3,000 yuan. The heavier tier is 10 to 15 days of detention. Where it becomes a crime: up to 3 years. One person posted 2 messages slandering Yuan Longping in a 499-member village WeChat group and got 6 months of public surveillance — not locked up, but with restricted movement.

Cost
Costs nothing. With content involving heroes and martyrs, the national flag, the national emblem, or the national anthem: no commenting, no editing images, no forwarding. The hard part is holding back a quip when others in the group are trading jokes.
Benefit
Insulting or fabricating facts to infringe the names, portraits, reputations, or honors of heroes and martyrs in a way that harms the public interest is punished at the tier below: 5 to 10 days of detention, or a fine of 1,000 to 3,000 yuan. Desecrating or denying the deeds and spirit of heroes and martyrs, or producing and spreading speech, images, or audiovisual content glorifying wars of aggression, thereby disrupting public order, falls in the same tier. The heavier tier is 10 to 15 days of detention, plus a fine of up to 5,000 yuan. At "serious circumstances" it becomes a crime: up to 3 years. Insulting the national flag or emblem in public, or altering the anthem's lyrics or music, or singing it in a distorted, disparaging way — where circumstances are serious, also up to 3 years. Official cases: Xiao posted 2 messages slandering and insulting Yuan Longping in a 499-member village WeChat group and was sentenced to 6 months of public surveillance (a penalty of restricted movement without imprisonment). Qiu used a Weibo account with over 2.5 million followers to post 2 items distorting the deeds of border-defense troops and got 8 months, plus a public apology in national media (nationwide)
Note
This provision of the Public Security Administration Punishments Law was added only in the 2025 revision. Before that, such matters could go only through the Criminal Law, or a civil public-interest lawsuit filed by the procuratorate. A WeChat group of a few hundred members counts as a public venue in the courts' eyes.

3

What's on overseas websites: read and close; no screenshots, no forwarding, no moving into group chats, no echoing it in the comments

Grade AValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

These provisions punish passing things on, not reading. If you forward, move into groups, or echo in the comments, it all counts as dissemination when a case is handled. Where it reaches inciting subversion or inciting separatism: up to 5 years, and over 5 years for ringleaders. Books and audiovisual material on terrorism and extremism are the exception: knowingly holding onto them, where circumstances are serious, is up to 3 years.

Cost
Costs nothing. Close the page and the matter ends there. No archiving, no forwarding, no moving onto domestic platforms. Don't use an account that can be tied to your identity to post political content long-term on overseas platforms. Don't take fees or funding from overseas institutions, organizations, or individuals either. The hard part is not screenshotting or sharing when you see something provocative.
Benefit
Inciting others to subvert state power or overthrow the socialist system by spreading rumors, slander, or other means: up to 5 years. Ringleaders (the statute's term is "prime movers") or those whose crimes are grave: 5 years or more, with a maximum fixed-term sentence of 15 years. Inciting separatism or undermining national unity carries the same sentences. Colluding with overseas institutions, organizations, or individuals to do either draws heavier punishment. Where institutions, organizations, or individuals at home or abroad fund others to do it, those directly responsible get up to 5 years, and 5 years or more in serious circumstances. Stealing, spying out, buying, or unlawfully supplying state secrets or intelligence for overseas institutions, organizations, or personnel: 5 to 10 years. Especially serious cases under this item: 10 years or more or life imprisonment; lighter ones, up to 5 years. Crimes endangering national security always carry supplemental deprivation of political rights for 1 to 5 years, during which voting rights and eligibility for public office are stripped away. Confiscation of property may also be imposed, turning personal property over to the state. There are administrative rules too: no individual or organization may use the network to engage in activities that endanger national security, honor, or interests; may not incite subversion of state power or overthrow of the socialist system; and may not incite separatism or undermine national unity. Publishing or transmitting such information is punished under the relevant laws and administrative regulations (nationwide). Another category stands without any spreading at all: knowingly holding unlawfully onto material that propagates terrorism or extremism is enough to convict where circumstances are serious. The material includes books, audio and video files, or other items. The sentence is up to 3 years of fixed-term imprisonment, criminal detention (short-term custody), or public surveillance (no custody but restricted movement), plus a fine imposed concurrently or separately — a fine alongside the sentence, or in some cases only the fine. The basis is Article 120-6 of the Criminal Law, added by Criminal Law Amendment (IX).
Note
The provisions cited here punish inciting others, spreading outward, and supplying to others; merely looking is not among them. Terrorism and extremism materials are an exception written into the statute — mere possession can convict (Article 120-6) — so never archive this category. Once seen, stop there: no screenshot archives, no forwarding, no commenting, no pulling others in to share. Forwarding and echoing in the comments both count as dissemination when a case is handled; "I only shared it" is no defense. Content originating from overseas platforms can draw heavier punishment. If you can't tell whether something is true, all the more reason not to pass it along — see No. 1 in this section (don't forward messages of unknown veracity). For how VPN tools themselves are punished, see No. 11 in Section 11. Forwarding this kind of content brings no real benefit, while the cost is prison time, deprivation of political rights, and confiscation of property. Comparable publicly documented cases appear only in overseas media and in documents released by family members — for example, a blogger who had long posted political commentary on overseas platforms was sentenced to 7 years in 2023. This book could not obtain a verdict verifiable through official channels, so it sticks to the statutes and attaches no case.

Cybersecurity Law (2025 amendment, effective January 1, 2026, Paragraph 2 of Article 13 and Item 1 of Article 71). https://www.cac.gov.cn/2025-12/29/c_1768735112911946.htm; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2015). Criminal Law Amendment (IX) (adding Article 120-6). Full text reposted by the National Public Complaints and Proposals Administration https://www.gjxfj.gov.cn/gjxfj/fgwj/flfg/webinfo/2017/03/16…
4

Porn videos: watching privately is your own business — don't send them to groups, don't sell 'resources,' don't create groups

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Watching privately is not within the punishment provisions. Send one video to a group and it counts as disseminating to the whole group: 10 to 15 days of detention plus a fine of up to 5,000 yuan, and up to 2 years where circumstances are serious. Selling "resources" for money: up to 3 years, with life imprisonment at the extreme. For dissemination groups of 30 or more members, the creator, the admins, and the main posters are all treated as criminals.

Cost
Costs nothing. Don't forward, don't save into group files, and don't serve as owner or admin of such groups.
Benefit
Disseminating obscene information online: 10 to 15 days of detention plus a fine of up to 5,000 yuan. The lighter tier is up to 5 days of detention or a fine of 1,000 to 3,000 yuan. Content involving minors draws heavier punishment. Disseminating obscene materials at the "serious circumstances" level: up to 2 years. Selling or spreading them for profit: up to 3 years plus a fine. Serious cases under this item: 3 to 10 years; especially serious: 10 years or more or life imprisonment. Creating a group mainly for disseminating obscene electronic information with 30 or more members is handled as a crime, and so is causing serious consequences. The group creator, the admins, and the main posters are all convicted of the crime of disseminating obscene materials (nationwide)
Note
Both laws punish "dissemination"; private viewing is not within the provisions. But one send to a group counts as disseminating to the whole group. How much volume "serious circumstances" requires is set by judicial interpretation; this section did not verify the specific figures.

5

Any 'part-time job' asking you to receive money, withdraw cash, or transfer funds with your own card is off-limits, whatever the cut

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

These "part-time jobs" pay a few hundred yuan and leave you a record. One man took his ID card and 1 bank card to a designated spot to help with transfers and withdrawals and earned just over 500 yuan. The procuratorate declined to prosecute him, but the police still detained him for 10 days and fined him 1,000 yuan. Another handed his own and others' bank cards and phone cards to a gang for receiving payments and cash withdrawals: 2 years and 3 months, plus a fine of 22,000 yuan.

Cost
Costs nothing. Walk away from gigs like "a few hundred a day, just bring your card to the bank."
Benefit
Knowingly helping transfer, buy, or sell money or property obtained from crime, or otherwise helping cover it up: up to 3 years, plus a fine imposed concurrently or separately (a fine alongside the sentence, or possibly only the fine). Official case: Wang, following instructions, took his ID card and 1 bank card to a designated location to help with transfers and withdrawals, earning just over 500 yuan. The procuratorate did not prosecute him; the police detained him for 10 days and fined him 1,000 yuan under the Anti-Telecom and Online Fraud Law. Man handed his own and others' bank cards and phone cards to a gang for receiving payments, transfers, and cash withdrawals: 2 years and 3 months plus a fine of 22,000 yuan (nationwide). Converting to virtual currency and moving it out is the same thing: An and two others, on a fraud gang's instructions, collected money with their own bank cards, bought virtual currency on trading platforms, and transferred it to accounts the gang designated, taking a percentage cut. Over 500,000 yuan of confirmed victim losses was involved. The three were convicted of concealing or disguising criminal proceeds and sentenced to 2 years and 8 months to 3 years and 3 months, each fined 30,000 to 40,000 yuan (Tongzhou, Beijing)
Note
For the consequences of lending out your bank card or running "money mule" payments for others, see No. 8 in Section 8 (lending out your bank card). This entry is about withdrawing and transferring money yourself. Taking money, converting it into virtual currency like Tether, and sending it out is the same offense. For why you can't get your own money back after a crypto loss, see No. 45 in Section 5 (don't buy virtual currency). "I didn't know where the money came from" won't necessarily be accepted when a case is handled. Absurdly high pay, requests to verify with face scans, transactions that look abnormal from any angle — on these alone you can be found to have actually known. The lightest outcome is still 10 days of detention, plus a record.

If someone recruits you to 'package documents' for loans and splits the fee by loan size, do none of it

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Help "package documents" for a loan and take a cut, and it's handled as fraud. One 126-member gang dressed up jobless people as "premium clients" and defrauded more than 80 banks of over 30 million yuan. The front signers took 30 percent of the loan as their cut; of the 80 already sentenced, 76 got 1 year and 4 months to 6 years and 6 months. Whoever's name the loan is in, the debt is theirs.

Cost
Costs nothing. Just refuse. Don't lend your ID card or credit record to anyone, don't sign loan contracts you haven't read, and don't attend in-person bank signings for someone else.
Benefit
Obtaining loans, bill acceptance, letters of credit, letters of guarantee, or the like from a bank or other financial institution by deception: where major losses are caused to the bank or other financial institution, up to 3 years, plus a fine imposed concurrently or separately (a fine alongside the sentence, or possibly only the fine). Especially major losses or other especially serious circumstances: 3 to 7 years plus a fine. The threshold for police to open an investigation is direct economic losses of 500,000 yuan or more. Never intending to repay, and defrauding loans with fabricated reasons for introducing funds or projects, fake economic contracts, fake supporting documents, or fake property certificates, is the crime of loan fraud. Under this item, 50,000 yuan defrauded is enough to open a case: up to 5 years plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan. Huge amounts or other serious circumstances: 5 to 10 years; especially huge: 10 years or more up to life imprisonment. Forging, altering, or trading official documents, certificates, or seals of state organs: up to 3 years, or 3 to 10 years in serious circumstances. Official case: a 126-member gang in 16 provinces and cities dressed up jobless people as "premium clients" and defrauded more than 80 bank branches of over 30 million yuan. The "clean-credit" front borrowers took 30 percent of the loan amount as their cut. The procuratorate prosecuted 105 "clean-credit" borrowers. Of the 80 sentenced at first instance in 2026, 76 got 1 year and 4 months to 6 years and 6 months for loan fraud plus fines. Another 4, for withdrawing cash for the gang, received combined punishment for loan fraud and money laundering (sentences for the two crimes counted together): 2 years and 4 months to 7 years and 6 months (nationwide). The crime of fraudulently obtaining loans in this entry follows the text as amended by Criminal Law Amendment (XI) from March 2021.
Note
"But I intended to repay" was not accepted in that case. The procuratorate established that these people had no jobs and no fixed assets, could never repay, and had spent their cut — so they were found to have never intended to repay. Those who withdrew the gang's cash may also face an additional money laundering charge. Whoever's name the loan is in and whoever signed the contract is the borrower. Even short of a crime, the debt and the credit record are yours. Fleeing abroad with the money doesn't close the matter either: once a case is filed, you can be pursued no matter how many years pass. Those with unserved sentences, or currently treated as criminal suspects or defendants, may not leave the country. Where a civil case is unresolved, a court can bar you from leaving; where a judgment debtor fails to comply, the court can also restrict exit. For withdrawing and transferring money for others, see No. 5 in this section ("part-time jobs" that have you collect money with your own card); for finding out you've been impersonated into a loan, see No. 9 in Section 8.

7

Found a bank card? Don't withdraw money. Found a phone or wallet? Contact the owner or hand it to the police — don't pocket it

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Keep found property for yourself and, once the amount reaches "relatively large," refuse to hand it over: up to 2 years; "huge" amounts, 2 to 5 years. Using a found bank card at an ATM is worse — it counts as fraudulently using another person's credit card: 5 years or less for relatively large amounts, plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan. For the ATM kind, the police open the case themselves; the owner doesn't have to sue.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes minutes. Call the owner, or drop the item at a police station.
Benefit
Found property must be returned to the owner, with prompt notice to come collect it, or handed to public security or other departments. Keeping what someone else left behind for your own use and, once the amount is "relatively large," refusing to hand it over constitutes the crime of embezzlement: up to 2 years. Huge amounts: 2 to 5 years. Taking someone else's found credit card to an ATM is "fraudulent use of another person's credit card." Where it rises to a crime, it's handled as credit card fraud: relatively large amounts, up to 5 years plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan; huge amounts or other serious circumstances, 5 to 10 years plus a fine of 50,000 to 500,000 yuan (nationwide)
Note
Embezzlement is "handled only upon complaint": the owner must sue in court themselves; the police don't act on their own. Withdrawing money from a found card is different — the owner need not sue; the police open the case directly. What counts as "relatively large" is set by judicial interpretation; this section did not verify the figure. After an item is handed to the relevant department, the owner pays storage fees when collecting it (Civil Code, Article 317).

8

Claim discounts under your real identity; don't buy virtual numbers to mass-register sockpuppets, and don't farm a loophole for repeated claims

Grade AValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Claiming a coupon once per account under your real identity is not within the scope of punishment. Mass-registering fake users, or placing and accepting your own orders to claim more, is handled as fraud: 3,000 yuan is enough for up to 3 years, and from 30,000 yuan it's 3 to 10 years. Delivery riders used virtual numbers bought at 0.1 yuan apiece to farm coupons and cashed out over 90,000 yuan; all 12 co-defendants were sentenced.

Cost
Costs nothing. Walk away from the gigs in "freebie task groups." If you find a platform loophole, leave it alone. The hard part is not treating discounts as income you can mass-produce.
Benefit
Defrauding others or the public of property: relatively large amounts, up to 3 years plus a fine imposed concurrently or separately (a fine alongside the sentence, or possibly only the fine). Huge amounts or other serious circumstances: 3 to 10 years plus a fine. Especially huge amounts or other especially serious circumstances: 10 years or more or life imprisonment, plus a fine or confiscation of property. The three tiers — relatively large, huge, and especially huge — are set locally by each province within these ranges: relatively large is 3,000 yuan to 10,000 yuan or more; huge is 30,000 yuan to 100,000 yuan or more; especially huge is 500,000 yuan or more. Teaching the method to others or selling "tutorials": up to 5 years for the crime of teaching criminal methods, 5 to 10 years in serious circumstances, and 10 years or more or life imprisonment in especially serious ones. The upstream and downstream trades in phone numbers and verification codes: up to 3 years for infringing citizens' personal information, 3 to 7 years in especially serious cases. Bulk accounts, automatic network-address switching systems, and SMS-code-receiving platforms for bulk verification are themselves expressly banned by Article 14 of the Anti-Telecom and Online Fraud Law. Illegally buying, selling, renting, or lending phone cards and internet accounts, and helping others pass real-name verification, fall under Article 31. Violating Article 14: all earnings confiscated, plus a fine of 1 to 10 times the earnings; where nothing was earned, or under 50,000 yuan, a fine of up to 500,000 yuan, and in serious circumstances also up to 15 days of detention. Violating Article 31: the same 1-to-10-times fine; where nothing was earned or under 20,000 yuan, a fine of up to 200,000 yuan, and in serious circumstances also up to 15 days of detention. Participating in telecom and online fraud that falls short of a crime: 10 to 15 days of detention, earnings confiscated, plus a fine of 1 to 10 times; where nothing was earned or under 10,000 yuan, a fine of up to 100,000 yuan. Official case one: delivery rider Liu bought virtual phone numbers at 0.1 yuan apiece to register as new users on a platform. He claimed the "15 off 29" newcomer coupon in full on his orders, then resold the goods to small shops for cash. He also used the virtual numbers to invite one another and collect reward money of 2 to 20 yuan. He and fellow rider Tan defrauded just over 90,000 yuan and just over 70,000 yuan respectively. The Shanghai Yangpu District procuratorate prosecuted 12 people for fraud, and the court sentenced them to 3 years and 6 months down to 3 months of criminal detention. Official case two: Wang exploited the time lag between refunds at his online store and the return of virtual lottery tokens. He refunded 1,156 orders and walked off with 224 collectible figures worth just over 249,000 yuan, cashing out on secondhand platforms. The court sentenced him to 3 years, suspended for 4, for fraud, plus a fine of 30,000 yuan. During the trial he returned the proceeds and prepaid the fine, 330,000 yuan in total. Official case three: a ride-hailing platform's new-user coupons and driver subsidies were defrauded through fake runs in which the same person hailed and accepted the ride — across 19 provinces and more than 70 cities, totaling over 2 million yuan. The Liaoning Chaoyang Longcheng district procuratorate prosecuted 163 people, all convicted. Ringleaders Huang and Cai received combined sentences for fraud, infringing citizens' personal information, and teaching criminal methods (sentences for several crimes counted together), 3 years and 6 months each. Another 34 minor accomplices were declined prosecution but still referred to the police for administrative punishment (nationwide)
Note
The line isn't "how much did you farm" but "did you fabricate anything." Joining a promotion under your real identity, claiming once per account, and using the coupon on yourself is a discount the platform gave you. Registering fake users, inventing transactions, or concealing that you've already refunded, in order to claim more — that's making the other side hand over goods on a false belief, and it's treated as fraud; the amount only decides how long the sentence is. Free EV charging has been farmed this way too. In August 2026 Kankan News reported that two people in Shanghai bought large quantities of virtual phone numbers and took turns binding them as sub-accounts on an EV maker's app. Each number charged twice under "charge now, pay later," then unbound with no one paying the electricity bill, and the charging sessions were resold to truck drivers. The Pudong New Area procuratorate deemed it fraud, not theft, and approved arrest. This case has media reports only — no verdict or official notice. Even amounts too small to prosecute have consequences: platforms can ban the account, claw back the discount, and demand return of "money you shouldn't have" under unjust enrichment. Participating in telecom fraud below the criminal threshold still brings the detention-and-fine tier. "Someone in the group led it and paid me per order" doesn't change the nature of your own share. Teaching the method to others or reselling accounts and phone numbers are separate offenses, and several crimes get counted together. The beneficiary is you. For writing and selling scripts yourself, see No. 3 in Section 11; for selling cards and accounts, see No. 8 in Section 8 (lending out your bank card) and No. 16 in this section (never lend out your ID card).

9

Throw nothing from balconies or windows — cigarette butts, garbage bags, and bottles all count

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Throw things off a building and even without hitting anyone you can get 5 days of detention and a 1,000-yuan fine; in serious circumstances, 10 to 15 days of detention. Hit someone and the charge changes: one drunk man threw empty bottles and a glass from the 21st floor onto a playground below, struck a 13-year-old student, and caused grievous injury — 10 years. Another threw 8 bricks from the 32nd floor and killed one person, with a death sentence approved in 2024.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time. Cigarette butts, garbage bags, bottles — take them all to the trash bin inside instead of tossing them out the window or off the balcony.
Benefit
Throwing objects from buildings or other high places, where there is a danger of injuring people, damaging property, or endangering public safety: up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Serious circumstances: 10 to 15 days of detention plus a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Serious enough to constitute the crime of throwing objects from heights: up to 1 year, plus a fine imposed concurrently or separately (a fine alongside the sentence, or possibly only the fine). Injuring or killing someone is handled under heavier charges. Official cases: Li, drunk, threw empty bottles and a glass from the 21st floor onto the playground below, striking a 13-year-old student and causing grade-II grievous injury — 10 years for endangering public safety by dangerous means. Zhou threw 8 bricks from the 32nd floor into a crowd, killing one person; the Supreme People's Court approved the death penalty in 2024 (nationwide)
Note
Detention applies even without hitting anyone — the provision requires only "a danger." The Civil Code has a separate provision on civil compensation for objects thrown from heights (Article 1,254). The original text could not be opened while this section was written, so it is not cited.

Don't buy replica guns, steel-ball guns, or airguns online; don't buy 'toy guns' of unknown origin

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Steel-ball guns and airguns bought online are classified as firearms once muzzle specific kinetic energy reaches 1.8 joules per square centimeter. Holding one without a permit: up to 3 years, or 3 to 7 years in serious circumstances. One couple sold "toy guns"; 18 of 43 were forensically classified as firearms, and they escaped prosecution only because their knowledge couldn't be proven.

Cost
Costs nothing. Want to shoot? Go to a proper shooting range.
Benefit
Possessing or secretly keeping firearms without a permit: up to 3 years, or 3 to 7 years in serious circumstances. Non-standard guns that cannot fire standard-issue ammunition are classified as firearms whenever muzzle specific kinetic energy is 1.8 joules per square centimeter or more. Muzzle specific kinetic energy means the energy per square centimeter the projectile carries as it leaves the barrel. Many steel-ball guns and airguns bought online exceed this figure. Since 2018, the Supreme People's Court and Supreme People's Procuratorate have required that, for airguns with relatively low specific kinetic energy, appearance, materials, price, intended use, and whether the person knew be weighed together before deciding whether to convict. Official case: the Zhao couple sold "toy guns" at a market; 43 were seized, 18 of which met the firearm standard upon forensic examination. Because there was insufficient evidence they knew they were firearms, prosecution was declined on evidentiary grounds (nationwide)
Note
The key to non-prosecution in that case was the finding that they "did not know." An adult who deliberately goes online to buy a steel-ball gun or airgun will have a hard time claiming afterward not to have known it was a gun. For the penalties on carrying crossbows and controlled knives, see No. 26 in this section (don't buy batons, stun guns, or daggers for self-defense).

11

After buying a drone, register it under your real name; don't fly near airports, military zones, or restricted urban airspace, and don't crack the altitude limiter

Grade AValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Fly without real-name registration: a fine of up to 200 yuan, or 2,000 to 20,000 yuan in serious circumstances. Fly in controlled airspace without approval: a fine of up to 500 yuan; in serious circumstances the drone is confiscated plus a fine of 1,000 to 10,000 yuan. Relatively serious violations can also mean 5 to 10 days of detention. One person paid to crack the altitude limiter, flew to nearly 3,000 meters to film cloud layers and post them online, and got 5 days of detention.

Cost
Real-name registration costs nothing and takes a few minutes. Before every flight, check through official channels whether the area you plan to fly is controlled airspace.
Benefit
Flying without real-name registration: ordered to correct, plus a fine of up to 200 yuan, or 2,000 to 20,000 yuan in serious circumstances. Flying micro, light, or small drones in controlled airspace without approval: ordered to stop flying, plus a fine of up to 500 yuan. Serious circumstances under this item: drone confiscated plus a fine of 1,000 to 10,000 yuan. Flying in violation of airspace management rules, in relatively serious cases: 5 to 10 days of detention. Official cases: Li paid to crack the altitude limiter, flew a drone to nearly 3,000 meters to film clouds and publish the footage — 5 days of detention. Zhang cracked altitude and no-fly zone restrictions for others more than 20 times, earning over 15,000 yuan. He was convicted of providing programs or tools for intruding into or unlawfully controlling computer information systems: 6 months, 1 year of probation, plus a fine (nationwide, since January 2024)
Note
Micro and light drones need no approval to fly in eligible airspace. Micro means an unladen weight under 0.25 kilograms. Eligible airspace is everything outside controlled airspace, and the areas around airports, military installations, and government offices mostly count as controlled. The MPS's original page was inaccessible when this section was written, so the Hubei Provincial Public Security Department's reposted page is cited.

Don't secretly film people; don't install cameras in rentals, guesthouses, or hotel rooms

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Secretly filming, peeping, or spreading someone's private life: up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan; relatively serious, 5 to 10 days. Using specialized covert-filming equipment and causing serious consequences: up to 2 years. Two men installed equipment in rooms at three hotels to film remotely, and got 1 year and 3 months and 1 year respectively. Security cameras in your own home don't count; cameras in rooms other people occupy do.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time. Don't secretly film people, and don't install cameras in rentals, guesthouses, or hotel rooms.
Benefit
Peeping, secretly filming, wiretapping, or spreading others' privacy: up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Relatively serious: 5 to 10 days of detention plus a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Unlawfully using dedicated wiretapping or covert-photography equipment and causing serious consequences: up to 2 years. Dedicated wiretapping or covert-photography equipment means devices made specifically for secret listening and filming. Official case: Yan and Yan bought covert-photography equipment online, installed it in multiple rooms across three hotels, and filmed remotely — 1 year and 3 months and 1 year respectively (nationwide)
Note
Once the footage is sold or spread, it is separately handled under crimes such as producing or selling obscene materials for profit — the same batch of cases includes a 10-year sentence. Cameras in your own home don't count; cameras in rooms other people use do.

Mahjong and poker are fine; no rake, no being the house, no organizing games for money, and no online gambling

Grade BValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Small-stakes cards among family and friends are none of the law's business. Take a rake from the game, be the house, or organize games for money, and the nature changes: gambling with relatively large stakes means up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Gathering people to gamble or living off gambling: up to 3 years; running a casino: up to 5 years. What counts as "relatively large stakes" is set locally — there is no national figure.

Cost
Costs nothing. Keep playing small-stakes games with family and friends. No skimming, no being the house, no organizing for money. The hard part is not taking over when someone starts setting a game up.
Benefit
Providing facilities for gambling for profit, or gambling with relatively large stakes: up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Serious circumstances: 10 to 15 days of detention plus a fine of 1,000 to 5,000 yuan. Gathering people to gamble for profit, or living off gambling: up to 3 years plus a fine. Running a casino: up to 5 years plus a fine, or 5 to 10 years in serious circumstances (nationwide)
Note
There is no national figure for "relatively large stakes"; localities set their own, which is why this entry is only Grade B. Skimming from games and collecting bets on behalf of online gambling platforms are often treated as running a casino when cases are handled. The relevant judicial interpretation was not verified for this section. No official case was found either.

Don't eat wild game; don't trade or keep protected animals as pets

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Eat animals under state key protection and they are confiscated, plus a fine of 2 to 20 times their value. Buying, transporting, or selling rare and endangered animals: up to 5 years, or 5 to 10 years in serious circumstances. Captive-bred animals traded as pets generally aren't crimes — one seller of 40-plus captive-bred parrots was not prosecuted. Wild-caught animals and those of unknown origin are another matter.

Cost
Costs nothing. Buy only legally sourced, captive-bred species as pets.
Benefit
Eating wildlife under state key protection, or buying it in order to eat it: the animals are confiscated plus a fine of 2 to 20 times their value. Breeding wildlife under state key protection without a permit: confiscation plus a fine of 1 to 10 times. Illegally purchasing, transporting, or selling rare and endangered wildlife under state key protection, or their products: up to 5 years plus a fine. Serious circumstances under this item: 5 to 10 years; especially serious: 10 years or more. Hunting, buying, transporting, or selling other terrestrial wild animals for food, in serious circumstances: up to 3 years. Official case: breeder Wang and two others sold 40-plus captive-bred Fischer's lovebirds (state second-class protection) worth under 400 yuan in total; in 2021 the procuratorate decided not to prosecute. From 2022, the Supreme People's Court and Supreme People's Procuratorate have made clear that captive breeding with mature techniques, already at scale, and traded or transported as pets is generally not treated as a crime (nationwide)
Note
"Generally not treated as a crime" covers only the captive-bred, kept-as-pets category. Wild-caught animals and those of unknown origin don't qualify. Which animals count as state key protected species is determined by the official list. Check the list before buying — easier than explaining yourself after the fact.

When collecting a debt: no seizing people, no locking them up, no following them home and refusing to leave

Grade AValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Even if the money really is owed to you, you can't seize or confine anyone. The statute says it outright: seizing or confining someone to collect a debt is still handled as unlawful detention. The lighter tier is 10 to 15 days of detention plus a fine of 1,000 to 2,000 yuan. The crime of unlawful detention: up to 3 years; causing grievous injury, 3 to 10 years; causing death, 10 years or more. To collect a debt, sue in court.

Cost
Costs nothing. If they won't repay, sue in court. For how to write an IOU, see No. 18 in Section 8 (IOUs). The hard part is not getting physical or following them home when they welch.
Benefit
Unlawfully restricting someone's personal freedom, barging into their home uninvited, or unlawfully searching their person: 10 to 15 days of detention plus a fine of 1,000 to 2,000 yuan. Relatively light: 5 to 10 days of detention plus a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Unlawful detention carries up to 3 years of fixed-term imprisonment, criminal detention (short-term custody), public surveillance (no custody but restricted movement), or deprivation of political rights. Causing grievous injury: 3 to 10 years; causing death: 10 years or more. Seizing or confining someone to collect a debt is punished under this same set of provisions, even when the debt is real (nationwide)
Note
"He really did owe me money" doesn't work here. The statute says explicitly that seizing or confining someone to collect a debt is handled as unlawful detention. China Courts Online carried several cases of people sentenced to 7 months to 1 year for locking up debtors over lawful debts. The site was down when this section was written, so they are not cited.

Never lend out your ID card, never use someone else's, and never check in, open cards, or buy tickets with another person's documents

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Lend, rent out, or transfer your ID card to someone else: a warning plus a fine of up to 200 yuan. Use someone else's ID card, or one obtained by fraud: a fine of 200 to 1,000 yuan, or up to 10 days of detention. Using fake or borrowed documents for real-name-required things like train tickets or hotel check-ins can, in serious circumstances, mean criminal detention or public surveillance.

Cost
Costs nothing. If someone asks to borrow it, refuse. When you must hand over a copy, write on the copy what specific matter it is for.
Benefit
Renting out, lending, or transferring your resident ID card to others: a warning plus a fine of up to 200 yuan. Using another person's ID card, or one obtained by fraud: a fine of 200 to 1,000 yuan, or up to 10 days of detention. Buying, selling, or using forged or altered ID cards falls in the same tier. Some situations require proof of identity under state rules. Using forged, altered, or stolen documents in those situations, where circumstances are serious, brings a criminal sentence. Documents include ID cards, passports, social security cards, driver's licenses, and so on. The penalty is criminal detention (short-term custody) or public surveillance (no custody but restricted movement), plus a fine imposed concurrently or separately — a fine alongside the sentence, or possibly only the fine (nationwide)
Note
A lent-out ID card can be used to register companies or open bank cards. For the consequences of those two, see Nos. 28 and 8 in Section 8 (don't be a nominal legal representative; don't lend out your bank card). Buying train tickets or checking into hotels with someone else's ID falls under "activities requiring proof of identity" in the statute. No official case was found for this entry. The same goes at internet cafés: always use your own card. Cafés must verify and register ID cards, and keep the registration and browsing records for at least 60 days, available to public security and culture authorities at any time. Whatever happens on that machine during your session is on the head of whoever's card was used.

When police stop or take you in, cooperate: no pushing, no hitting, no grabbing their body camera — with alcohol in you, hold back all the more

Grade AValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Obstructing enforcement on the spot: a warning or a fine of up to 500 yuan; serious circumstances, 5 to 10 days of detention. Laying hands on police is another tier: biting, slapping, kicking, tackling, throwing things — causing minor injury or worse counts as violent assault on police, up to 3 years. Using a gun, a controlled knife, or a car to ram: 3 to 7 years. Shaking off a grip and other ordinary resistance don't count.

Cost
Costs nothing. Keep your hands to yourself on the spot. Raise objections afterward: file a complaint, apply for administrative reconsideration, or sue in court. The hard part is holding your temper in those few minutes when you're stopped — especially after drinking.
Benefit
Obstructing state functionaries performing official duties according to law: a warning or a fine of up to 500 yuan. Serious circumstances: 5 to 10 days of detention plus a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Obstructing people's police draws heavier punishment. Violently attacking a people's police officer lawfully performing duties: up to 3 years. Using a gun, a controlled knife, or ramming with a car — seriously endangering an officer's personal safety: 3 to 7 years. Biting, slapping, kicking, tackling, or throwing objects causing minor injury or above is what counts as "violent attack." Shaking off a grip, struggling free, and kicking away are ordinary resistance and don't count (nationwide)
Note
Per a 2021 Supreme People's Procuratorate briefing, in the first month after assaulting police became a standalone crime, 405 people were approved for arrest. Of 42 cases in Jiangsu, 47.6 percent stemmed from drunken altercations. Of 16 cases in Hubei, 12 involved nothing worse than punching, kicking, and biting. Laying hands on auxiliary officers is handled as obstructing official duties. No official case spelling out individual circumstances was found for this entry.

No sex with anyone under 14 — 'she agreed' is no defense

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Sex with someone under 14 is handled as rape with heavier punishment regardless of whether she agreed, with a base sentence of 3 to 10 years. Under 12: you are deemed to "have known" without exception. Between 12 and 14: if her physical development, manner, or dress shows she might be a child, and you proceed anyway, you are deemed to have "knowingly" known. Claims of genuine ignorance face a very strict bar in court.

Cost
Costs nothing. If the other person's age is uncertain, don't have sex.
Benefit
Sex with a girl under 14 is handled as rape with heavier punishment; the base sentence is 3 to 10 years. The Supreme People's Court's line: where violence, coercion, or other forceful means are used, it is rape regardless of whether the offender knew she was a child. Without forceful means, for those under 12, "should have known" is found without exception. For ages 12 to 14, where physical development, speech and manner, or dress shows she might be a child and the offender proceeds anyway, "actual knowledge" is found. The "genuinely didn't know" exception is applied very strictly (nationwide)
Note
The original pages of the two-supreme-two-ministries opinion on handling criminal cases of sexual assault against minors, and of the Supreme People's Court's 2003 reply, were inaccessible when this section was written. So the standard for finding "knowledge" cites the reply on the SPC's official website. The statute's term is "young girl." This entry makes no distinction between male and female perpetrators.

Before you hit someone, do the math: detention, compensation, prison

Grade AValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

The bill for one swing: 5 to 10 days of detention plus a fine of 500 to 1,000 yuan. Cause minor injury and it's a criminal case: up to 3 years; grievous injury, 3 to 10 years. Money is separate: one man broke three of the other man's ribs and paid 113,000 yuan in a settlement to escape prosecution. Another broke the other man's radius, paid nothing, and got 10 months.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time. The hard part is the few seconds before you swing.
Benefit
Beating someone or intentional injury: 5 to 10 days of detention plus a fine of 500 to 1,000 yuan. Gang beatings, beating disabled people, pregnant women, the elderly, or children, repeated beatings, or beating several people at once: 10 to 15 days of detention plus a fine of 1,000 to 2,000 yuan. Minor injury makes it the crime of intentional injury: up to 3 years of fixed-term imprisonment, criminal detention (short-term custody), or public surveillance (no custody but restricted movement). Grievous injury: 3 to 10 years. Civilly, you also pay medical expenses, lost wages (money not earned from missed work), nursing fees, transport costs, hospital meal allowances, and nutrition fees. If the victim is left disabled, disability compensation is added on. Disability compensation is calculated as the previous year's per-capita disposable income of urban residents where the court sits, times 20 years. For victims over 60, one year is subtracted for each additional year of age; over 75, it's 5 years. In 2022, procuratorates nationwide accepted more than 70,000 minor-injury cases, most arising from marriage, family, and neighborhood disputes or chance incidents. Supreme People's Procuratorate typical cases: Lu broke three of the other man's ribs (grade-II minor injury) and paid 113,000 yuan in a settlement to be spared prosecution. Shi broke the other man's radius (grade-II minor injury), paid nothing, and got 10 months of fixed-term imprisonment (nationwide; Public Security Administration Punishments Law effective January 1, 2026)
Note
For avoiding conflict, why striking first loses, and where the line of justifiable defense sits, see No. 10 in Section 8 (conflict and justifiable defense). For the bill on lashing out at someone in anger, see Nos. 11 to 14 in Section 8. Fights arising from civil disputes with relatively minor circumstances can be mediated by the police. For minor injuries, agreeing on compensation with the other side and actually paying it can bring a lighter sentence or even non-prosecution — but not a yuan of the compensation is waived. What counts as minor injury is set by forensic standards; this section did not verify them. Lost wages and nursing fees are calculated from actual income and days missed; there is no uniform figure.

Can't raise a child you've had? Civil-affairs adoption registration is the only legal way out: taking money to give the child away can be prosecuted as trafficking, and abandonment is a crime

Grade AValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

There is a way out if you can't raise the child, but only one legal one: adoption registration with the civil affairs department — the adoption takes effect only from the day of registration. Privately giving a child away, especially for money, can turn from "placing for adoption" into child trafficking, whose starting sentence is 5 years or more. Abandoning a child and refusing to support them, in vile circumstances, is the crime of abandonment: up to 5 years.

Cost
Costs nothing. Adoption registration at a civil affairs department at or above the county level requires submitting materials and waiting for review and an adoption assessment, which takes some time.
Benefit
Criminal Law Article 240: "Whoever abducts and traffics women or children shall be sentenced to 5 to 10 years of fixed-term imprisonment and fined." With aggravating circumstances: 10 years or more of fixed-term imprisonment or life imprisonment, plus a fine or confiscation of property. "Where circumstances are especially serious, the death penalty applies, with confiscation of property." Article 17 of the Opinion on Punishing Crimes of Abducting and Trafficking Women and Children According to Law addresses how to distinguish selling one's own child from private placement. The test is "the key lies in whether the actor had the purpose of unlawful gain" — that is, whether they meant to profit from it. Three situations can be found to be selling one's own child and convicted as trafficking women or children. The first is "treating childbearing as a means of unlawful gain and selling the child immediately after birth." The second is "'placing' the child with others for money while knowing the recipient has no intention of raising it, or giving no thought at all to whether they intend to raise it." The third is "'placing' the child with others for a huge sum clearly beyond 'nutrition fees' or 'gratitude fees.'" Conversely, private placement out of genuine hardship rather than for profit, accepting only small nutrition or gratitude fees, is private placement and is not convicted as trafficking. Then Criminal Law Article 261: "Whoever has a duty to support the elderly, the young, the ill, or others without independent living capacity and refuses to do so, in vile circumstances, shall be sentenced to up to 5 years of fixed-term imprisonment, criminal detention, or public surveillance." Civil Code Article 1,094 provides that only three parties may place a child for adoption: the guardian of an orphan, a child welfare institution, or birth parents with special difficulties who are unable to raise the child. Article 1,105: "Adoption shall be registered with the civil affairs department of a people's government at or above the county level. The adoption relationship is established from the date of registration."
Note
Whether to have the child is not discussed here. After the child is born, this sequence is the smoothest. Step one: give birth at a hospital — prenatal care and hospital delivery are covered in Section 27. The birth certificate is the prerequisite for every procedure after. Step two: if placing the child for adoption, go directly to a civil affairs department at or above the county level; don't go through intermediaries. Once money changes hands, the nature can change. Within a year after giving birth, if thoughts of harming yourself or the child appear, treat it as an emergency. For the list of pregnancy and postpartum signs requiring an immediate hospital visit, see No. 7 in Section 27. The 42-day postpartum check doubles as postpartum depression screening — see No. 16 in Section 27. For suicidal thoughts, call 12356 — see No. 25 in Section 1. No case is attached to this entry: the official typical cases on trafficking one's own children were not verified case by case this round, so only the statutes and the opinion's text are cited.

Don't stage accidents or inflate losses for insurance claims: that's insurance fraud, and anyone who testifies, repairs, or appraises for you is implicated too

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Inventing accidents or inflating losses to claim insurance is insurance fraud: relatively large amounts, up to 5 years plus a fine of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan. Anyone who testifies, appraises, or values property for you and deliberately issues false documents is convicted as an accomplice alongside you. In one case in Xuancheng, Anhui, 8 people got 2 to 4 years, each fined 10,000 yuan.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time — just don't do it.
Benefit
Criminal Law Article 198 lists five situations. (1) The policyholder deliberately fabricates the insurance subject — inventing an insured object that doesn't exist at all. (2) The policyholder, insured, or beneficiary fabricates false causes for an insured event that occurred, or inflates the extent of the losses. (3) Fabricating an insured event that never happened. (4) The policyholder or insured deliberately causing an insured event that damages property. (5) The policyholder or beneficiary deliberately causing the insured's death, disability, or illness. Relatively large amounts: up to 5 years of fixed-term imprisonment or criminal detention, plus a fine of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan. Huge amounts or other serious circumstances: 5 to 10 years, plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan. Especially huge amounts or other especially serious circumstances: 10 years or more, plus a fine of 20,000 to 200,000 yuan or confiscation of property. The final paragraph of this article covers the helpers: appraisers, witnesses, and property valuers in insurance matters. Those who deliberately issue false documents and create conditions for others' insurance fraud are treated as accomplices to insurance fraud and convicted together with the fraudster. Insurance Law Article 27: claiming an insured event that never happened lets the insurer rescind the contract without refunding the premiums. Where forged or altered supporting materials are used, or accident causes fabricated or losses inflated, the insurer doesn't pay the overstated portion, and what was already paid must be returned or made good. Case: in the Zhang case in Xuancheng, Anhui, 8 people including Wang were sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment ranging from 4 years down to 2 years for insurance fraud, each with a fine of 10,000 yuan. A sham litigation spun off from the case: the insurer assessed the losses at 20,000 yuan, but the party used a forged vehicle transfer agreement to gain standing to sue, and the court awarded just over 70,000 yuan. That final civil judgment was set aside on retrial on September 26, 2019. The Anti-Insurance Fraud Work Measures require risk information checks at both ends — underwriting and claims. They also call for exploring a multi-line industry anti-fraud information platform and an anti-fraud intelligence center. These platforms screen suspicious fraud data in bulk, passing leads to industry associations, anti-fraud organizations, and insurers to verify. Suspected crimes are reported to the public security organs promptly. The financial regulator and its local offices must build sound mechanisms linking administrative law enforcement with criminal justice alongside the public security organs, people's procuratorates, and people's courts (nationwide, issued July 31, 2024)
Note
Several practices that feel harmless fall within these five items: after a minor accident, asking the repair shop to "pad the claim a little"; folding old damage into this one claim; deliberately bumping cars with a friend and then filing; or inventing an accident that never happened. For how to buy car insurance, see No. 26 in Section 5 (buy enough third-party liability). Deliberately causing an insured family member's death after taking out a policy is expressly subject to combined punishment for multiple crimes — see No. 38 in Section 8 (insuring family members). Medical insurance runs on a different set of rules: swiping a health insurance card with no treatment, or cashing out the personal account, is handled as fraud — see the note to No. 13 in Section 5.

Don't sell your organs or find donors for others: the seller nets just over 20,000 yuan per kidney while the same one resells for 200,000 — proceeds are confiscated plus a fine of 10 to 20 times the deal

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Living organs can only be donated to a spouse, lineal relatives, or collateral relatives within three generations; any buying or selling is illegal. In a Beijing case, the kidney seller received only a bit over 20,000 yuan, while the same kidney was sold to the patient for 180,000 to 220,000 yuan. The proceeds are confiscated, plus a fine of 10 to 20 times the deal. For the physical cost of losing a kidney, see No. 35 in Section 1 (one kidney doing the work of two).

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time — just don't do it.
Benefit
Regulations on Human Organ Donation and Transplantation, Article 5: "No organization or individual may buy or sell human organs in any form, or engage in activities related to the buying and selling of human organs." Article 10: "No organization or individual may obtain living organs from citizens under 18 for transplantation." Article 11: "Recipients of living organs are limited to the donor's spouse, lineal relatives, or collateral relatives within three generations." Article 37 sets out the penalties for organ trading. Buying and selling human organs, or engaging in related activities, is investigated and handled by the health departments of local people's governments at or above the county level. First, illegal gains are confiscated — every yuan from the deal is taken. Then a fine of 10 to 20 times the transaction amount is imposed. Medical personnel involved have their practice certificates revoked and are banned for life from providing medical and health services. Where a crime is constituted, criminal responsibility is pursued according to law (nationwide, effective May 1, 2024; the former Regulations on Human Organ Transplantation repealed at the same time). Criminal Law Article 234-1: "Whoever organizes others to sell human organs shall be sentenced to up to 5 years of fixed-term imprisonment and fined; in serious circumstances, 5 years or more, plus a fine or confiscation of property." Three more situations are convicted and punished under Criminal Law Articles 234 and 232: taking someone's organs without their consent; taking the organs of a person under 18; and forcing or deceiving someone into donating an organ. These are handled as intentional injury or intentional homicide. Case one: the case of Zheng Wei and 14 others, final at the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court on August 20, 2014, involved 51 kidneys and over 10.34 million yuan. The sellers (donors) "received only 20,000 to 25,000 yuan each." On the buyers' (recipients') side, "a kidney used to cost 180,000 or 190,000, later 210,000 or 220,000." The removal site was a four-story building rented for 7,500 yuan a month; the gang's head nurse testified that the place was "filthy beyond description, with no rescue equipment at all." Organizer Zheng Wei got 12 years for organizing the sale of human organs; the other 14 got 3.5 to 9 years. Case two: the "teen sells kidney for an iPhone" case published by the Supreme People's Procuratorate. Wang, 17, had his right kidney removed in Chenzhou on the night of April 28, 2011. The operating venue was a department contracted out by a hospital without transplant qualifications. When discharged on May 2 he had received 22,000 yuan; the recipient side paid the brokers 150,000 yuan and 10,000 US dollars, and the lead offender cleared just over 56,000 yuan. Wang was left with renal insufficiency after the surgery; "the injury was assessed as grievous bodily harm, grade-III disability."
Note
The beneficiary is you. The deal looks like "20,000 in one payout"; in reality it's an organ traded for a phone. The teen kidney case's forensic finding was grievous bodily harm and grade-III disability — months of rest won't fix that. In that case, the prosecutors found the 5 defendants violated Paragraph 2 of Criminal Law Article 234 and prosecuted them for intentional injury. One reason: the medical staff removed the right kidney without verifying whether the "donor" was a minor. If the same thing happened today, the recruiters would be handled for organizing the sale of human organs, and removing the organs of anyone under 18 is still convicted and punished as intentional injury under Article 234. Black-market brokers do the surgery in rented rooms or borrowed venues — no evaluation beyond tissue matching, no post-op follow-up, and no one to own up to complications. To genuinely donate to a family member, take the Article 11 route: done at a qualified transplant institution, reviewed by an ethics committee, unpaid throughout. Posthumous donation of organs from the deceased is unpaid and outside this entry's scope. For what losing a kidney costs your body, see No. 35 in Section 1 (one kidney doing the work of two). When money is so tight that selling an organ crosses your mind, first look at the assistance channels in Section 7 (unemployment insurance, temporary assistance, minimum living allowance). For the traps of online loans and "packaged document" loans, see No. 6 in this section.
