Don't buy sex: the default tier is 10 to 15 days of detention, not a small fine

Grade AValue: FairBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Getting caught is not a matter of paying a small fine and walking away. The statute's default tier is 10 to 15 days of detention, plus a fine of up to 5,000 yuan. Only relatively light cases get up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. And knowingly having syphilis or gonorrhea and buying sex anyway is a crime: up to 5 years.

Cost
Costs nothing and takes no time — just don't do it.
Benefit
Public Security Administration Punishments Law Article 78: prostitution and buying sex — 10 to 15 days of detention, and a fine of up to 5,000 yuan may be imposed concurrently. Relatively light circumstances: up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Soliciting in public places: up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to 1,000 yuan. Article 79: enticing, harboring, or procuring others into prostitution — 10 to 15 days of detention, and a fine of up to 5,000 yuan may be imposed concurrently. Relatively light circumstances: up to 5 days of detention or a fine of 1,000 to 2,000 yuan. Article 87: staff of hotels, food service, culture and entertainment businesses, taxi companies, and the like who tip off offenders during police crackdowns on prostitution or otherwise provide conditions for such activities — 10 to 15 days of detention. Criminal Law Article 360 is the crime of spreading venereal disease: knowingly having syphilis, gonorrhea, or another serious venereal disease and prostituting oneself or buying sex — up to 5 years of fixed-term imprisonment, criminal detention, or public surveillance, plus a fine (nationwide; Public Security Administration Punishments Law effective January 1, 2026)
Note
The detention here is administrative detention — you go to a detention house; it's not pay-and-leave. Procuring for someone or providing premises draws the same penalty as buying sex yourself; that's what the Article 79 tier covers. Hotel and KTV staff who tip off clients about police checks are likewise detained 10 to 15 days under Article 87. Criminal Law Article 360 once had a Paragraph 2, the crime of soliciting underage girls, deleted by Criminal Law Amendment (IX) in 2015; such acts are now punished directly as rape with heavier weight — see No. 18 in this section (no sex with anyone under 14). Signs like "in-home wellness" or "massage therapy" don't change the nature of what happens; the actual conduct governs. For the risks of venereal disease and HIV, see No. 30 in Section 1 (condoms throughout sex) and No. 38 in Section 13 (get post-exposure prophylaxis within 72 hours). For what to watch out for in entertainment venues themselves, see Section 22.

24

Fan-translated comics, re-uploaded shows, shared cloud-drive resources, and pirated e-books infringe even when free of charge; with ads or membership fees, prison becomes possible

Grade AValue: HighBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Translate and post someone's work without permission, or upload it online, and it's infringement even free of charge: take it down, pay damages. Add advertising or membership fees and it counts as for profit. 30,000 yuan earned, 500 works uploaded, or 1,000 members is enough for prison — up to 10 years. The head of the YYeTs subtitle group got 3 years and 6 months.

Cost
Costs nothing. Watching what you bought or downloaded yourself, even translating it for fun, is fine — just don't upload it for everyone to see. Don't run ad-supported or membership-charging resource sites and groups, and don't sell cloud-drive links. The hard part is not joining the re-upload line when "everyone's sharing it."
Benefit
Civil law first. Among an author's rights under the Copyright Law is the translation right — the right to turn the work from one language into another. There is also the right of communication through information networks — the right to put the work online for the public to access anytime, anywhere. Translating someone's work without permission is infringement; so is uploading it without permission. The infringer must stop the infringement and pay damages. Only personal study, research, or appreciation of an already published work exempts you from permission and payment. Damages are first calculated from the right holder's actual losses or your gains; where neither can be determined, the court sets a figure between 500 yuan and 5 million yuan. Willful infringement in serious circumstances can draw 1 to 5 times. The right holder's reasonable costs of stopping the infringement are also yours to pay. Now criminal law. Criminal Law Article 217 presupposes "for the purpose of profit." Putting others' works online for the public in order to make money, past the thresholds, is the crime of copyright infringement: up to 3 years plus a fine, or only the fine. Huge amounts or especially serious circumstances: 3 to 10 years plus a fine. What counts as for profit: besides selling, running paid ads on the page counts, as does charging registration or other fees under a membership system. Service fees, membership fees, and ad revenue all count as illegal gains. The criminal thresholds — clearing any one is enough: illegal gains of 30,000 yuan or more. Unlawful business revenue of 50,000 yuan or more — in the YYeTs case this was counted as total revenue from membership fees, advertising, and hard-drive sales. Distributing others' works online totaling 500 items (works) or more. Downloaded 10,000 times or more, or viewed 100,000 times or more. Membership-based distribution with 1,000 or more registered members. Below all of these, two items each reaching over half also counts. At 10 times these figures, you're in the 3-to-10-year tier. Fines are generally 1 to 10 times the illegal gains. Official case one: Liang Yongping and others downloaded unauthorized films and shows from overseas sites, organized translation and subtitling, and uploaded them for online viewing and download on the "YYeTs subtitle group" website and app. The site held 32,824 unauthorized film and TV works and over 6.83 million members. From January 2018 to January 2021 it collected over 2.7 million yuan in membership fees and over 8.8 million yuan in ad revenue. Selling portable hard drives loaded with the shows brought in over 1 million yuan more. The site displayed a "donation" QR code — donate and receive membership perks. The procuratorate found this was membership fees under another name. On November 22, 2021, Liang was sentenced to 3 years and 6 months and fined 1.5 million yuan. The other 14 got 1 year and 6 months to 3 years, all suspended, with fines of 40,000 to 350,000 yuan. Official case two: Ke used crawler software to harvest the playback addresses of over 50,000 films and shows and put them on his own website and app for free viewing. He sold advertising on the splash screen by impressions, earning just over 350,000 yuan. In 2023 he was sentenced to 3 years, suspended for 4, with a fine of 400,000 yuan. Official case three: Huang rented servers from his home and built a music download forum. He uploaded over 100,000 songs to 18 cloud drives and posted links on the forum. Members had to top up for forum coins to get the links and extraction codes; top-ups totaled over 500,000 yuan. In 2023 he was sentenced to 3 years, suspended for 4, with a fine of 550,000 yuan (nationwide; judicial interpretation effective April 26, 2025)
Note
The beneficiary is you. Watching what you bought and translating it for yourself sits within what the statutes allow. The line is "putting it online for everyone." Unpaid subtitle and fan-translation groups fall short of the crime of copyright infringement, because that crime requires profit-seeking. But civil infringement still stands, and right holders can demand takedowns and damages. In Japan, even without charging you may break the law. In February 2018 several Chinese nationals in Japan were arrested on suspicion of violating Japan's Copyright Act, and the Chinese Consulate General in Nagasaki followed with a reminder: translating, publishing, or distributing works without authorization may be unlawful even without profit. Run ads, charge membership, or trade "donations" for member perks, and you fall into the for-profit tier. In the YYeTs case, those who only translated or proofread had low participation and were treated as witnesses by the police. The Supreme People's Procuratorate spelled out in that case that organizers, profit-splitters, and platform operators face strict accountability. Hired accomplices can receive leniency, and temporarily recruited minor participants may be spared criminal liability. The three old intellectual-property criminal judicial interpretations of 2004, 2007, and 2020 were repealed effective April 26, 2025. The 2011 three-department opinion was not named as repealed; where it conflicts with the new interpretation, the new one governs. The view-count threshold, for instance, moved from 50,000 to 100,000. For the other risk of publishing fan fiction and derivative works, see No. 25 in this section (fan fiction). For printing others' images on merchandise to sell, see No. 21 in Section 12 (buy image licenses). For running a platform and receiving a right holder's infringement notice, see No. 9 in Section 26 (receiving an infringement notice).

Chinese Consulate General in Nagasaki Reminds Chinese Nationals in Japan to Comply with the Copyright Act. http://nagasaki.china-consulate.gov.cn/chn/tzgg/201802/t201…

Publishing or selling fan fiction and derivative works: get the original author's permission first, or replace the borrowed characters' names and relationships with your own

Grade BValue: HighBasis: MoneyMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Fan fiction that borrows only character names, personalities, and relationships can still be judged infringing when published. Jiang Nan's "Youth in Bygone Days" borrowed more than 60 characters from Jin Yong; on appeal he was ordered to pay 1.68 million yuan plus 200,000 yuan in costs. The lawsuit ran 9 years, ended in mediation, and he agreed not to republish the book as-is. For fan fiction shared free as a pastime, the courts say it must be analyzed case by case.

Cost
Costs nothing. Before publishing or selling, negotiate authorization with the original work's right holder. If that fails, replace the borrowed names, personalities, and character relationships with your own. And don't ride the original's name in the book title, subtitle, or taglines either.
Benefit
Jiang Nan's novel "Youth in Bygone Days" used the names of Guo Jing, Huang Rong, Qiao Feng, Linghu Chong, and other characters from Jin Yong's novels, telling of their days on a university campus. When published in 2002, the subtitle was "The College Years of the Condor Heroes." By the time of the lawsuit the book had come out in multiple editions and sold over a million copies. Jin Yong sued Jiang Nan and the publishers in 2016, seeking 5 million yuan. First instance found no copyright infringement: apart from the specific plot, mere character names, relationships, and personalities are hard to call protected concrete expression. But it found that Jiang Nan had borrowed the original's fame to attract readers, constituting unfair competition, and awarded 30 percent of the 5.6 million yuan in royalties across editions — 1.68 million yuan — plus 200,000 yuan in attorney fees. On appeal, the Guangzhou Intellectual Property Court reversed and found copyright infringement. It held that the two books' plots were not substantially similar — the plot wasn't copied — but that the "group portrait" of 60-plus characters, with their names, personalities, relationships, and backgrounds, was Jin Yong's choice and arrangement, expression protected by the Copyright Law, and that Jiang Nan had infringed the copyright of four of Jin Yong's novels. The subtitle's deliberate linkage to "The Legend of the Condor Heroes" separately constituted unfair competition. The appeal court ordered Jiang Nan to stop the unfair competition, publish a statement to eliminate its effects, and pay 1.68 million yuan plus 200,000 yuan in reasonable costs; the two publishing and distribution companies bore joint liability for 330,000 yuan of it — meaning they pay that part together. The appeal did not order the infringement stopped, but required that future reprints pay the original right holder 30 percent of reprint royalty income. After the appeal, both sides applied to the Guangdong High People's Court for retrial. On September 19, 2025, the parties reached a settlement under the court's auspices. In it, the parties agreed not to characterize the matter as "plagiarism." Jiang Nan acknowledged that he lacked knowledge of copyright law when writing, had not obtained Jin Yong's adaptation permission beforehand, and had caused him harm. He agreed not to republish the book as-is, and in future reprints to stop using the original character names and related content from Jin Yong's works. The parties confirmed that the subtitle constituted unfair competition. The compensation ordered on appeal had already been paid by Jiang Nan. Once the mediation statement was signed for, the first- and second-instance judgments lost legal effect. The defendant in another case was Zhang Muye, pen name Tianxia Bachang, author of "Ghost Blows Out the Light." In 2006 he transferred all property rights in the series' copyright to Shanghai Xuanting Entertainment Information Technology Co. He later authorized publication of a new book, "Mojin Xiaowei," using the character names, character relationships, and tomb-raiding rules of "Ghost Blows Out the Light"; the new book's cover used the poster of "Mojin: The Lost Legend," a film adapted from the series. Xuanting sued for 20 million yuan. The Shanghai Pudong court held that the new book had its own independent plot and was not copyright infringement, but that the cover misled readers into thinking the book was connected to the film's source material, constituting false advertising. The court ordered the two publishing and distribution companies to pay 900,000 yuan, with the publisher jointly liable for 600,000 yuan of it; the appeal upheld this. In statutory terms, the adaptation right is the right to alter a work and create a new original work from it. Using a work by adaptation, translation, annotation, or other means without the copyright holder's permission brings civil liability such as stopping the infringement and paying damages (nationwide)
Note
The beneficiary is you. It's Grade B because the legal boundaries of fan fiction are still unsettled. The two instances reached different conclusions and the case ended in mediation; neither judgment remains in effect. The handling judge at the Guangdong High Court said in a Q&A that the settlement binds only the parties to this case. Whether fan fiction infringes "must be analyzed case by case; it cannot be generalized." The judge's three-step sequence: first, whether what the two works share is an abstract idea or concrete expression; second, whether that expression is original to the original author; third, whether it falls under fair use or other non-infringing situations. So borrowing just a theme or a premise carries different risk from lifting a whole cast's names, personalities, and relationships. For fan fiction posted free online, this book found no official court rulings. The Copyright Law contains no exception saying "free means not infringing." Count the process cost too: from the July 2016 lawsuit to the September 2025 settlement, 9 years passed, through first instance, appeal, and retrial review — and Jin Yong himself died during the appeal. After an original author sells the copyright, their own sequel can still be sued by the buyer, as Tianxia Bachang found out. In copyright cases, the winner's reasonable costs of stopping the infringement count toward damages; the 200,000 yuan awarded at first instance here was attorney fees. For the risks of fan translations, re-uploads, and sharing others' works, see No. 24 in this section (fan-translated comics, re-uploaded shows).

"Jin Yong v. Jiang Nan" Copyright and Unfair Competition Dispute Settled in Guangdong. https://www.gdcourts.gov.cn/xwzx/fayuanxinmeiti/content/pos…; National Copyright Administration (2020). Shanghai's Ten Copyright Cases of 2019 Released (issued by the Shanghai Copyright Bureau; Case 6: the "Ghost Blows Out the Light" copyright infringement and unfair competition dispute). https://www.ncac.gov.cn/xxfb/ywxx/202004/t20200430_47269.html; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2020). Copyright Law (2020 amendment, Article 3, Article 10 Paragraph 1 Item 14, Article 52 Item 6, and Article 54). http://www.npc.gov.cn/npc/c2/c30834/202011/t20201119_308796…
26

Don't buy expandable batons, stun guns, daggers, or pepper spray for self-defense; keeping them in the car still counts as carrying

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: FreeMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Daggers, switchblades, police batons, stun guns and the like, carried out and found in a check: up to 5 days of detention. Brought into stations, malls, or buses: 5 to 10 days. Actually pulling one out tends to backfire too: one man, punched bare-handed, stabbed his attacker with a knife he had hidden in advance — 4 years for excessive defense.

Cost
Costs nothing. Keep anything already bought at home — don't take it out, don't put it in the car. If something happens, back away and call the police first; fight back only if you can't escape.
Benefit
Start with Public Security Administration Punishments Law Article 38. Unlawfully carrying crossbows, daggers, or other controlled implements under state rules: up to 5 days of detention, and a fine of up to 1,000 yuan may be added. Relatively light: a warning or a fine of up to 500 yuan. Taking them into public places or public transport: 5 to 10 days of detention, and a fine of up to 1,000 yuan may be added. Criminal Law Article 130 is heavier: unlawfully carrying controlled knives into public places or public transport, endangering public safety in serious circumstances — up to 3 years. Which knives count as controlled is set out in five categories in the Ministry of Public Security's 2007 recognition standards. The first is daggers: with handle, guard, and blood groove, tip angle under 60 degrees. The second is triangular scrapers. The third is spring knives with self-locking mechanisms, commonly called flick knives. The fourth is knives with tip angle under 60 degrees and blades over 150 millimeters. The fifth is knives with tip angle over 60 degrees and blades over 220 millimeters. Martial arts and gift knives with unsharpened edges and rounded tips don't count. Police batons are police equipment. The People's Police Law provides that only police may possess and use them; others found holding them face confiscation, up to 15 days of detention or a warning, plus a fine of up to 5 times the illegal gains. The railway prohibited-items list classes batons, tear gas devices, stun guns, and defense sprays as controlled implements — on trains these may not be carried on your person or checked in. Left in the car gets checked too: one driver carrying controlled knives was stopped at a checkpoint by police and given administrative detention. For the bill when you actually use one, see the guiding opinions on justifiable defense, which list "whether a weapon was used or readied for use" among the factors separating defense from mutual combat. Official case: Yang quarreled with someone who threatened to bring people back for revenge; he went home and strapped on two knives. The man returned and punched him bare-handed in the face; Yang stabbed him in the chest and abdomen, and the man died. The court found his act had a defensive character, but since the other man only punched bare-handed while Yang stabbed at vital areas, it was excessive defense. He was sentenced to 4 years for intentional injury (nationwide; Public Security Administration Punishments Law effective January 1, 2026)
Note
The beneficiary is you. Carrying a knife doesn't automatically defeat justifiable defense. In Procuratorate Case No. 45, student Chen was mobbed by 9 attackers and fought back with a fruit knife he carried; it was still found to be justifiable defense. The procuratorate spelled out that what affects the finding is not whether you carried a tool but whether there was intent to brawl. The downside lands in two places. First, the item itself is unlawful — a penalty on any routine check, used or not. Second, with a knife at hand it's easy to stab in response to a punch or a shove, and injuries reaching grievous harm or worse can turn it into excessive defense. For pepper spray, this book found no national-level text banning personal possession — only that it can't be taken on trains. Whether expandable batons sold online count as police batons, this book likewise found no unified national recognition text. If something happens, first see No. 10 in Section 8 (conflict breaks out: call the police, don't fight). When there's no way back, see No. 11 in Section 8 (assault you can't escape — you may fight back). For being cornered for money in the wild, see No. 36 in Section 13 (strangers demanding money in the wilderness).
Sources (10 references)

Notice on Issuing the "Standards for Recognizing Controlled Knives" (Gong Tong Zi [2007] No. 2). https://www.gd.gov.cn/zwgk/wjk/zcfgk/content/post_2937075.html (reposted by the Guangdong Provincial People's Government); Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2012 amendment). People's Police Law (Article 36). https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/203770/index.html (reposted by the Beijing Public Security Traffic Management Bureau); State Council (1996). Announcement on Publishing the "Catalog of Items Prohibited or Restricted from Carrying and Checking on Railways" (2022 No. 1). https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/2022-05/31/content_569…; Jinjiang Municipal People's Government (2022).
