3

Sudden facial droop, one-sided arm weakness, or slurred speech: call 120 immediately — don't wait, don't drive yourself

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Drooping mouth, an arm that won't lift on one side, slurred speech — call 120 immediately. If the clot-busting drug goes in within 3 hours of onset, the odds of recovering to the point of basically managing daily life on your own are about 1.75 times those without the drug. Drag it out to 3 to 4.5 hours and the multiple falls to 1.26. Past 4.5 hours, no difference can be seen. Write down the exact time symptoms started. No water, no medicine, and don't drive yourself.

Cost
Free. Three actions, learnable by watching once: have them smile, hold both arms out level, and say a complete sentence.
Benefit
Individual-patient data from 16 randomized trials of intravenous thrombolysis and 6,756 patients, pooled (a meta-analysis). Intravenous thrombolysis means injecting a drug to reopen the blocked vessel. With alteplase within 3 hours of onset, the odds ratio for recovering to the point of basically managing daily life independently (modified Rankin Score 0-1) was 1.75, 95% CI 1.35-2.27 (the credible range) — the odds of that outcome were about 1.75 times those without thrombolysis. From 3 to 4.5 hours it was 1.26 (1.05-1.51). Past 4.5 hours it was 1.15 (0.95-1.40) — statistically, no difference can be seen
Note
The earlier the thrombolysis, the better it works; past 4.5 hours it is basically useless. Call 120 rather than driving because the ambulance goes straight to a hospital with a stroke center and calls ahead so they can prepare. Write down the exact time symptoms started — doctors need it to decide whether thrombolysis is possible. No water, no medication, and no "let's rest a bit and see"
Sources (1 reference)
Emberson J, Lees KR, Lyden P, et al. (2014). Effect of treatment delay, age, and stroke severity on the effects of intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase for acute ischaemic stroke: a meta-analysis of individual patient data from randomised trials. Lancet, 384(9958), 1929-1935. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(14)60584-5
4

Sudden violent dizziness, double vision, one eye going dark, or a finger that can't find your own nose tip: treat as stroke and call 120

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Checking only "face droop, raise the arm, speak," more than a tenth of strokes get missed, because some strokes start without a drooping mouth or a paralyzed arm. Add unsteadiness, double vision, or a missing patch of vision, and the miss rate drops to 4.4%. Sudden spinning dizziness you can't stand through, seeing double, or a finger that can't find your own nose tip — call 120 all the same, and note the time all the same.

Cost
Free. Two additions to the three actions "face droop, raise the arms, speak" (item 3, sudden facial droop and slurred speech). One: have them stand straight and close their eyes, watch whether they sway, then ask whether their vision is doubled or missing a patch. The other: when you suspect it yourself, touch your nose tip with a fingertip, then do it again with eyes closed.
Benefit
In 2014 the University of Kentucky Stroke Center reviewed the medical records of 736 cases of acute ischemic stroke (a stroke caused by a blocked vessel). 14.1% of those patients showed none of the three FAST symptoms at onset — face droop, arm weakness, slurred speech. Adding "unsteady walking, weak legs, and visual symptoms" to the screen brought the missed share down from 14.1% to 4.4%
Note
When the blocked vessels are in the cerebellum and brainstem region (posterior circulation infarct), there is often no drooping mouth and no paralyzed arm. There is only the spinning dizziness, veering while walking, double vision, and coughing when drinking or eating — the picture most easily mistaken for a cervical spine problem, low blood sugar, or inner-ear crystals, and delayed accordingly. Missing the nose tip and being unable to stand with eyes closed are signs of cerebellar involvement. But no single action can rule a stroke out in reverse: if it comes on suddenly and doesn't ease off, call 120 and record the exact time it began. The study reviewed only one hospital's charts, and the authors themselves note it still needs further validation
Sources (1 reference)
Aroor S, Singh R, Goldstein LB (2017). BE-FAST (Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time): Reducing the Proportion of Strokes Missed Using the FAST Mnemonic. Stroke, 48(2), 479-481. https://doi.org/10.1161/STROKEAHA.116.015169
5

One eye suddenly blacking out like a curtain falling — even if it clears in minutes — still means the ER that day as a stroke

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

One eye suddenly going black like a curtain falling means a vessel at the back of the eye is blocked — the longer it stays blocked, the less retina can be saved. It is also a form of brain ischemia, and a stroke is likely in the following days. Among people evaluated and treated the same day, the rate of another stroke within 90 days drops from 10.3% to 2.1%. Go that day to an ER with a stroke center; don't wait until tomorrow to book an ophthalmology appointment.

Cost
Free. The ER evaluation and vascular testing will take half a day to a day.
Benefit
The American Heart Association's 2021 scientific statement on central retinal artery occlusion (the main vessel at the back of the eye blocked) states plainly: "Acute central retinal artery occlusion is an emergency." Care systems should recognize it as an emergency and triage it by urgency. The longer the blood supply is cut off, the less retina can be salvaged. The Oxford EXPRESS study looked at two groups of patients: minor stroke, and brain ischemia whose symptoms resolved on their own (medically, a transient ischemic attack). After these patients were switched to same-day evaluation and same-day treatment, the rate of recurrent stroke within 90 days fell from 10.3% (32/310) to 2.1% (6/281)
Note
It's graded B because EXPRESS was not a randomized trial. It compared the same population across two periods, before and after the practice change, and other conditions may also have shifted between the two — that part can't be separated out. A few minutes of blackness that clears on its own is most easily waved off as "being tired" or "low blood sugar." It is one form of transient ischemic attack, and the next few days are exactly the high-risk window for stroke. Vision loss in one eye that comes without pain, redness, or tearing deserves particular attention. Don't wait for the next day's ophthalmology clinic; go straight to the ER of a hospital with a stroke center.
Sources (2 references)
Mac Grory B, Schrag M, Biousse V, et al. (2021). Management of Central Retinal Artery Occlusion: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association. Stroke, 52(6), e282-e294. https://doi.org/10.1161/STR.0000000000000366 ; Rothwell PM, Giles MF, Chandratheva A, et al. (2007). Effect of urgent treatment of transient ischaemic attack and minor stroke on early recurrent stroke (EXPRESS study): a prospective population-based sequential comparison. Lancet, 370(9596), 1432-1442. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(07)61448-2
6

One eye aching, pressurized, and red, with a rainbow ring around lights plus headache and nausea: same-day eye emergency

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

This is an acute glaucoma attack. The fluid inside the eye can't drain out, and the pressure spikes at once. The longer it drags on, the more the optic nerve gets crushed, and the damage doesn't come back. During Wuhan's lockdown, patients waited an average of 241 hours before treatment, and 21.87% went blind. The same period the next year, with no lockdown, the average wait was 121 hours and 7.84% went blind.

Cost
Free. An eye-ER visit to measure pressure and examine the anterior chamber takes half a day.
Benefit
An eye hospital in Wuhan compared acute primary angle-closure glaucoma patients across two periods. In the 76 lockdown days of 2020 there were 54 patients and 64 eyes; the same period in 2021 had 46 patients and 51 eyes, with similar demographics between the two groups. From symptom onset to treatment, the lockdown group took 241.84±211.95 hours versus 121.53±96.12 hours in the control group (P=0.001). Pressure at presentation was 52.63±12.45 mmHg versus 45.16±9.79 mmHg (P=0.001). Blindness rates were 21.87% versus 7.84%. Glaucomatous optic neuropathy was found in 20/64 eyes (31.25%) versus 7/51 eyes (13.73%) (P=0.03). A Korean hospital reviewed 50 eyes that had a single attack and later had the lens removed. A year later, 25 (50%) were left with some degree of visual field defect. The longer the stretch from symptom onset to getting the pressure down, the greater the odds of a lasting defect (P=0.005). Another prospective study had 43 people with shallow anterior chambers lie face down in a dark room for 1 hour. Pressure in both eyes rose significantly (P<0.01). The median rise was 3.60 mmHg in the dominant eye and 2.70 mmHg in the other (P<0.05)
Note
Two reasons it's graded B. First, the Wuhan comparison was dug out of old medical records, and the lockdown itself brought other differences that can't be separated from the "delay" factor. Second, the Korean group had only 50 eyes and was retrospective too. The trigger described is not screen time; it is two things stacked together: in the dark the pupil dilates, and long hours head-down or face-down push the lens forward. People whose anterior chamber is already shallow are prone to being set off this way, so the truly high-risk are those over 50, farsighted, or with a family member who has had angle-closure glaucoma. Young people gaming all night almost never trigger it this way. The most common misjudgment during an attack is to take it for gastroenteritis, migraine, or high blood pressure, because the headache and vomiting overshadow the eye symptoms. Painless, non-red vision loss in one eye is a different matter — see item 5 (One eye suddenly going dark). For whether blue-light-blocking glasses work, see Section 6, item 16 (Blue-light-blocking glasses).
Sources (3 references)
Zhou L, Wu S, Wang Y, Bao X, Peng T, Luo W, Ortega-Usobiaga J (2022). Clinical presentation of acute primary angle closure during the COVID-19 epidemic lockdown. Frontiers in Medicine, 9, 1078237. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2022.1078237 ; Sung MS, Kim HJ, Park SW (2023). Predictors of long-term visual field outcome after an episode of acute primary angle closure. Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology, 51(4), 291-299. https://doi.org/10.1111/ceo.14206 ; Wang J, Wang J, Ng TK, Huang C (2025). Asymmetric intraocular pressure changes in dominant and contralateral eyes: the dark room prone provocative test. Seminars in Ophthalmology, 40(4), 325-331. https://doi.org/10.1080/08820538.2024.2443972
7

Chest pressure, pain, or tightness lasting more than 15 minutes: call 120 — don't tough it out and don't drive yourself

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Chest pain like something pressing down, tightness, or squeezing that lasts more than 15 minutes — call 120. For those whose vessel is reopened within 55 minutes of reaching the hospital, 30-day mortality is 2.8%. Past 55 minutes, 9.7%. Every stretch of delay kills off another patch of heart muscle. Don't drive yourself: losing consciousness on the road is a second accident.

Cost
Free.
Benefit
Israel ran a national survey of acute coronary syndrome. The analysis covered ST-elevation myocardial infarction patients, one class of heart attack. It measured the interval from hospital arrival to opening the blocked vessel with a balloon (balloon dilation). With intervals ≤55 minutes, 5/178 (2.8%) died within 30 days. With intervals >55 minutes, 15/155 (9.7%) died within 30 days
Note
The study compared the delay after arriving at the hospital, not the stretch from onset to hospital. But the logic is the same: every bit of delay kills off another patch of heart muscle. The pain may sit in the upper abdomen, the back, or the jaw, or it may show up as numbness in the left arm. Diabetics and the elderly may feel no pain at all, just breathlessness. Don't drive yourself — losing consciousness on the road is a second accident
Sources (1 reference)
Karkabi B, Meir G, Zafrir B, et al. (2021). Door-to-balloon time and mortality in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction. European Heart Journal - Quality of Care and Clinical Outcomes. https://doi.org/10.1093/ehjqcco/qcaa037
8

Sudden tearing pain migrating from chest to back to flank: call 120 and say clearly that 'the pain is moving'

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

A tearing pain that migrates from the chest to the back and down toward the flank: when you call 120, say it straight out — "it feels like tearing, and the pain is moving downward." Without surgery, on medication alone, this disease kills 58%. Its treatment is the opposite of a heart attack's: only if the doctor thinks of it will they order a contrast CT instead of putting you on blood thinners and clot-busters. A big blood-pressure gap between the two arms, or a pulse missing on one side — report those too.

Cost
Free.
Benefit
The International Registry of Acute Aortic Dissection (IRAD) collected 464 cases from 12 centers. Aortic dissection is the disease behind that tearing chest-and-back pain. Among the symptoms patients reported first, the most common was sudden, severe, sharp pain. Overall in-hospital mortality was 27.4%. For type A dissections treated with medication only, no surgery, mortality was 58%
Note
Dissection and heart attack get opposite treatment. A heart attack calls for anticoagulants and thrombolytics — drugs that keep blood from clotting; used on a dissection, they amount to draining the patient through the tear. So at the hospital, volunteer "tearing pain, moving downward" so the doctor thinks to order a contrast CT. A large blood-pressure gap between the arms, or a pulse you can't find on one side, is a clue. Higher risk: poorly controlled blood pressure, Marfan syndrome, or a family history of aortic aneurysm or dissection. Likewise, don't drive yourself, and don't hold out until the next day
Sources (1 reference)
Hagan PG, Nienaber CA, Isselbacher EM, et al. (2000). The International Registry of Acute Aortic Dissection (IRAD): new insights into an old disease. JAMA, 283(7), 897-903. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.283.7.897
9

A sudden 'worst headache of your life' hitting peak within an hour: go to the ER now for a head CT

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

What matters is how fast the pain peaks. A severe headache that hits its worst within an hour is, about 6% of the time, a burst vessel on the surface of the brain. Over 40, neck pain or stiffness, someone saw you pass out, it started during exertion, it exploded in an instant, or your neck won't bend forward — hit any one and go to the ER for a head CT. Most people who get checked turn out fine, but missing one re-bleed is death.

Cost
The ER visit itself costs little. A head CT in the ER runs a few hundred yuan.
Benefit
Ten Canadian ERs ran a prospective cohort study of 2,131 cases of "severe headache reaching peak pain within an hour," fixing the criteria in advance and then following and recording every case. Of these, 132 (6.2%) were subarachnoid hemorrhage (a vessel on the brain's surface burst). The Ottawa SAH rule has six items: age 40 or over, neck pain or stiffness, a witnessed loss of consciousness. The other three: onset during exertion, instantaneous thunderclap onset, and limited forward neck flexion on the doctor's exam. Meeting any one item calls for imaging. The rule caught every single bleeding patient — sensitivity 100%, 95% CI 97.2%-100.0% (the credible range). The price: among people without a bleed, only 15.3% could be ruled out by it (specificity 15.3%)
Note
What to watch is not "how bad" but "how fast to worst" — a headache that explodes within seconds to a minute is the danger signal; a migraine that builds gradually is not. With vomiting, a stiff neck, light sensitivity, or a brief faint, take it even more seriously. A specificity of 15.3% means the vast majority of people checked under this rule turn out fine. But missing one re-bleed is death, so the check is worth it. Don't swallow a painkiller, push it down, and go back to sleep
Sources (1 reference)
Perry JJ, Stiell IG, Sivilotti MLA, et al. (2013). Clinical decision rules to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage for acute headache. JAMA, 310(12), 1248-1255. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2013.278018
10

Two weeks to months after a head bump, an older person becoming unsteady, sluggish, drowsy, or weak on one side: get a head CT

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

After an elderly person bumps their head, the blood usually doesn't pool until the third week. At the moment of impact they can be perfectly fine, and the person may not even remember the bump. After surgery this disease recurs up to 33% of the time, and fatality can reach 32%. If an older person suddenly turns confused, walks as if floating, sleeps all the time, or has a weak hand, first ask backward over the past two or three months whether they fell or hit their head — then get the CT.

Cost
A head CT costs two to three hundred yuan.
Benefit
The Chinese Medical Association's Neurosurgery Branch and others published the Chinese Expert Consensus on Drug Treatment of Chronic Subdural Hematoma. A chronic subdural hematoma is a pool of blood that slowly collects between the membranes covering the brain — in technical terms, a chronic space-occupying collection formed between the arachnoid and the dura mater. It "usually forms in the third week after a traumatic brain injury" and is mostly seen in the elderly. After surgery, recurrence can reach 33% and fatality 32%. Among patients over 90, overall only 24% make a good recovery. A systematic review: worldwide, 3.39 to 39.1 new cases per 100,000 people per year, rising with age — over 80, up to three times that. The most common causes are trauma and falls, followed by long-term heavy drinking, blood-thinning medication (anticoagulants), and violence. A geriatrics review: the typical presentation "includes confusion, cognitive decline, gait disturbance, or drowsiness, and can resemble other geriatric syndromes"
Note
At the moment of impact they can be completely fine — the person may not even recall bumping their head. So when the family notices "suddenly confused lately, walking as if floating, sleeping all the time, one hand weak," first ask backward over the past two or three months about falls and head bumps, then get the CT. Don't file it straight under "senile dementia" or "after-effects of that last stroke" — a wrong label means delay. Older people on aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, or a newer oral anticoagulant are at higher risk, and so are long-term heavy drinkers. For fall prevention, see Section 1, item 13 (Training balance and leg strength).
Sources (3 references)
Zhang J et al. (2021). Expert consensus on drug treatment of chronic subdural hematoma. Chinese Neurosurgical Journal, 7(1), 47. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41016-021-00263-z ; Dziho A et al. (2025). Global prevalence and incidence of chronic subdural hematoma: A systematic review. Brain and Spine, 5, 105893. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bas.2025.105893 ; Mathon B, Shotar E (2026). Diagnostic and therapeutic management of chronic subdural hematoma in elderly patients. Gériatrie et Psychologie Neuropsychiatrie du Vieillissement, 24(1), 30-41. https://doi.org/10.1684/pnv.2026.1274
11

One leg suddenly swollen, tight, and tender to the touch: see a doctor promptly; add sudden breathlessness or chest pain and call 120 now

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

One leg suddenly swollen, tight, a size bigger than the other, tender to the touch — get a leg vein ultrasound promptly. Add sudden breathlessness, chest pain on a deep breath, a racing heart, or lightheadedness, and the clot may already be in the lungs: call 120 directly. Of people diagnosed with pulmonary embolism, 17.4% die within 3 months. Sitting still for more than 4 hours roughly doubles the risk, but the risk to any one person stays low.

Cost
An ultrasound of the leg vessels (lower-limb venous ultrasound) costs one to two hundred yuan.
Benefit
The International Cooperative Pulmonary Embolism Registry (ICOPER) collected 2,454 confirmed acute pulmonary embolism patients from 52 hospitals in 7 countries. Pulmonary embolism is a clot blocking the pulmonary artery. All-cause mortality at 3 months in this group was 17.4% (426/2454). The WHO WRIGHT project: travel of more than 4 hours at a stretch "roughly doubles" the risk of a clot forming in a vein and traveling to the lungs (venous thromboembolism). But the probability per person remains very low — for more than 4 hours of immobility it is "about one in six thousand"
Note
Both legs swelling together is usually a heart, liver, kidney, or vein-function problem. One leg suddenly swollen and a size bigger than the other is the classic picture of deep vein thrombosis. Higher-risk situations: long car or plane trips, bed rest after surgery or a fracture, a cast, the period around pregnancy and childbirth, cancer, oral contraceptives. When a clot breaks off and blocks a pulmonary artery, that is a pulmonary embolism: sudden breathlessness, sharper chest pain on a deep breath, racing heart, lightheadedness, coughing up blood (hemoptysis). At that stage, call 120 directly. The 17.4% is the death rate among confirmed pulmonary embolism cases, not "a swollen leg carries this much risk" — don't scare yourself with that number.
Sources (2 references)
Goldhaber SZ, Visani L, De Rosa M (1999). Acute pulmonary embolism: clinical outcomes in the International Cooperative Pulmonary Embolism Registry (ICOPER). Lancet, 353(9162), 1386-1389. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(98)07534-5 ; WHO (2007). Study results released on travel and blood clots. https://www.who.int/news/item/29-06-2007-study-results-rele…
12

Heavy bleeding: press the wound hard with your hand first; if a limb can't be controlled, apply a tourniquet — and call 120

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Press hard with your hand or clothing first; if a limb can't be controlled, put on a tourniquet; then call 120, and once it's on, don't loosen it. Among battlefield casualties, those tourniqueted before shock set in survived nine in ten; after shock, only one in ten; the 5 who needed one and didn't get it all died. Place it above the wound, twist until the blood stops, and note the time. Don't substitute shoelaces or rope. Neck and torso wounds can only be pressed, never tourniqueted.

Cost
A windlass tourniquet costs a few dozen to a hundred-odd yuan; keep one in the car and in the first-aid kit. Learning "place above the wound, twist until the blood stops, note the time" takes a few minutes.
Benefit
Over 6 years, 11 Level I trauma centers in Texas admitted 1,026 limb vascular injuries, of which 181 (17.6%) got a tourniquet before reaching the hospital. Crude numbers, no adjustment: deaths with a tourniquet 3.9%, without one 5.2%. After leveling the other conditions (multivariable adjustment), tourniquet use remained independently associated with survival. Adjusted OR 5.86, with the credible range 95% CI 1.41 to 24.47. Of 232 casualties at a Baghdad combat hospital: those tourniqueted before shock appeared survived 90%; after shock, only 10%. All 5 who needed a tourniquet and didn't get one died; among those who got one, 87% survived. The order: direct pressure — clothing or a towel will do → tourniquet for limb bleeding that won't stop → call 120 → don't loosen it
Note
Don't use rope, shoelaces, or other narrow things as a tourniquet — they can't compress the artery and they cut into skin. Once on, don't loosen the tourniquet every little while to "let some blood through." Bleeding from the neck or torso can only be pressed, never tourniqueted. In that battlefield data, the tourniquet itself cost no one a limb; 4 cases had transient nerve palsy. Chinese emergency physicians' expert consensus says the same: once applied in prehospital care, loosening is not recommended unless some other means can stop the bleeding completely. For upper-arm bleeding, place it on the upper third of the upper arm; for thigh bleeding, at the groin. Don't place it on the forearm, lower leg, elbow, or knee. The consensus advises keeping total time, before and after hospital arrival, under 2 hours where possible — but if the hospital can't be reached and there is no other way to stop the bleeding, don't untie it until proper rescue arrives. A makeshift tourniquet from a belt, tie, or sleeve can hardly stop bleeding on its own; pair it with a stick and twist it tight.
Sources (4 references)
Teixeira PGR et al. (2018). Civilian Prehospital Tourniquet Use Is Associated with Improved Survival in Patients with Peripheral Vascular Injury. Journal of the American College of Surgeons. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jamcollsurg.2018.01.047 ; Kragh JF et al. (2009). Survival with emergency tourniquet use to stop bleeding in major limb trauma. Annals of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/SLA.0b013e31818842ba ; Emergency Physician Branch of the Chinese Medical Doctor Association et al. (2020). Expert consensus on the emergency application of tourniquets. Chinese Journal of Emergency Medicine 29(6):773-779: "In prehospital emergency care, once a tourniquet is applied, loosening is not recommended unless alternative treatment that stops the bleeding completely is available" "Maximum duration of use should not exceed 2 h. But if circumstances make hospital treatment impossible or there is no alternative means of hemostasis, the tourniquet is not released until formal rescue arrives". https://doi.org/10.3760/cma.j.issn.1671-0282.2020.06.006, full text http://www.cem.org.cn/rhtml/20200606/index.htm
13

Bitten or scratched by a dog or cat: alternate rinsing with soap solution and running water for 15 minutes, then get the vaccine that day

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Once rabies symptoms appear, fatality is nearly 100% — washing plus vaccine is the only way through. First alternate rinsing with soap solution and clean running water for 15 minutes, then get the vaccine that same day. A bite that breaks through, or a licked break in the skin, is Category III exposure and adds an injection of passive immunization. "It's a family pet, it's had its shots" changes nothing: the category is set by the wound, not by the dog's pedigree.

Cost
Rinsing is free. The full rabies vaccine course costs a few hundred yuan. Category III exposure adds rabies passive immunization (pre-made antibody injected directly), several hundred to over a thousand yuan.
Benefit
The 2023 national protocol from the National Disease Control and Prevention Administration and the National Health Commission states verbatim: "Rabies fatality reaches almost 100%." The required care: "thoroughly rinse all bite and scratch wounds for about 15 minutes, alternating soap solution (or another mildly alkaline cleanser) with running water under some pressure." A light bite on unbroken skin, or a scratch that doesn't bleed, is Category II exposure — the vaccine is required. A bite that pierces through, or broken skin that gets licked, is Category III exposure: "the wound should be managed and rabies passive immunization given along with the rabies vaccine." WHO: rabies kills about 59,000 people worldwide each year, 99% of it transmitted by dogs
Note
Don't skip treatment because "it's a family pet, it's had its shots." The protocol looks at what category the wound has reached (exposure level), not at the dog's background. Don't bandage the wound yourself. The ten-day observation rule can only decide whether to stop the shots, never whether to start them. Bites from wild animals or bats get the same treatment.
Sources (2 references)
General Department of the National Disease Control and Prevention Administration and the General Office of the National Health Commission (2023). Notice on issuing the Work Protocol for Rabies Exposure Prevention and Management (2023 edition). https://www.ndcpa.gov.cn/jbkzzx/c100014/common/content/cont… ; WHO. Rabies fact sheet. https://www.who.int/zh/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/rabies
14

Burn: immediately flush with cool running water for 20 minutes; no toothpaste or soy sauce

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Flush with cool running water for a full 20 minutes within 3 hours of the burn, and the odds of later needing a skin graft drop to roughly 60% of those who didn't rinse. Cool water, not ice water — icing makes the injury worse. If clothing sticks to the wound, don't tear it off; after rinsing, cover it with a clean cloth and go to the hospital. No toothpaste, soy sauce, sesame oil, or flour. If you only remember a while later, flushing within three hours still helps.

Cost
Free. Takes 20 minutes.
Benefit
Australia followed 2,495 children with burns. For kids flushed with cool running water for 20 minutes within 3 hours of injury, the odds ratio for later needing a skin graft was 0.6, 95% CI 0.4-0.8 (the credible range) — roughly 60% of those who didn't. Pooling 7 studies found the same: "20 minutes of cool running water within three hours of injury significantly lowered the chance of needing a skin graft and surgical wound management"
Note
Cool water, not ice water — icing makes the injury worse. If clothing sticks to the wound, don't tear it off; after rinsing, cover it with a clean cloth and go to the hospital. No toothpaste, soy sauce, sesame oil, or flour — they muddy the doctor's read of burn depth and invite infection. Flushing within three hours still helps
Sources (2 references)
Griffin BR, Frear CC, Babl F, Oakley E, Kimble RM (2020). Cool Running Water First Aid Decreases Skin Grafting Requirements in Pediatric Burns: A Cohort Study of Two Thousand Four Hundred Ninety-five Children. Annals of Emergency Medicine, 75(1), 75-85. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annemergmed.2019.06.028; Griffin B, Cabilan CJ, Ayoub B, et al. (2022). The effect of 20 minutes of cool running water first aid within three hours of thermal burn injury on patient outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Australasian Emergency Care, 25(4), 367-376. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.auec.2022.05.004
15

Sudden whole-body rash, breathlessness, or faintness: treat as anaphylactic shock — call 120 right away and say why

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

A sudden rash over the whole body, plus breathlessness or faintness — treat it as anaphylactic shock. Call 120 immediately and say straight out "suspected anaphylactic shock," so the ambulance brings epinephrine. Antihistamines and steroids act slowly; they are no substitute for epinephrine. Anyone who has had one episode should get a doctor to prescribe an auto-injector — into the mid-outer thigh, through clothing if need be.

Cost
Free. For people with a known severe allergy, keeping your own epinephrine auto-injector costs money, and it is a prescription drug.
Benefit
Epinephrine is the first-choice drug (first-line) for anaphylactic shock grade II and above, and the guideline lists it as a strong recommendation. Antihistamines and steroids act too slowly to stand in for it
Note
That allergy guideline (EAACI) itself states that in this field "the evidence mostly sits at very low levels." It lists epinephrine as a strong recommendation because the benefit far outweighs the risk, not because of large trials. In China epinephrine is prescription-only, and ordinary households usually don't have it on hand. What you can do is call 120 and say "suspected anaphylactic shock" so the ambulance brings the drug. Anyone who has had one severe allergic episode should get a doctor to prescribe an auto-injector and learn to use it in the mid-outer thigh (outer, slightly toward the front) — through trousers works too.
Sources (2 references)
China Association for Pharmaceutical Education et al. (2022). Clinical practice guideline for emergency management of anaphylactic shock (2020). Frontiers in Pharmacology: "Epinephrine is the first-line medicine in GRADE II to IV anaphylaxis" "Intramuscular epinephrine should be injected in the mid-anterolateral thigh"; the adult intramuscular ceiling is 0.5 mg and 0.3 mg for under 14, repeatable every 5-15 minutes if there is no response. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2022.845689; Muraro A, et al. (2022). EAACI guidelines: Anaphylaxis (2021 update). Allergy. https://doi.org/10.1111/all.15032
16

Someone convulsing: clear the surroundings, lay them on their side, time it on a watch, and put nothing in their mouth

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Move hard objects out of the way, lay them on their side with mouth down, and time it on a watch. Don't pin them down, don't pry the mouth open, don't stuff anything in — that only damages teeth and jaw. Call an ambulance if it lasts over 5 minutes, if it restarts quickly after stopping, if they can't be roused or can't breathe well afterward, if it happens in water, or if it's the first-ever seizure. Offer water only when they are fully alert.

Cost
Free.
Benefit
Prevents the tooth and jaw injuries caused by prying the mouth open and stuffing in hard objects. Prevents fractures from forcibly pinning someone down. More than 5 minutes without stopping is the red line that requires an ambulance
Note
The same page lists several other situations that call for an immediate ambulance: another seizure soon after one ends, can't be roused or breathing is labored afterward, injured during the seizure, it happens in water, or it's the first seizure. Once it stops, lay them on their side with mouth down, and offer water only when fully alert. For families with an epilepsy patient, these steps matter most. Do the same for a stranger: the odds of the benefit flowing back to you are smaller, but it won't create liability either (Civil Code Article 184 — see item 2 in this section, don't rush to lift the person).
Sources (1 reference)
US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Seizure first aid: "Don't hold the person down or stop their movements" "Don't put anything in their mouth. This can hurt their teeth or jaw" "Don't offer water or food until they are fully alert" "Time the seizure to track if it lasts more than 5 minutes. If it does, seek immediate medical attention or call 911". https://www.cdc.gov/epilepsy/first-aid-for-seizures/index.html
17

A diabetic suddenly shaking, cold-sweating, or slurring: give 15 grams of sugar first, then recheck after 15 minutes

Grade AValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Sugar first — 15 grams; sugar cubes or a small juice box both work. Recheck after 15 minutes, and if it's still low, do it again. Blood sugar below 3.0 mmol/L is hypoglycemia serious enough for medicine to take seriously. Once it takes someone else's help to handle, it can be fatal. Feed nothing at all to anyone not fully conscious — it goes down the windpipe. Call 120 directly.

Cost
Free. Carry a few sugar cubes or a small juice box.
Benefit
Blood sugar below 3.0 mmol/L counts as clinically significant hypoglycemia. When it changes mental state or behavior and someone else's help is needed to manage it, that is severe hypoglycemia, and it can be fatal
Note
Feed nothing to anyone not fully conscious — it goes into the windpipe; call 120 directly. The same standard recommends that everyone on insulin or prone to lows keep glucagon on hand. The original text: "All individuals treated with insulin or who are at high risk of hypoglycemia...should be prescribed glucagon". Nasal spray and prefilled injectors work better than kits you have to mix on the spot. These steps are written for yourself or the diabetic in your household, and the sugar you carry is for them too.
Sources (1 reference)
American Diabetes Association (2025). Standards of Care in Diabetes 2025, Chapter 6: Glycemic targets and hypoglycemia. Diabetes Care: classification "Level 1: Glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L)" "Level 2: Glucose <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)" "Level 3: A severe event characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment of hypoglycemia, irrespective of glucose level"; management "For most individuals, 15 g carbohydrates should be ingested" "Fifteen minutes after initial treatment, repeat the treatment if hypoglycemia persists". https://doi.org/10.2337/dc25-S006
18

Someone electrocuted: cut the power first, then move the source away with a dry stick or the like; never grab them bare-handed

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Cut the power first, or knock the source away with a dry stick or the like, before touching the person. Grab them bare-handed and one casualty becomes two. If they're not breathing once free of the source, start compressions immediately per item 1 (hard chest compressions) — an electrical injury doesn't make CPR off-limits. Downed high-voltage lines and transformer equipment are not do-it-yourself: back off and wait for the power company to cut the current.

Cost
Free.
Benefit
Prevents the rescuer from being shocked too, turning one casualty into two. If they're not breathing once free of the source, do CPR per item 1 in this section (hard chest compressions). The US CDC's first-aid steps: look first, don't touch — the person may still be connected to the current. Cut the power if you can; if not, push the source away with something non-conductive like cardboard, plastic, or wood. Once free of the source, anyone with no breathing or pulse gets CPR immediately. One review notes that people whose hearts stop after electrocution and are revived often have good outcomes
Note
"Cut the power before touching the person" is a purely self-interested rule: grab bare-handed and you're the second one down. Downed high-voltage lines and transformer equipment are not do-it-yourself; back off and wait for the power company to cut the power. For cardiac arrest caused by electrocution, compress and defibrillate as usual — "electrical injury" is no reason to keep your hands off.
Sources (2 references)
US CDC. What to Do to Protect Yourself From Electrical Hazards (the First aid section). https://www.cdc.gov/natural-disasters/response/what-to-do-p…; Spies C, Trohman RG (2006). Narrative review: Electrocution and life-threatening electrical injuries. Annals of Internal Medicine 145(7):531-537. https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-145-7-200610030-00011
19

CO alarm sounds, or everyone in the room has headache and nausea at once: get outside first, then call

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Alarm sounding, or a whole room of people with headache, nausea, and dizziness at once: get everyone outside first, then call. Don't stay in to find the cause, and don't go back for the valve. The symptoms feel like a cold; "better the moment you step out" is the strongest tell. China reported 11,523 deaths from carbon monoxide poisoning in 2018, most in winter, most of them dying at home.

Cost
Free.
Benefit
China CDC's cause-of-death surveillance system reported 11,523 carbon monoxide poisoning deaths in 2018. The heaviest months were January (2,845), February (2,321), and December (2,010). In those three winter months, 66% to 73% of the deaths happened at home. These are the numbers reported into the system, not estimates projected onto the national population. In the US, more than 400 people die each year from unintentional CO poisoning not linked to fires; more than 100,000 visit an emergency department and more than 14,000 are hospitalized
Note
The symptoms look like a cold, and also like being drunk. A whole room of people feeling sick together, better the moment they step out — that is the strongest tell. Don't stay inside hunting for the cause, don't go back for the valve; get the people out first, then call. For how to install an alarm, see Section 1, item 3.
Sources (3 references)
You J, Liu J, Zhou M (2020). Number of Deaths due to Carbon Monoxide Poisoning by Month and by Place of Death — China, 2018. China CDC Weekly 2(2):32: "In 2018, there were 11,523 deaths caused by carbon monoxide poisoning reported in China". https://doi.org/10.46234/ccdcw2020.008; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Carbon monoxide poisoning: "More than 400 Americans die from unintentional CO poisoning not linked to fires" "More than 100,000 visit an emergency department" "More than 14,000 are hospitalized", common symptoms "headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion". https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html; US Consumer Product Safety Commission. Carbon Monoxide Information Center: "If you suspect CO poisoning, get outside to fresh air immediately, and then call 911". https://www.cpsc.gov/Safety-Education/Safety-Education-Cent…
20

Swallowed cleaner, pesticide, or medication: don't induce vomiting; bring the bottle and get care immediately; splashed in eye or on skin, flush with plenty of water for at least 15 minutes

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

If someone swallows cleaner, pesticide, or medication, don't induce vomiting — a corrosive liquid coming back up burns the esophagus a second time. Drink a suitable amount of milk or egg white first, then take the bottle and its label straight to the hospital. Splashed on skin or in the eye, flush with plenty of clean water for at least 15 minutes — hold the eyelids open and don't rub. Mixing disinfectant with toilet cleaner produces chlorine gas.

Cost
Free. Keep cleaners, disinfectants, pesticides, and medications on high shelves out of children's reach, or in a locked cabinet. Never decant them into beverage bottles.
Benefit
The China CDC's National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control gives four sets of instructions. Swallowed (ingested): drink a suitable amount of milk or egg white immediately — "remember, do not induce vomiting." Get to a doctor as soon as possible, bringing the packaging or instructions "so the doctor can quickly identify the ingredients and plan treatment." Inhaled: move immediately to a well-ventilated area and loosen the collar to keep the airway clear; with severe coughing, rapid breathing, or breathing difficulty, get medical care immediately. Skin contact: rinse the area with plenty of clean water for at least 15 minutes, taking care not to splash the rinse water into the eyes or other unharmed skin. Eye contact: rinse the eyes with plenty of clean water or saline for at least 15 minutes. Hold the eyelids open so the water reaches the eyeball and the inside of the lids — "never rub the eyes." Go straight to ophthalmology afterward. High-risk products are identified by acidity (pH). Below pH 3: toilet cleaners, descalers, floor cleaners, stainless-steel polish; some heavy-duty drain uncloggers also contain dilute sulfuric acid. Above pH 11: drain uncloggers, heavy-duty kitchen degreasers, dishwasher powder, oxygen bleach, scouring powder. And one combination that goes wrong on the spot: disinfectant used together with an acid-containing toilet cleaner produces chlorine gas, which irritates the airway, triggers violent coughing and shortness of breath, and can even be life-threatening
Note
Graded B because the official guidance only says how to handle it and how to recognize it — there is no "how much less harm if you follow this" number. The logic against vomiting: corrosive liquid coming back up burns the esophagus (the tube from throat to stomach) a second time. If you're not sure what was swallowed, bring the bottle and instructions to the hospital along with any vomit. Prevention is far cheaper than first aid: store by category, never alongside food and drink, cap tightly and discard empty bottles when done, and never pour leftovers into a water bottle. Wear rubber gloves and goggles when using them, open windows for ventilation, and never mix different types. Carbon monoxide is item 19; burns are item 14. For acids and alkalis splashed on the body — how to strip clothing and how long to rinse — see item 21 (Chemicals splashed on the body).
Sources (1 reference)
National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (2025). Summer safety tips: beware of strong acid and strong alkali cleaners. https://niohp.chinacdc.cn/kpdw/202507/t20250722_308659.htm
21

Acids, alkalis, and other chemicals on skin: strip contaminated clothing and flush with plenty of running water; for eyes, hold the lids open and flush — finish the full time before leaving

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Three steps. First, strip off the soaked clothing, shoes, and socks immediately — wherever the fabric held the chemical against the skin burns worst. Second, flush with lots of running water, at least 15 minutes for both skin and eyes; Hunan's Emergency Management Department says 20 to 30 minutes — go with the longer figure. Third, for the eyes, hold the lids open while flushing, and go straight to ophthalmology afterward. Use room-temperature water, never hot.

Cost
Free. On your first day on the job, note where the eyewash stations and drench showers are — don't wait for an accident to go looking.
Benefit
On the spot, three steps. First, strip off contaminated clothing, shoes, and socks immediately: the poison keeps absorbing through skin, and where the fabric held it against the body is hurt worst. Second, flush with plenty of running water. The floor set by the China CDC's National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control is "at least 15 minutes" each for skin and eyes. Hunan's Emergency Management Department puts wound flushing at 20 to 30 minutes, "longer for strong chemicals." Take the longer of the two. Third, for the eyes "hold the eyelids open, making sure the water fully reaches the eyeball and the inside of the lids," and "never rub the eyes"; go straight to ophthalmology after flushing. Use cool or lukewarm water; hot water is forbidden. Don't smear ointment, mercurochrome, or anything else on a fresh wound, and don't wrap it in dirty cloth — whatever you apply muddies the doctor's read of the depth. Legally, "chemical skin burns" and "chemical eye burns" are both on the statutory occupational disease list; when they happen at work, they go through the occupational disease and work-injury channels. Where an acute occupational hazard accident occurs, the employer "must promptly organize treatment, health examinations, and medical observation, with all costs borne by the employer" (nationwide)
Note
Graded B because on how long to rinse, one official document says 15 minutes and another says 20 to 30 — there is no unified national standard number. When you go to the hospital, bring the chemical's name, its packaging, or its safety data sheet (SDS); the doctor plans treatment from it. Don't grab another acid or alkali to "neutralize": mixing the two releases heat, and there is no controlling how much. The "neutralizing solution" in the Hunan document means a dedicated rinse solution the workplace keeps ready in advance, not grabbing something on the spot. Dry powders like lime and cement: brush off first, then flush (some local emergency pages draw from this that concentrated sulfuric acid should also be wiped dry first — sources differ here, so this book takes no position). For household cleaners and swallowed chemicals, see item 20. For pre-job protection and medical exams, see Section 19, items 9 and 10 (reading the hazard disclosure before starting the job; the employer must provide protective equipment).
Sources (4 references)
National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (2025). Summer safety tips: beware of strong acid and strong alkali cleaners. https://niohp.chinacdc.cn/kpdw/202507/t20250722_308659.htm; Hunan Provincial Department of Emergency Management (2015). Emergency handling and treatment of common chemical poisoning accidents. http://yjt.hunan.gov.cn/yjt/tszt/aqzs/201509/t20150919_3113…; National Health Commission and three other departments (2024). Classification and Catalogue of Occupational Diseases (effective August 1, 2025). https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengceku/202412/content_6992843…; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2018). Law on the Prevention and Control of Occupational Diseases (Article 37). https://www.beijing.gov.cn/zhengce/zhengcefagui/qtwj/201711… (reproduced by the Beijing Municipal People's Government)
22

In heat: dizziness, nausea, no sweating, or confusion — move to shade at once, remove clothing, douse with water to cool; if confused, give no water and call 120

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Hot red skin, slurred speech, confusion — that is heat stroke. From dizzy to unconscious can be a matter of tens of minutes, and the fatality rate is extremely high. Move at once to a shaded, airy spot, strip off clothing, and cool with cool water and wet towels — and call 120 at the same time. Feed no water at all to anyone not fully conscious; it goes down the wrong pipe.

Cost
Free.
Benefit
The US National Weather Service: heat stroke is "a serious medical emergency." Its signs: body temperature above 103°F (39.4°C), confusion, slurred speech, hot red skin. The response: call for help immediately, move to a cool place, cool with cool water and wet cloths, and "do not give fluids." Heat exhaustion shows heavy sweating, weakness, cool damp skin, a fast weak pulse; the response is to move to a cool place, loosen clothing, and sip water; with vomiting, worsening, or no relief after more than 1 hour, seek care. Yunnan Provincial CDC tips: move immediately to a shaded, ventilated spot, cool with cold wet towels, give salted drinks to those fully conscious, and call emergency services at once for severe cases; severe heat stroke has an "extremely high fatality rate." China CDC advice: cool first, transport second — get the cooling done within the "golden half hour" after consciousness is lost. Where conditions allow, healthy young and middle-aged adults can be rapidly cooled by cold water immersion; for the elderly and those with underlying conditions, spray water on the skin and cool by evaporation. The Wilderness Medical Society's 2024 updated heat-illness guideline says cold water immersion is the most important treatment for severe heat illness and cools fastest. No ice water? Use the coldest water on hand; if immersion is not possible, spray plus fanning, at roughly half the speed of immersion
Note
Don't wait to "see if it passes" — heat stroke can go from dizziness to coma in tens of minutes. Don't pour water into anyone not fully conscious; it goes down the wrong pipe. Where to put ice packs: the two sources differ. China CDC says neck, armpits, and groin; the Wilderness Medical Society says studies show no cooling effect from those spots. Its advice: if ice packs are all you have, cover the whole body; if there are not enough, put them on cheeks, palms, and soles. Both agree: where conditions allow, use cold water immersion.
Sources (7 references)
US National Weather Service. Heat Related Illnesses. https://www.weather.gov/safety/heat-illness ; Yunnan Provincial Administration of Disease Control and Prevention (2026). With these symptoms, you may have heatstroke. https://ynsjkj.yn.gov.cn/html/2026/jikongkepu_0719/2606.html ; Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention. In hot weather, China CDC reminds you to guard against heatstroke: "Where conditions allow, cold water immersion can be used to rapidly cool healthy young and middle-aged adults with no underlying conditions. The elderly and those with underlying conditions can spray water on the skin and cool by evaporation. Cooling should follow the principle of 'cool first, transport later.'" https://www.chinacdc.cn/jkkp/ggws/hjyssj/202409/t20240906_2… ; National Health Commission (2010). Key points on preventing heat stroke. https://www.nhc.gov.cn/wjw/jbyfykz/201007/1edb19b7dd4e4bdf8… ; Eifling KP et al. (2024). Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Heat Illness: 2024 Update. Wilderness & Environmental Medicine 35(1_suppl):112S-127S. https://doi.org/10.1177/10806032241227924 (the full-text site blocks automated retrieval; the specific recommendations were checked against the update summary on the Wilderness Medical Society's website: "cold water immersion … is the most important method of treating severe heat illness" "If CWI is unavailable, evaporative cooling is the recommended second-line treatment. … generally half as fast as CWI" https://wms.org/magazine/magazine/1540/Heat-Illness-CPG/def…); Lipman GS et al. (2019). Same guideline, 2019 edition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wem.2018.10.004
23

A heatstroke victim who's still alert: give cool lightly salted water or a sports drink in small, frequent sips — no gulping, no alcohol or sugary drinks

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Only the alert get to drink. Cool lightly salted water or a sports drink, in small amounts often — 500 to 1,000 ml per hour. No gulping; vomit sucked into the windpipe is deadlier than the heat itself. No alcohol or sugary drinks — they make the body lose more water. Cool first — sponge with cool water, ice packs on neck, armpits, and groin — then rehydrate. For anyone unconscious or slurring, not a single drop.

Cost
Free. A bottle of sports drink costs a few yuan.
Benefit
China CDC published the Public Guide to Preventing and Handling Heat Stroke (2014 edition). It says "drink at least 2-4 cups of cool water per hour (500-1000ml); the water should not be too warm, and drinking should be in small, frequent amounts." It also says "don't drink alcohol or drinks with lots of sugar. These drinks cause the body to lose more fluid. Also avoid drinks that are icy cold." For heat stroke it states flatly "do not give the patient water." US NIOSH: for heat exhaustion, "encourage frequent small sips of cool water"; for heat cramps, a sugar-and-electrolyte sports drink every 15 to 20 minutes, and "no salt tablets"
Note
After heavy sweating, gulping plain water alone dilutes the salt in your blood (low blood sodium) — that is why the water should carry a little salt. Gulping in one go easily brings vomiting, and vomit sucked into the windpipe kills faster than the heatstroke itself. "No ice-cold drinks" is advice from China CDC's 2014 edition, on fears of stomach cramps, with no quantified evidence behind it — don't misread it as "no cold things at all." Item 22 (stripping clothes and dousing with water when dizzy and nauseated in the heat) covers several cooling methods: sponging with cool water, cold water immersion, ice packs on the neck, armpits, and groin. These are exactly the official first-line cooling methods — applied to the body, not poured into the mouth. Cooling always comes before rehydration. For anyone unconscious or slurring, not a single drop
Sources (2 references)
National Institute of Occupational Health and Poison Control, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (2014). Public guide to preventing and handling heat stroke (2014 edition). https://niohp.chinacdc.cn/sndt/201405/t20140530_97623.htm ; US CDC/NIOSH. Heat-Related Illnesses. https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/heat-stress/about/illnesses.html
24

In a fire: crawl low, touch the door before opening — if it's hot, don't; take the stairs, never the elevator; once out, don't turn back

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Get on the floor and crawl under the smoke toward the exit. Before opening any door, feel the handle and the door itself: hot, or smoke seeping through the gap — don't open it, take a second route. Open slowly, and shut it immediately if thick smoke pours in. Stairs, never the elevator — one power cut and you're trapped inside. Once out, don't go back for anything. If clothes catch fire: stop, drop, roll, hands shielding your face.

Cost
One or two standalone smoke alarms at home, a few dozen yuan. Glance at the two exits in your hallway ahead of time.
Benefit
FEMA's escape text: "get down low and crawl under the smoke toward the exit." Feel the handle and the door before opening: "if it's hot, or smoke is coming through the gap, don't open that door — use your second way out." Open slowly; if heavy smoke appears, close it immediately. If clothes catch fire, "stop, drop, and roll," hands covering your face. If you can't get out, close the door, block the gaps and vents with cloth or tape, and call in your location. The Ministry of Emergency Management's fire self-rescue tips agree: never take the elevator while escaping; when the fire is small, head downstairs as far as possible; cover nose and mouth with a wet towel or mask, and evacuate crawling or bent low
Note
No elevators — a power cut traps you inside. Don't turn back for valuables. Don't run upward unless you have confirmed the roof door is open. Don't jump. A wet towel should be folded in half 3 times into 8 layers, and not too wet — soaked through, it actually makes breathing harder. When smoke and toxic gas are too thick, even the towel won't hold.
Sources (3 references)
US FEMA Ready.gov. Home Fires. https://www.ready.gov/home-fires; Ministry of Emergency Management (2019). Self-rescue methods for fires in public places: "never take the elevator while escaping; when the fire is not large, run downstairs as far as possible" "cover the nose with a wet towel or mask and evacuate crawling or bent over". https://www.mem.gov.cn/kp/shaq/201904/t20190401_366015.shtml; Guizhou Provincial Fire and Rescue Corps (2020). Fire safety basics: three keys to escaping: "a wet towel folded in half 3 times (into 8 layers) filters smoke fairly well, but when smoke and toxic gas are too concentrated, the filtering effect can no longer be guaranteed. Also, a towel that is too wet makes breathing difficult". https://gz.119.gov.cn/xfkp/xfcs/202010/t20201026_71437855.html
25

Seeing someone drowning: first call for help and dial 110/120, extend a pole or throw flotation — don't go in yourself

Grade CValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

A drowning person will instinctively push the rescuer under, and the one who goes in can drown too. The order: yell for help → dial 110/120 → extend a pole or rope → throw a life ring, an empty bucket, or plastic bottles → if they're out of the water and not breathing, start compressions immediately. Never enter the water in a hand-linked chain. About 300,000 people drown worldwide each year, and it is the fourth leading cause of death for children aged 1 to 4.

Cost
Free. The hard part is resisting the urge to jump in.
Benefit
WHO: about 300,000 people drown worldwide each year, 92% in low- and middle-income countries. Drowning is the fourth leading cause of death among children aged 1 to 4, and the third among ages 5 to 14. WHO's recommended intervention is "safe rescue and resuscitation training" — learning, for instance, rescues that never enter the water. The order: yell for help → call → extend a pole or rope, throw a life ring, empty bucket, or plastic bottles → if the person is out of the water and not breathing, start compressions immediately
Note
It is graded C because no official text could be found for the "don't go in the water" rule — only WHO's death figures and the "safe rescue" direction. Don't enter the water hand-in-hand in a chain. Without training, don't go pulling at people; a drowning person pushes the rescuer under. "Don't go in" is likewise a self-interested rule: the one who goes in drowns, and it makes no difference who is in the water. The person you will most likely be saving is your own child; prevention is in Section 1, item 12 (Never losing sight of children near water). If someone falls through the ice, likewise don't run onto the ice to pull them out; for ice safety, see Section 1, item 41 (Measuring ice thickness before crossing).
Sources (1 reference)
WHO. Drowning fact sheet. https://www.who.int/zh/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/drowning
26

Someone choking and unable to speak: stand behind, give 5 back blows plus 5 abdominal thrusts; if they collapse, start CPR

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

First ask: "Are you choking? Can you speak?" If they can still cough hard and make sound, keep your hands off and let them cough. If they can't speak, get behind them — 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts, repeating until the object comes out or they collapse. If they collapse, start CPR, and have someone call an ambulance at the same time. For pregnant women and the very heavy, switch to chest thrusts. Never reach into the mouth after something you can't see.

Cost
Free. Watch the motion once: one fist pressed just above the navel, the other hand wrapped around it, quick inward-and-upward thrusts.
Benefit
The US National Library of Medicine's text: first ask "Are you choking? Can you speak?" "If they can cough hard and can speak, don't intervene" — coughing alone usually dislodges the object. If they can't speak, "repeat 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the person loses consciousness." "If consciousness is lost, begin CPR," while having someone call an ambulance. For pregnant women and people with obesity, switch to chest thrusts
Note
Don't reach into the mouth after something you can't see — you'll push it deeper. Don't strike someone who can still cough. Choking most often happens at your own dinner table; the main beneficiaries are your family. The domestic teaching is the same set: the Fujian Red Cross Emergency Rescue Training Center says that for children over 1 and adults, the Chinese Red Cross system has always taught 5 back blows plus 5 abdominal thrusts in a cycle. Plenty of old tutorials online teach only abdominal thrusts — that is the outdated version. For infants under 1, no abdominal presses; switch to chest presses — see item 43 in this section (An infant choking).
Sources (2 references)
US National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Choking – adult or child over 1 year. https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000047.htm; Fuzhou Municipal Health Commission (2026). The Heimlich maneuver has been updated: "For toddlers over 1, children, and adults: the old single abdominal thrust is replaced by a cycle of '5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts'" "First-aid training in the Chinese Red Cross system has always been taught as a '5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts' cycle". https://www.fuzhou.gov.cn/zgfzzt/swjw/fzwj/jkkp/202601/t202…
27

Lost or broken down in gobi, desert, or uninhabited areas: stay put or stay by the vehicle, report your location first, then shade and insulate yourself, ration water, and don't wander

Grade CValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: a lotTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: large

Stay where you are or stay with the vehicle — the car is the biggest shade there is. The order: with signal, send your location before calling → shade and warmth → ration water, moving only at night when it cools → don't wander → signal with a mirror, smoke, or three fires. Before going in, tell someone your route, destination, return date, and vehicle model and plate.

Cost
Before entering uninhabited areas, tell someone your route, destination, return date, and vehicle model and plate. Water starts at 4 liters per person per day. A satellite communicator or BeiDou short-message device costs over a thousand yuan; a few hundred yuan per rental. The hard part is holding to "stay put and don't wander."
Benefit
The US National Park Service's Mojave Desert page has three sentences verbatim. One: "at least 1 gallon (about 3.8 liters) of water per person per day; 2 gallons per person per day for hikers and cyclists." Another: "tell someone your route, destination, return date, vehicle model, and license plate." And one more: "cell phone signal comes and goes." Death Valley verbatim: "don't hike on the valley floor and at low elevations in the heat"; the wilderness areas have "almost no cell signal," and a satellite phone is recommended. The Mojave desert-driving page: "in an emergency, staying with your vehicle is the most important thing you can do." The page adds that this does not happen often, but people have died of exposure to extreme heat or cold while walking back toward the road. Priorities in five steps. First, check in and send your coordinates — with signal, send your location before calling. Second, shade and warmth; the vehicle is the biggest shelter. Third, water — no moving by day; move when it cools at night. Fourth, don't wander. Fifth, signaling. Chongqing's Emergency Management Bureau tips: three fires laid in a triangle are the internationally recognized distress signal. If you are close by, shout "three short, three long, then three short again," repeating every 1 minute. In sunshine, flash with something shiny — a mirror, a can lid. The Ministry of Culture and Tourism warns self-driving tourists to be cautious about uninhabited areas, travel in multiple vehicles where possible, and rent a satellite phone when necessary
Note
Graded C because these are official tips, not research data. The water amounts, the check-in, the signal coverage, staying with the vehicle, the distress signals are all official wording. The folk "groups-of-three shouts" had no official text to be found, so it is rewritten as the official three fires and the three-short-three-long-three-short. Don't hike around looking for your way at midday. Don't drink urine. Don't skip drinking to save water.
Sources (5 references)

Desert Driving Safety. https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/desertdrivingsafety.htm ; Chongqing Municipal Administration of Emergency Management (2024). Emergency tips >> the distress signals you need to know in the wild (infographic): "Lighting three fires is the internationally recognized distress signal; arrange the fires in a triangle" "Three short, three long, then three short again; repeat after an interval of 1 minute". https://yjj.cq.gov.cn/yjkp/scshaq/202409/t20240918_13639172… ; Ministry of Culture and Tourism (2018). Ministry of Culture and Tourism reminds tourists to choose outdoor adventure travel with care: "be cautious about heading into uninhabited and sparsely populated areas" "travel in multiple vehicles where possible, prepare walkie-talkies in advance, and rent a satellite phone when necessary". https://www.mct.gov.cn/zxbs/cxts/201811/t20181127_836244.htm

Shivering, slurred words, unsteady steps mean hypothermia: change out of wet clothes, wrap up, warm the trunk first, and drink hot sweet drinks — no alcohol

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Body temperature dropping below 35°C is hypothermia: shivering, slurred speech, a wobbling walk, fuzzy thinking. Change out of wet clothes, wrap up in a thermal blanket or dry clothes, and warm the trunk first, not the hands and feet. Hot sweet drinks to sip, no alcohol — alcohol suppresses shivering. The shivering stopping is not improvement; it is worsening. No consciousness, start CPR.

Cost
A foil thermal blanket costs a few yuan, plus a spare set of dry clothes. Learning to read the signs is free.
Benefit
The US National Weather Service's text: body temperature below 95°F (35°C) is hypothermia — "if someone feels cold, sluggish, or can't think clearly, see a doctor immediately." The response: "get medical care immediately, move the person to a heated indoor space, and rewarm starting from the body's center first," with warm drinks. "Alcohol reduces shivering," so no drinking. "If unconscious, do CPR." Frostbite gets warmed with lukewarm water or body heat — "not hot water or radiant heat like a fireplace." The Wilderness Medical Society's 2019 hypothermia guideline is the practice guideline in this field
Note
Don't rub the hands and feet. Don't put them in a hot bath. Don't drag or haul them around — in severe hypothermia the heart stops easily. Don't take "no more shivering" as improvement; the trembling stopping (shivering ceased) is deterioration. The Wilderness Medical Society guideline's full text requires a subscription; only the abstract was checked this time.
Sources (2 references)
US National Weather Service. During Extreme Cold. https://www.weather.gov/safety/cold-during ; Dow J et al. (2019). Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update. Wilderness & Environmental Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wem.2019.10.002

Snakebite: sit down and stay still, remove rings and watches, reach hospital fast for antivenom — no cutting, no sucking, no tight binding

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Sit down and stay still, and immobilize the bitten limb. Rings and watches come off first — the limb will swell. Get to a hospital that stocks antivenom as fast as possible; antivenom is the only thing that can reverse most of the venom's effects. No cutting, no sucking with the mouth, no icing, no rope tight enough to turn the limb purple. No alcohol, no running. If you can photograph the snake from a distance, do; don't try to catch it.

Cost
Free. Know ahead of time which nearby hospital has antivenom. The hard part is resisting the urge to treat the wound yourself.
Benefit
WHO's text has three sentences. One: "immediately immobilize the bitten body part completely and get to the nearest medical facility quickly." One: "avoid using a tourniquet, and avoid cutting the wound." And one: "treat with appropriate antivenom targeted at the local snake species." "High-quality antivenom is the most effective treatment to prevent or reverse most of the toxic effects of snakebite." Worldwide, roughly 81,000 to 138,000 people die of snakebite each year, and amputations and permanent disability run about 3 times the death count. China's 2024 snakebite guideline estimates 250,000 to 280,000 venomous snakebites a year domestically, striking mostly people over 50. Hospitals in 11 provinces along the Yangtze basin and in the south admitted 40,817 snakebite patients from 2017 to 2021, with 23 deaths (0.06%) during hospitalization
Note
Photograph the snake from a distance if you can; don't catch it. No alcohol, no running, no sucking, no icing, no rope tight enough to turn the limb purple. China has no official count of nationwide snakebite deaths. That 11-province in-hospital death rate looks low, but over a tenth of the patients checked themselves out before finishing treatment, and whatever happened to them afterward is not in the statistics.

(2026). Clinical epidemiology of snakebite envenoming in hospitals 11 provinces of Yangtze River Basin and southern regions of China. PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases: "withdrawal (4346, 10.65%), and death (23, 0.06%)". https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0013247

In an earthquake, first note what building you're in: in structures built to seismic standards, shelter in place; in old buildings that may collapse with a door a few steps away, get out

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

First look at what building you're in. In buildings put up after 2001 to code, where getting out means stairs or a lobby, shelter in place: shield your head and neck under a sturdy table and grip the table legs. Single-story homes, old brick buildings, and self-built houses with no seismic design — if the door is a few steps away, get out. In no case do you jump from a building, take the elevator, or head down the stairs while things are shaking.

Cost
Free. Check in advance how many steps it takes to get out of your home, which route, and which table is sturdy.
Benefit
China Earthquake Administration's science film "The earthquake is here — hide or run?" teaches the maxim "take cover nearby during the quake, evacuate quickly after," with the explicit qualifier "this refers to being inside buildings that meet seismic design requirements." The reasoning: in such buildings "the chance of overall collapse is small." The original says that "falling building components and decorative items" "are the greatest threat to life safety." And "running around blindly without protection during the quake" "actually makes you easier to be struck by falling ceilings, chandeliers (fans), and the like." The hiding method: "protect the head and neck with your hands or some soft object" "and grip the table legs firmly"; with no table, "quickly crouch close against a load-bearing wall" "avoiding exterior walls, windows, and balconies." "If outdoors," then "evacuate to open ground to take cover as soon as possible." Now the other side: the 1988 Armenia earthquake brought Soviet-style precast panel buildings down in whole rows. That earthquake's case-control study states that "leaving the building after the first shock was protective." People who stayed indoors were 4.40 times as likely to be injured as those who ran out (odds ratio 4.40), 95% CI 2.24-8.71 (the credible range). Being injured inside a building was 12.20 times as likely as being outdoors (3.62-63.79). Being in a building of 5 stories or more was 3.65 times the risk of a shorter building (2.12-6.33)
Note
It's contested — the two conclusions are about two kinds of buildings. The China Earthquake Administration itself conditions "hiding" on "being inside buildings that meet seismic design requirements." It also calls for adapting to the place and the person: weigh together whether the building is seismically sound, where you are in it, and whether you can still run. In Armenia, whole buildings pancaked; there was nowhere to shelter, so getting out won. US FEMA, for homes in its own country, says "drop in place, cover head and neck, hold on — don't run outside," where injuries come mostly from falling objects and from falling while moving during the shaking. The Northridge study adds that reaching out to catch things and grabbing onto things that "look stable" worsens injuries. So just asking "run or hide" is useless; judge "will this building collapse, and can you reach open ground within seconds." For buildings built to code after 2001, where getting out requires stairs or a lobby: shelter in place. Single-story homes, old brick buildings, and self-built houses with no seismic design, door a few steps away: get out. The Armenia study compared injured versus uninjured survivors only; the dead were not counted, and the paper doesn't say whether the effect of floor height was adjusted away. People who could run out were probably on lower floors to begin with — read those numbers at a discount. In no case do you jump from a building, take the elevator, or head down the stairs while the shaking is on. Once outside, stay away from tall buildings, overpasses, utility poles, glass curtain walls, and billboards.
Sources (4 references)
China Earthquake Administration (produced by the Anhui Earthquake Administration). The earthquake is here — hide or run? (science video, transcript). https://www.cea.gov.cn/cea/dzpd/dzcs/5537260/index.html; Armenian HK, Noji EK, Oganesian AP (1992). A case-control study of injuries arising from the earthquake in Armenia, 1988. Bulletin of the World Health Organization, 70(2), 251-257. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/1600585; US FEMA Ready.gov. Earthquakes. https://www.ready.gov/earthquakes; Mahue-Giangreco M, Mack W, Seligson H, Bourque LB (2001). Risk factors associated with moderate and serious injuries attributable to the 1994 Northridge Earthquake. Annals of Epidemiology, 11(5), 347-357. https://doi.org/10.1016/s1047-2797(01)00220-4

Meeting bears, wild boars, or packs of feral dogs: don't run, don't scream, don't make eye contact; back away slowly at an angle

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

Don't run — a bear runs like a racehorse uphill and down. Don't climb trees either; black bears and brown bears both climb. Stand still, keep talking to it in a low voice, and once it stops moving, back away slowly at an angle. If a brown bear charges, drop and play dead, hands clasped behind your neck, legs apart. If a black bear charges, don't play dead — run for the car or a building; if there's no escape, fight back with whatever is at hand. For dog bites and scratches, rinse and get the shot per item 13.

Cost
Free. Carry a trekking pole in the mountains, walk with company and make noise so animals know you're coming first. The hard part is standing still instead of running.
Benefit
The US National Park Service's bear text has six sentences. One: "don't run — bears can run as fast as a racehorse, uphill and down." One: "stay calm; most bears don't want to attack you, they just want to be left alone." One: "keep talking to the bear in a low voice." One: "when the bear isn't moving, back away slowly at an angle, so you can keep an eye on the bear without tripping." One: "make yourself look as big as possible." And one: "don't climb trees — both grizzly bears and black bears can climb." Attacked by a brown bear: "play dead — lie flat, hands clasped behind your neck, legs apart." Attacked by a black bear: "don't play dead; run to a car or building, and if you can't escape, fight back with anything at hand." Dog bites are handled per item 13
Note
Grade B covers only bears. For wild boars and feral dogs, "don't run, back off slowly, get to higher ground or something solid between you" is accumulated experience, graded C; no official tips from the national or provincial forestry authorities could be found this time. Don't lure animals with food, don't crowd in for photos, don't take dogs into boar country. China's bears are mostly black bears and brown bears — play dead or not, decided separately for these two.
Sources (2 references)
US National Park Service. Staying Safe Around Bears. https://www.nps.gov/subjects/bears/safety.htm ; General Department of the National Disease Control and Prevention Administration and the General Office of the National Health Commission (2023). Work Protocol for Rabies Exposure Prevention and Management (2023 edition). https://www.ndcpa.gov.cn/jbkzzx/c100014/common/content/cont…
