Thunderstorm in the open: get inside a hard-topped vehicle or a building; avoid ridgelines, lone trees, water, and metal

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Outdoors within a thunderstorm's range, there is no safe place. Get into a hard-topped car or a building — convertibles, motorcycles, tents, pavilions, trees, and overhanging rocks don't count. Avoid open fields, ridgelines and hilltops, lone trees, water, and metal railings. If the group can't move, spread out and stand apart. Retreat at the first sound of thunder; it's only safe 30 minutes after the last rumble.

Cost
Free. The price is having your trip interrupted for half an hour or more. The hard part is turning back while the thunder is still far off.
Benefit
Outdoors within a thunderstorm's range, there is no safe place. Only 30 minutes after the last rumble of thunder is it safe
Note
Tents, pavilions, trees, and rock overhangs don't count as shelter. Hard-topped cars count; convertibles and motorcycles don't. Start withdrawing at the first sound of thunder — don't wait for the rain to come down.
Sources (1 reference)
US National Weather Service. Lightning safety outdoors: "There is no safe place outside when thunderstorms are in the area" "Avoid open fields, the top of a hill or a ridge top. Stay away from tall, isolated trees or other tall objects" "Stay away from water, wet items, such as ropes, and metal objects, such as fences and poles"; if you truly can't move, "If you are in a group, spread out to avoid the current traveling between group members"; resuming activity, "Wait 30 minutes until after the last rumble of thunder". https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-outdoors

Going to altitude: ascend slowly by sleeping altitude (how high you sleep each night); descend if symptoms worsen — don't push through

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: someBenefit: large

What counts is how high you sleep, not how high you went by day. Above 2,450 m of sleeping altitude there is altitude illness risk. Past 3,000 m, add only 500 m of sleeping altitude per night, and allow an extra acclimatization day for every 1,000 m gained. Headache plus nausea, a wobbling walk, changed mental state, or breathlessness at rest — go down. Descending comes before oxygen and medication.

Cost
An extra day or two spent acclimatizing. The preventive drug is prescription-only; ask a doctor before departure. The hard part is holding on to those days when the itinerary is tight.
Benefit
Above 2,450 m of sleeping altitude there is altitude illness risk. High-altitude cerebral edema and pulmonary edema (fluid in the brain and lungs) kill if you don't get down in time
Note
What counts is "how high you sleep," not how high you went by day. Headache plus nausea, a wobbling walk, changed mental state, or breathlessness at rest are all signals to go down. Descending takes priority over oxygen and medication; climbing higher while on oxygen is the wrong move.
Sources (2 references)
US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Clinical practice guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of acute altitude illness (2024 update). Wilderness & Environmental Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wem.2023.05.013

Tick embedded: pull it straight out with pointed tweezers close to the skin; no oils, no burning

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Grip the tick's head with pointed tweezers right against the skin and pull steadily straight out. No oils, no burning, no twisting — that aggravates it into pumping pathogen-laden fluid into the skin, and it also tends to leave the mouthparts stuck in the flesh. Note the date after removal. Fever, rash, or fatigue in the following weeks: tell the doctor unprompted that you were bitten by a tick.

Cost
A pair of fine-tipped tweezers.
Benefit
Oils, burning, and twisting aggravate the tick into squeezing pathogen-laden fluid into the skin. Done that way, it also tends to leave the part of its mouth (the hypostome) stuck in the flesh. For severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome, the disease ticks transmit in China, the nation reported 6,602 cases and 306 deaths in 2024 — both the highest since the disease was discovered. From 2010 to 2024 the average case fatality rate was 4.79%, rising with age to 9.15% among those 85 and over
Note
Write down the date after removal. Fever, rash, or fatigue in the following weeks: bring up the tick bite yourself at the appointment. If the doctor doesn't ask and you don't say, it easily gets treated as a cold.
Sources (2 references)
US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. After a tick bite: "Grasp the tick as close to the skin's surface as possible using clean fine-tipped tweezers" "Pull tick away from the skin with steady, even pressure" "Do not use petroleum jelly, heat, nail polish, or other substances to try and make the tick detach from the skin. This may agitate the tick and force infected fluid from the tick into the skin". https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/after-a-tick-bite/index.html; Ren Q et al. (2026). Epidemiological characteristics of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) in China, 2010–2024: a fifteen-year national surveillance analysis. BMC Infectious Diseases 26:1497: "The number of reported cases (6,602 cases) and deaths (306 cases) in 2024 were both the highest levels since the discovery of this disease" "The average CFR was 4.79%, and the CFR increased with age, reaching 9.15% among those aged 85 years and above". https://doi.org/10.1186/s12879-026-14066-z

Boil all wilderness water before drinking; a rolling boil for one minute suffices — no need to boil longer at altitude

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Every microbe that can make you sick through drinking water dies within seconds at boiling temperature. The extra rolling minute is just margin for "misjudging the boil" — no need to boil longer because of the altitude. If you can't boil, use a filter or disinfection tablets; each misses pathogens the other catches, so boil when you can. Crystal-clear stream water and snowmelt can carry parasites just the same.

Cost
The extra weight of a stove and fuel.
Benefit
Every microbe that can cause illness through drinking water is killed (inactivated) within seconds at boiling temperature. "Water doesn't boil hot enough at high altitude" is a common misconception
Note
The same page notes you don't literally need a rolling boil: holding water at 60°C for 30 minutes works just as well; boiling is simply the visible endpoint you can see without a thermometer. If you can't boil, use a filter or chemical disinfection tablets — each covers pathogens the other misses; boil when you can. Clear-looking stream water and snowmelt can still carry parasites; don't judge by looks.
Sources (1 reference)
US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. A stranger demands money in the wild: give it, don't fight, note their features, and call the police once you're clear

Grade CValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: yesBenefit: large

Hand over the money, don't fight, don't mouth off. For a few hundred yuan the other person is risking robbery: three to ten years to start, ten-plus years up to the death penalty for home invasion, armed robbery, or causing serious injury or death. Once he takes the money and turns to go, chasing him down no longer counts as self-defense. The moment you're clear, note looks, accent, license plate, and direction of escape, and dial 110.

Cost
The cash you're carrying. The hard part is swallowing your anger.
Benefit
Life is dearer than money; for a few hundred yuan the other person is risking a felony. Article 263 of the Criminal Law provides that whoever robs public or private property by violence, coercion, or other means is sentenced to three to ten years' imprisonment and fined. With a gun, home invasion, serious injury or death, and similar circumstances, the sentence runs ten years and up, to the death penalty. Article 20's justifiable defense only protects "stopping an unlawful assault in progress." Once the person takes the money and turns away, chasing and striking is no longer defense. Once you're clear, note looks, accent, license plate, and escape direction immediately, and dial 110
Note
Graded C because "giving money rather than resisting is safer" has no direct literature; the statutes only describe the other side's risk and your limits. Don't follow them somewhere secluded "to get the money." Don't hand over your phone password. Don't get in their car. Paying first applies only when you're cornered face to face and your personal safety is threatened — you still report to the police once you're clear. Someone demanding money online over private photos or nude-chat recordings is the reverse case: not a cent, ever — see Section 8, item 32 (When the other side blackmails you for money). Don't count on a carried baton, stun gun, or dagger; carrying them out the door is itself punishable — see Section 9, item 26 (Don't buy a baton or stun gun for self-defense).
Sources (1 reference)
National People's Congress (amended 2020). Criminal Law (Articles 20 and 263). https://jtgl.beijing.gov.cn/jgj/jgxx/flfg/fl/11033925/index… (integrated text reproduced by the Beijing Public Security Traffic Administration)
37

Stumbling on a group brawl: walk away; don't break it up, don't gawk, don't pick up anything off the ground; to report, retreat to a safe distance and call 110

Grade BValue: FairBasis: freedomMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

The moment you lay hands on someone, breaking up the fight becomes joining it. Taking part in group brawling draws up to 3 years; with big crowds, on the road, or with weapons, 3 to 10 years. Bystanders get hurt by mistake easily, too. What to do is step back and leave. If you're willing to report it, retreat to a safe distance and dial 110; state the location, how many people, whether anyone has knives or clubs, and whether anyone is lying motionless.

Cost
Free. The hard part is resisting two urges: stepping in to pull someone away, and standing around to watch. After reporting, you may be called back to give a statement — at most half a day.
Benefit
Criminal Law Article 292: "For group brawling, the principal elements and other active participants are sentenced to up to three years of imprisonment, criminal detention, or public surveillance." For repeated group brawls, large crowds and scale with vile social impact, serious disorder of public order in public places or on key traffic arteries, or carrying weapons: "three to ten years of imprisonment." "Group brawling causing serious injury or death" is convicted and punished as intentional injury or intentional homicide. The Public Security Administration Punishments Law has penalties too: for beating a person, 5 to 10 days' detention plus a 500 to 1,000 yuan fine. Group brawling handled as picking quarrels and provoking trouble: up to 15 days' detention plus a 2,000 yuan fine. The Guiding Opinions on the Lawful Application of Justifiable Defense, Article 5: an unlawful assault "includes assaults against oneself and also those endangering the state or the public interest, or against others." Article 9 of the same: where one side strikes first with plainly excessive means, or strikes first and keeps attacking while the other side tries hard to avoid the conflict, the party that fights back should generally be recognized as acting in defense
Note
Graded B because the consequences half has hard statutory text, but "step back and report, don't wade in" has no official text of its own — it is inferred from the statutes and from how "mutual combat" is distinguished. "I was just breaking it up" is no talisman; the determination turns on whether you laid hands and on whom. If the other person is already down or has run, chasing and striking is no longer defense. If you see someone being beaten one-sidedly by a crowd, the law does allow you to stop it. Justifiable defense protects others, not only yourself. But wading in barehanded mostly just adds one more casualty. Shouting for people, filming from far off, calling the police — those work better. "Hands off, don't gawk" is pure upside for you. The benefit of calling 110 lands mainly on the person on the ground — the lowest tier of beneficiary in this book — so weigh the time yourself. A few things to know before weighing. The duty to testify already exists: Criminal Procedure Law Article 62 states that everyone who knows about a case has a duty to testify, and skipping this call doesn't make it go away. If serious injury or death results, the police will still find who was present through surveillance footage; standing and gawking is what gets you registered most easily. A reporting person unwilling to reveal their name: the case-handling organ "shall keep it confidential for them" (Article 111). State the location, the numbers, whether anyone is armed, and you can hang up — no need to stay put. It only reaches admonishment or detention of up to ten days if the court summons you to appear and you refuse to testify without a valid reason (Article 193); bystanders almost never get that far. Not reporting is not itself illegal: Criminal Procedure Law Article 110's "have the right and the duty" carries no penalty, and the Criminal Law has no offense of a private person failing to report what they know — walking away is a legal option. After walking away, only two red lines remain. One: helping hide the person afterward or giving false evidence to shield them (Criminal Law Article 310, up to 3 years, 3 to 10 if serious). Two: deliberately giving false testimony when asked to testify (Article 305, up to 3 years, 3 to 7 if serious). Silence and honest answers are fine; making things up is not. For being drawn into a conflict yourself, see Section 8, item 10; for a stranger demanding money, see item 36 in this section; for money after being injured in a rescue, see item 39 in this section.
Sources (4 references)
National People's Congress (1997). Criminal Law (Articles 232, 234, 292, 305, and 310). https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/201802/t20180206_364975.shtml; Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (2025). Public Security Administration Punishments Law (revised 2025, Articles 30 and 51). https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202506/t20250627_699863.shtml; Supreme People's Court, Supreme People's Procuratorate, and Ministry of Public Security (2020). Guiding Opinions on the Lawful Application of Justifiable Defense (Fa Fa [2020] No. 31, Articles 5 and 9). https://www.court.gov.cn/zixun/xiangqing/251611.html; National People's Congress (2018). Criminal Procedure Law (revised 2018, Articles 62, 110, 111, and 193). Full text reproduced by the People's Procuratorate of the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region https://www.nx.jcy.gov.cn/zwsy/qwfb/202011/t20201119_608817…
38

Possible HIV exposure: get post-exposure prophylaxis within 72 hours — the earlier the better

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: a lotTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

If you suspect you've been infected with HIV, 72 hours is the hard line — ideally the drugs are in you within 2 hours. They run for 28 straight days. Past 72 hours this road is gone, so don't wait until the next day to decide.

Cost
A 28-day course costs over a thousand yuan, self-paid in most regions. You'll be making a hospital run that same night. The hard part is admitting on the spot that you may have been infected, and walking out the door immediately.
Benefit
The Beijing Municipal People's Government's HIV-prevention FAQ puts it this way: the preventive drugs taken after exposure are called post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), and they should be started "within 2 hours where possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours." Then "take them continuously for 28 days." Past 72 hours, starting is no longer recommended — a hard deadline
Note
Where to get it: the HIV designated medical institutions named by the local CDC, usually under infectious disease (STI/HIV clinic). Many cities now have 24-hour clinics — Chongqing's published figure is 29 clinics across 26 districts and counties, 14 of them around the clock. Before going, call the local CDC to ask which has the drugs; don't burn time in the ER. Situations that count as "exposure" include unprotected sex, a broken condom, a needlestick, or blood on a mucous membrane; whether to use the drugs is the doctor's call. The full 28 days must be taken — a few missed doses noticeably weaken the effect. Afterward, recheck at 4 to 6 weeks and at 3 months per medical advice. PEP is only a remedy; for routine prevention and testing, see Section 1, items 30 and 31 (Condoms every time; get tested after any high-risk encounter).
Sources (2 references)
Beijing Municipal People's Government. Can't tell before from after? Six questions and answers on HIV pre-exposure/post-exposure prophylaxis. https://www.beijing.gov.cn/fuwu/bmfw/jhsyfwzdzx/sjazbr/fakp…; National Center for AIDS/STD Control and Prevention, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (2020). Technical guideline for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (trial). https://www.chinacdc.cn/jkyj/crb2/yl/azb/jswj_azb/202410/t2…
39

Injured or out of pocket from rescuing someone: first go after the wrongdoer and medical insurance, then apply for good-samaritan recognition

Grade BValue: HighBasis: moneyMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Injured or out of pocket from a rescue, you don't have to write it off as bad luck. For good-samaritan injuries, treatment comes first and payment after. Medical costs are borne by the wrongdoer; if they fled or can't pay, it goes through basic medical insurance. With no wrongdoer, the person you saved is legally required to give appropriate compensation. At the same time, apply for good-samaritan recognition — the injured get their benefits settled under work-injury insurance standards.

Cost
Free. The application means submitting materials and waiting for determination — several trips, a few weeks to a few months.
Benefit
Civil Code Article 183: "Where a person suffers harm protecting another's civil rights and interests, the tortfeasor bears civil liability, and the beneficiary may give appropriate compensation. Where there is no tortfeasor, the tortfeasor has fled, or the tortfeasor cannot bear civil liability, and the victim requests compensation, the beneficiary shall give appropriate compensation." State Council Office Document [2012] No. 39 covers what happens to people injured in good-samaritan acts. Medical institutions must open a green channel, "upholding the principle of 'treatment first, payment after.'" On medical costs, the original reads: "Medical costs incurred in emergency treatment shall be borne by the wrongdoer or responsible party where one exists; where there is none, or the wrongdoer or responsible party has fled or cannot bear them, they are resolved through the basic medical security system as specified." For deaths: "where the conditions for martyr designation are met, the person shall be designated a martyr in accordance with law"; "where the case counts as deemed work-related death, survivors receive the one-time work-related death benefit plus a special survivor allowance equal to 40 months of the person's own wages." For disability: "where the conditions for work-injury insurance benefits are met, the corresponding benefits are implemented under the Work Injury Insurance Regulations; where not, the civil affairs department grades the disability and implements the corresponding benefits." On employment, they are "included in employment assistance as a priority and given key support," and public-interest posts "give priority to qualified good-samaritan persons." On housing, they are "included in the housing security system as a priority, with priority allocation and sale of government-subsidized housing or issuance of housing rental subsidies"
Note
Graded B because the benefits available are fixed by national documents, but the bonus amounts and the recognition process are governed by each province's own good-samaritan regulations — the numbers differ by locality and were not verified province by province this round. Generally you apply to the public security organ where it happened or to the good-samaritan work body (foundation). Recognition depends on evidence: the police report receipt, surveillance footage from the scene, witnesses' names and phone numbers, hospital records — keep them from the spot. If you need to sue, the civil rights and interests of good samaritans already fall within free legal aid. For the national standard of the one-time work-related death benefit and how disability grades convert to money, see Section 19, items 14 and 15. For how to apply for legal aid, see Section 7, item 3.
Sources (2 references)
National People's Congress (2020). Civil Code (Article 183). https://www.spp.gov.cn/spp/fl/202006/t20200602_463888.shtml; General Office of the State Council forwarding the Ministry of Civil Affairs and other departments (2012). Opinions on strengthening the protection of the rights and interests of good-samaritan persons (Guo Ban Fa [2012] No. 39). https://www.gov.cn/zwgk/2012-07/26/content_2191928.htm
40

Knife, rebar, or glass stuck in the body: press around it to stop the bleeding — never pull it out

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: large

Pulling it out can trigger massive bleeding and makes it harder for doctors to gauge the damage. The method: call 120, press with your hand or dressings around the object to stop the bleeding, and pad the object steady so it doesn't shift. With abdominal wounds and organs showing, don't push them back in — cover them with a clean wet dressing. A chest wound that bubbles: don't seal it with plastic; sealing can collapse the lung.

Cost
Free. The hard part is resisting the "pull it out first" instinct and staying with the person while waiting for the ambulance.
Benefit
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies' 2025 international first aid guideline: "The first aider should press around an embedded object (such as a knife), steady it, and not pull it out." "Do not remove any impaled object from an abdominal or chest wound; pulling it out can cause massive bleeding and makes it harder for the doctor to judge how bad the injury is." "An object embedded in the body should be steadied; if it pulses with the heartbeat, let it pulse and hold it loosely steady." "The first aider should not push protruding organs back into the body." An open chest-wall wound that is not gushing blood "can be left uncovered, without a dressing, because sealing the wound can trap air in the chest cavity and collapse the lung partially or fully (pneumothorax)". All penetrating chest and abdominal wounds should get an immediate call for emergency help
Note
Graded B because this is accepted guideline practice with no randomized trial — you can't exactly split casualties into "pull" and "don't pull" groups to test it. The only exception is an object blocking the airway so the person can't breathe. At the hospital, go straight to the triage desk at the ER entrance and report "penetrating injury." That is the tier that goes into the resuscitation room immediately; don't queue at the registration window (see Section 24, item 7). If it truly went all the way through, call 120 — the ambulance calls the hospital ahead to prepare for arrival. For pressing heavy bleeding and applying a tourniquet, see item 12.
Sources (1 reference)
International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025). International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025, pp. 256-257, 267-268. https://www.ifrc.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/IFRC%20Int…
41

Suspected fracture: stop moving it, support it in place, ice for no more than 20 minutes, and never straighten it yourself

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Treat any limb injury as a possible fracture first — being able to stand or move rules nothing out; only an X-ray can settle it. Keep the injured part still, support it with your hand, or brace it in its original position with a sling or rigid board. Ice as early as possible, no more than 20 minutes at a stretch. Never straighten it yourself. If a broken bone has pierced the skin, stop the bleeding and cover with a clean dressing — don't press the bone back in.

Cost
Free. Find a rigid board, a rolled magazine, or clothing as a splint. Put a layer of cloth between skin and the cold pack.
Benefit
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies published the 2025 International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines. It says "any injury to a hand or foot should first be treated as a possible fracture." It also says "the only accurate way to confirm a fracture is an X-ray. When in doubt, treat it as a fracture." The purpose of immobilization is "to minimize movement and pain." Cold packs: "at most 20 minutes at a stretch, which eases pain; icing longer than that can damage the skin." "When a long bone like the femur is injured, the blood lost from the bone alone can be fatal." Call for emergency help when pain or swelling is marked, shock signs appear, the femur (thigh bone) is fractured, or the limb is visibly out of position. For a fracture bent at an angle, straightening it on the spot (reduction) is considered only when two conditions hold together. One: "the location is remote (or resources limited), and the limb below the bend is cold or pale, or the first aider cannot immobilize it well enough for transport." Two: the rescuer is trained. For open fractures (bone through the skin), the priorities are stopping bleeding and preventing infection
Note
Graded B because these are accepted practices. For traction splinting a fractured femur (thigh bone) before hospital, there is only one chart-review study behind it, and the evidence is of very low confidence. Its results: less transfusion within 24 hours and shorter stays, with differences in death and complications too small to call. As for reducing first (setting the bone back) versus immobilizing as-is, no evidence was found at all. Three common misconceptions to drop: being able to stand and walk doesn't mean no fracture; use cold only, never heat, and no alternating cold and hot; a sprain doesn't get "walked off" — rest it first. For the movement prohibitions after an elderly fall with suspected fracture, see item 2. One leg swelling after a cast or bed rest raises the alarm for a clot — see item 11. For whether to pursue a disability assessment or a disability certificate after treatment, see Section 24, items 9 and 10.
Sources (1 reference)
International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025). International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025, pp. 301-302. https://www.ifrc.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/IFRC%20Int…
42

After sexual assault: get somewhere safe and call 110; don't shower, don't wash clothes, don't tidy the room before the forensic exam, and get to a hospital within 72 hours

Grade BValue: FairBasis: freedomMoney: littleTime: moderateWillpower: yesBenefit: large

Traces on your body, your clothes, and in the room are the most important evidence for identifying the perpetrator. So avoid showering before the forensic exam, and don't wash clothes or tidy the room; call 110 as early as you can. Emergency contraception is on pharmacy shelves, and the sooner it's taken the better it works. Get to a hospital within 72 hours and let the doctor decide about the blocking drugs.

Cost
Reporting is free. Emergency contraception is over the counter; any pharmacy stocks it. A course of PEP costs over a thousand yuan, and whether to take it is the doctor's call — see item 38 in this section (Getting PEP within 72 hours). The hard part is that it's hard to speak up, and you badly want to shower right away.
Benefit
A prosecutor with the Beijing People's Procuratorate says: "Whether minor or adult, when harmed, you should call 110 the moment it happens." Timely reporting and medical care "make it easier for investigators to examine the scene, collect physical traces, and secure evidence." The People's Daily anti-sexual-assault handbook, reproduced by the Guizhou Civil Affairs Department, writes: "once you have the misfortune of suffering sexual assault, the most important thing is preserving evidence." Keep "evidence such as bodily fluids, hair, skin flakes, and communication records," and "after being assaulted, do not shower, wash clothes, tidy the room, or throw things away on your own initiative." When the assailant is an acquaintance, keep call and message records. If they threaten or offer money afterward, keep that evidence too. The Beijing Xicheng District People's Procuratorate writes: "try not to shower before the physical examination." The World Health Organization says emergency contraception can be used "when a woman suffers sexual assault without effective contraceptive protection." It is recommended within 5 days; the earlier, the more effective. Emergency contraception containing levonorgestrel (a progestin) leaves a pregnancy rate of 1.2% to 2.1% among women who take it. Levonorgestrel tablets sold in Chinese pharmacies are over the counter. The Wuhan Health Commission's formulation: after unprotected sex, "within 72 hours, the earlier the pill is taken, the better the prevention of pregnancy." For HIV PEP, take it within 2 hours where possible, no later than 72 (nationwide)
Note
It is graded B because these are official case-handling experience and medication advice — there is no "how much higher the conviction rate if you follow this" number. The beneficiary is mainly you and your family. The 72-hour window for emergency contraception is the domestic label's line; the WHO says it works within 5 days, but later is worse — don't drag. If already pregnant, emergency contraception does nothing. When reporting, tell it as it is — no concealing, no exaggerating. If the other side comes back afterward to settle privately, offer money, or threaten you, keep records of all of it; delete nothing. You may report once you've thought it through, but evidence fades with time. Whether or not you report, get to a hospital within the time limits. For recording, see Section 8, item 41 (Recording). If they later use photos or the report itself to threaten you, that is also a crime — see Section 8, item 32 (When the other side uses police reports or photos to extort money). If a friend goes through this, go with them to report and to the hospital; don't start by telling them to take a shower and rest.
Sources (6 references)

Why they are silent no more.... https://www.bjjc.gov.cn/c/xicheng/xjjsl/320654084.jhtml; World Health Organization (2021). 43

An infant under 1 who's choking and can't cry: 5 back blows face-down, then 5 chest presses face-up, alternating — never the abdomen

Grade BValue: ExceptionalBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: large

If the baby can still cough and cry out, let them cough while you watch closely. If they can't cry and their face is going purple, have someone call 120; lay the baby face-down along your forearm and give 5 blows with the heel of your hand between the two shoulder blades. If it doesn't come out, flip them over and give 5 quick presses to the center of the chest, alternating the two — never the abdomen. If the baby goes unresponsive, switch to CPR.

Cost
Free. Watch the motion once or take an infant first-aid course, minutes to half a day. The hard part is getting the baby face-down and positioned amid the panic.
Benefit
The American Heart Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics issued 2025 pediatric basic life support guidelines. The guideline writes: choking (such as a foreign object blocking the airway) "is one of the leading causes of death in infants and children." What infants most often choke on is liquid. Still coughing and able to make sound is mild: let the child cough while you watch for worsening. Very weak coughing, or unable to cough, unable to cry, or going purple in the face, is severe. Severe means calling emergency help first, then "repeating 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts until the object comes out or the infant becomes unresponsive." The guideline does not recommend abdominal thrusts for infants, because they can injure the abdominal organs. Chest thrusts are now recommended with the heel of one hand, because it presses deeper than the old two-finger method. If the infant becomes unresponsive, start CPR, compressions first, no pulse-checking. Before giving breaths, remove any object you can see. The guideline states plainly "do not perform blind finger sweeps." The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies' 2025 international first aid guideline is the same set: first give up to 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades; failing that, flip the baby over and give up to 5 chest presses; failing that, call emergency help immediately. Its chest presses use encircling hands with two thumbs. The Fujian Red Cross Emergency Rescue Training Center says infants under 1 get "5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts." For back blows, lay the baby face-down on your forearm, head lower than the trunk
Note
Graded B because the technique rests mainly on case reports; there is no "how many fewer deaths if you follow this" number. Benefit is set to "large" by judgment: a fully blocked airway stops a child's heart within minutes. The beneficiaries are almost always your own children. For children over 1 and adults, switch to abdominal thrusts — see item 26 in this section (Choking: back blows plus abdominal thrusts). On the hand technique for chest presses, sources differ. The US guideline and the new domestic Red Cross version use the heel of one hand; the International Red Cross uses two thumbs; old tutorials use two fingers. The 2025 US guideline no longer recommends two fingers, because they don't press deep enough. In an emergency, any of these beats not pressing. Even after the object comes out, take the baby to the hospital — fragments may be left in the lungs. Keep coins, small toys, and the like out of children's reach. For what to do after the baby goes unresponsive, see item 44 in this section (Infant CPR).
Sources (4 references)
Joyner BL et al. (2025). Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support: 2025 American Heart Association and American Academy of Pediatrics Guidelines for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Emergency Cardiovascular Care. Circulation 152(suppl 2):S424–S447. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001370, full text at https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-…; International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025). International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2025, pp. 238-240. https://www.ifrc.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/IFRC%20Int…; Fuzhou Municipal Health Commission (2026). The Heimlich maneuver has been updated. https://www.fuzhou.gov.cn/zgfzzt/swjw/fzwj/jkkp/202601/t202…
44

An infant under 1 unresponsive and not breathing normally: call 120 on speaker and do infant CPR — 30 compressions, 2 breaths

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: moderateWillpower: noneBenefit: large

Tapping the soles gets no response and breathing isn't normal: call 120 on speaker and don't stop your hands. Encircle the chest with both hands and press with two thumbs; if you can't encircle it, use the heel of one hand — press down about 4 cm, about 2 presses per second. After every 30 presses, cover the baby's mouth and nose with your mouth and give 2 breaths. An infant's heart usually stops because breathing has stopped; with breaths included in CPR, more of them survive.

Cost
Free. Infant CPR takes one practice course, half a day to a day. The hard parts are giving mouth-to-mouth breaths and daring to press hard.
Benefit
The American Heart Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics issued 2025 pediatric basic life support guidelines. The guideline writes: for infants and children, cardiac arrest is still caused mainly by breathing going wrong. Of infants suffering out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, only 6.6% survive to discharge. For a layperson facing an unresponsive infant or child with no normal breathing and no signs of life, "CPR should be started immediately," without checking a pulse. Compression depth is at least one-third of the chest's front-to-back diameter — for infants, "about 1.5 inches (4 cm)." Rate: 100 to 120 per minute. One rescuer: 30 compressions, 2 breaths. Two rescuers: 15 compressions, 2 breaths. For infants, press with the heel of one hand, or encircle with both hands and press with two thumbs; if you can't encircle, use the heel. The two-finger technique has been dropped, because it doesn't press deep enough. The guideline adds that for infants and children in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, adding breaths to compressions improves survival. A US registry counted 3,900 children under 18 with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, 59.4% of them infants. Where a bystander did CPR, adjusted survival to discharge was 13.2%, versus 9.5% without. Adjusted OR 1.57 (about 57% higher odds of survival), 95% CI 1.25-1.96 (the credible range). In infants, CPR with breaths was associated with higher survival, and the surviving children's brains recovered better too. Compression-only CPR turned out about the same as no CPR at all. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies' 2025 international first aid guideline writes: to check an infant's responsiveness, pick the baby up or tap the soles. If you're alone, call emergency services on speaker yourself. With no phone you can press and talk on at once, do 1 minute of CPR first, then call. The Capital Institute of Pediatrics has a science piece, reproduced by the Beijing Health Commission. It writes: "if only one person is present, do 2 minutes of CPR first, then call the 120 ambulance." Compression depth "4 cm for infants." For under 1, breaths go "mouth over mouth and nose"
Note
Graded B because the survival numbers come from registry studies that only track records, and they count all children; infant-specific figures were not given in the abstract. Benefit is set to "large" using the all-children numbers: survival to discharge rose from 9.5% to 13.2%, a relative gain of about forty percent. The beneficiaries are almost always your own children. Three differences from item 1 in this section (hard chest compressions). First, infants need breaths; compression-only works poorly on them. Second, use two thumbs or the heel of one hand, pressing about 4 cm — not stacked hands. Third, when alone and unable to press and call at once, press first, then call. How long to press first varies: the Capital Institute of Pediatrics and the US guideline say 2 minutes for a single rescuer, the International Red Cross 1 minute. A phone on speaker dissolves the problem. The European Resuscitation Council teaches 5 breaths before compressions; the US guideline teaches compressions first — both beat doing nothing. Old domestic tutorials teach two-finger compressions; the 2025 US guideline has dropped that technique. When choking caused it, glance in the mouth before breaths and remove only what you can see — see item 43 in this section (An infant choking).
Sources (6 references)
Joyner BL et al. (2025). Circulation 152(suppl 2):S424–S447. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001370, full text at https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-…; Naim MY et al. (2017). Association of Bystander Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation With Overall and Neurologically Favorable Survival After Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in the United States: A Report From the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival Surveillance Registry. JAMA Pediatrics 171(2):133–141. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2016.3643; International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2025).
