After week 20 of pregnancy, don't take ibuprofen-type painkillers on your own

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

After week 20 of pregnancy, most of the amniotic fluid is made by the fetus's kidneys. Taking ibuprofen-type drugs at this stage can injure the fetal kidneys and make the amniotic fluid drop. Among the reports of this kind the US has received are cases of newborn death. Low-dose aspirin prescribed by a doctor is not included.

Cost
Free.
Benefit
In October 2020, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a safety warning: using NSAIDs at about 20 weeks of pregnancy or later can cause fetal kidney problems, leading to too little amniotic fluid. The warning covers both prescription and OTC drugs, including aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, and celecoxib. The FDA reviewed adverse event reports through July 2017 and found 35 cases of too little amniotic fluid or impaired newborn kidney function, all with serious outcomes. Five were newborn deaths, all accompanied by newborn kidney failure. In the literature, most cases of low amniotic fluid resolved within 72 hours to 6 days of stopping the drug. The FDA advises pregnant women not to use this class of drugs at 20 weeks or later unless a doctor explicitly recommends it. Doctor-prescribed 81 mg low-dose aspirin for specific problems of pregnancy is not covered by this restriction. For pain and fever, the FDA points to acetaminophen and other alternatives — ask a pharmacist or doctor first.
Note
The FDA notes that many OTC medicines for colds, flu, and insomnia also contain this class of ingredient; check the ingredient list. US OTC labels used to warn only about the last 3 months of pregnancy; this moved the line up to about 20 weeks. For low-dose aspirin to prevent preeclampsia, see Section 27, item 5 (low-dose aspirin). Rated B because the numbers come from adverse event reports, and no one knows how many people took the drug without anything happening. Benefit is rated "medium" by judgment: the outcomes are severe, but they happen rarely.
Sources (1 reference)
U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2020-10-15). FDA recommends avoiding use of NSAIDs in pregnancy at 20 weeks or later because they can result in low amniotic fluid. Drug Safety Communication. https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-…

For acid reflux and heartburn, buy omeprazole yourself but take it at most 7 days; difficulty swallowing, vomiting blood, or black stools mean going straight to the hospital

Grade BValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Omeprazole enteric-coated tablets can be bought without a prescription as of 2022, but the insert says self-treatment lasts no more than 7 days and no repeat course within two months. Do not self-treat if you have difficulty or pain swallowing, are vomiting blood, or have blood in your stool or black stools — these can be signals of something serious. The drug can also mask the symptoms of stomach cancer and delay diagnosis.

Cost
Free. Take it for exactly the number of days the insert says.
Benefit
In Announcement No. 68 of 2022, the NMPA switched omeprazole enteric-coated tablets from prescription to OTC status and issued a model package insert. The insert's indication is "short-term relief of heartburn and acid regurgitation caused by excess stomach acid." The precautions state: do not use for more than 7 days; consult a physician or pharmacist if symptoms are not relieved; do not take it again within two months; seek medical care immediately if symptoms recur; do not use if you have difficulty or pain swallowing, are vomiting blood, or have blood in your stool or black stools, which may be signs of a serious condition; when alarm symptoms such as marked weight loss, repeated vomiting, difficulty swallowing, vomiting blood, or black stools appear, malignancy must be ruled out first, because treatment can mask symptoms and delay diagnosis; consult a doctor if new symptoms appear or symptoms change at age 55 or older; and people taking clopidogrel should avoid taking omeprazole at the same time.
Note
Clopidogrel is a common anti-clotting drug for people who have had a stent put in or a heart attack. Omeprazole weakens it; if you take it, ask a doctor first. Rated B because these are package-insert rules, and no study has calculated how many problems following them prevents. Benefit is rated "medium" by judgment: it guards against stomach bleeding and stomach cancer being caught too late, but most acid reflux and heartburn is not serious.
Sources (1 reference)

7

Don't ask a doctor for antibiotics for a common cold

Grade AValue: HighBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

Antibiotics do not clear a cold any faster than taking nothing. In adults, they raise the risk of side effects to more than twice that of taking none. For a pus-filled runny nose lasting less than 10 days, antibiotics have no proven benefit either.

Cost
Free, and it saves the cost of the medicine.
Benefit
A Cochrane systematic review pooled 6 randomized trials with 1,147 people. For the common cold, antibiotics versus placebo showed no clear difference in the proportion who did not recover or had persistent symptoms (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.60–1.14, not significant). The risk of adverse effects was 1.8 times that of the placebo group (95% CI 1.01–3.21); among adults 2.62 times (1.32–5.18), while children showed no increase (0.91, 0.51–1.63). For acute purulent rhinitis with a pus-filled runny nose lasting less than 10 days, antibiotics showed no clear benefit either (RR 0.73, 0.47–1.13), while adverse effects rose (RR 1.46, 1.10–1.94, about 46% higher). The authors' conclusion: routine antibiotics are not recommended for either condition.
Note
This edition was republished in 2025, and the abstract states the literature search ran through 2013. Antibiotics are prescription drugs in China, and pharmacies may sell them only against a prescription; do not take leftover antibiotics at home on your own either. Benefit is rated "medium" by judgment: what this prevents is adverse effects, not death.
Sources (1 reference)
Kenealy T, Arroll B (2025). Antibiotics for the common cold and acute purulent rhinitis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 11:CD000247. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000247.pub4

For diarrhea, rehydrate with oral rehydration salts first; no anti-diarrheal medicine for children under 5

Grade AValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: littleTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: medium

With diarrhea, the priority is replacing fluids, not stopping the diarrhea. Mix oral rehydration salts with water as the package directs and drink that; do not substitute juice or soft drinks — too much sugar actually leaves you more dehydrated. Do not give anti-diarrheal drugs such as loperamide to children under 5; in severe cases they cause intestinal obstruction, which can be fatal.

Cost
A box of oral rehydration salts costs a few yuan to a dozen or so yuan; keep one at home.
Benefit
The World Health Organization's diarrhea treatment manual states that "anti-diarrheal" drugs and antiemetics have no practical benefit in children with acute or prolonged diarrhea. They do not prevent dehydration or improve nutrition. Some have dangerous, sometimes fatal side effects, and they must never be given to children under 5. Drugs that slow the gut's movement, such as loperamide, can cause severe paralytic ileus, which can be fatal, and may prolong the infection. The manual also notes that drinks with too much sugar draw water from the body into the gut and cause hypernatremic dehydration — soft drinks and commercial juice drinks, for example. The WHO manual recommends a reduced-osmolarity formula with a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L. Compared with the old formula, it cut unplanned intravenous fluid therapy by 33%. A Cochrane review pooling 8 trials found similar results (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.45–0.79, about 40% fewer).
Note
When buying, check the osmolarity printed on the package and choose a reduced-osmolarity formula. The manual states that blood in a child's stool is most often bacterial dysentery, which calls for a doctor and antibiotics — rehydrating at home alone is not enough. Benefit is rated "medium" by judgment: the numbers at hand compare two kinds of rehydration salts, not drinking versus not drinking.
Sources (2 references)
World Health Organization (2005). The treatment of diarrhoea: a manual for physicians and other senior health workers, 4th revision. https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/43209; Hahn S, Kim S, Garner P (2002). Reduced osmolarity oral rehydration solution for treating dehydration caused by acute diarrhoea in children. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, (1):CD002847. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD002847

Take painkillers no more than 15 days a month, and combination painkillers no more than 10 — otherwise your headache may be caused by the medication itself

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: medium

If your headaches keep coming back and you take a painkiller every day, the pills may be making the pain worse. The international headache classification calls this medication-overuse headache. Plain painkillers on more than 15 days a month, or combination painkillers on more than 10 days a month, for more than 3 months in a row, is enough to qualify. Most people get better after stopping the overused drug.

Cost
Free. You have to keep count of the days you take it and resist swallowing one casually.
Benefit
The International Headache Society's International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition, gives the diagnostic criteria: a person with a pre-existing headache disorder, headaches on 15 or more days a month, and regular overuse of headache medication for more than 3 months. For non-opioid painkillers such as acetaminophen, aspirin, and ibuprofen, the overuse threshold is 15 or more days a month; for combination painkillers, 10 or more days a month. Combination painkillers are those that put two or more pain-relieving drugs together, or add helper ingredients such as caffeine — acetaminophen plus codeine, for example. If you rotate several non-opioid painkillers, add the days together. The classification notes that epidemiological evidence from many countries shows that among people with headaches on 15 or more days a month, more than half have this kind of headache. Most patients improve after stopping the overused drug, and preventive headache treatment works better too.
Note
Painkiller tablets with "ka" (caffeine) in the Chinese name usually contain caffeine; count them as combination products under the 10-day rule. If the number of headache days a month keeps growing, see a neurologist rather than just adding medication. Rated B because the classification provides diagnostic thresholds, not a controlled trial. Benefit is rated "medium" by judgment: what it buys back is days without headache, not survival.
Sources (2 references)
Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society (2018). The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition. Cephalalgia, 38(1):1-211. https://doi.org/10.1177/0333102417738202; ICHD-3 online edition, 8.2 Medication-overuse headache (including 8.2.3 and 8.2.5). https://ichd-3.org/8-headache-attributed-to-a-substance-or-…

Clear out expired and leftover medicines regularly, bin them with the packaging in the hazardous-waste bin, and don't keep them at home

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: noneBenefit: small

Of the medicines young children swallow without an adult knowing, nearly half are prescription tablets. Of the prescription drugs children swallow, about three in ten belong to grandma or grandpa. Clear out the medicines you have no use for, and there is one fewer thing a child can dig up. Put the cleared-out medicines in the hazardous-waste bin with their packaging, or hand them to a pharmacy that collects old medicines.

Cost
Free. One pass through the medicine cabinet a year, fifteen minutes or so.
Benefit
US emergency department surveillance data estimate that from 2004 to 2013, unsupervised medicine swallowing by children under 6 led to about 640,000 emergency department visits (estimate 640,161). In 2013 alone, about 59,000 (59,092). From 2010 to 2013, the most common were oral prescription tablets, 45.9%. Among prescription drugs, the most common were opioid painkillers (13.8%) and benzodiazepine sleep and sedative drugs (12.7%). In 2017, five US poison control centers surveyed parents who phoned for help. Of the children who swallowed a prescription medicine, 30.7% had taken a grandparent's. For more than half (51.5%) of the prescription drugs, an adult had already taken them out of the original packaging before the child got hold of them. In China, the National Hazardous Waste Catalog (2025 edition) lists waste medicines and their packaging generated in everyday household life as hazardous waste within household garbage. Shanghai's sorting and disposal guide places waste medicines under hazardous waste, specifying that this includes expired medicines, medicine capsules, tablets, and inner packaging, and that "discarded medicines should preferably be put out together with their packaging." Shanghai also stipulates that expired household medicines collected by pharmacies are handled through temporary transfer points set up by each district's market regulation department. The US FDA says the best way to dispose of expired and unused medicines is to hand them in at a collection site.
Note
Waste-sorting catalogs are not exactly the same everywhere; go by the list posted at your complex's garbage room. In Shanghai, leftover Chinese-medicine dregs count as wet garbage, not hazardous waste. Store the medicines you keep in their original boxes — do not empty them into pill organizers or other bottles — and keep them out of children's reach; see Section 13, item 20 (accidental swallowing). Do not take leftover antibiotics at home on your own either; see item 7 of this section (antibiotics). Where the US has no collection site, it tells people to mix medicines into coffee grounds or cat litter, seal the bag, and throw it in the regular trash; a few strong painkillers are allowed to be flushed down the toilet. That is the US practice; in China, sort and put out according to local rules. Rated B because the US figures are registry data only, and no study has calculated how many accidental swallowings clearing out the medicine cabinet prevents. Benefit is rated "small": the numbers at hand are emergency visits, not deaths, and the effect of the clearing-out action cannot be computed.

No alcohol while taking antibacterials like cephalosporins or metronidazole, nor for 7 days after stopping — and steer clear of alcohol-containing medicines such as Huoxiang Zhengqi water and cough syrups

Grade BValue: FairBasis: mortalityMoney: noneTime: littleWillpower: someBenefit: small

When some cephalosporins and metronidazole meet alcohol, they make people flush, with a racing heart, chest tightness, and vomiting; in severe cases blood pressure drops. It is not just baijiu and beer — alcohol-containing medicines such as Huoxiang Zhengqi water and cough syrups can trigger it too. Avoid all of it while taking the drug and for 7 days after stopping.

Cost
Free. Skip alcohol for a little over a week, and check whether ethanol appears in the ingredients before taking any other medicine.
Benefit
This is called a disulfiram-like reaction. A 2023 safe-medication explainer from the Fujian Provincial Medical Products Administration says that drinking alcohol before or after taking some cephalosporins can trigger the reaction, which "can seriously damage health and even endanger life." Symptoms include facial flushing, sweating, and palpitations, and in worse cases breathing difficulty, falling blood pressure, and anaphylactic shock. Following the Clinical Medication Guidelines of the Pharmacopoeia of the People's Republic of China, the explainer lists cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefoperazone, metronidazole, tinidazole, furazolidone, and others. It states that "for 7 days after taking the medicine, drinking alcohol and consuming alcohol-containing medicines, foods, and the like are forbidden," with liquor-filled chocolates and Huoxiang Zhengqi water as examples. The reason: the enzyme the drug suppresses often needs 4 to 5 days to recover. A hospital in Guangzhou compiled 82 cases over 2 years. 57 (69.51%) were caused by cephalosporins and 10 (12.20%) by nitroimidazoles (metronidazole, tinidazole, and the like). The alcohol came from alcoholic drinks in 40 cases (48.78%) and from ethanol-containing medicines in 31 (37.80%); the oral ones included Huoxiang Zhengqi water, cough syrups, and motherwort liquid extract. Of the 82 cases, 68 were mild, 9 moderate, and 5 severe; they resolved within 1 to 3 hours, with no deaths. The US metronidazole label requires no alcohol while taking it and for at least 3 days after stopping, and no products containing propylene glycol.
Note
Not every cephalosporin does this, but ordinary people cannot tell which do; following this rule for all of them is the simplest course. When a doctor prescribes a cephalosporin or metronidazole, volunteer whether you have drunk alcohol in the past few days. That explainer suggests not drinking in the 3 days before starting the medicine either, while admitting there is no authoritative word on that interval yet. If you flush and your heart starts racing, stop everything containing alcohol at once. The explainer says mild cases settle on their own and severe ones need the hospital. Do not drink while taking acetaminophen either; see item 1 of this section (acetaminophen). Rated B because the evidence is a case series and package inserts, with no controls. Benefit is rated "small": all 82 cases resolved within a few hours, with no deaths, and only 5 were severe.
